1️⃣ IoC Container & Bean Lifecycle

Every Spring Boot feature you will be asked about (transactions, security, caching, MVC) is built out of the same three mechanisms: bean definitions, dependency injection and post-processors. Interviewers start here because a candidate who can say where @Autowired is actually processed, why a prototype inside a singleton is stale, and how a circular reference gets resolved (or refused) will not be fooled by any framework "magic" later. The path: injection basics → how beans are declared → scopes → the full lifecycle → post-processors → circular references → the context itself → events, configuration properties, conditions, ordering and startup hooks.

IoC & Dependency Injection: constructor vs setter vs field

Why interviewers ask: the very first Spring question in most loops. They want the reason constructor injection won, not just "Spring recommends it".

Inversion of Control: your class no longer looks up or constructs its collaborators; the container builds the object graph and hands each object what it declared it needs. Dependency Injection is the mechanism: the container calls your constructor / setter / writes your field. Analogy: instead of every engineer going to the store for a laptop, IT (the container) reads the requisition (the constructor signature) and delivers one to the desk.

Three styles: constructor (dependencies are parameters; fields can be final; the object is never in a half-built state; a plain new works in tests; a 9-parameter constructor is a loud smell telling you to split the class), setter (optional or reconfigurable dependencies; object exists before it is complete), field (@Autowired private Repo repo; — shortest to write, but hides dependencies, needs reflection or Spring to test, cannot be final, and makes circular references silently possible). Since Spring 4.3 a single constructor needs no @Autowired at all.

@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repo;      // final: cannot be null after construction
    private final Clock clock;

    // single constructor → @Autowired is implicit (Spring 4.3+)
    public OrderService(OrderRepository repo, Clock clock) {
        this.repo = Objects.requireNonNull(repo);
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    @Autowired(required = false)              // optional collaborator via setter
    public void setAuditor(Auditor auditor) { this.auditor = auditor; }
    private Auditor auditor = Auditor.NOOP;
}
// Lombok equivalent: @RequiredArgsConstructor generates the constructor for final fields
StyleImmutabilityTestable with newCircular refsBest for
ConstructorYes (final)YesFails fast at startup (good)All mandatory dependencies
SetterNoYesResolvable (early reference)Optional / re-settable dependencies
FieldNoNeeds reflection / @InjectMocksResolvable (hidden)Test classes only
Interview angle: "Your team's code base uses field injection everywhere; is it worth migrating?" Answer with cost/benefit: circular references become visible, unit tests stop needing Spring, and null fields become compile-time impossible; do it class-by-class with Lombok's @RequiredArgsConstructor, and use the Boot 2.6+ circular-reference ban as the safety net.

Pitfalls

  • Calling an injected dependency from inside the constructor of a field-injected class: the field is still null because population happens after instantiation.
  • A @Component with two constructors and no @Autowired: Spring falls back to the no-arg constructor, or fails if there is none; annotate the one you want.
  • Injecting a concrete class instead of its interface works, but a JDK-proxy (interface-based) AOP proxy will then fail with "bean is not of required type"; Boot defaults to CGLIB proxies precisely to avoid this.
Interview questions
  • Why does Spring recommend constructor injection? — Dependencies are explicit and mandatory, fields can be final so the object is immutable and thread-safe by construction, tests use new without a container, and circular dependencies fail fast instead of hiding.
  • What happens if a field-injected dependency is used inside the constructor? — NullPointerException: Spring instantiates first, then populates fields; use constructor injection or @PostConstruct for post-population logic.
  • Is @Autowired required on the constructor? — Not since Spring 4.3 when the class has exactly one constructor; with several, annotate one (only one may have required=true).
  • Difference between @Autowired, @Inject and @Resource? — @Autowired (Spring) and @Inject (JSR-330, jakarta.inject in Boot 3) resolve by type then qualifier; @Resource (JSR-250, jakarta.annotation) resolves by name first, then type, and is processed by a different post-processor (CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor).
  • How would you inject a dependency that may not exist? — Optional<T>, ObjectProvider<T>, @Autowired(required=false) on a setter, or @Nullable on the parameter.
  • Spring Boot 2 vs 3: anything changed here? — The injection model is unchanged; the namespace moved from javax.annotation/javax.inject to jakarta.*, and Boot 3 requires Java 17 so records and final constructor injection are idiomatic.

@Autowired resolution rules, @Qualifier, @Primary, collections

Why interviewers ask: "you have two PaymentGateway beans; which one gets injected?" is the most common "predict the outcome" question in Spring interviews, and the fallback order is precise.

Resolution for a single injection point goes: (1) collect all beans assignable to the declared type (generics included: Repo<Order> and Repo<User> are different); (2) if exactly one, inject it; (3) otherwise narrow by @Qualifier (custom qualifier annotations count); (4) then prefer the bean marked @Primary; (5) then the highest @Priority (jakarta.annotation.Priority); (6) finally match the parameter/field name against bean names; (7) still ambiguous → NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException; none found → NoSuchBeanDefinitionException unless required=false.

Collections are special: List<Gateway>, Set, array and Map<String, Gateway> (key = bean name) receive all matching beans. Lists are sorted by @Order / Ordered / @Priority (lowest value first); a plain Map keeps registration order. ObjectProvider<T> is the lazy, programmatic view: getIfAvailable(), getIfUnique(), orderedStream(), getObject(args) for prototypes.

public interface Gateway { String charge(long cents); }

@Component @Order(1) class StripeGateway implements Gateway { … }
@Component @Order(2) @Primary class AdyenGateway implements Gateway { … }
@Component @Qualifier("legacy") class LegacyGateway implements Gateway { … }

@Service
class CheckoutService {
    CheckoutService(Gateway defaultGw,                       // → AdyenGateway (@Primary)
                    @Qualifier("legacy") Gateway legacy,     // → LegacyGateway (qualifier beats @Primary)
                    Gateway stripeGateway,                   // → StripeGateway (name fallback, only if no @Primary!)
                    List<Gateway> all,                       // [Stripe, Adyen, Legacy] sorted by @Order
                    Map<String, Gateway> byName,             // {"stripeGateway"=…, …}
                    ObjectProvider<FraudCheck> fraud) {      // optional, resolved on demand
        fraud.ifAvailable(FraudCheck::warmUp);
    }
}
Careful with the third parameter: because AdyenGateway is @Primary, step 4 wins before the name fallback in step 6, so stripeGateway actually receives Adyen. Name matching only applies when no primary/priority resolves the tie. This is exactly the trap interviewers set.
MechanismWhere declaredWins overTypical use
@Qualifier("x")Injection point + beanEverything belowPick a specific implementation
@PrimaryOne bean of the typePriority, nameSensible default when several exist
@Priority(n)Bean classNameRank candidates, also orders lists
Parameter / field nameImplicitNothingLast-resort tie-break; brittle under refactoring (-parameters flag needed)

Pitfalls

  • Two @Primary beans of the same type → NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException "more than one 'primary' bean found".
  • @Order on a @Component affects only collection ordering and some Spring-managed lists (filters, advisors); it does not influence bean creation order — use @DependsOn for that.
  • Relying on parameter names requires compiling with -parameters (Boot's Maven/Gradle plugins add it; a plain javac build silently loses it).
  • Injecting List<Gateway> into a bean that is itself a Gateway excludes itself (self-references are skipped unless it is the only candidate).
Interview questions
  • Two beans implement the same interface and you inject the interface. What happens? — NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException at startup unless a @Qualifier, @Primary, @Priority or a parameter name matching a bean name disambiguates.
  • @Qualifier and @Primary both present; which wins? — @Qualifier: it filters candidates first; @Primary is only consulted among what survives the filter.
  • How do you inject all implementations in a defined order? — Inject List<T> and annotate implementations with @Order/@Priority; or use ObjectProvider<T>.orderedStream().
  • When would you use ObjectProvider over a plain injection? — Optional dependencies without required=false, breaking a cycle by resolving lazily, and obtaining a fresh prototype instance per call with getObject().
  • Why did a working injection break after renaming a constructor parameter? — It was relying on the name fallback; two candidates existed and only the parameter name matched a bean name. Make it explicit with @Qualifier.
  • How do you write a custom qualifier? — Meta-annotate: @Qualifier @Retention(RUNTIME) @interface Legacy {}, then use @Legacy on both the bean and the injection point; it is type-safe and refactor-proof.
  • How do you debug "which bean was injected?" in production? — ApplicationContext.getBeanNamesForType(Gateway.class), the /actuator/beans endpoint (shows each bean's dependencies), or --debug for the condition report.

@Component vs @Bean vs @Configuration (and proxyBeanMethods)

Why interviewers ask: "if @Bean method a() calls b() twice, how many B instances exist?" tests whether you know a @Configuration class is silently subclassed by CGLIB. The answer changes with proxyBeanMethods=false and with @Component.

@Component (and its stereotypes @Service, @Repository, @Controller) marks your own class for classpath scanning; Spring calls its constructor. @Bean is a factory method you write, usually to register a class you do not own (a DataSource, a RestClient) or one that needs conditional wiring; the return value becomes the bean, named after the method. @Configuration is itself a @Component plus one crucial extra: full mode. The class is subclassed at runtime by CGLIB, and every @Bean method call — including this.dataSource() from another @Bean method — is intercepted and routed through the container's singleton registry, so you always get the one managed instance.

With @Component holding @Bean methods, or @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false), you are in lite mode: no subclass, plain Java method calls, a fresh object per call. Lite mode starts faster (no CGLIB generation, GraalVM-native friendly; nearly every Boot auto-configuration uses it) but requires inter-bean dependencies to be passed as method parameters instead of called directly. Analogy: full mode is a receptionist who intercepts every "get me the printer" and hands you the office's single printer; lite mode lets you walk to the store and buy a new one each time.

@Configuration                      // full mode: CGLIB subclass, inter-bean calls are safe
public class DataConfig {
    @Bean DataSource dataSource() { return new HikariDataSource(cfg()); }
    @Bean OrderRepo orderRepo()   { return new OrderRepo(dataSource()); }  // same singleton
}

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)   // lite mode: faster startup, no subclass
public class DataConfigLite {
    @Bean DataSource dataSource() { return new HikariDataSource(cfg()); }
    @Bean OrderRepo orderRepo(DataSource ds) { return new OrderRepo(ds); } // inject as parameter
}
@Component@Bean in @Configuration@Bean in lite mode
Who writes the classYouAnyone (3rd-party OK)Anyone
Instantiated byContainer via constructorYour factory methodYour factory method
Inter-bean method calln/aIntercepted → singletonPlain call → new object
Class must be non-finalOnly if AOP-proxiedYes (CGLIB subclass)No
Startup / native costLowCGLIB generation per configLowest (Boot auto-configs use this)

Pitfalls

  • A private or final @Bean method in full mode cannot be overridden by CGLIB; Spring fails at startup with a clear message.
  • Two @Bean methods with the same name in different configs: by default Boot 2.1+ refuses bean overriding (BeanDefinitionOverrideException) unless spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding=true.
  • @Bean methods are non-static by default; a BeanFactoryPostProcessor bean method must be static or it forces early instantiation of the whole config class (Spring logs a warning).
  • Returning a bean of an interface type from @Bean hides the concrete type from autowiring; declare the most specific return type you can.
Interview questions
  • What is the difference between @Component and @Bean? — @Component is a class-level marker picked up by scanning and instantiated by Spring; @Bean is a method that returns an object you construct, registered under the method name, used for third-party types or conditional wiring.
  • Why is @Configuration not just @Component? — Full mode: CGLIB subclassing makes inter-bean method calls return the managed singleton. A @Component with @Bean methods is lite mode and each call creates a new object.
  • When would you set proxyBeanMethods=false? — When no @Bean method calls another (dependencies passed as parameters), to shave startup time and support GraalVM native images; Boot's own auto-configurations all do this.
  • What happens if you make a @Configuration class final? — Startup fails: CGLIB cannot subclass it. Use lite mode or remove final.
  • Is @Service functionally different from @Component? — No behaviour difference in the core container; @Repository is the exception, adding PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor exception translation into DataAccessException.
  • How would you debug two connection pools showing up in metrics? — Check for a @Bean method called directly from a lite-mode class or from a non-@Bean helper; /actuator/beans lists one bean, but the second pool was created by a plain method call and is invisible to Spring.
  • Boot 2 vs 3: any change in configuration classes? — The CGLIB naming changed to $$SpringCGLIB$$ (Spring 6 repackaged CGLIB), and AOT processing in Boot 3 pre-generates bean definitions so lite mode is strongly preferred for native images.

Bean scopes, scoped proxies and the prototype-in-singleton trap

Why interviewers ask: "is a singleton bean thread-safe?" and "I marked my bean prototype but I keep getting the same instance" are the two classic scope questions; both hinge on who is holding the reference.

singleton (default): one instance per container, created eagerly at startup, shared by every thread, so it must be stateless or synchronise its state. prototype: a new instance every getBean() / injection; Spring does not track it after creation, so @PreDestroy is never called. Web scopes: request, session, application (servlet context), websocket. Custom scopes (e.g. a thread scope, or a tenant scope) implement Scope and register via CustomScopeConfigurer.

The trap: injecting a prototype (or request-scoped) bean into a singleton resolves it once, at singleton creation; the singleton then holds that single instance forever. Fixes, in order of preference: inject ObjectProvider<T> and call getObject() per use; declare the narrow bean with proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS so the singleton holds a proxy that resolves the current instance on every method call (mandatory for request/session beans injected into singletons); or a @Lookup abstract method that Spring overrides via CGLIB. Analogy: a scoped proxy is a hotel front desk; you always talk to the desk, and it routes you to whichever guest currently occupies the room.

@Component @Scope("prototype")
class ReportBuilder { /* mutable state per report */ }

@Component @Scope(value = WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_REQUEST,
                  proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)
class RequestContext { String correlationId; }

@Service
class ReportService {
    private final ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder> builders;   // fresh per call
    private final RequestContext ctx;                       // proxy → current request

    ReportService(ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder> builders, RequestContext ctx) {
        this.builders = builders; this.ctx = ctx;
    }
    Report build() {
        ReportBuilder b = builders.getObject();   // new instance every time
        return b.withId(ctx.correlationId).build();
    }
}
ScopeInstancesDestroy callbackInjecting into a singleton
singleton1 per contextYes, on close()Direct
prototype1 per request to the containerNo (container forgets it)ObjectProvider / @Lookup
request1 per HTTP requestYes, end of requestScoped proxy required
session1 per HTTP sessionYes, session invalidationScoped proxy required

Pitfalls

  • Prototype beans that hold expensive resources leak: nobody calls @PreDestroy. Use try-with-resources or a DisposableBean you close yourself.
  • Accessing a request-scoped proxy from a non-request thread (an @Async method, a scheduler) throws "No thread-bound request found"; copy the values into your task first.
  • ScopedProxyMode.INTERFACES proxies only the interfaces; injecting the concrete class then fails with a BeanNotOfRequiredTypeException.
Interview questions
  • Are singleton beans thread-safe? — Not automatically; Spring only guarantees one instance. Keep them stateless or use thread-safe state (ConcurrentHashMap, atomics, ThreadLocal with cleanup).
  • I annotated a bean @Scope("prototype") but always get the same object. Why? — It is injected into a singleton, which received one instance at its own creation. Use ObjectProvider.getObject(), a scoped proxy or @Lookup.
  • How does a request-scoped bean get injected into a singleton controller? — Through a CGLIB scoped proxy (proxyMode=TARGET_CLASS); each method call on the proxy looks up the bean bound to the current request via RequestContextHolder.
  • Does Spring call @PreDestroy on prototype beans? — No. Prototypes are handed over and forgotten; the client owns their lifecycle.
  • Singleton scope vs the Singleton design pattern? — Pattern: one instance per JVM class loader enforced by the class; Spring scope: one per container, enforced by the registry; two contexts can hold two instances.
  • How would you implement a per-tenant scope? — Implement Scope (get, remove, registerDestructionCallback) backed by a map keyed on the tenant in a ThreadLocal/MDC, register it with CustomScopeConfigurer, and inject via a scoped proxy.

The complete bean lifecycle: definition → instance → ready → destroyed

Why interviewers ask: "walk me through what happens when Spring creates a bean" is the single most reliable question for measuring Spring depth. The order of @PostConstruct vs afterPropertiesSet() vs init-method, and where proxies appear, are the details they listen for.

A bean starts as a BeanDefinition (class, scope, constructor args, property values, init/destroy method names) registered by scanning or @Bean parsing and possibly rewritten by BeanFactoryPostProcessors. When a singleton is needed, AbstractAutowireCapableBeanFactory.doCreateBean runs, in this order: instantiate (constructor chosen, constructor args injected) → populate (@Autowired, @Value, @Resource on fields/setters) → Aware callbacks (BeanNameAware, BeanClassLoaderAware, BeanFactoryAware; then via a post-processor EnvironmentAware, ApplicationContextAware…) → BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization → initialisation: @PostConstruct, then InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet(), then @Bean(initMethod=…) → BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization (this is where AOP wraps the bean in a proxy) → stored in the singleton registry → ready.

Once all singletons exist, SmartInitializingSingleton.afterSingletonsInstantiated() runs, then SmartLifecycle.start() (Kafka listeners, schedulers, the web server), then ContextRefreshedEvent. Shutdown mirrors it: ContextClosedEvent → SmartLifecycle.stop() → @PreDestroy → DisposableBean.destroy() → destroyMethod (Boot infers close()/shutdown() for @Beans automatically). Analogy: hiring: the job description (definition) → the hire (instantiate) → equipment issued (populate) → told their name and manager (Aware) → onboarding checks (BPP before) → orientation day (init) → badge printed with access rules (BPP after = proxy) → on the floor.

@Component
public class CacheWarmer implements InitializingBean, DisposableBean, BeanNameAware {
    private final CatalogClient client;          // 1. constructor
    private String beanName;

    CacheWarmer(CatalogClient client) { this.client = client; }

    @Override public void setBeanName(String n) { beanName = n; }      // 3. Aware
    @PostConstruct void warm() { client.preload(); }                   // 5a. first init callback
    @Override public void afterPropertiesSet() { /* 5b. second */ }
    @PreDestroy void flush() { client.flush(); }                         // 8. on close()
    @Override public void destroy() { /* after @PreDestroy */ }
}
HookRunsCoupling to SpringRecommended?
@PostConstruct / @PreDestroy1st init / 1st destroyNone (jakarta.annotation)Yes, default choice
InitializingBean / DisposableBean2ndSpring interfaceFramework code only
@Bean(initMethod, destroyMethod)3rdNone (third-party classes)Yes for classes you do not own
SmartLifecycle.start/stopAfter all singletons are readySpring interfaceLong-running components (listeners, servers)

Pitfalls

  • Calling a @Transactional/@Cacheable/@Async method of the same bean from @PostConstruct runs without advice: the proxy does not exist yet (step 7 comes later). Use ApplicationRunner or an ApplicationReadyEvent listener instead.
  • Throwing from @PostConstruct aborts the whole context with BeanCreationException; that is often desirable (fail fast) but makes "warm-up" logic a startup risk.
  • Boot infers close()/shutdown() as the destroy method of @Beans; set destroyMethod="" for beans whose close() must not be called (e.g. a shared DataSource owned elsewhere).
  • Prototype beans never get destroy callbacks; request/session beans do (end of request/session).
Interview questions
  • Walk me through bean creation. — Definition → instantiate via constructor → populate fields/setters → Aware callbacks → BPP before-init → @PostConstruct → afterPropertiesSet → init-method → BPP after-init (AOP proxy) → cached singleton; destroy is @PreDestroy → destroy() → destroy-method.
  • Why is @Transactional ignored when called from @PostConstruct? — The proxy is created in postProcessAfterInitialization, after init callbacks; inside @PostConstruct this is the raw object.
  • @PostConstruct vs constructor for initialisation? — With constructor injection, dependencies are already available in the constructor; @PostConstruct is still useful for logic that needs all injection (including setters/fields) or that should not run in unit tests that new the class.
  • Where do Aware interfaces fit, and are they still recommended? — After population, before init; they couple you to Spring, so prefer injecting ApplicationContext/Environment directly or using ObjectProvider.
  • What happens if a bean's init method throws? — BeanCreationException, the context refresh fails, already-created singletons are destroyed, and Boot exits with a non-zero code (after the FailureAnalyzer report).
  • How do you run code after every bean is ready? — SmartInitializingSingleton, an ApplicationReadyEvent/ContextRefreshedEvent listener, or ApplicationRunner; not @PostConstruct, which sees only earlier beans.
  • Boot 2 → 3: what changed in lifecycle annotations? — Package only: javax.annotation.PostConstruct became jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct; a leftover javax import compiles (if the jar is present) but is silently ignored by Spring 6.

BeanFactoryPostProcessor vs BeanPostProcessor: how @Autowired, @Value and AOP really work

Why interviewers ask: the "magic" annotations are ordinary post-processors. Naming AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor and AbstractAutoProxyCreator shows you have read the stack traces, and it explains why a BPP bean itself cannot be @Autowired-processed or proxied.

A BeanFactoryPostProcessor runs once, before any bean is instantiated, and edits bean definitions: ConfigurationClassPostProcessor parses @Configuration/@ComponentScan/@Import and registers definitions; PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer resolves ${…} in definition metadata. A BeanPostProcessor runs per bean instance, around initialisation, and may modify or replace the object: AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor (fields/setters/constructors for @Autowired, @Value, @Inject), CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor (@Resource, @PostConstruct, @PreDestroy), AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator (AOP, @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async proxies), ScheduledAnnotationBeanPostProcessor.

The consequence interviewers probe: BPPs are instantiated first (in registerBeanPostProcessors), before ordinary singletons; so a BPP and anything it depends on are created too early to be processed by other BPPs — Spring logs "Bean X is not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors". Analogy: BFPP edits the blueprint before the factory starts; BPP inspects each car coming off the line and may swap it for an armoured version (proxy).

@Component
class RenameScope implements BeanFactoryPostProcessor {           // edits definitions
    public void postProcessBeanFactory(ConfigurableListableBeanFactory bf) {
        bf.getBeanDefinition("auditLog").setScope("prototype");
    }
}

@Component
class TimingBpp implements BeanPostProcessor {                    // wraps instances
    public Object postProcessAfterInitialization(Object bean, String name) {
        if (bean instanceof PaymentService p) return timedProxy(p);   // replace the bean
        return bean;
    }
}

@Service
class PaymentService {
    @Value("${pay.timeout:3s}") Duration timeout;                 // injected by AutowiredAnnotationBPP
    @Autowired AuditLog auditLog;
    @PostConstruct void init() { /* timeout and auditLog are set here */ }
}
  1. All BFPPs (Spring-internal first, ordered by PriorityOrdered/Ordered, then yours) run once. Not a single application bean exists yet.
  2. BPPs are created eagerly and registered in order. If TimingBpp had injected PaymentService, that service would be created here, too early to be proxied by AOP.
  3. Pre-instantiation of remaining singletons starts. PaymentService is constructed.
  4. InstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor.postProcessProperties is the hook: AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor reflects over the class once (metadata cached) and writes both fields.
  5. @PostConstruct executes from CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor; everything injected is available.
  6. After-init: every BPP in order. Ours returns a proxy; the container stores the proxy under the name paymentService.
  7. Done. This is the whole trick behind @Transactional: no bytecode weaving, just a BPP swapping the reference.
BeanFactoryPostProcessorBeanPostProcessor
Operates onBeanDefinition metadataLive bean instances
RunsOnce per context, before instantiationTwice per bean (before/after init)
Can replace the beanCan change class / scope / propertiesYes: return a different object (proxy)
ExamplesConfigurationClassPostProcessor, PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurerAutowiredAnnotationBPP, CommonAnnotationBPP, AutoProxyCreator
Declare asstatic @Bean (avoid early config instantiation)@Component or static @Bean

Pitfalls

  • A BPP with @Autowired dependencies pulls those beans forward; they miss AOP and @ConfigurationProperties binding. Keep BPPs dependency-free or use ObjectProvider lazily.
  • BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor (a BFPP sub-interface) runs even earlier and can add definitions; this is how @Imported ImportBeanDefinitionRegistrars and MyBatis mapper scanning work.
  • @Value("${x}") in a BFPP's own fields cannot be resolved by the placeholder configurer (it is a sibling BFPP); read from Environment directly.
Interview questions
  • How does @Autowired actually work? — AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, an InstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor, scans the class for injection metadata (cached), resolves each dependency via BeanFactory.resolveDependency and sets it reflectively during populateBean.
  • How is @Transactional implemented without bytecode weaving? — AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator (a BPP) checks each bean for matching advisors in postProcessAfterInitialization and returns a JDK/CGLIB proxy that wraps calls with TransactionInterceptor.
  • BFPP vs BPP in one sentence? — BFPP mutates definitions before any bean exists; BPP mutates or replaces each bean instance around its initialisation.
  • Why does Spring warn "not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors"? — A bean was instantiated during BPP registration (as a BPP dependency), so BPPs registered later never saw it; AOP or @Autowired may silently not apply to it.
  • Why declare a BFPP @Bean method static? — So the container can invoke it without instantiating the enclosing @Configuration class, which would otherwise be created before its own placeholders and BPPs are ready.
  • How would you write a BPP that applies to only one bean? — Check beanName or the type in postProcessAfterInitialization and return the bean unchanged for everything else; never return null.
  • What is InstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInstantiation used for? — It can short-circuit creation by returning a ready object (used by AOP's TargetSource path and by mocking frameworks such as @MockBean).

Circular dependencies: the three-level cache, why constructors fail, Boot 2.6+ ban

Why interviewers ask: it combines lifecycle, injection styles and a real Boot behaviour change. "A→B→A: does it start?" has three different correct answers depending on injection style and Boot version, and the strong candidate explains the cache that makes any of it possible.

DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry keeps three maps: L1 singletonObjects (fully initialised beans), L2 earlySingletonObjects (instantiated but not yet populated/initialised, possibly already a proxy), L3 singletonFactories (an ObjectFactory that can produce the early reference, applying SmartInstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor.getEarlyBeanReference — i.e. creating the AOP proxy early if needed). Right after instantiation, a bean's factory is put in L3. While populating A, Spring needs B; while populating B, it needs A: getSingleton("a") misses L1, misses L2, hits L3, calls the factory, moves the early A into L2 and hands it to B. B finishes, A finishes, both land in L1.

This only works for setter/field injection, because A must already be instantiated to have an early reference. With constructor injection, A's constructor needs a finished B, whose constructor needs A, which is "currently in creation" → BeanCurrentlyInCreationException. Since Boot 2.6, spring.main.allow-circular-references defaults to false, so even the field/setter case is refused with a clear "The dependencies of some of the beans form a cycle" report. The right fix is to break the cycle in the design (extract the shared piece into a third bean, use events, or invert the dependency); the tactical fixes are @Lazy on one parameter (injects a resolving proxy), ObjectProvider<B>, or setter injection plus re-enabling the flag. Analogy: two people who each refuse to enter the room until the other is seated (constructor). With setters, both walk in, then exchange business cards.

// Preferred: break the cycle. Both depended on "notify"; extract it.
@Service class OrderService { OrderService(Notifier n) { … } }
@Service class InvoiceService { InvoiceService(Notifier n) { … } }

// Tactical: @Lazy injects a CGLIB proxy that resolves InvoiceService on first call
@Service class OrderService {
    OrderService(@Lazy InvoiceService invoices) { … }
}

// Tactical: resolve on demand (also works for prototypes)
@Service class OrderService {
    private final ObjectProvider<InvoiceService> invoices;
    OrderService(ObjectProvider<InvoiceService> invoices) { this.invoices = invoices; }
    void place() { invoices.getObject().issue(); }
}

Pitfalls

  • @Lazy proxies require a non-final class (CGLIB) or an interface; the first call to the proxy can throw if the target fails to create, far from startup.
  • Early-reference + AOP: if a BPP other than the auto-proxy creator wraps A in postProcessAfterInitialization, B holds a different object than L1 → Spring detects it and throws "Bean with name 'a' has been injected into other beans … in its raw version".
  • @Async beans in a cycle are a classic failure: the async proxy is created late, so the early reference differs; use @Lazy on that injection.
  • Re-enabling allow-circular-references globally hides design problems; if you must, do it while refactoring, not permanently.
Interview questions
  • A depends on B and B on A, both constructor-injected. What happens? — BeanCurrentlyInCreationException (Boot reports "The dependencies of some of the beans in the application context form a cycle"); a constructor cannot receive a half-built partner.
  • Same cycle with field injection? — Spring Framework can resolve it through the early-reference cache, but Boot 2.6+ refuses by default; set spring.main.allow-circular-references=true to restore the old behaviour.
  • Why three caches, not two? — L3 holds a factory so the early reference (possibly an AOP proxy) is created lazily and only when a cycle actually occurs; L2 caches the produced reference so repeated lookups return the same object.
  • How does @Lazy break the cycle? — The parameter receives a proxy immediately; the real bean is resolved on the first method call, after both beans are fully created.
  • How would you fix a cycle without @Lazy? — Extract the shared responsibility into a third bean, replace one direction with an ApplicationEvent, inject ObjectProvider, or switch that one dependency to setter injection.
  • How do you find cycles in a large code base? — Start the app: Boot's FailureAnalyzer prints the exact cycle; or use ArchUnit/IDE dependency graphs to fail the build on package cycles.
  • Boot 2 vs 3? — The prohibition arrived in 2.6 and is unchanged in 3.x; Boot 3's AOT mode additionally cannot generate code for cycles, so they are a hard error for native images.

ApplicationContext vs BeanFactory, context hierarchy, and refresh()

Why interviewers ask: "what does SpringApplication.run actually do?" and "can a child context see the parent's beans?" test whether you understand the container as a thing with phases, not a black box.

BeanFactory (DefaultListableBeanFactory) is the bare registry: definitions, lazy getBean, DI. ApplicationContext wraps one and adds eager singleton pre-instantiation, automatic BeanPostProcessor/BeanFactoryPostProcessor detection, Environment and property sources, event publishing, MessageSource i18n, ResourceLoader, and web integration. Boot creates an AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext (or the reactive/plain variants) and calls refresh(), whose sequence is the skeleton every lifecycle question hangs on.

Contexts form a hierarchy: a child sees its parent's beans (getBean falls back to the parent), the parent never sees the child's. Classic Spring MVC used root (services) + servlet (controllers) contexts; Boot uses a single context by default, but SpringApplicationBuilder.parent()/child() and Spring Cloud's BootstrapApplicationContext still build hierarchies. Test slices (@WebMvcTest) and @SpringBootTest caching rely on the context being a self-contained, restartable unit.

public void refresh() {
    prepareRefresh();                              // start time, Environment, early listeners
    ConfigurableListableBeanFactory bf = obtainFreshBeanFactory();   // load BeanDefinitions
    prepareBeanFactory(bf);                        // ApplicationContextAwareProcessor, ignore Aware ifaces
    postProcessBeanFactory(bf);                    // web scopes (request/session) registered
    invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors(bf);           // ConfigurationClassPostProcessor, placeholders
    registerBeanPostProcessors(bf);                // Autowired/CommonAnnotation/AutoProxy BPPs created
    initMessageSource();
    initApplicationEventMulticaster();             // SimpleApplicationEventMulticaster
    onRefresh();                                   // Boot: create the embedded web server (not started)
    registerListeners();                           // @EventListener + ApplicationListener beans
    finishBeanFactoryInitialization(bf);           // preInstantiateSingletons(): YOUR beans here
    finishRefresh();                               // SmartLifecycle.start(), web server starts, ContextRefreshedEvent
}
  1. The bean factory is created; for annotation contexts the definitions of the primary source (your @SpringBootApplication class) are registered, nothing else yet.
  2. Infrastructure BPPs and special resolvable dependencies are registered; web contexts add request/session scopes.
  3. The big one: ConfigurationClassPostProcessor parses configuration classes recursively, evaluating @Conditionals, and registers every definition. Then PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer and your own BFPPs run.
  4. All BPPs are instantiated and ordered. This is why BPP dependencies are "not eligible" for full processing.
  5. Message source, event multicaster and (in Boot) the embedded web server are created; listeners are registered.
  6. Your beans are created here, one doCreateBean at a time, recursing into dependencies. Lazy beans and prototypes are skipped.
  7. LifecycleProcessor.onRefresh() starts SmartLifecycle beans in phase order (the web server has a very late phase), then ContextRefreshedEvent; Boot follows with runners and ApplicationReadyEvent.
CapabilityBeanFactoryApplicationContext
Bean instantiationLazy, on getBeanEager for singletons (fail-fast at startup)
BPP / BFPPManual addBeanPostProcessorAuto-detected from definitions
Events, i18n, resources, EnvironmentNoYes
Use in practiceNever directly (embedded only)Always

Pitfalls

  • Calling refresh() twice on a GenericApplicationContext throws; contexts are refresh-once (the XML/classpath ones support re-refresh).
  • Injecting the context to call getBean at runtime is the service-locator anti-pattern; it hides dependencies and breaks tests. Use ObjectProvider.
  • In a hierarchy, @EventListener in a child does not hear events published in the parent, but parent listeners do hear child events (events propagate up).
Interview questions
  • BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext? — BeanFactory is the minimal DI registry with lazy lookup; ApplicationContext extends it with eager singleton creation, automatic post-processor detection, events, Environment, i18n and resource loading; you always use the context.
  • What does SpringApplication.run() do before and after refresh()? — Before: build Environment, print banner, choose the context class, apply initializers, load the primary source. After: call runners, publish ApplicationStartedEvent/ApplicationReadyEvent, or on failure run FailureAnalyzers.
  • Where does component scanning happen in refresh()? — Inside invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors, by ConfigurationClassPostProcessor, before any BPP or ordinary bean exists.
  • Can a parent context inject a bean defined in a child? — No. Lookup is child → parent only; siblings are invisible to each other.
  • How do you get a bean when you only have a name at runtime? — Inject ApplicationContext or better ObjectProvider/Map<String, T>; avoid the static ApplicationContextAware holder hack outside legacy code.
  • Why does @SpringBootTest reuse contexts and why does @MockBean slow tests? — The test framework caches contexts by configuration key; each distinct set of @MockBeans/properties is a new key, forcing another full refresh().
  • Boot 2 vs 3 here? — Spring 6 adds AOT: refresh() can run at build time to pre-compute definitions (ApplicationContextAotGenerator), which is what makes native images and faster startup possible; the runtime sequence is unchanged.

Application events: @EventListener, @TransactionalEventListener, async events

Why interviewers ask: events are the standard way to decouple "order placed" from "send email" inside one JVM, and the follow-up "is the listener in the same transaction/thread?" separates people who have been burned from those who have not.

ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(Object) (any POJO since Spring 4.2; no need to extend ApplicationEvent) delivers to every @EventListener method whose parameter type matches (generics respected via ResolvableType), plus ApplicationListener<E> beans. By default the SimpleApplicationEventMulticaster is synchronous: listeners run on the publishing thread, inside the publisher's transaction, and an exception propagates back to the publisher. Add @Async (with @EnableAsync) to a listener to hand it to the task executor, or define a bean named applicationEventMulticaster with a task executor to make all events async.

@TransactionalEventListener defers delivery to a transaction phase: AFTER_COMMIT (default), AFTER_ROLLBACK, AFTER_COMPLETION, BEFORE_COMMIT. Published outside a transaction the event is dropped unless fallbackExecution=true. Boot itself speaks in events: ApplicationStartingEvent → EnvironmentPreparedEvent → ContextInitializedEvent → PreparedEvent → ContextRefreshedEvent → StartedEvent → ReadyEvent (and FailedEvent); the early ones fire before the context exists, so they need listeners registered in META-INF/spring.factories or SpringApplication.addListeners, not @EventListener.

public record OrderPlaced(long orderId, String email) {}     // plain POJO event

@Service
class OrderService {
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;
    OrderService(ApplicationEventPublisher events) { this.events = events; }

    @Transactional
    void place(Order o) {
        repo.save(o);
        events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(o.id(), o.email())); // still inside the tx
    }
}

@Component
class MailListener {
    @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
    @Async                                   // off the request thread; needs @EnableAsync
    public void onPlaced(OrderPlaced e) { mailer.send(e.email(), "Order " + e.orderId()); }

    @EventListener(condition = "#e.orderId() > 1000")   // SpEL filter
    public void audit(OrderPlaced e) { log.info("big order {}", e.orderId()); }
}
Listener styleThreadSees publisher's tx?Exception effect
@EventListenerPublisher'sYes (same tx)Propagates to publisher, can roll back
@EventListener @AsyncExecutorNoLogged by AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler
@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)Publisher's (after commit)Committed; new writes need REQUIRES_NEWLogged, cannot roll back the committed tx

Pitfalls

  • AFTER_COMMIT listener doing @Transactional writes: the outer transaction is finished but its resources are still bound, so the listener's default REQUIRED joins a "completed" tx and the writes are silently not committed; use REQUIRES_NEW.
  • A synchronous listener that throws rolls back the order; if the email service is flaky, the order fails. Make side effects async or after-commit.
  • @EventListener methods are called through the bean proxy only if the listener is a bean; @Async on them requires the class to be proxyable.
  • Listening for ApplicationReadyEvent with @EventListener works; listening for ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent that way silently never fires (no context yet).
Interview questions
  • Are Spring events synchronous? — By default yes: same thread, same transaction, exceptions propagate. Make them async per listener with @Async or globally by configuring the multicaster with an executor.
  • When would you use @TransactionalEventListener? — For side effects that must only happen if the business transaction committed (emails, outbox publishing, cache eviction); with AFTER_COMMIT the listener never sees a rolled-back order.
  • Why did my after-commit listener's DB write vanish? — It joined the already-committed transaction; annotate it @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW).
  • Event vs direct method call vs message broker? — Events decouple within one JVM with no delivery guarantee; a broker (Kafka/SQS) gives durability and cross-service delivery. Use the outbox pattern when you need both transactional consistency and a broker.
  • Can a listener return a value? — Yes: a non-void return from @EventListener is published as a new event (or each element of a collection), enabling small event chains.
  • Order of multiple listeners for the same event? — Undefined unless you add @Order on the listener methods.
  • Which Boot startup events cannot be caught with @EventListener? — Everything before ContextRefreshedEvent (starting, environment-prepared, context-initialized/prepared); register those via SpringApplication.addListeners or spring.factories.

@Value, @ConfigurationProperties, relaxed binding, validation, @Profile & property precedence

Why interviewers ask: "which value wins: application.yml, an env var, or -D?" and "why did my @Value field stay null?" are daily-life questions; senior candidates are expected to prefer typed, validated properties over scattered @Value.

@Value("${key:default}") injects one value (placeholder resolved by PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer, converted by the ConversionService; supports SpEL with #{…}). @ConfigurationProperties(prefix="app.mail") binds a whole tree into a typed object using the Binder, with relaxed binding: app.mail.smtp-host, smtpHost, smtp_host and env var APP_MAIL_SMTPHOST all map to the property smtpHost (canonical form in files is kebab-case, env vars are upper snake with dots → underscores and dashes removed). Boot 3 binds records via constructor binding (Java 17 idiom; @DefaultValue for defaults), supports List/Map/Duration/DataSize, generates IDE metadata via spring-boot-configuration-processor, and validates with @Validated + Bean Validation annotations, failing startup with a precise report.

The Environment is an ordered list of PropertySources; first match wins. From highest to lowest (the ones that matter): devtools global settings → @TestPropertySource → @SpringBootTest(properties) → command-line args → SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON → servlet params → JNDI → Java system properties (-D) → OS environment variables → profile-specific application-{profile}.yml (outside jar, then inside) → application.yml (outside jar, then inside) → @PropertySource on config classes → SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties. @Profile("prod") registers a bean only when that profile is active (spring.profiles.active; !prod, prod & eu expressions); spring.profiles.group composes profiles; a profile-specific file overrides the base file per key, not wholesale.

@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.mail")
public record MailProps(
        @NotBlank String smtpHost,
        @DefaultValue("587") int port,
        @DefaultValue("PT5S") Duration timeout,
        List<@Email String> admins) {}

@SpringBootApplication
@ConfigurationPropertiesScan          // or @EnableConfigurationProperties(MailProps.class)
class App {}

@Service
class Mailer {
    Mailer(MailProps props,
           @Value("${app.mail.from:noreply@acme.com}") String from) { … }
}
app:
  mail:
    smtp-host: smtp.acme.com      # canonical kebab-case
    admins: [ops@acme.com, sre@acme.com]
---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: prod            # Boot 2.4+ multi-document style (replaces spring.profiles)
app:
  mail:
    port: 465                     # overrides only this key in prod
# env var equivalent: APP_MAIL_SMTPHOST=smtp.acme.com ; list: APP_MAIL_ADMINS_0_=ops@acme.com
@Value@ConfigurationProperties
GranularityOne valueWhole prefix, nested, lists, maps
Relaxed bindingNo: exact keyYes
ValidationNo@Validated + JSR-380
SpELYesNo
IDE metadata / docsNoYes (configuration processor)
Use forOne-off, SpELAnything with 2+ related keys

Pitfalls

  • @Value on a static field is silently ignored; on a field of an object created with new it is also ignored (Spring only processes beans).
  • Env var names cannot contain dots or dashes; APP_MAIL_SMTP_HOST binds fine to smtp-host via relaxed rules, but @Value("${app.mail.smtp-host}") also resolves it only because Boot's SystemEnvironmentPropertySource maps names; @Value with a camelCase key does not.
  • @Profile on a @Configuration class hides all its @Beans; on a single @Bean method it hides just that bean; there is no "default when nothing else matched" except a bean with no profile or @Profile("default").
  • Boot 2.4 changed file processing: spring.profiles in YAML became spring.config.activate.on-profile, profile-specific files always override the base regardless of order, and spring.config.import replaced bootstrap.yml for config servers.
Interview questions
  • Property precedence: env var vs application.yml vs command line? — Command-line args > Java system properties > OS env vars > profile-specific files > application.yml > defaults; first source that has the key wins.
  • @Value or @ConfigurationProperties? — @ConfigurationProperties for anything structured: relaxed binding, validation at startup, one typed object to inject and test; @Value for single values or when SpEL is needed.
  • How does relaxed binding map APP_MAIL_SMTPHOST? — Env vars are lower-cased, underscores become dots, and the binder matches ignoring case and dashes, so it lands on app.mail.smtp-host.
  • How do you make invalid config fail fast? — @Validated on the properties class with Bean Validation constraints; Boot's BindValidationException lists every failing key at startup.
  • How do you bind an immutable properties object? — A Java record or a class with one constructor (constructor binding is automatic in Boot 3; @ConstructorBinding only needed to pick among several).
  • What is @Profile("!prod") and how do profile groups work? — Bean active when prod is not active; spring.profiles.group.prod=prod-db,prod-mq activates several profiles when prod is.
  • How do you inspect the effective configuration at runtime? — /actuator/env (shows every property source and which wins) and /actuator/configprops; enable management.endpoint.env.show-values=always carefully.
  • Boot 2 vs 3? — Constructor binding no longer needs @ConstructorBinding for single-constructor classes/records; jakarta.validation namespace; the 2.4 config-file model (spring.config.import, on-profile) is the only one.

The @Conditional family in user code

Why interviewers ask: conditions are how auto-configuration works (next section) and how you ship feature-flagged or environment-specific beans without profiles for everything; the trap question is "why did @ConditionalOnBean not see my bean?".

@Conditional(MyCondition.class) asks a Condition.matches(context, metadata) at definition-registration time (inside ConfigurationClassPostProcessor). Boot ships the useful ones: @ConditionalOnProperty(name="feature.x", havingValue="true", matchIfMissing=false) (feature flags), @ConditionalOnMissingBean / @ConditionalOnBean (defaults that users can override), @ConditionalOnClass / OnMissingClass (by class name string, so the class need not be on the classpath), @ConditionalOnExpression (SpEL), @ConditionalOnWebApplication, @ConditionalOnResource, @ConditionalOnJava, @ConditionalOnCloudPlatform. @Profile itself is just @Conditional(ProfileCondition.class).

The rule that trips people: @ConditionalOnBean/OnMissingBean only see definitions registered so far. Auto-configurations run after user config (that is why the library's default @ConditionalOnMissingBean yields to yours), but two user configurations have no guaranteed order, so a bean-presence condition between them is a coin flip. Use them in auto-configuration classes (ordered via @AutoConfiguration(before/after)), and use property/class conditions in user code.

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class PaymentConfig {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "payments", name = "provider", havingValue = "stripe", matchIfMissing = true)
    Gateway stripe(StripeProps p) { return new StripeGateway(p); }

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "payments", name = "provider", havingValue = "adyen")
    Gateway adyen(AdyenProps p) { return new AdyenGateway(p); }

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(FraudCheck.class)      // library default; app can replace it
    FraudCheck noopFraud() { return FraudCheck.NOOP; }
}

// Custom condition: only when running on Kubernetes
class OnK8s implements Condition {
    public boolean matches(ConditionContext ctx, AnnotatedTypeMetadata md) {
        return ctx.getEnvironment().containsProperty("KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST");
    }
}

Pitfalls

  • @ConditionalOnMissingBean with no attributes on a @Bean method uses the method's return type; if the return type is an interface, any bean of that interface suppresses it.
  • Conditions on a @Configuration class are evaluated before its @Bean methods; a false class-level condition skips all of them, including @Imports.
  • @ConditionalOnExpression is evaluated against the Environment only; it cannot reference beans.
  • Run with --debug (or hit /actuator/conditions) to read the ConditionEvaluationReport: positive and negative matches with the reason.
Interview questions
  • When is a @Conditional evaluated? — Once, at configuration-class parsing inside refresh(); it cannot depend on runtime state and it never re-evaluates.
  • Why does @ConditionalOnBean in my own config not see a bean from another of my configs? — User configurations have no defined order, so the other definition may not be registered yet; bean conditions are safe only in auto-configurations, which run after user code.
  • How would you implement a feature flag for a bean? — @ConditionalOnProperty(name="feature.x.enabled", havingValue="true") on the @Bean or config; for runtime toggling inject a flag service instead, since conditions are startup-only.
  • @Profile vs @ConditionalOnProperty? — Profile: coarse environment switch, many beans at once; property: fine-grained, self-describing, testable with a single property override.
  • How do you debug "bean X was not created"? — --debug or /actuator/conditions shows the negative match and which condition failed, e.g. "@ConditionalOnClass did not find required class".
  • Can you combine conditions? — Stacking annotations is an AND; for OR/NOT extend AnyNestedCondition/NoneNestedConditions/AllNestedConditions.

@Lazy, @DependsOn, @Order vs @Priority

Why interviewers ask: quick checks that you know what controls creation order versus collection order; candidates routinely believe @Order affects startup.

Bean creation order is driven by dependencies: a bean is created when first needed, otherwise in definition registration order during preInstantiateSingletons. @DependsOn("flywayInitializer") forces an ordering where there is no injected dependency (e.g. a schema migration before a cache warmer). @Lazy on a bean defers creation to first use; on an injection point it injects a lazy-resolving proxy (used for cycles and expensive optional dependencies). spring.main.lazy-initialization=true makes everything lazy: faster startup, but errors move from boot time to first request, and Boot excludes some infrastructure via LazyInitializationExcludeFilter.

@Order(int) (Spring, lower = first, default LOWEST_PRECEDENCE) and @Priority(int) (jakarta.annotation) sort collections of beans, filters, interceptors, advisors and listeners; @Priority additionally acts as a tie-breaker in single-bean injection (a candidate with the highest priority wins), which @Order does not. Neither influences instantiation order.

@Component
@DependsOn("flywayInitializer")            // forces creation after the migration bean
class ReferenceDataCache { … }

@Component @Lazy                           // created on first getBean / first proxy call
class HeavyPdfRenderer { … }

@Component @Order(10) class AuthFilter implements Filter { … }   // runs before Order(20)
@Component @Order(20) class LogFilter  implements Filter { … }

@Component @Priority(1) class FastGateway implements Gateway { … } // wins single injection over unranked
AnnotationAffectsDoes not affect
@DependsOnCreation (and reverse destruction) orderInjection selection
@LazyWhen a bean/injection is resolvedScope
@OrderList/array injection, filters, aspects, listenersCreation order, single-bean choice
@PrioritySame as @Order + single-bean tie-breakCreation order
Interview questions
  • Does @Order change bean creation order? — No; it orders sorted collections and Spring-managed chains. Use dependencies or @DependsOn for creation order.
  • @Order vs @Priority? — Both sort; @Priority is the Jakarta standard and also breaks ties for single injection; @Order works on methods and @Beans too.
  • Downside of global lazy initialisation? — Misconfiguration surfaces on first request rather than at deploy; first-call latency; some beans (web endpoints, listeners) must be excluded.
  • What does @Lazy on a constructor parameter inject? — A CGLIB/JDK proxy that resolves the real bean on first method call; the class must be proxyable.
  • Why can @DependsOn be an anti-pattern? — It encodes a hidden dependency by string name; injecting the dependency directly is refactor-safe and expresses the same ordering.

ApplicationRunner / CommandLineRunner, startup hooks & graceful shutdown

Why interviewers ask: "where do you put code that must run once after startup?" and "what happens to in-flight requests on kill/pod termination?" are operational questions every senior is expected to answer precisely.

ApplicationRunner (run(ApplicationArguments): parsed --name=value options) and CommandLineRunner (run(String... rawArgs)) are beans invoked by SpringApplication.run after the context is refreshed and ApplicationStartedEvent, before ApplicationReadyEvent; all beans exist and are proxied, so @Transactional works here (unlike @PostConstruct). Order them with @Order. An exception in a runner aborts startup. For "run when traffic can be served" use an ApplicationReadyEvent listener; for "run before the context" use ApplicationContextInitializer or EnvironmentPostProcessor.

Shutdown: Boot registers a JVM shutdown hook; on SIGTERM it calls context.close(): ContextClosedEvent → SmartLifecycle.stop() in reverse phase order → @PreDestroy/destroy() on singletons → executor shutdown. With server.shutdown=graceful (Boot 2.3+) the web server first stops accepting new connections and waits up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase (default 30s) for in-flight requests; Kubernetes needs terminationGracePeriodSeconds above that and a preStop sleep to drain the Service endpoints. Analogy: graceful shutdown is closing the restaurant door but letting seated guests finish, with a hard "lights out" after 30 minutes.

@Component @Order(1)
class SchemaCheckRunner implements ApplicationRunner {
    @Override public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {
        if (args.containsOption("skip-checks")) return;   // --skip-checks
        schema.verify();                                  // throws → startup aborts, exit code 1
    }
}

@Component
class PollerLifecycle implements SmartLifecycle {          // long-running component
    private volatile boolean running;
    public void start() { running = true; poller.start(); }
    public void stop()  { running = false; poller.drain(); }  // called on SIGTERM before @PreDestroy
    public boolean isRunning() { return running; }
    public int getPhase() { return Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1; }  // stop early (before web server), start late
}
server:
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 20s
# k8s: terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30, lifecycle.preStop.exec: ["sleep","5"]

Pitfalls

  • kill -9 (SIGKILL) bypasses everything; only SIGTERM/SIGINT run hooks. Kubernetes sends SIGKILL after the grace period.
  • Runners run on the main thread; a runner that blocks forever (a manual message loop) means ApplicationReadyEvent and readiness probes never fire.
  • Custom thread pools not registered as beans (or created with new) are not shut down; tasks are lost. Declare them as beans so ThreadPoolTaskExecutor.destroy() runs; set waitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown.
  • Graceful shutdown covers the web server and SmartLifecycle beans; @Scheduled tasks and Kafka listeners stop via their own lifecycle phases, order matters.
Interview questions
  • CommandLineRunner vs ApplicationRunner? — Same timing; ApplicationRunner receives parsed ApplicationArguments (options vs non-option args), CommandLineRunner the raw strings. Prefer ApplicationRunner.
  • @PostConstruct vs runner vs ApplicationReadyEvent? — @PostConstruct: per bean, before proxies, other beans may not exist. Runner: all beans ready, before "ready". ApplicationReadyEvent: after runners, app is serving; best for warm-ups that may fail without aborting startup.
  • What happens to an in-flight request during a rolling deploy? — Without graceful shutdown the connection is cut; with server.shutdown=graceful Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow/Netty stop accepting and wait up to the phase timeout for active requests to finish.
  • How do you return a specific exit code? — Implement ExitCodeGenerator or throw an exception implementing it, and call System.exit(SpringApplication.exit(ctx)).
  • In what order do things stop? — ContextClosedEvent, then SmartLifecycle.stop() highest phase first (web server is among the first to stop accepting), then @PreDestroy/DisposableBean in reverse creation order, then executors.
  • How do readiness/liveness probes tie in? — Boot 2.3+ exposes /actuator/health/readiness and /liveness; readiness flips to REFUSING_TRAFFIC as soon as shutdown begins so the load balancer drains before requests are cut.

@Bean method orderRepo() inside a plain @Component class calls this.dataSource() (another @Bean method in the same class). How many DataSource objects exist after startup?

b. A @Component with @Bean methods is lite mode: no CGLIB subclass, so this.dataSource() is an ordinary Java call and creates an unmanaged second instance. a is true only in full-mode @Configuration. c is wrong: lite-mode @Beans are registered. d needs two definitions with the same name.

A @Service has a field-injected @Autowired Repo repo; and calls repo.count() inside its constructor. Result?

c. Lifecycle order is instantiate → populate; a field cannot be written before the object exists, so it is null in the constructor. d only happens with an explicit @Lazy. This is one of the strongest arguments for constructor injection.

Which is the correct order of initialisation callbacks on one bean?

a. Annotation, then interface, then configured method, all inside initializeBean, and only afterwards do BPPs get the after-init callback (where AOP proxies are created). c would mean the proxy exists during @PostConstruct, which is exactly what does not happen.

A @Transactional method of the same bean is called from its @PostConstruct method. What happens?

d. Two reasons, either sufficient: the auto-proxy creator runs in postProcessAfterInitialization (after @PostConstruct), and even later, this.method() never goes through the proxy. Use an ApplicationRunner or a TransactionTemplate.

Where is @Autowired actually processed?

b. It is an InstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor whose postProcessProperties reflectively writes fields/setters. c is a BeanFactoryPostProcessor: it works on definitions and never touches instances. Knowing this explains why a BPP's own dependencies can miss injection features.

Boot 3.2, default settings. A has @Autowired B b; (field) and B has @Autowired A a; (field). What happens at startup?

c. The framework can resolve this (option a describes pre-2.6 behaviour and what happens with the flag set to true), but Boot now prohibits it by default and the FailureAnalyzer prints the cycle. Spring never leaves a required dependency null (d).

Why does constructor-injection A(B) / B(A) fail even when circular references are allowed?

a. The three-level cache needs an object to hand out; with constructors there is none until the constructor returns, which needs the partner, which needs this bean → BeanCurrentlyInCreationException. c confuses BFPP with BPP. @Lazy on one parameter works because a proxy stands in for the not-yet-created bean.

Three beans of type Gateway: stripe (@Order(1)), adyen (@Primary), legacy (@Qualifier("legacy")). A constructor parameter is declared Gateway stripe with no annotation. Which is injected?

d. Resolution: type → qualifier → primary → priority → name. A primary candidate exists, so the name fallback (a) is never reached. @Order (b) sorts collections and never picks a single bean. c would occur with no primary and a non-matching name.

An @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) method annotated @Transactional saves an audit row. The row never appears, no exception. Why?

b. The listener runs on the publishing thread while the completed transaction's synchronisation is still active; a REQUIRED tx silently participates and its work is lost. a is wrong (same thread unless @Async); d would mean the listener never ran at all, but here it did.

Which is the highest-precedence source among these for server.port?

c. Command-line args outrank system properties (d), which outrank environment variables (b), which outrank every application*.yml (a). Only test-level sources (@TestPropertySource) and devtools go higher.

Practice

Scenario: which bean gets injected, and what fails?

For each of the four injection points, state the outcome (which bean or which exception) on Spring Boot 3 with default settings.

interface Notifier { void send(String m); }

@Component("emailNotifier") @Priority(5)          class EmailNotifier implements Notifier { … }
@Component                 @Primary                class SmsNotifier   implements Notifier { … }
@Component                 @Qualifier("push")      class PushNotifier  implements Notifier { … }
@Component                 @Primary                class SlackNotifier implements Notifier { … }

@Service
class AlertService {
    AlertService(Notifier n1,                          // (1)
                 @Qualifier("push") Notifier n2,       // (2)
                 Notifier emailNotifier,               // (3)
                 List<Notifier> all,                   // (4) what order?
                 ObjectProvider<Notifier> provider) {}
}
Tests: resolution order, multiple primaries, collection ordering
Hint 1
Count how many beans carry @Primary. What does determinePrimaryCandidate do when it finds more than one?
Hint 2
Injection point (2) filters by qualifier before primaries are considered. But does the container even get to construct AlertService?
Reveal solution

The context fails to start. Injection point (1) has four type candidates, no qualifier, and two primaries → NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException: more than one 'primary' bean found among candidates [emailNotifier, smsNotifier, pushNotifier, slackNotifier]. Constructor injection is all-or-nothing, so AlertService is never created; Boot's failure analyzer reports the parameter index.

If you remove @Primary from SlackNotifier:

  • (1) → SmsNotifier (single primary).
  • (2) → PushNotifier: the qualifier narrows to one candidate; primaries are irrelevant.
  • (3) → SmsNotifier, not EmailNotifier: the primary is chosen at step 4, the parameter-name fallback at step 6 is never reached. (With no primary at all, @Priority(5) on EmailNotifier would win at step 5, again before the name.)
  • (4) → all four, sorted: @Priority(5) first is not guaranteed to be first overall; AnnotationAwareOrderComparator treats unannotated beans as LOWEST_PRECEDENCE, so EmailNotifier comes first and the other three follow in registration (scan) order.
  • provider.getIfUnique() returns SmsNotifier (primary counts as unique); provider.orderedStream() gives the same order as (4).

Debug: @PostConstruct runs twice and the cache warms twice

Logs show warming catalog cache… twice at startup and two HikariPool-1/HikariPool-2 pools. Nothing is annotated prototype. Find every cause and fix it.

@SpringBootApplication
@ComponentScan({"com.acme", "com.acme.catalog"})
public class App { public static void main(String[] a) { SpringApplication.run(App.class, a); } }

@Component
public class CatalogCache {
    @PostConstruct void warm() { log.info("warming catalog cache…"); load(); }
}

@Configuration
public class DataConfig {
    @Bean DataSource dataSource() { return new HikariDataSource(); }
    @Bean JdbcTemplate jdbc() { return new JdbcTemplate(dataSource()); }
    @Bean CatalogCache catalogCache() { return new CatalogCache(); }
}
Tests: definition registration, bean overriding rules, context hierarchy, full-mode configs
Hint 1
Boot refuses bean-definition overriding by default; so how can two CatalogCache beans exist? Look at the names, not the types.
Hint 2
DataConfig is full-mode, so dataSource() from jdbc() is fine. Where else might a second context or a second definition come from: tests? @SpringBootTest + @WebMvcTest in the same run? A DevTools restart?
Reveal solution

Cause 1: two definitions with different names. Scanning registers CatalogCache as bean catalogCache; the @Bean method also registers catalogCache… same name, so Boot would throw BeanDefinitionOverrideException, unless spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding=true is set (check application.yml). If the @Bean were named differently (e.g. catalog()), you would get two silent singletons of the same class, each running @PostConstruct once. Fix: register the class one way, not both (drop the @Bean or the @Component).

Cause 2: overlapping scan packages is not a cause: com.acme.catalog is inside com.acme; Spring de-duplicates by bean name, so the double @ComponentScan is redundant but harmless. Remove it anyway (@SpringBootApplication already scans its package).

Cause 3 (two Hikari pools): if the app also has a test or a Spring Cloud bootstrap context, each ApplicationContext builds its own singletons: two contexts → two pools and two warm-ups. Confirm by logging context.getId() or checking for a parent via ctx.getParent(). DevTools restart also produces a second pool in the log until the first context closes.

Robust fix: keep one registration path per class; make the warm-up idempotent and move it to an ApplicationReadyEvent listener (it can then use transactional/cached beans safely); and set spring.datasource.hikari.pool-name so duplicate pools are obvious in metrics.

Scenario: "prototype" bean is not fresh under load

Under concurrent requests, report data from one user leaks into another's PDF. ReportBuilder is @Scope("prototype"). Explain and give two fixes, stating which you would choose.

@Component @Scope("prototype")
class ReportBuilder { private final List<Row> rows = new ArrayList<>(); … }

@RestController
class ReportController {
    private final ReportBuilder builder;               // injected once
    ReportController(ReportBuilder builder) { this.builder = builder; }

    @GetMapping("/report") byte[] report(@RequestParam long userId) {
        builder.reset();
        builder.addAll(repo.rowsFor(userId));
        return builder.render();
    }
}
Tests: prototype-in-singleton, ObjectProvider, scoped proxies, thread safety
Hint 1
When exactly is builder resolved, and how many times?
Reveal solution

The controller is a singleton; its constructor ran once at startup, so the container produced one prototype instance then and never again. All requests share it → concurrent reset()/addAll() interleave and rows leak between users.

Fix 1 (preferred): inject ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder> and call getObject() per request. Explicit, no proxies, works in unit tests with a lambda.

private final ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder> builders;
@GetMapping("/report") byte[] report(@RequestParam long userId) {
    ReportBuilder b = builders.getObject();      // new instance per request
    b.addAll(repo.rowsFor(userId));
    return b.render();
}

Fix 2: @Scope(value = "prototype", proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS): the controller holds a proxy and every method call goes to a brand-new instance — which is worse here, because addAll and render would hit different instances. A request-scoped proxy would work (one instance per request), but couples the builder to the web layer. Fix 3: stop making it a bean: new ReportBuilder() per request is the simplest correct code when the builder has no injected dependencies.

Fix the design: circular dependency at startup, without @Lazy or the global flag

Startup fails: "The dependencies of some of the beans in the application context form a cycle: orderService ↔ inventoryService". Both use constructor injection. Propose a fix that keeps constructor injection, keeps the flag at its default, and does not use @Lazy. Explain what the three-level cache would have done if these were field-injected on Boot 2.5.

@Service
class OrderService {
    private final InventoryService inventory;
    OrderService(InventoryService inventory) { this.inventory = inventory; }
    void place(Order o) { inventory.reserve(o.items()); repo.save(o); }
    void cancel(long id) { … }
}

@Service
class InventoryService {
    private final OrderService orders;
    InventoryService(OrderService orders) { this.orders = orders; }
    void reserve(List<Item> items) { … }
    void onStockOut(String sku) { orders.cancelAllFor(sku); }   // the back-edge
}
Tests: dependency inversion, events, ObjectProvider, three-level cache reasoning
Hint 1
Which of the two edges is the "real" dependency and which is a notification? A notification does not need a reference to its consumer.
Hint 2
Two structural options: publish an event for the back-edge, or extract the shared piece so both depend on a third bean. A third, lighter option keeps the reference but resolves it on demand.
Reveal solution

Diagnosis: OrderService → InventoryService is a genuine call dependency; InventoryService → OrderService exists only to notify about stock-outs. Cycles caused by a "call-back" edge are the common case and should be replaced by an event or a callback interface.

Fix A (events, preferred): InventoryService publishes StockOut(sku); OrderService listens. No reference from inventory to orders, and the cancellation can be made AFTER_COMMIT.

@Service
class InventoryService {
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;
    InventoryService(ApplicationEventPublisher events) { this.events = events; }
    void onStockOut(String sku) { events.publishEvent(new StockOut(sku)); }
}

@Service
class OrderService {
    OrderService(InventoryService inventory) { … }          // one direction only
    @EventListener void on(StockOut e) { cancelAllFor(e.sku()); }
}

Fix B (dependency inversion): define interface StockOutHandler { void stockOut(String sku); } in the inventory package; OrderService implements StockOutHandler; InventoryService depends on List<StockOutHandler>. The graph is now Orders → Inventory → (interface) with Orders implementing the interface: no cycle, and multiple handlers plug in.

Fix C (tactical): InventoryService(ObjectProvider<OrderService> orders) and orders.getObject().cancelAllFor(sku). The cycle disappears because the provider is resolved lazily; keeps constructor injection but leaves the design smell in place.

Why field injection "worked" on 2.5: Spring instantiates OrderService (raw), stores an ObjectFactory in singletonFactories, and while populating it creates InventoryService, whose population asks for orderService; the lookup misses L1/L2, hits L3, and hands out the early (unpopulated) OrderService, promoting it to earlySingletonObjects. Both finish and move to singletonObjects. If OrderService were @Transactional, the L3 factory would create the proxy early so InventoryService holds the proxy. Boot 2.6 turned this off because the "works by accident" ordering silently breaks with @Async or custom BPPs, and because it hides design cycles like this one.

⚡ Rapid-fire: IoC container & bean lifecycle

  • IoC vs DI? — IoC is the principle (the container drives object creation and wiring); DI is the mechanism (constructor/setter/field injection).
  • Default bean scope? — Singleton, eager, one per ApplicationContext.
  • Is a Spring singleton the GoF singleton? — No; one per container, not per JVM, and not enforced by the class.
  • Why constructor injection? — Immutability, mandatory dependencies, testability with new, cycles fail fast.
  • Is @Autowired needed on a single constructor? — Not since Spring 4.3.
  • @Autowired vs @Resource? — Type-first vs name-first; different post-processors.
  • Two candidates, no qualifier: what happens? — NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException unless @Primary, @Priority or a matching parameter name resolves it.
  • @Qualifier vs @Primary: which wins? — @Qualifier.
  • How to inject all implementations? — List<T>/Map<String,T>/ObjectProvider<T>.stream(); order with @Order.
  • @Component vs @Bean? — Class marker for scanning vs factory method for objects you construct (third-party types).
  • What does @Configuration add over @Component? — CGLIB "full mode": inter-bean method calls return the singleton.
  • proxyBeanMethods=false? — Lite mode: no subclass, faster startup, pass dependencies as parameters.
  • Bean lifecycle in one breath? — Definition → instantiate → populate → Aware → BPP-before → @PostConstruct → afterPropertiesSet → init-method → BPP-after (proxy) → ready → @PreDestroy → destroy → destroy-method.
  • Where is the AOP proxy created? — postProcessAfterInitialization of the auto-proxy creator (a BeanPostProcessor).
  • BFPP vs BPP? — Definitions before instantiation vs instances around initialisation.
  • Which BPP handles @Autowired? @PostConstruct? — AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor; CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor.
  • Does @Transactional work inside @PostConstruct? — No: no proxy yet, and self-invocation.
  • Are prototype beans destroyed by Spring? — No; @PreDestroy is never called for them.
  • Prototype injected into singleton gives the same instance. Fix? — ObjectProvider.getObject(), scoped proxy, or @Lookup.
  • Request-scoped bean in a singleton? — proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS scoped proxy.
  • Circular dependency with constructors? — BeanCurrentlyInCreationException; with fields it is resolvable but Boot 2.6+ forbids it by default.
  • Three-level cache names? — singletonObjects, earlySingletonObjects, singletonFactories.
  • What does @Lazy on a parameter inject? — A proxy that resolves the bean on first call.
  • BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext? — Bare registry vs registry + eager init, BPP auto-detection, events, Environment, i18n.
  • Where does component scanning happen? — invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors → ConfigurationClassPostProcessor, inside refresh().
  • Are Spring events synchronous? — Yes by default; @Async or an executor on the multicaster makes them async.
  • @TransactionalEventListener default phase? — AFTER_COMMIT; dropped outside a transaction unless fallbackExecution=true.
