  • Property precedence, top three? — Command line > system properties > environment variables (then profile files, then application.yml).
  • @Value vs @ConfigurationProperties? — Single value with SpEL vs typed, validated, relaxed-bound tree.
  • When are @Conditionals evaluated? — Once, at definition parsing; never at runtime.
  • Does @Order control bean creation order? — No; use dependencies or @DependsOn.
  • Runner vs @PostConstruct? — Runners run after all beans are ready and proxied, before ApplicationReadyEvent.
  • Enable graceful shutdown? — server.shutdown=graceful + spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase.
  • Boot 2 → 3 namespace change? — javax.* → jakarta.* for annotations, validation, persistence, servlet; Java 17 baseline.

2️⃣ Auto-configuration & Boot Internals

Spring Boot is "Spring with opinions": starters pick your dependencies, auto-configuration builds the beans you did not write, and an embedded server turns the project into one runnable jar. Interviewers use this section to check that you can explain why a bean appeared or disappeared, which property value actually won, and what changed between Boot 2 and 3. The path runs from what Boot adds, through the startup sequence and the conditions engine, to configuration precedence, servers, Actuator, packaging, testing and migration.

What Boot adds over Spring & what @SpringBootApplication really is

Why interviewers ask: the opening question of almost every Spring interview. They want four concrete things (defaults, starters, embedded server, executable jar), not "it makes Spring easy", and they want you to decompose the one annotation everybody copies.

Spring Framework gives you the container, AOP, MVC, transactions; it gives you no opinion on which beans to create or how to run. Spring Boot layers four things on top: opinionated defaults (a DataSource, a DispatcherServlet, Jackson, a thread pool, all configured to sane values and overridable by properties), starters (curated dependency bundles with tested versions), an embedded server (Tomcat by default, so there is no WAR and no external container) and production plumbing (Actuator, metrics, externalized config, executable "fat" jar). Analogy: Spring is a well-stocked kitchen; Boot is the chef who has already prepped everything so you only cook the part that is yours.

@SpringBootApplication is nothing more than three meta-annotations: @SpringBootConfiguration (a @Configuration that test slices can locate with @SpringBootTest), @EnableAutoConfiguration (imports AutoConfigurationImportSelector, the whole magic) and @ComponentScan with two filters that exclude TypeExcludeFilter'd types and other auto-configuration classes. Because scanning starts at the annotated class's package, putting the main class in the root package is the single most important layout rule.

// What you write
@SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = "com.acme", exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)
public class App {
    public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(App.class, args); }
}

// What it means (Boot 3.x source, trimmed)
@SpringBootConfiguration                    // = @Configuration (+ marker for @SpringBootTest search)
@EnableAutoConfiguration                    // @Import(AutoConfigurationImportSelector.class)
@ComponentScan(excludeFilters = { @Filter(type = CUSTOM, classes = TypeExcludeFilter.class),
                                  @Filter(type = CUSTOM, classes = AutoConfigurationExcludeFilter.class) })
public @interface SpringBootApplication { … }
Interview angle: "Can I use Spring Boot without @SpringBootApplication?" Yes: put @Configuration @EnableAutoConfiguration @ComponentScan on any class, or even skip auto-configuration and only use SpringApplication for the runner/banner/embedded-server plumbing. "Does Boot generate code?" No (except AOT/native): everything is ordinary @Configuration classes evaluated at runtime.
Spring FrameworkSpring Boot
Bean setYou declare every beanAuto-configured, backs off when you declare your own
DependenciesPick and version each jarStarters + BOM pin ~500 versions
DeploymentWAR into Tomcat/Jettyjava -jar app.jar with embedded server (WAR still possible)
Configuration@PropertySource, XMLLayered Environment: yml, env vars, args, cloud config
OpsDIYActuator health/metrics/probes, graceful shutdown

Pitfalls

  • Main class in com.acme.app.boot while controllers live in com.acme.web: nothing is scanned, no error, just 404s. Fix with scanBasePackages or move the class up.
  • @ComponentScan declared explicitly on the main class replaces the one inside @SpringBootApplication, dropping the exclude filters, so @WebMvcTest slices start pulling in everything.
  • Two @SpringBootApplication classes on the test classpath (e.g. one in src/test) make @SpringBootTest pick the wrong one or fail with "Found multiple @SpringBootConfiguration".
Interview questions
  • What does Spring Boot add over Spring, concretely? — Opinionated auto-configuration that backs off to user beans, starters with a curated BOM, an embedded servlet/reactive server, an executable jar layout and production features (Actuator, externalized config, graceful shutdown).
  • Decompose @SpringBootApplication. — @SpringBootConfiguration (a @Configuration), @EnableAutoConfiguration (imports AutoConfigurationImportSelector) and @ComponentScan rooted at the class's package with filters that keep auto-config classes out of the scan.
  • Why must the main class sit in the root package? — Component scan and JPA entity/repository scanning default to that package; beans in sibling packages are silently missed.
  • Is Boot's DI container different from Spring's? — No; it is the same DefaultListableBeanFactory and refresh(). Boot only adds bean definitions and an Environment around it.
  • How do you switch off one piece of auto-configuration? — exclude/excludeName on the annotation, or spring.autoconfigure.exclude in properties; declaring your own bean of that type is usually enough because of @ConditionalOnMissingBean.
  • Boot 2 vs 3 for this annotation? — Unchanged; what changed underneath is the registration file (AutoConfiguration.imports instead of spring.factories), Jakarta namespaces and the Java 17 baseline.

Starters & dependency management: parent POM vs BOM import, overriding versions

Why interviewers ask: version conflicts are the most common real-world build problem; they check that you know where the versions come from and the two correct ways to override one.

A starter (spring-boot-starter-web, -data-jpa, -actuator, -test…) is an almost-empty jar whose only job is a POM with transitive dependencies; -web pulls spring-webmvc, Jackson, validation hooks and spring-boot-starter-tomcat. Starters carry no version numbers: every version comes from the spring-boot-dependencies BOM, which pins roughly 500 artifacts that the Boot team tested together.

You reach the BOM in one of two ways. spring-boot-starter-parent as your Maven parent: you inherit the BOM, plus Java 17 compiler settings, UTF-8, resource filtering with @..@ placeholders and the spring-boot-maven-plugin config; versions are exposed as properties (<jackson-bom.version>) that a child can override with one line. dependencyManagement import (scope import, type pom) when you already have a corporate parent: same version pins, but property overrides do not work; you must declare the artifact before the Boot BOM in your own dependencyManagement. Gradle uses the io.spring.dependency-management plugin or Gradle's native platform(...) with the same BOM.

<!-- Option A: parent (properties override works) -->
<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>3.3.2</version>
</parent>
<properties><mysql.version>8.4.0</mysql.version></properties>

<!-- Option B: import the BOM (own parent); override by declaring FIRST -->
<dependencyManagement><dependencies>
  <dependency><groupId>com.mysql</groupId><artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId><version>8.4.0</version></dependency>
  <dependency><groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId><artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
              <version>3.3.2</version><type>pom</type><scope>import</scope></dependency>
</dependencies></dependencyManagement>

<!-- Swap the server: exclude Tomcat, add Jetty -->
<dependency><groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId><artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
  <exclusions><exclusion><groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId><artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId></exclusion></exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency><groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId><artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jetty</artifactId></dependency>
Real world: "we need Jackson 2.17.x for a CVE but Boot 3.2 pins 2.15" → with the parent, set <jackson-bom.version>; with BOM import, add the jackson-bom to dependencyManagement above the Boot BOM. Then run mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core to prove it. Overriding a Spring-managed version is "supported but untested"; note it in the PR.

Pitfalls

  • Adding <version> directly on a starter dependency silently overrides the BOM for that one artifact only and often leaves its siblings mismatched (e.g. spring-web 6.1 with spring-core 6.0).
  • Two starters that bring two servers (-web + -jetty without excluding Tomcat) still boot, with Tomcat, because Boot's ServletWebServerFactory conditions pick the first found; the surprise is only visible in the conditions report.
  • Test scope leakage: putting h2 in compile scope makes DataSourceAutoConfiguration pick an in-memory DB in production when no URL is set.
Interview questions
  • What is inside a starter jar? — Practically nothing; it is a POM of transitive dependencies with no versions. The versions come from spring-boot-dependencies.
  • spring-boot-starter-parent vs importing the BOM? — Parent gives BOM + plugin config + compiler settings + version properties; BOM import gives only the version pins and is used when you already have a corporate parent.
  • How do you override a managed version with a BOM import? — Declare the artifact (or its own BOM) in dependencyManagement before the Boot BOM import; properties like jackson-bom.version only work with the parent.
  • How would you debug a NoSuchMethodError after adding a library? — mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose (or gradle dependencyInsight) to find the conflicting transitive version; fix with the BOM/exclusion, never by copying a random version.
  • Why does Boot ship spring-boot-starter-logging with Logback and how do you switch to Log4j2? — Logging is a starter too; exclude -logging from every starter (or globally in Gradle) and add -log4j2, otherwise both bindings are on the classpath.
  • Should a company build its own starter? — Yes for cross-cutting concerns (tracing headers, security defaults, a client library); it is the same autoconfigure+starter split Boot itself uses (see custom starters).

SpringApplication.run(): the startup sequence step by step

Why interviewers ask: "walk me through what happens when I run main" is the canonical senior Spring question. The answer separates people who know the order (Environment before context, initializers before refresh, runners after) from people who say "it scans and starts Tomcat".

SpringApplication is a plain Java object. Its constructor already does work: it deduces the WebApplicationType (SERVLET if DispatcherServlet is on the classpath, REACTIVE if only DispatcherHandler, NONE otherwise), loads BootstrapRegistryInitializers, ApplicationContextInitializers and ApplicationListeners from META-INF/spring.factories (still used for these in Boot 3, only auto-configs moved) and finds the main class from the stack trace.

run() then executes a fixed script: start the StartupStep timer → create the BootstrapContext → get the SpringApplicationRunListeners (EventPublishingRunListener) and fire ApplicationStartingEvent → build and prepare the Environment (property sources, profiles; fires ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent, which is where ConfigDataEnvironmentPostProcessor loads application.yml) → print the banner → instantiate the context class (AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext) → prepareContext: apply initializers, fire ApplicationContextInitializedEvent, register the primary source as a bean definition, fire ApplicationPreparedEvent → refresh() (everything from section 1: BFPPs, auto-configuration parsing, singletons, and for a servlet app onRefresh() creates and starts Tomcat) → fire ApplicationStartedEvent → call ApplicationRunner/CommandLineRunner beans → fire ApplicationReadyEvent. Any exception is routed through FailureAnalyzers (the "APPLICATION FAILED TO START / Description / Action" block), ApplicationFailedEvent is fired, and the context is closed.

Analogy: a theatre opening night. The stage manager reads the house rules (Environment), the set is built (context + refresh), the doors open (server started), the pre-show announcements run (runners), and only then is the show declared "ready". Note where ApplicationListeners registered via spring.factories differ from @EventListener beans: the former see the early events (Starting, EnvironmentPrepared), the latter exist only after refresh and see Started/Ready.

public ConfigurableApplicationContext run(String... args) {
    Startup startup = Startup.create();
    DefaultBootstrapContext bootstrapContext = createBootstrapContext();
    ConfigurableApplicationContext context = null;
    SpringApplicationRunListeners listeners = getRunListeners(args);
    listeners.starting(bootstrapContext, this.mainApplicationClass);   // ApplicationStartingEvent
    try {
        ApplicationArguments appArgs = new DefaultApplicationArguments(args);
        ConfigurableEnvironment env = prepareEnvironment(listeners, bootstrapContext, appArgs);
        Banner printedBanner = printBanner(env);
        context = createApplicationContext();                            // servlet/reactive/none
        prepareContext(bootstrapContext, context, env, listeners, appArgs, printedBanner);
        refreshContext(context);                                         // AbstractApplicationContext.refresh()
        afterRefresh(context, appArgs);
        startup.started();
        listeners.started(context, startup.timeTakenToStarted());        // ApplicationStartedEvent
        callRunners(context, appArgs);                                   // ApplicationRunner / CommandLineRunner
    } catch (Throwable ex) {
        throw handleRunFailure(context, ex, listeners);                  // FailureAnalyzers + ApplicationFailedEvent
    }
    listeners.ready(context, startup.ready());                           // ApplicationReadyEvent
    return context;
}
  1. Constructor work is done (web type deduced, initializers/listeners loaded). starting() publishes ApplicationStartingEvent to spring.factories listeners only.
  2. prepareEnvironment builds the property-source stack and fires ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent; the config-data listener adds application*.yml, spring.config.import sources and activates profiles. The context does not exist yet, so @Value cannot see any of this.
  3. Banner, then the context object is instantiated by ApplicationContextFactory. It is empty: no definitions, no beans.
  4. prepareContext: environment attached, ApplicationContextInitializers run (this is the hook Spring Cloud uses for bootstrap), singletons like springApplicationArguments are registered, and the main class becomes the first bean definition.
  5. refresh(): BFPPs parse the main class, component scan and the auto-configuration import selector fill the definition registry, then onRefresh() creates the embedded WebServer, singletons are instantiated and finishRefresh() starts the server and publishes ContextRefreshedEvent.
  6. ApplicationStartedEvent is published (all @EventListener beans now exist), then runners execute in @Order. Tomcat is already accepting connections here.
  7. On any throwable, FailureAnalyzers try to turn the exception into a human explanation (Description/Action), ApplicationFailedEvent fires, the context is closed and the JVM exits with code 1 (or an ExitCodeGenerator value).
  8. ApplicationReadyEvent is the last event: context refreshed, server up, runners done. Kubernetes readiness (via Actuator) turns green only now, which is why long warm-ups belong in a runner or a listener of this event.
// Programmatic customisation instead of static run()
new SpringApplicationBuilder(App.class)
        .web(WebApplicationType.SERVLET)
        .bannerMode(Banner.Mode.OFF)
        .lazyInitialization(true)
        .initializers(ctx -> ctx.getEnvironment().getPropertySources()
                .addFirst(new MapPropertySource("override", Map.of("server.port", 9090))))
        .listeners((ApplicationListener<ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent>) e ->
                System.out.println("profiles=" + Arrays.toString(e.getEnvironment().getActiveProfiles())))
        .run(args);

// A FailureAnalyzer for your own exception type
class QuotaFailureAnalyzer extends AbstractFailureAnalyzer<QuotaExceededException> {
    protected FailureAnalysis analyze(Throwable root, QuotaExceededException cause) {
        return new FailureAnalysis("License quota exceeded: " + cause.getMessage(),
                                   "Set license.key or reduce worker.count", cause);
    }   // register in META-INF/spring.factories under org.springframework.boot.diagnostics.FailureAnalyzer
}
Interview angle: "My @EventListener(ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent.class) never fires." Correct: that event is published before the context exists, so no bean can listen; register the listener in spring.factories, via SpringApplicationBuilder.listeners(), or use an EnvironmentPostProcessor. "Why does server.port set in an ApplicationContextInitializer work but the same in a @PostConstruct not?" The port is read when Tomcat is created inside onRefresh(), before any singleton's @PostConstruct.

Pitfalls

  • Blocking work in a CommandLineRunner delays ApplicationReadyEvent and thus the readiness probe; a runner that throws kills the app after Tomcat already bound the port.
  • ContextRefreshedEvent fires before runners and before ApplicationStartedEvent; in a context hierarchy it fires once per context.
  • SpringApplication.run() returns the context; tests or CLIs that ignore it and call System.exit skip the graceful shutdown that SpringApplication.exit(ctx) would do.
  • The banner is printed before the context exists, so banner.txt can use ${application.version} from the manifest but not bean data.
Interview questions
  • Order the events: Starting, EnvironmentPrepared, ContextInitialized, Prepared, ContextRefreshed, Started, Ready, Failed. — Exactly that order; the first four are pre-refresh (only spring.factories/builder listeners hear them), ContextRefreshedEvent is Spring's, Started fires after refresh, Ready after runners, Failed on any exception.
  • Where does Tomcat actually start? — Created in ServletWebServerApplicationContext.onRefresh() (during refresh()), started in finishRefresh() through the WebServerStartStopLifecycle, i.e. before runners run.
  • How does Boot decide between servlet, reactive and none? — WebApplicationType.deduceFromClasspath(): reactive if DispatcherHandler present and no DispatcherServlet/Jersey; servlet if Servlet + ConfigurableWebApplicationContext; else none. Override with spring.main.web-application-type.
  • What is an ApplicationContextInitializer and when would you write one? — A callback invoked on the context after creation but before refresh; used to add property sources, set the id, or register definitions programmatically (Spring Cloud's bootstrap and Testcontainers' ConfigDataApplicationContextInitializer use it).
  • ApplicationRunner vs CommandLineRunner vs @PostConstruct for a warm-up? — Runners run after the whole context is ready and proxied and before Ready; @PostConstruct runs mid-refresh on a single bean with no guarantee other beans exist. ApplicationRunner gives parsed --option=value args.
  • Where does "APPLICATION FAILED TO START" come from? — FailureAnalyzers in handleRunFailure; each analyzer matches a root cause type (PortInUseException, BindException, NoSuchBeanDefinitionException) and prints Description + Action instead of a 200-line stack trace.
  • How would you make the app exit with a custom code? — Expose an ExitCodeGenerator bean or throw an exception implementing ExitCodeGenerator; call System.exit(SpringApplication.exit(ctx)).
  • Boot 2 vs 3 differences in startup? — Boot 2.4 introduced BootstrapContext and config-data processing; Boot 3 adds AOT-optimised startup (-Dspring.aot.enabled=true) that skips configuration parsing entirely and uses pre-generated bean definitions.

How auto-configuration works: import selector, AutoConfiguration.imports, filtering, ordering, exclusions

Why interviewers ask: "how does Boot know to create a DataSource?" is the follow-up to every "what is Boot" answer. A strong answer names the selector, the imports file, the two-phase filtering and why auto-configs are always parsed after user configuration.

@EnableAutoConfiguration is @Import(AutoConfigurationImportSelector.class). The selector is a DeferredImportSelector: ConfigurationClassParser processes all your @Configuration, @ComponentScan and @Imports first and only then asks deferred selectors for their imports. That single design choice is what lets auto-configurations "back off": by the time @ConditionalOnMissingBean runs, every user bean definition is already registered.

Candidates come from META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports, one fully qualified class per line, loaded by ImportCandidates.load() from every jar on the classpath (Boot 2.7 introduced the file; Boot 3.0 removed spring.factories support for the EnableAutoConfiguration key; spring.factories still works for listeners, initializers, failure analyzers). The selector then: removes duplicates → removes exclusions (exclude=, excludeName=, spring.autoconfigure.exclude) → applies AutoConfigurationImportFilters (OnClassCondition, OnWebApplicationCondition, OnBeanCondition) using the pre-computed META-INF/spring-autoconfigure-metadata.properties so that ~150 classes are discarded without loading them → fires AutoConfigurationImportEvent → sorts the survivors with AutoConfigurationSorter (alphabetical, then @AutoConfigureOrder, then @AutoConfigureBefore/After as a topological sort). Finally each class is parsed as a normal @Configuration, evaluating class- and method-level conditions in REGISTER_BEAN phase.

Analogy: a buffet where the chef waits until every guest has served themselves, then fills only the dishes that are still empty.

# src/main/resources/META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports
com.acme.fooclient.autoconfigure.FooClientAutoConfiguration
com.acme.fooclient.autoconfigure.FooClientMetricsAutoConfiguration

# properties: turn one off without touching code
spring.autoconfigure.exclude=org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration

# --debug output (ConditionEvaluationReport), trimmed
Positive matches:
   DataSourceAutoConfiguration matched:
      - @ConditionalOnClass found required classes 'javax.sql.DataSource', 'EmbeddedDatabaseType'
Negative matches:
   DataSourceAutoConfiguration.PooledDataSourceConfiguration:
      Did not match:
         - @ConditionalOnMissingBean (types: javax.sql.DataSource) found beans of type 'javax.sql.DataSource' myDs
Interview angle: "Why can I not use @ConditionalOnMissingBean reliably in my own @Configuration?" Because user configs are parsed in an undefined order among themselves; the only guarantee is user-before-auto. "Why are auto-config classes excluded from component scanning?" So that they are registered only via the selector, keeping their deferred ordering; scanning one would parse it too early and its bean conditions would see an empty registry.

Pitfalls

  • Using @Import(SomeAutoConfiguration.class) or @ComponentScan over an auto-config package makes it a user config: it loses deferred ordering and its @ConditionalOnMissingBeans can fire before your beans exist.
  • @AutoConfigureAfter orders only among auto-configurations; it does nothing relative to user configuration.
  • Boot 3 ignores the EnableAutoConfiguration key in spring.factories: an internal Boot 2 starter silently stops contributing beans after the upgrade.
  • Excluding a class that is not an auto-configuration throws at startup ("The following classes could not be excluded because they are not auto-configuration classes").
Interview questions
  • Where does Boot 3 discover auto-configurations? — META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports in every jar, one class per line, loaded via ImportCandidates; spring.factories is no longer consulted for that key.
  • Why does user configuration always win? — AutoConfigurationImportSelector is a DeferredImportSelector, processed after all non-deferred configuration, so bean-presence conditions see the user's definitions.
  • What is spring-autoconfigure-metadata.properties for? — Generated by the spring-boot-autoconfigure-processor; it records class-level conditions so the selector can reject candidates by string comparison before loading the class, cutting startup time.
  • Three ways to disable an auto-configuration? — exclude/excludeName on @SpringBootApplication/@EnableAutoConfiguration, spring.autoconfigure.exclude, or making its condition fail (your own bean, missing class, property).
  • How do @AutoConfigureBefore, After and Order interact? — Sorter first orders alphabetically, then by @AutoConfigureOrder (lower first), then applies Before/After constraints as a topological sort; a cycle fails startup.
  • How would you debug "my bean was replaced by Boot's"? — Run with --debug or open /actuator/conditions, search for the auto-config class, read its positive match, then check whether your bean type/name really matched the @ConditionalOnMissingBean attributes.
  • What phase are auto-config conditions evaluated in? — Class-level @ConditionalOnClass/OnWebApplication as import filters (early); everything else in ConfigurationPhase.REGISTER_BEAN during class parsing; none at runtime.
  • Boot 2.7 vs 3.0 on this? — 2.7 added the .imports file and @AutoConfiguration while still reading spring.factories; 3.0 dropped the spring.factories path for auto-configs, so libraries had to migrate.

The @Conditional* family in depth: evaluation order, "user config wins", and @ConditionalOnMissingBean traps

Why interviewers ask: section 1 covered what the annotations mean; here they probe timing. "You put @ConditionalOnMissingBean on your own config and Boot still created a second bean, why?" separates people who have debugged this from people who have read about it.

Every @ConditionalOn* is a SpringBootCondition with a ConfigurationPhase. PARSE_CONFIGURATION conditions (OnClass, OnMissingClass, OnProperty, OnExpression, OnResource, OnWebApplication, OnJava, OnCloudPlatform) look only at the classpath and Environment, so they are evaluated the moment the class is encountered and can veto parsing the whole class. REGISTER_BEAN conditions (OnBean, OnMissingBean, OnSingleCandidate) inspect the BeanDefinitionRegistry; they are evaluated later, when definitions are actually registered, and the answer depends entirely on what has been registered so far.

On a single element the conditions are sorted so that cheap classpath/property checks run before bean checks, and the first failure short-circuits. OnMissingBean matches by type (default: the @Bean method's return type, including generics since Boot 2.x), by name, by annotation, and honours search = SearchStrategy.ALL|ANCESTORS|CURRENT for context hierarchies. Because the registry is only complete after all user configs and after each auto-config in sorted order, the reliable places for bean conditions are auto-configurations (ordered with @AutoConfigureAfter) and nothing else.

ConditionPhaseLooks atTypical use
@ConditionalOnClass / OnMissingClassPARSE_CONFIGURATION (also as import filter)Classpath (by name; use name= when the class may be absent from a @Bean method signature)Gate a whole auto-config on a library
@ConditionalOnPropertyPARSE_CONFIGURATIONEnvironment; havingValue, matchIfMissingFeature toggles, enabled flags
@ConditionalOnWebApplication(type=SERVLET|REACTIVE)PARSE_CONFIGURATIONContext type / classpathWeb-only beans
@ConditionalOnExpression / OnResource / OnJavaPARSE_CONFIGURATIONSpEL over Environment / resource exists / JVM versionRare, complex switches
@ConditionalOnBean / OnMissingBean / OnSingleCandidateREGISTER_BEANRegistry so far (definitions, not instances)Back-off defaults in auto-config only
@AutoConfiguration(after = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)
@ConditionalOnClass(name = "com.acme.foo.FooClient")      // string form: safe if class absent
@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "foo", name = "enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
@EnableConfigurationProperties(FooProperties.class)
public class FooClientAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(FooClient.class)          // user-defined FooClient always wins
    FooClient fooClient(FooProperties p, ObjectProvider<FooCustomizer> customizers) {
        var c = new FooClient(p.baseUrl(), p.timeout());
        customizers.orderedStream().forEach(cz -> cz.customize(c));
        return c;
    }

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnBean(MeterRegistry.class)               // safe: MetricsAutoConfiguration is ordered before
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    FooMetrics fooMetrics(FooClient client, MeterRegistry registry) { return new FooMetrics(client, registry); }
}
Interview angle: "I have two DataSource beans and Boot's DataSourceAutoConfiguration still backed off, but JdbcTemplateAutoConfiguration did not create a JdbcTemplate." Right: JdbcTemplate is guarded by @ConditionalOnSingleCandidate(DataSource.class); with two candidates and no @Primary it backs off silently. Mark one @Primary.

Pitfalls

  • @ConditionalOnMissingBean without attributes on a method returning an interface backs off for any implementation; returning a concrete type narrows the match, sometimes too much (a user bean typed as the interface will not suppress it).
  • @ConditionalOnBean checks definitions, not whether the bean will actually be created; a definition that later fails its own creation still satisfies it.
  • Conditions never re-run. A bean registered later via BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor or @Import(ImportBeanDefinitionRegistrar) is invisible to conditions that already matched.
  • @ConditionalOnClass(SomeType.class) on a @Bean method whose signature references SomeType can blow up with NoClassDefFoundError while the annotation is being read; put the condition on a nested class or use name=.
Interview questions
  • In which order are conditions evaluated on one @Bean? — Boot sorts them: parse-phase conditions (class, property, web, expression) first, register-bean conditions last; the first non-match stops evaluation and records the reason.
  • Why is @ConditionalOnMissingBean "only for auto-configuration"? — It compares against the registry at evaluation time; only deferred auto-configs are guaranteed to be parsed after all user beans, so only there is the answer deterministic.
  • What happens if I use it anyway in a user config? — It works or not depending on scan order; renaming a package or adding a test config can silently produce duplicate beans or a missing bean.
  • Difference between @ConditionalOnBean and @ConditionalOnSingleCandidate? — OnBean: at least one definition; OnSingleCandidate: exactly one, or several with one @Primary. Boot uses the latter for JdbcTemplate, EntityManagerFactory consumers.
  • How would you debug why a conditional bean was not created? — --debug or /actuator/conditions; the negative-match entry names the failing condition and what it found ("found beans of type … named …"); Unconditional classes at the bottom lists what always loads.
  • What is the string-name form of @ConditionalOnClass for? — Referencing a class that may be absent without the annotation processor triggering class loading; needed on @Bean methods whose return type would otherwise load the class.
  • Can a custom Condition see beans? — It gets a ConditionContext with the registry and BeanFactory, but the same ordering caveats apply; implement ConfigurationCondition to declare REGISTER_BEAN phase.
  • Boot 2 vs 3? — Semantics unchanged; Boot 3 adds @ConditionalOnThreading(VIRTUAL) (3.2) and @ConditionalOnBooleanProperty (3.5), and removes @ConditionalOnEnabledResourceChain-style legacy web conditions.

Writing your own starter: autoconfigure module + starter module, @AutoConfiguration, properties metadata

Why interviewers ask: a practical design question that reveals whether you understand the back-off model from the library author's side: optional dependencies, conditions, properties with IDE metadata and the naming convention.

Boot's own split is the template. acme-foo-spring-boot-autoconfigure holds the @AutoConfiguration classes, @ConfigurationProperties, the AutoConfiguration.imports file and declares the library it configures as optional so the module compiles even where the library is absent. acme-foo-spring-boot-starter is a POM-only module: autoconfigure + the library + any transitive starters. Users add the starter; the conditions do the rest. Name third-party starters xyz-spring-boot-starter; spring-boot-starter-xyz is reserved for Boot's own.

@AutoConfiguration (Boot 2.7+) is @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods=false) plus @AutoConfigureBefore/After attributes, and marks the class so @ComponentScan excludes it. Add spring-boot-configuration-processor (annotation processor scope) to generate META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json, which gives IDE completion and documentation; hand-written extras (deprecations, value hints) go into additional-spring-configuration-metadata.json. Optionally ship a FailureAnalyzer and test with ApplicationContextRunner.

// autoconfigure module
@ConfigurationProperties("acme.foo")
public record FooProperties(@DefaultValue("true") boolean enabled,
                            @DefaultValue("https://foo.acme.com") String baseUrl,
                            @DefaultValue("PT2S") Duration timeout) {}

@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnClass(FooClient.class)
@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "acme.foo", name = "enabled", matchIfMissing = true)
@EnableConfigurationProperties(FooProperties.class)
public class FooAutoConfiguration {
    @Bean @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    FooClient fooClient(FooProperties p) { return FooClient.builder().baseUrl(p.baseUrl()).timeout(p.timeout()).build(); }
}

// test: no Spring Boot app needed
@Test void backsOffWhenUserDefinesClient() {
    new ApplicationContextRunner()
        .withConfiguration(AutoConfigurations.of(FooAutoConfiguration.class))
        .withUserConfiguration(UserClientConfig.class)
        .withPropertyValues("acme.foo.base-url=http://localhost:1")
        .run(ctx -> assertThat(ctx).getBean(FooClient.class).isSameAs(UserClientConfig.CLIENT));
}
acme-foo-spring-boot-autoconfigure/
  src/main/java/com/acme/foo/autoconfigure/FooAutoConfiguration.java
  src/main/resources/META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports
  src/main/resources/META-INF/additional-spring-configuration-metadata.json   (optional hints)
  pom.xml  -> spring-boot-autoconfigure (compile), foo-client (optional), configuration-processor (provided)
acme-foo-spring-boot-starter/
  pom.xml  -> autoconfigure module + foo-client (compile), no code

Pitfalls

  • Forgetting optional on the configured library in the autoconfigure module forces it onto every consumer even when they only wanted the conditions.
  • Component-scanning the autoconfigure package (main class above it) turns auto-configs into user configs and breaks back-off.
  • Using @Component inside an autoconfigure module: nothing scans it, so beans never appear; everything must be reachable from the @AutoConfiguration class.
  • Property prefix collisions (spring.*, server.*, management.*) are reserved; use your company namespace.
Interview questions
  • Why two modules? — The autoconfigure module can be depended on by people who bring their own version of the library; the starter is the convenience bundle. It also keeps the conditions compiling against optional classes.
  • What does @AutoConfiguration give over @Configuration? — proxyBeanMethods=false by default, inline before/after ordering, and exclusion from component scan; the imports file is what actually registers it.
  • How do you expose typed properties with IDE support? — @ConfigurationProperties record/class + spring-boot-configuration-processor; enable with @EnableConfigurationProperties in the auto-config rather than @ConfigurationPropertiesScan.
  • How do you let users customise the client without replacing it? — Inject ObjectProvider<FooCustomizer> (or a Customizer functional interface) and apply in order; that is the pattern Boot uses for RestClientCustomizer, TomcatConnectorCustomizer.
  • How do you test an auto-configuration in isolation? — ApplicationContextRunner/WebApplicationContextRunner with AutoConfigurations.of(...), property values and FilteredClassLoader to simulate a missing class.
  • What breaks when migrating a Boot 2 internal starter to 3? — spring.factories registration is ignored (move to the imports file), javax → jakarta, constructor-binding annotations are implicit, and any use of removed conditions or WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter.

Externalized configuration: the precedence stack, profiles & profile groups, spring.config.import, YAML vs properties

Why interviewers ask: "the value in the env var is not applied, what wins?" is an everyday production question; the strong answer recites the top of the stack from memory, explains profile-specific overrides and knows what changed in Boot 2.4.

The Environment is a MutablePropertySources list searched top-down; first hit wins. Boot's documented order (highest first): 1 DevTools global settings (~/.config/spring-boot) → 2 @TestPropertySource → 3 @SpringBootTest(properties) → 4 command-line --key=value → 5 SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON (inline JSON in an env var/system property) → 6 ServletConfig init params → 7 ServletContext init params → 8 JNDI java:comp/env → 9 Java system properties (-D) → 10 OS environment variables → 11 random.* → 12 config data files: profile-specific application-{profile}.yml outside the jar → inside the jar → plain application.yml outside → inside → 13 @PropertySource on configuration classes → 14 SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties. Within config data, spring.config.imported documents override the importing document, and spring.config.additional-location adds files with higher precedence than the defaults while spring.config.location replaces the defaults.

Profiles: spring.profiles.active (from anywhere except a profile-specific document) selects them; spring.profiles.include adds unconditionally; profile groups (spring.profiles.group.prod=proddb,prodmq) expand one name into several. In YAML, --- separates documents and spring.config.activate.on-profile: prod (Boot 2.4+, replaces spring.profiles) activates one; on-cloud-platform: kubernetes is the other activation key. Config trees (spring.config.import=configtree:/etc/secrets/) map Kubernetes-mounted files to properties named by path. YAML and .properties are equivalent except that YAML supports lists natively and multi-document files, cannot be loaded with @PropertySource, and .properties wins when both exist for the same location (both are loaded; properties has higher precedence).

spring:
  application.name: orders
  profiles:
    group:
      prod: [prod-db, prod-mq]          # activating "prod" activates all three
  config:
    import:
      - optional:configtree:/etc/secrets/    # /etc/secrets/db/password -> db.password
      - optional:file:./override.yml         # imported docs override this one
server.port: 8080
---
spring.config.activate.on-profile: prod-db
spring.datasource.url: jdbc:postgresql://db.prod:5432/orders
---
spring.config.activate.on-cloud-platform: kubernetes
management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled: true
MechanismExampleNote
Command linejava -jar app.jar --server.port=7070Highest of the runtime sources; disable with setAddCommandLineProperties(false)
Env varSPRING_DATASOURCE_URL, APP_ADMINS_0_=a@xRelaxed: upper-snake, indices for lists; wins over all files
System property-Dspring.profiles.active=prodAbove env vars
Profile fileapplication-prod.ymlAlways above application.yml; outside-jar above inside-jar
Importsspring.config.import=vault://, configserver:Boot 2.4 replaced the bootstrap context for Cloud Config

Pitfalls

  • spring.profiles.active inside a profile-specific document (on-profile) throws InvalidConfigDataPropertyException; use spring.profiles.include or groups.
  • Env var relaxed binding is one-way: SERVER_PORT binds, but @Value("${SERVER_PORT}") also works only because the env source is consulted literally; @Value("${server.port}") and @ConfigurationProperties are the portable spellings.
  • YAML gotchas: on/off/yes become booleans in YAML 1.1 (SnakeYAML), 010 may parse as octal; quote them.
  • The Boot 2.4 config-data rewrite: spring.config.use-legacy-processing=true restored old behaviour in 2.x; it is gone in 3.x.
Interview questions
  • A property set as an env var is not applied. Where do you look? — Something higher: a --arg in the launch command or Dockerfile CMD, a -D in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON, or a test override; check /actuator/env, which lists every source and which one is winning.
  • Order the top five sources. — Test annotations, command line, SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON, system properties, environment variables; then profile files, then application.yml.
  • Does application-prod.yml override application.yml even if listed first? — Yes since Boot 2.4: profile-specific documents are always processed after and override non-profile ones; order between files no longer matters.
  • spring.config.location vs additional-location vs import? — location replaces the default search locations; additional-location adds higher-precedence locations; import is declared inside config and supports non-file sources (config trees, Vault, Config Server).
  • How would you pass a secret from a Kubernetes Secret mount? — spring.config.import=optional:configtree:/mnt/secrets/; each file becomes a property named by its relative path, no env var exposure in ps.
  • YAML or properties? — YAML for structure, lists and multi-document profile activation; properties for @PropertySource and tooling. If both exist for the same name, both load and .properties takes precedence.
  • What are profile groups for? — One flag (prod) that fans out to several finer profiles so each document stays single-purpose; also good for @Profile("prod-db") beans.
  • Boot 2.3 vs 3 differences? — 2.4 rewrote config processing (spring.config.import, activate.on-profile, profile files always win, bootstrap context optional); 3.x removed legacy processing and adds spring.config.import=optional: semantics everywhere.

Embedded servers: Tomcat vs Jetty vs Undertow, thread pools, server.*, servlet vs reactive detection

Why interviewers ask: "how many concurrent requests can your service take?" and "what happens to request 201?" are capacity questions that come down to Tomcat's connector settings; senior candidates know the three numbers and the Boot 3 threading options.

Boot picks the server from the classpath: spring-boot-starter-web brings Tomcat (default), swap the starter for Jetty or Undertow; spring-boot-starter-webflux brings Reactor Netty. The corresponding ServletWebServerFactoryAutoConfiguration/ReactiveWebServerFactoryAutoConfiguration registers a TomcatServletWebServerFactory etc., created in onRefresh() and bound to server.* properties via ServerProperties. Customise programmatically with a WebServerFactoryCustomizer<TomcatServletWebServerFactory> or TomcatConnectorCustomizer bean.

Tomcat's capacity model: server.tomcat.threads.max (200) worker threads handle requests; server.tomcat.max-connections (8192) sockets can be open (NIO keeps idle keep-alive connections without a thread); beyond that, server.tomcat.accept-count (100) connections queue in the OS backlog, after which connection refused. So 200 slow requests block the pool while the 201st waits on a connection, not a thread; the client sees latency, not an error. Boot 3.2 adds spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true (Java 21): Tomcat/Jetty use a virtual thread per request, removing the 200-thread ceiling for blocking I/O. Boot 3 targets Jakarta EE 10: Servlet 6.0 (jakarta.servlet), Tomcat 10.1, Jetty 12 (3.2+), Undertow 2.3.

server:
  port: 8080
  shutdown: graceful                       # stop accepting, finish in-flight (spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase)
  http2.enabled: true
  ssl.bundle: web                          # Boot 3.1 SSL bundles (spring.ssl.bundle.pem.web.*)
  tomcat:
    threads: { max: 200, min-spare: 10 }
    max-connections: 8192
    accept-count: 100
    connection-timeout: 20s
    keep-alive-timeout: 60s
    mbeanregistry.enabled: true            # expose Tomcat metrics via JMX
spring:
  threads.virtual.enabled: true            # Boot 3.2+, Java 21
  mvc.servlet.path: /api                   # DispatcherServlet mapping (not context-path)
TomcatJettyUndertowReactor Netty
StackServlet (default)ServletServletReactive (WebFlux)
ThreadingPool, 200 max; virtual threads in 3.2+Pool; virtual threads in 3.2+XNIO I/O + worker threadsEvent loop, cores × 1 threads; never block
StrengthsUbiquitous, best docs, JMX metricsLow footprint, HTTP/2 & WebSocket maturityLowest memory, fastest static I/OBack-pressure, high fan-out
Watch outBlocking pool exhaustionJetty 12 API changes in Boot 3.2Smaller community; no virtual-thread support in BootOne blocking call stalls an event loop
Interview angle: "Requests hang after 200 concurrent users." Every Tomcat worker is blocked (slow downstream, DB pool exhausted, synchronized block); connection 201 sits in max-connections/accept-count. Diagnose with a thread dump (/actuator/threaddump) and tomcat.threads.busy metric; fix the downstream timeout first, then consider virtual threads or WebFlux, not just raising threads.max.

Pitfalls

  • Both -web and -webflux on the classpath: Boot picks the servlet stack, and WebFlux endpoints silently do not exist; set spring.main.web-application-type or drop a starter.
  • server.servlet.context-path prefixes everything including Actuator; spring.mvc.servlet.path only prefixes MVC endpoints.
  • Raising threads.max to 2000 usually moves the bottleneck to the DB pool (Hikari default 10) and increases context-switch and memory cost (~1 MB stack each).
  • Virtual threads + synchronized around I/O pin the carrier thread on Java 21 (fixed in Java 24); prefer ReentrantLock in hot paths.
Interview questions
  • How does Boot know whether to start Tomcat or Netty? — WebApplicationType.deduceFromClasspath(); then the matching *WebServerFactoryAutoConfiguration creates the factory bean whose getWebServer() is called in onRefresh().
  • What are Tomcat's three capacity knobs? — threads.max (workers, 200), max-connections (open sockets, 8192), accept-count (TCP backlog, 100). Threads are the bottleneck for blocking work; connections for slow clients.
  • How would you change the port programmatically? — A WebServerFactoryCustomizer<ConfigurableWebServerFactory> bean calling setPort, or server.port=0 for random (read it back from WebServerInitializedEvent / @LocalServerPort).
  • Servlet vs reactive: when do you pick WebFlux? — Many concurrent, mostly-waiting calls (streaming, fan-out gateways) with a fully non-blocking stack; with JDBC/JPA or blocking clients stay on MVC, and in Boot 3.2+ virtual threads cover most of the scalability argument.
  • What does server.shutdown=graceful do? — On SIGTERM the connector stops accepting new requests and in-flight ones get up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase (30 s) to finish before the context closes.
  • Can you still build a WAR? — Yes: extend SpringBootServletInitializer, set packaging war, mark the Tomcat starter provided; the target container must be Jakarta EE 10 (Tomcat 10.1+) for Boot 3.
  • Boot 2 vs 3 for servers? — Tomcat 9 → 10.1 (javax → jakarta), Jetty 9/10 → 12, HTTP/2 and SSL via spring.ssl.bundle (3.1), virtual threads (3.2), server.tomcat.max-keep-alive-requests naming changes.

Actuator: endpoints & exposure, health groups and Kubernetes probes, info, Micrometer metrics, securing it

Why interviewers ask: it is the "production readiness" question. They want to hear liveness vs readiness, how you add a custom health check without taking down the pod, what management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=* exposes, and how you lock it down.

spring-boot-starter-actuator registers endpoints (health, info, metrics, env, beans, conditions, configprops, loggers, threaddump, heapdump, mappings, scheduledtasks, shutdown…) under /actuator. Two switches control visibility: an endpoint must be enabled (all are, except shutdown) and exposed over a technology; over HTTP only health is exposed by default (Boot 2.x also exposed info; 3.x does not). Everything else needs management.endpoints.web.exposure.include.

Health aggregates HealthIndicator beans (auto-registered for DB, disk, Redis, Kafka, Mongo…) through a StatusAggregator: any DOWN makes the whole endpoint 503. Health groups subset them: on Kubernetes (auto-detected) Boot enables /actuator/health/liveness (only LivenessState) and /actuator/health/readiness (ReadinessState), backed by ApplicationAvailability; publishing AvailabilityChangeEvent.publish(ctx, ReadinessState.REFUSING_TRAFFIC) pulls the pod out of the Service without a restart. Readiness flips to ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC on ApplicationReadyEvent. Metrics come from Micrometer: a MeterRegistry (Prometheus, Datadog, OTLP…) with auto-instrumented JVM, Tomcat, HTTP server/client, DataSource, cache and logging meters; Boot 3 adds the Observation API (@Observed, Micrometer Tracing replacing Sleuth) so one instrumentation yields metrics + traces.

management:
  server.port: 9091                            # separate port, firewall it
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,metrics,prometheus,loggers
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when-authorized            # never "always" on a public port
      probes.enabled: true                     # liveness/readiness groups outside k8s too
      group:
        readiness.include: readinessState,db,redis    # deps you cannot serve without
        liveness.include: livenessState               # NEVER include external deps here
    shutdown.enabled: false
  observations.key-values.app: orders
  tracing.sampling.probability: 0.1
  info.env.enabled: true                       # info.* properties into /actuator/info
@Component
class QueueLagHealth implements HealthIndicator {
    public Health health() {
        long lag = lagGauge.get();
        return lag < 10_000 ? Health.up().withDetail("lag", lag).build()
                            : Health.down().withDetail("lag", lag).build();   // affects only groups that include it
    }
}

@Configuration
class ActuatorSecurity {
    @Bean @Order(1)
    SecurityFilterChain actuatorChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.securityMatcher(EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint())
            .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
                .requestMatchers(EndpointRequest.to(HealthEndpoint.class)).permitAll()
                .anyRequest().hasRole("OPS"))
            .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults());
        return http.build();
    }
}
ProbeQuestionShould includeFailure consequence
LivenessIs the process wedged?Internal state only (livenessState)Container restarted
ReadinessCan it serve traffic now?readinessState + hard dependencies (DB)Removed from Service endpoints
StartupHas it finished booting?Same as liveness, longer thresholdProtects slow-starting apps from liveness kills

Pitfalls

  • A DB HealthIndicator in the liveness group turns a DB outage into a restart storm; liveness must never depend on external systems.
  • exposure.include=* on the app port publishes env (secrets are sanitised only for well-known keys; Boot 3 hides all values unless management.endpoint.env.show-values=always), heapdump (full memory) and loggers (POST changes levels).
  • /actuator/health hits every indicator on each probe call; a slow indicator (remote HTTP) makes probes time out; cache with management.endpoint.health.cache.time-to-live or make it a readiness-only check.
  • Counting with registry.counter("orders." + customerId) creates unbounded tag cardinality; use bounded tags and a MeterFilter deny list.
Interview questions
  • Which endpoints are exposed by default over HTTP in Boot 3? — Only health. JMX exposes more but JMX is off by default. Boot 2 also exposed info.
  • Liveness vs readiness in Spring terms? — LivenessState.CORRECT/BROKEN and ReadinessState.ACCEPTING/REFUSING_TRAFFIC held by ApplicationAvailability; health groups liveness/readiness render them; any bean can change them via AvailabilityChangeEvent.
  • How do you add a custom health check that only affects readiness? — Implement HealthIndicator (bean name minus "HealthIndicator" is the key) and add that key to management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include.
  • How would you secure Actuator? — Separate management.server.port reachable only inside the cluster, expose a minimal list, show-details=when-authorized, and a SecurityFilterChain using EndpointRequest matchers with a dedicated role.
  • How do you get a Prometheus scrape? — Add micrometer-registry-prometheus, expose prometheus; Boot registers PrometheusMeterRegistry and /actuator/prometheus.
  • How would you debug a bean or property issue in a running pod? — /actuator/beans, /actuator/conditions, /actuator/env/{key} (shows which property source wins), /actuator/configprops, and POST /actuator/loggers/com.acme with {"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}.
  • What replaced Spring Cloud Sleuth in Boot 3? — Micrometer Tracing (Brave or OpenTelemetry bridge) on top of the Observation API; spring-boot-starter-actuator + a tracing bridge + an exporter (Zipkin/OTLP).
  • What does info show and how do you populate it? — info.* properties (opt-in via management.info.env.enabled), build info from spring-boot-maven-plugin:build-info, git info from git-commit-id-plugin, Java/OS info, and custom InfoContributor beans.

DevTools & the restart classloader

Why interviewers ask: a quick check that you know why a restart takes 1 s instead of 10 s, why DevTools is excluded from the fat jar, and the classloader-related ClassCastException it can cause.

spring-boot-devtools splits the classpath in two: jars (unchanging) load in the base classloader; your project's classes load in a throw-away RestartClassLoader. When a compiled class changes, DevTools closes the context, drops the restart loader, creates a new one and runs main again; the JVM, the jars and Tomcat's port stay. It also sets dev-friendly property defaults (template caches off, server.error.include-*, H2 console), enables LiveReload, and is automatically disabled when the app is launched with java -jar or a non-development classloader; the Boot Maven/Gradle plugins exclude it from the repackaged jar (excludeDevtools, default true).

spring.devtools.restart.exclude=static/**,public/**
spring.devtools.restart.additional-paths=../shared-lib/target/classes
spring.devtools.restart.trigger-file=.reloadtrigger   # restart only when this file changes
spring.devtools.livereload.enabled=false
# ~/.config/spring-boot/spring-boot-devtools.properties applies to every project (highest precedence source)

Pitfalls

  • An object created by the base loader (a cached entity in a library-level cache, a serialised session, a Kryo/JPA proxy) cast to the same class from the restart loader fails with ClassCastException: X cannot be cast to X; the fix is to put that jar into the restart loader via META-INF/spring-devtools.properties (restart.include.*) or disable restart.
  • DevTools' relaxed defaults (e.g. spring.h2.console.enabled, disabled caches) must never leak: keep it optional/developmentOnly and verify the fat jar has no devtools entry.
  • Restart is not hot-swap: static state and connection pools are recreated; for field-level hot swap use JRebel or the IDE's HotSwap.
Interview questions
  • Why is a DevTools restart faster than a cold start? — Only the project classes are reloaded in a fresh RestartClassLoader; third-party jars and the JVM stay warm, and the JIT keeps its profile for library code.
  • Why is DevTools excluded in production? — The repackage plugin drops it by default, and it self-disables under java -jar; its defaults (disabled caches, H2 console, remote restart) would be a security and performance problem.
  • What causes "X cannot be cast to X" with DevTools? — Two classloaders defining the same class; instances from the base loader meet a class from the restart loader. Move the jar into the restart loader or disable restart.
  • How do you keep Maven's Tomcat port and DB across restarts? — Automatic: the JVM and base loader survive; but connection pools, caches and static fields belonging to project classes are rebuilt.
  • Where do DevTools global settings sit in the precedence stack? — At the very top (above test properties and command-line args), but only when DevTools is active.

Packaging: fat jar layout, layered jars, buildpacks/OCI images, GraalVM native image & AOT constraints

Why interviewers ask: "how does java -jar work when jars-in-jars are not supported by the JDK?" tests internals; "how would you cut cold start / image size?" tests whether you know layering, buildpacks, CDS and where native image's closed-world rules bite Spring.

The spring-boot-maven-plugin:repackage (Gradle bootJar) wraps your normal jar: your classes go to BOOT-INF/classes/, dependencies uncompressed to BOOT-INF/lib/, and the manifest's Main-Class becomes org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher (Boot 3.2 moved the loader to .loader.launch), with your class in Start-Class. The launcher builds a LaunchedClassLoader that reads nested jars in place (stored, not deflated, so they can be random-accessed) and calls your main. Layered jars (default on) add BOOT-INF/layers.idx ordering content as dependencies → spring-boot-loader → snapshot-dependencies → application; java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers (3.3; -Djarmode=layertools before) splits them so a Dockerfile can COPY each layer separately and reuse cached layers when only application code changed.

Buildpacks: mvn spring-boot:build-image uses Paketo buildpacks to produce an OCI image without a Dockerfile, choosing a JRE, memory calculator (JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS derived from the container limit) and layering. GraalVM native image (Boot 3.0+ via native-maven-plugin or build-image with -Pnative) compiles ahead of time under a closed-world assumption: no runtime classpath scanning, reflection, proxies or resources unless declared. Spring's AOT engine therefore runs a build-time refresh() up to bean-definition creation and generates Java source that registers every bean directly plus RuntimeHints for reflection/resources/proxies; conditions are evaluated at build time, so a profile or property that changes which beans exist must be fixed at build. Trade: ~50 ms startup and a fraction of the RSS versus longer builds, lower peak throughput than JIT, and limits on dynamic code (@Profile switching, @Conditional on runtime state, hand-rolled reflection, JPA byte-code enhancement needing hints). For JVM deployments, Boot 3.3's CDS support (extract + -XX:SharedArchiveFile) is the low-risk middle ground.

# Dockerfile using layers (Boot 3.3+ jarmode)
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre AS builder
COPY target/app.jar app.jar
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers --destination extracted
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre
COPY --from=builder extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=builder extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder extracted/application/ ./
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]

# OCI image without a Dockerfile / native binary
mvn spring-boot:build-image -Dspring-boot.build-image.imageName=acme/orders
mvn -Pnative native:compile          # needs GraalVM JDK; ./target/orders
// Declaring what native image cannot see
@ImportRuntimeHints(OrdersHints.class)
@SpringBootApplication class App {}

class OrdersHints implements RuntimeHintsRegistrar {
    public void registerHints(RuntimeHints hints, ClassLoader cl) {
        hints.reflection().registerType(LegacyDto.class, MemberCategory.INVOKE_DECLARED_CONSTRUCTORS, MemberCategory.DECLARED_FIELDS);
        hints.resources().registerPattern("templates/*.ftl");
        hints.proxies().registerJdkProxy(PaymentGateway.class);
    }
}
// or on a type: @RegisterReflectionForBinding(LegacyDto.class)

Pitfalls

  • mvn package without the plugin's repackage execution (easy to lose when you drop the parent) produces a plain jar: no main manifest attribute.
  • java -cp app.jar com.acme.App fails: nested jars are not on the classpath; use -jar, or the extracted layout.
  • Native: Class.forName on a string, Jackson on an undeclared DTO, @Profile chosen at runtime, Mockito, and libraries lacking reachability metadata all fail at runtime, not at compile; test with mvn -PnativeTest test.
  • Building native with the spring.profiles.active you use in dev bakes dev beans into the production binary.
Interview questions
  • How does java -jar run nested jars? — Boot's JarLauncher is the manifest main class; it builds a LaunchedClassLoader over BOOT-INF/classes and BOOT-INF/lib/*.jar (stored entries, random-access) and invokes Start-Class.main reflectively.
  • Why are layered jars useful? — Docker caches image layers; separating rarely-changing dependencies from your classes means a code change rebuilds and pushes only the last small layer.
  • Buildpacks vs Dockerfile? — Buildpacks give a reproducible, patched base image and JVM memory tuning with zero Dockerfile; a Dockerfile gives full control (custom base, extra tools). Many teams use buildpacks by default and Dockerfile for exceptions.
  • What does Spring AOT do and why is it needed for native? — It executes the container's definition phase at build time, generating code that registers beans and RuntimeHints, because GraalVM's closed world forbids runtime scanning, reflection and proxy generation unless pre-declared.
  • What Spring features break or change under native image? — Conditions and profiles frozen at build time; no CGLIB class generation at runtime (@Configuration subclasses are generated at build); JDK proxies need hints; SpEL and reflection-based libraries need metadata; Mockito-based tests do not run natively.
  • When would you not use native image? — Throughput-sensitive long-running services (C2 JIT beats AOT peak), heavy reflection/dynamic libraries, or when build time (minutes, GBs RAM) hurts CI. Use CDS or plain JVM with tuned JVM flags instead.
  • How would you cut JVM cold-start without going native? — Boot 3.3 CDS (extract then run with -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit/SharedArchiveFile), spring.main.lazy-initialization, fewer auto-configs (exclude), -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 for dev, and Project Leyden/CRaC where supported.
  • Boot 2 vs 3 for packaging? — Native support moved from the experimental Spring Native project into Boot 3.0 core (AOT engine); the loader package moved to loader.launch in 3.2; jarmode=tools and CDS in 3.3.

Testing: @SpringBootTest modes, slices, @MockBean → @MockitoBean, @TestConfiguration, context caching, Testcontainers @ServiceConnection

Why interviewers ask: "why does your test suite take 12 minutes?" and "why does a bean exist in the app but not in @WebMvcTest?" are the two classic questions; both are answered by understanding what a slice loads and how contexts are cached.

@SpringBootTest finds the @SpringBootConfiguration upward from the test package and starts the whole context. webEnvironment: MOCK (default; servlet environment mocked, use MockMvc, no port), RANDOM_PORT/DEFINED_PORT (real embedded server, inject TestRestTemplate/WebTestClient, @LocalServerPort), NONE (no web layer). Slices load only one layer plus its auto-configs: @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class) = MVC infrastructure, @ControllerAdvice, converters, security filters, MockMvc, and no @Service/@Repository beans; @DataJpaTest = entities, repositories, an embedded DB (unless @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)), each test transactional and rolled back; @JsonTest = Jackson + JacksonTester; @RestClientTest = RestClient/RestTemplate builder + MockRestServiceServer. Anything the slice does not load is supplied with @MockBean, which replaces (or adds) a Mockito mock in the context. Boot 3.4 deprecates @MockBean/@SpyBean in favour of Spring Framework 6.2's @MockitoBean/@MockitoSpyBean (field-level, same idea, part of spring-test).

Contexts are expensive, so the TestContext framework caches them across test classes keyed by the full configuration: classes, profiles, properties, mock beans, initializers, context customizers. Two test classes with identical keys share one context; any difference (a different @MockBean set, one extra properties=, @DirtiesContext) forces another startup. Ten variants ≈ ten startups ≈ the 12-minute suite. @TestConfiguration classes are excluded from scanning and only picked up when nested inside the test or @Imported, and they may override beans. For real infrastructure, Testcontainers + Boot 3.1's @ServiceConnection on the container field lets Boot derive the JDBC/Kafka/Redis connection details automatically, replacing hand-written @DynamicPropertySource blocks; @Testcontainers/@Container (JUnit) or a static singleton container manage lifecycle.

@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class OrderControllerTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    @MockitoBean OrderService service;                 // Boot 3.4+ (was @MockBean)

    @Test void returns404WhenMissing() throws Exception {
        when(service.find("x")).thenReturn(Optional.empty());
        mvc.perform(get("/orders/x")).andExpect(status().isNotFound());
    }
}

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)
@Testcontainers
class OrderFlowIT {
    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> db = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16");   // no @DynamicPropertySource needed
    @Autowired TestRestTemplate rest;

    @TestConfiguration static class FixedClock {
        @Bean @Primary Clock clock() { return Clock.fixed(Instant.EPOCH, ZoneOffset.UTC); }
    }

    @Test void createsOrder() {
        var r = rest.postForEntity("/orders", new CreateOrder("sku-1", 2), OrderDto.class);
        assertThat(r.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.CREATED);
    }
}
AnnotationLoadsDoes not loadTypical extras
@SpringBootTestEverything—webEnvironment, properties, classes
@WebMvcTestControllers (optionally one), advice, filters, converters, security, MockMvcServices, repositories, @Component@MockitoBean for services; @Import for extra config
@DataJpaTestEntities, repositories, TestEntityManager, embedded DB, tx rollbackWeb, services@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace=NONE) + Testcontainers
@JsonTestObjectMapper, JacksonTesterEverything elseSerialisation contract tests
@RestClientTestRestClient.Builder, MockRestServiceServerWeb serverClient wrapper classes

Pitfalls

  • "No qualifying bean of type OrderService" inside @WebMvcTest: slices do not scan services; mock it or, if it really is web infrastructure, @Import it.
  • @MockBean in a base test class applied inconsistently across subclasses, or sprinkled per test, multiplies context variants; centralise mocks in a shared config.
  • @DataJpaTest replaces your DataSource with H2 by default even when Testcontainers is configured; add @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE).
  • @Transactional tests roll back, so AFTER_COMMIT event listeners and @Async paths never run; test those with RANDOM_PORT and real commits.
  • Starting one container per test class with @Container on a non-static field recreates it per test method; use static or a singleton-container base class.
Interview questions
  • Why are Spring tests slow and how do you fix it? — Each distinct context configuration starts a container (seconds each) and the cache is keyed by every annotation detail; fix by standardising configuration (shared mocks/properties), preferring slices, avoiding @DirtiesContext, and running Testcontainers as singletons.
  • MOCK vs RANDOM_PORT? — MOCK runs DispatcherServlet in-process through MockMvc (no socket, filters still run); RANDOM_PORT starts Tomcat and tests over HTTP, needed for real serialisation, async, and container behaviour.
  • What does @WebMvcTest include from Security? — The security auto-configuration and filter chain; with spring-security-test you use @WithMockUser/with(csrf()), otherwise POSTs get 401/403.
  • @MockBean vs @MockitoBean? — Same purpose; @MockitoBean lives in spring-test (6.2), is the replacement after Boot 3.4 deprecated @MockBean, and is more precise about which bean it targets; both affect the context cache key.
  • How does @ServiceConnection work? — Boot detects the container type and registers a ConnectionDetails bean (e.g. JdbcConnectionDetails) that auto-configuration prefers over spring.datasource.* properties; same mechanism Docker Compose support (3.1) uses.
  • When do you use @TestConfiguration? — To add or override a few beans (fixed Clock, stub client) for tests without touching the main configuration; as a nested static class it applies to that test only, as a top-level class it must be @Imported.
  • How would you debug a bean present in prod but missing in a test? — Check the slice's documented inclusions, look at @SpringBootConfiguration discovery (which main class was found), profiles/@ActiveProfiles, and run the test with debug=true to read the conditions report for that context.
  • Boot 2 vs 3 testing changes? — JUnit 4 vintage removed from the starter (3.0), @ServiceConnection/Docker Compose (3.1), @MockBean deprecated for @MockitoBean (3.4), MockMvcTester with AssertJ (3.4), RestClient test support (3.2).

Spring Boot 2 → 3 migration: Jakarta, Java 17, spring.factories, trailing slashes, observability, httpclient5, property renames

Why interviewers ask: most teams did (or are doing) this migration; they want the checklist and the two or three things that broke silently in yours.

Boot 3.0 (Nov 2022) sits on Spring Framework 6, Spring Security 6, Hibernate 6.1, Hibernate Validator 8, Jakarta EE 9/10 and requires Java 17. The visible change is the namespace: every javax.persistence, javax.servlet, javax.validation, javax.annotation (@PostConstruct) becomes jakarta.*, and every library that still ships javax servlet/JPA classes must be upgraded or replaced. The recommended path is Boot 2.7 first (deprecations, AutoConfiguration.imports, SecurityFilterChain beans already work there), then 3.x with spring-boot-properties-migrator on the classpath to log renamed properties at startup, then remove the migrator.

Silent breakers: trailing-slash matching is off (/orders/ no longer maps to /orders; add a redirect filter or fix clients); PathPatternParser is the default and rejects ** in the middle of patterns; WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter and antMatchers are gone (SecurityFilterChain bean, requestMatchers); spring.factories auto-config registration is ignored; Sleuth is replaced by Micrometer Tracing and the Observation API (trace IDs in logs need micrometer-tracing-bridge-*); RestTemplate/HttpComponents now needs httpclient5; Hibernate 6 changes ID generation defaults (SEQUENCE per entity with _SEQ suffix instead of hibernate_sequence) and query/type semantics; spring.redis.* → spring.data.redis.*, spring.jpa.hibernate.use-new-id-generator-mappings removed, management.metrics.export.* → management.<system>.metrics.export.*, server.max-http-header-size → server.max-http-request-header-size. New in 3.x worth naming: ProblemDetail (RFC 7807, spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled), RestClient and HTTP interface clients (3.2), virtual threads (3.2), SSL bundles (3.1), Docker Compose and Testcontainers integration (3.1), native image.

// Security: Boot 2 (removed)                     // Boot 3
// class Cfg extends WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter { … }
@Bean SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
                   .requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()   // was antMatchers
                   .anyRequest().authenticated())
               .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
               .build();
}

// Trailing slash: opt back in explicitly if clients depend on it
@Configuration class WebCfg implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    public void configurePathMatch(PathMatchConfigurer c) { c.setUseTrailingSlashMatch(true); } // deprecated; prefer fixing clients
}

// Hibernate 6 id generation: keep the old shared sequence explicitly
@Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "hib")
@SequenceGenerator(name = "hib", sequenceName = "hibernate_sequence", allocationSize = 1)
Long id;
AreaBoot 2.7Boot 3.x
BaselineJava 8+, Spring 5.3, Jakarta EE 8 (javax)Java 17+, Spring 6, Jakarta EE 9/10 (jakarta)
Auto-config registryspring.factories or .imports.imports only
Security configAdapter (deprecated) or SecurityFilterChainSecurityFilterChain, requestMatchers, lambda DSL only (6.1+)
ObservabilitySleuth + Micrometer metricsMicrometer Observation + Tracing (OTel/Brave)
URL matchingTrailing slash matchesStrict; PathPatternParser
HTTP client for RestTemplatehttpclient 4httpclient5; RestClient added in 3.2
NativeSpring Native (experimental)Built-in AOT + GraalVM

Pitfalls

  • A dependency that still bundles javax.servlet (old Swagger/Springfox, old Jersey, some SDKs) compiles but fails at runtime with NoClassDefFoundError: javax/servlet/Filter; replace it (springdoc-openapi 2.x) or use the Eclipse Transformer as a last resort.
  • Hibernate 6 sequence change breaks inserts on existing schemas ("sequence orders_seq does not exist") unless you keep the generator explicit or migrate the schema.
  • Custom Conditions or starters registered in spring.factories vanish without error; check /actuator/conditions after the upgrade.
  • Trace IDs disappear from logs until you add a tracing bridge and (for async/WebClient) propagate context; Sleuth's MDC keys changed to traceId/spanId.
Interview questions
  • Give the Boot 2 → 3 checklist. — Upgrade to 2.7 and fix deprecations; Java 17; javax → jakarta (imports and dependencies); replace WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter; move starters to .imports; add the properties migrator; Sleuth → Micrometer Tracing; httpclient5; verify Hibernate 6 behaviour and trailing-slash clients; run the conditions report and integration tests.
  • Why did Jakarta rename the packages at all? — Oracle kept the javax trademark when handing Java EE to Eclipse; EE 9 renamed to jakarta.* so the specs could evolve, which forced a whole-ecosystem binary break.
  • What broke silently in a typical migration? — Trailing-slash routes returning 404, Hibernate sequence naming, lost auto-configs from spring.factories, missing trace IDs in logs, and spring.redis.* properties no longer read.
  • How do you find renamed properties? — spring-boot-properties-migrator logs each old key with its replacement and temporarily maps it; remove after fixing.
  • What replaced Sleuth and why? — Micrometer Tracing on the Observation API: one Observation produces metrics and spans and Boot instruments MVC, WebClient, JDBC, Kafka once; bridges to OpenTelemetry or Brave.
  • What new Boot 3 features would you adopt after migrating? — ProblemDetail error responses, RestClient/HTTP interfaces, virtual threads (3.2), SSL bundles, @ServiceConnection tests, and optionally native image for small services.
  • Can Boot 3 run on Java 11? — No; Java 17 is the compiled baseline (class file 61). Boot 2.7 is the last line supporting 8/11.

Boot 3.2 app. Your @Configuration class declares @Bean DataSource myDs(). What does DataSourceAutoConfiguration do and why?

c. AutoConfigurationImportSelector is a DeferredImportSelector, processed after all user configuration, so bean conditions see user definitions. a would require the same bean name; b describes what happens for beans without a missing-bean guard; d is invented: any user config counts.

A Boot 2.7 internal starter registers its auto-config under org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.EnableAutoConfiguration in META-INF/spring.factories. After upgrading the consuming app to Boot 3.1, what happens?

b. Boot 3.0 removed the spring.factories path for auto-configuration; candidates come only from AutoConfiguration.imports. There is no error, which is why /actuator/conditions is the first check after an upgrade. spring.factories still works for listeners, initializers and failure analyzers, so c is half-true and wrong for this key.

Two user @Configuration classes: A has @Bean @ConditionalOnMissingBean Clock clock(), B has @Bean Clock fixed(). Which statement is correct?

d. OnMissingBean is evaluated in REGISTER_BEAN phase against the registry so far, and user configs are parsed in scan order with no ordering guarantee. The only deterministic home for such a fallback is an auto-configuration. a would be true if conditions re-ran at the end; they never do.

application.yml has server.port: 8080, application-prod.yml has 9090, the container sets SERVER_PORT=7070, and the entrypoint is java -Dserver.port=6060 -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod. Which port?

a. Java system properties (-D) sit above OS environment variables, which sit above every config file. The only thing that would beat 6060 here is a --server.port command-line argument or SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON. c is the trap: profile files beat application.yml but not runtime sources.

In SpringApplication.run(), which is the correct order?

c. The Environment must exist before the context (it is attached in prepareContext), initializers run on the unrefreshed context, Started fires right after refresh, runners follow, and Ready is last. b puts initializers after refresh, which would make them useless for adding property sources.

You want to log the active profiles the moment application.yml has been loaded. Which works?

b. ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent fires before the context exists, so no bean (a) can hear it. c and d run much later; they can read profiles but not "the moment" the Environment was prepared, and a runner runs last, not first.

Which Actuator setup is correct for Kubernetes?

d. Liveness failures cause restarts, which cannot fix an external outage and cause restart storms (a). Readiness removes the pod from the Service, which is the right reaction to a missing dependency. b exposes env, heapdump and loggers to the app's public port.

A @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class) fails with "No qualifying bean of type OrderService". Best fix?

a. The slice deliberately loads only the web layer; supplying the collaborator as a mock keeps the test fast and isolated. b and c load the world (and c also breaks the slice's filters); d is a lie to the framework.
