Why does java -cp app.jar com.acme.App fail for a Boot fat jar while java -jar app.jar works?

c. The JDK's classloader does not support jars inside jars; -jar starts JarLauncher (the manifest Main-Class) which builds a LaunchedClassLoader over BOOT-INF/classes and BOOT-INF/lib/*, then calls Start-Class. Extract the jar (jarmode=tools extract) if you need a flat classpath.

Which statement about GraalVM native image with Boot 3 is true?

b. The closed-world assumption forbids runtime scanning and undeclared reflection, so Spring pre-computes the bean graph and hints. a is the opposite of what happens; c is backwards (native wins on startup and memory, JIT on peak throughput); d is why RuntimeHintsRegistrar exists.

Practice

Scenario: "my @Bean DataSource is ignored" and, after a fix, "two DataSources"

A team reports two symptoms on Boot 3.2, one after the other. Explain each and give the fix.

// Symptom 1: the pool below is never used; Hikari still connects to spring.datasource.url
@Component
class DbConfig {
    @Bean
    DataSource reportingDs() { return new HikariDataSource(reportingCfg()); }
}

// Symptom 2 (after moving it to @Configuration): startup fails
// "Parameter 0 of method jdbcTemplate in JdbcTemplateConfiguration required a single bean, but 2 were found"
// ... and later "No qualifying bean of type DataSource: expected single matching bean but found 2: reportingDs, mainDs"
Tests: back-off rule, @ConditionalOnSingleCandidate, @Primary, scanning
Hint 1
Is DbConfig in a package under the main class? Check /actuator/beans for reportingDs. If it is not there, the auto-config never saw it.
Hint 2
Symptom 2 comes from JdbcTemplateAutoConfiguration, which is guarded by @ConditionalOnSingleCandidate(DataSource.class), and from DataSourceTransactionManagerAutoConfiguration/JPA needing one DataSource.
Reveal solution

Symptom 1. Either DbConfig is outside the scanned package (main class not in the root package), or it is scanned but nothing makes the bean the one Boot uses. Verify with /actuator/beans. If the bean is absent, fix scanning (scanBasePackages or move the main class). If it is present, DataSourceAutoConfiguration did back off (its PooledDataSourceConfiguration is @ConditionalOnMissingBean({DataSource.class, XADataSource.class})); the "still connects to spring.datasource.url" observation then means reportingCfg() itself reads those properties, or a second explicit DataSource exists. @Component vs @Configuration does not matter for back-off; lite mode only affects inter-bean calls.

Symptom 2. Now there are two DataSource beans (mainDs and reportingDs). Auto-configurations that consume a DataSource are written for a single candidate: JdbcTemplateAutoConfiguration uses @ConditionalOnSingleCandidate (so it backs off, later producing "no JdbcTemplate"), while HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration, Flyway and DataSourceTransactionManagerAutoConfiguration inject DataSource by type and fail with the "expected single matching bean" error.

Fix. Mark the main pool @Primary (auto-configs then resolve it, and @ConditionalOnSingleCandidate accepts several candidates with exactly one primary). Inject the other with @Qualifier("reportingDs"). Bind both from properties with @ConfigurationProperties("app.datasource.reporting") on a DataSourceProperties/HikariDataSource bean. Give the reporting side its own JdbcTemplate/TransactionManager beans explicitly, and if JPA must span both, configure two EntityManagerFactory beans with @EnableJpaRepositories(basePackages, entityManagerFactoryRef, transactionManagerRef). Confirm with /actuator/conditions: DataSourceAutoConfiguration.PooledDataSourceConfiguration negative, JdbcTemplateAutoConfiguration positive.

Scenario: the env var is set but the app ignores it

Kubernetes manifest sets SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db-blue:5432/orders. The pod still connects to db-green. The Dockerfile ends with:

ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-Xmx1g -Dspring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://db-green:5432/orders"
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar", "--spring.profiles.active=prod"]

Explain which source wins and list two ways to prove it from inside the running pod. Then say what would happen if the URL were instead in application-prod.yml inside the jar and the env var were still set.

Tests: precedence stack, /actuator/env, relaxed binding
Hint 1
Rank: command line, SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON, system properties, environment variables, files. Where does JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS -D… land?
Reveal solution

JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS is read by the JVM at startup, so -Dspring.datasource.url becomes a Java system property, which sits above OS environment variables in Boot's stack. The env var is present, relaxed-bound correctly (SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL ≡ spring.datasource.url), and simply shadowed.

Prove it: (1) GET /actuator/env/spring.datasource.url lists every property source containing the key in precedence order with the winning one first: systemProperties then systemEnvironment. (2) jcmd <pid> VM.system_properties | grep datasource or ps -o args/cat /proc/1/environ to see JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS; the JVM also prints "Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS" on stderr at start. (3) Startup log line The following 1 profile is active: "prod" confirms the arg parsing but not the URL; /actuator/configprops shows the bound DataSourceProperties.

Fix: remove the -D from the image (bake only JVM flags into JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, never application config) or override at an even higher level with a command-line argument.

Variant: if the URL lived only in application-prod.yml, the env var would win: any environment variable beats every config-data file, profile-specific or not, inside or outside the jar. Profile files only beat application.yml and @PropertySource.

Scenario: context fails with "no qualifying bean" only in the test slice

The application starts fine. This test fails at context load with NoSuchBeanDefinitionException: No qualifying bean of type 'com.acme.audit.AuditFilterSupport'.

@Component
class AuditFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {           // registered as a servlet filter
    AuditFilter(AuditFilterSupport support) { … }         // @Service in com.acme.audit
}

@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class OrderControllerTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    @MockitoBean OrderService orderService;
    @Test void ok() throws Exception { mvc.perform(get("/orders/1")).andExpect(status().isOk()); }
}

Why does the slice see AuditFilter but not AuditFilterSupport? Give three fixes and say which one you would pick, and what the context-cache implication is.

Tests: slice inclusion rules, @MockitoBean, @TestConfiguration, context caching
Hint 1
@WebMvcTest uses a TypeExcludeFilter that includes @Controller, @ControllerAdvice, Converter, Filter, WebMvcConfigurer, HandlerInterceptor… and excludes everything else.
Reveal solution

WebMvcTypeExcludeFilter keeps web-infrastructure types, and a jakarta.servlet.Filter is one of them, so AuditFilter is scanned into the slice; its constructor dependency AuditFilterSupport is a plain @Service, which the slice excludes. The full app has both; the slice has half.

Fixes. (1) @MockitoBean AuditFilterSupport support; in the test: the filter still runs, with a mock collaborator. (2) @WebMvcTest(controllers = OrderController.class, excludeFilters = @Filter(type = ASSIGNABLE_TYPE, classes = AuditFilter.class)) or @AutoConfigureMockMvc(addFilters = false) to keep the filter out entirely. (3) A nested @TestConfiguration providing a real or stub AuditFilterSupport, or @Import(AuditFilterSupport.class) if it is cheap and has no further dependencies.

Choice. Prefer (1) if audit behaviour matters to the controller tests (e.g. it sets a request attribute the controller reads); prefer (2) when the filter is irrelevant, because it keeps the slice minimal. Avoid (3) when AuditFilterSupport drags in a repository.

Cache implication. Every distinct set of @MockitoBeans, excludeFilters or nested configs is a different context key. If ten controller tests each mock a different set, ten contexts start. Put the shared mocks and slice settings in one meta-annotation or abstract base class so all @WebMvcTests share one cached context.

Implement: an auto-configuration for FooClient with a property toggle, back-off and metrics

Write a Boot 3 auto-configuration for a third-party com.foo.FooClient (built via FooClient.create(String url, Duration timeout)). Requirements: only active when the class is present and acme.foo.enabled is not false; typed properties with defaults and validation; user-defined FooClient wins; register a FooHealthIndicator only when Actuator's health is available; register metrics only when a MeterRegistry exists; make it discoverable; write a test that proves back-off and the disabled toggle.

Tests: conditions, ordering, properties, imports file, ApplicationContextRunner
Hint 1
Which conditions are parse-phase and which are register-bean? Which auto-configs must run before yours so your @ConditionalOnBean(MeterRegistry.class) is deterministic?
Hint 2
Health indicators need @ConditionalOnEnabledHealthIndicator("foo") plus a class condition on HealthIndicator; put Actuator-related beans in a nested configuration so a missing Actuator jar does not break the outer class.
Reveal solution
@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties("acme.foo")
public record FooProperties(@DefaultValue("true") boolean enabled,
                            @NotBlank @DefaultValue("https://api.foo.com") String baseUrl,
                            @DefaultValue("PT3S") Duration timeout) {}

@AutoConfiguration(after = { MetricsAutoConfiguration.class, CompositeMeterRegistryAutoConfiguration.class })
@ConditionalOnClass(name = "com.foo.FooClient")
@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "acme.foo", name = "enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
@EnableConfigurationProperties(FooProperties.class)
public class FooAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    FooClient fooClient(FooProperties p) { return FooClient.create(p.baseUrl(), p.timeout()); }

    @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
    @ConditionalOnClass(MeterRegistry.class)
    @ConditionalOnBean(MeterRegistry.class)                 // safe: ordered after metrics auto-config
    static class Metrics {
        @Bean @ConditionalOnMissingBean
        FooClientMetrics fooClientMetrics(FooClient c, MeterRegistry r) { return new FooClientMetrics(c, r); }
    }

    @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
    @ConditionalOnClass(HealthIndicator.class)
    @ConditionalOnEnabledHealthIndicator("foo")
    static class Health {
        @Bean @ConditionalOnMissingBean(name = "fooHealthIndicator")
        HealthIndicator fooHealthIndicator(FooClient c) { return () -> c.ping() ? Health.up().build() : Health.down().build(); }
    }
}
# META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports
com.acme.foo.autoconfigure.FooAutoConfiguration
class FooAutoConfigurationTests {
    private final ApplicationContextRunner runner = new ApplicationContextRunner()
            .withConfiguration(AutoConfigurations.of(FooAutoConfiguration.class));

    @Test void createsClientByDefault() {
        runner.run(ctx -> assertThat(ctx).hasSingleBean(FooClient.class).doesNotHaveBean(FooClientMetrics.class));
    }
    @Test void backsOffWhenUserDefinesClient() {
        runner.withUserConfiguration(UserCfg.class)
              .run(ctx -> assertThat(ctx).getBean(FooClient.class).isSameAs(UserCfg.CLIENT));
    }
    @Test void disabledByProperty() {
        runner.withPropertyValues("acme.foo.enabled=false").run(ctx -> assertThat(ctx).doesNotHaveBean(FooClient.class));
    }
    @Test void metricsWhenRegistryPresent() {
        runner.withBean(SimpleMeterRegistry.class).run(ctx -> assertThat(ctx).hasSingleBean(FooClientMetrics.class));
    }
    @Test void absentWithoutLibrary() {
        runner.withClassLoader(new FilteredClassLoader(FooClient.class)).run(ctx -> assertThat(ctx).doesNotHaveBean("fooClient"));
    }
    @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false) static class UserCfg {
        static final FooClient CLIENT = FooClient.create("http://stub", Duration.ofSeconds(1));
        @Bean FooClient fooClient() { return CLIENT; }
    }
}

Reasoning. Class and property conditions are parse-phase and gate the whole class cheaply (the string-name class condition avoids loading FooClient while reading annotations). @ConditionalOnMissingBean on the client is deterministic because this is a deferred auto-configuration. @ConditionalOnBean(MeterRegistry.class) is a register-bean condition, so the class declares after = MetricsAutoConfiguration; without that ordering the metrics bean would appear or not depending on the alphabetical sort. Nested static configurations isolate optional dependencies (Actuator, Micrometer) so NoClassDefFoundError cannot occur in the outer class. @ConditionalOnEnabledHealthIndicator honours management.health.foo.enabled. Ship it as acme-foo-spring-boot-autoconfigure (FooClient optional) plus acme-foo-spring-boot-starter, with spring-boot-configuration-processor for metadata.

⚡ Rapid-fire: auto-configuration & Boot internals

  • Spring vs Spring Boot in one line? — Framework vs opinionated auto-configuration + starters + embedded server + executable jar.
  • @SpringBootApplication = ? — @SpringBootConfiguration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan.
  • What does @EnableAutoConfiguration import? — AutoConfigurationImportSelector, a DeferredImportSelector.
  • Where are Boot 3 auto-configs listed? — META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports.
  • Is spring.factories dead? — Only for auto-configs; still used for listeners, initializers, failure analyzers, env post-processors.
  • Why does user config beat auto-config? — Deferred import: auto-configs are parsed after all user configuration.
  • Order auto-configs how? — @AutoConfigureBefore/After/Order; user configs cannot be ordered against them.
  • Disable one auto-config? — exclude= / spring.autoconfigure.exclude / define your own bean.
  • See why a bean was or was not created? — --debug or /actuator/conditions (ConditionEvaluationReport).
  • Parse-phase vs register-bean conditions? — OnClass/OnProperty/OnWebApplication vs OnBean/OnMissingBean/OnSingleCandidate.
  • @ConditionalOnMissingBean in user config? — Order-dependent; use only in auto-configuration.
  • What is a starter? — POM-only dependency bundle without versions; versions from spring-boot-dependencies.
  • Override a managed version? — Property with the parent (jackson-bom.version) or declare before the BOM import.
  • Startup order? — Starting → Environment prepared → context created → initializers → refresh → Started → runners → Ready.
  • Where does Tomcat start? — onRefresh() creates it, finishRefresh() starts it, inside refresh().
  • Events a @Component cannot hear? — Starting, EnvironmentPrepared, ContextInitialized, Prepared (pre-refresh).
  • "APPLICATION FAILED TO START" block from? — FailureAnalyzers in handleRunFailure.
  • Top of the property stack? — Test props → command line → SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON → system props → env vars → profile yml → yml.
  • Profile file vs base file? — Profile-specific always wins (Boot 2.4+).
  • Activate a YAML document per profile? — spring.config.activate.on-profile (was spring.profiles).
  • Profile group? — spring.profiles.group.prod=a,b expands one profile into several.
  • Kubernetes secret files as properties? — spring.config.import=configtree:/path/.
  • Tomcat defaults? — 200 max threads, 8192 max connections, 100 accept-count, port 8080.
  • Switch Tomcat → Jetty? — Exclude spring-boot-starter-tomcat, add spring-boot-starter-jetty.
  • Virtual threads? — spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true, Boot 3.2 + Java 21.
  • Actuator endpoints exposed by default? — health only (Boot 3).
  • Liveness vs readiness? — Restart me vs stop routing to me; never put external deps in liveness.
  • Custom health check? — Implement HealthIndicator, add its key to a health group.
  • Metrics library? — Micrometer; Boot 3 adds Observation API and Micrometer Tracing (replaces Sleuth).
  • Secure Actuator? — Separate management.server.port, minimal exposure, EndpointRequest matchers, show-details=when-authorized.
  • DevTools restart trick? — Two classloaders; only project classes reload in RestartClassLoader.
  • How does java -jar run nested jars? — JarLauncher + LaunchedClassLoader over BOOT-INF/classes and lib/.
  • Layered jar layers? — dependencies, spring-boot-loader, snapshot-dependencies, application.
  • Build an image without a Dockerfile? — mvn spring-boot:build-image (Paketo buildpacks).
  • Native image constraint? — Closed world: conditions fixed at build, reflection/proxies/resources need RuntimeHints.
  • @SpringBootTest default web environment? — MOCK.
  • @WebMvcTest loads services? — No; mock them with @MockitoBean (@MockBean before 3.4).
  • Why many contexts in a test suite? — Cache key includes mocks, properties, profiles; each variant starts a new context.
  • @ServiceConnection? — Boot 3.1: derives connection properties from a Testcontainers container automatically.
  • Boot 3 baseline? — Java 17, Spring 6, Jakarta EE 9/10 (jakarta.*), Hibernate 6.
  • Trailing slash in Boot 3? — No longer matches by default; /orders/ ≠ /orders.
  • WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter in Boot 3? — Removed; expose a SecurityFilterChain bean and use requestMatchers.
  • Find renamed properties during migration? — spring-boot-properties-migrator.

3️⃣ Web MVC & REST APIs

Almost every Spring Boot interview contains a "walk me through what happens when a request hits your controller" question, and the follow-ups fan out from there: where a filter runs versus an interceptor, why an @ExceptionHandler did not fire, why validation was silently ignored, why the API froze at 200 concurrent users. This section follows that request: servlet container → filter chain → DispatcherServlet → mapping, binding, validation → controller → response conversion → exception handling, then the REST design, HTTP client, async/reactive and testing questions that build on it.

Request lifecycle: Tomcat → Filters → DispatcherServlet → controller → response

Why interviewers ask: the canonical "explain the flow" question. A senior answer names the actual classes in order and knows which of them are pluggable, because every later question (filters, interceptors, converters, exception handling) is "where in this flow does X happen?".

Boot embeds Tomcat (default; Jetty/Undertow are swaps). A Tomcat worker thread (http-nio-8080-exec-N, pool default max 200) parses the bytes into an HttpServletRequest and runs the Filter chain (Boot registers your Filter beans, Spring Security's FilterChainProxy, CharacterEncodingFilter, RequestContextFilter…). The last link of that chain is the DispatcherServlet, Spring's front controller, mapped to /. Analogy: Tomcat is the building's mail room, filters are security checkpoints in the corridor, the DispatcherServlet is the receptionist who looks up which office (handler) should get the letter.

Inside doDispatch(): (1) the HandlerMapping list (RequestMappingHandlerMapping for @RequestMapping, others for static resources) returns a HandlerExecutionChain = handler + interceptors; (2) a HandlerAdapter (RequestMappingHandlerAdapter) knows how to invoke it: preHandle interceptors, then HandlerMethodArgumentResolvers build each parameter (@PathVariable, @RequestBody via an HttpMessageConverter, …), the method runs, and HandlerMethodReturnValueHandlers process the result: @ResponseBody/ResponseEntity → pick an HttpMessageConverter by content negotiation (Jackson's MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter for JSON) and write straight to the response; a String view name → ViewResolver (Thymeleaf) renders a template. (3) Exceptions from any of this go to the HandlerExceptionResolver chain (@ExceptionHandler lives in ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver). Finally afterCompletion interceptors run and the response flows back out through the filters.

// Simplified shape of DispatcherServlet.doDispatch (Spring 6)
HandlerExecutionChain chain = getHandler(request);          // HandlerMappings
HandlerAdapter ha = getHandlerAdapter(chain.getHandler());
if (!chain.applyPreHandle(request, response)) return;       // interceptors
ModelAndView mv = ha.handle(request, response, chain.getHandler()); // args → method → return value
chain.applyPostHandle(request, response, mv);
processDispatchResult(request, response, chain, mv, exception);      // exception resolvers, view
// afterCompletion runs in a finally-like path for every interceptor whose preHandle ran
Interview angle: "Is the DispatcherServlet a singleton? Is the controller?" Both are singletons, so a controller with a mutable instance field is a data race across Tomcat threads. Also: Boot registers exactly one DispatcherServlet (DispatcherServletAutoConfiguration) at spring.mvc.servlet.path=/; a second one is possible with a ServletRegistrationBean for a separately configured child context.

Pitfalls

  • Reading the request body in a filter consumes the InputStream; @RequestBody then sees an empty body. Wrap with ContentCachingRequestWrapper.
  • Expecting @ExceptionHandler to catch a filter exception: the resolver chain is inside the servlet; filters are outside. You get the BasicErrorController page instead.
  • Static resources: ResourceHttpRequestHandler is also a "handler" — a wildcard controller mapping like /{id} can shadow /favicon.ico.
Interview questions
  • Walk me through what happens when POST /orders hits a Boot app. — Tomcat worker parses the request → servlet filter chain (Security first) → DispatcherServlet.doDispatch → RequestMappingHandlerMapping finds the method and interceptors → preHandle → argument resolvers (Jackson reads @RequestBody, validation) → method → return value handler picks an HttpMessageConverter by Accept → postHandle/afterCompletion → response unwinds through filters.
  • What is the front controller pattern and why one servlet? — One entry point centralises routing, security hooks, exception translation and content negotiation; controllers stay plain classes instead of servlets each mapped in web.xml.
  • How does Spring choose the HttpMessageConverter? — It intersects the request's Accept with what the mapping produces, then iterates converters in order asking canWrite(type, mediaType); first match wins, so registration order matters when you add a custom one.
  • What if no handler matches? — DispatcherServlet.noHandlerFound → 404; with spring.mvc.throw-exception-if-no-handler-found=true (default in Boot 3.2+) a NoHandlerFoundException/NoResourceFoundException is thrown so your advice can format it.
  • Is the DispatcherServlet thread-safe? Where is per-request state? — Yes; per-request state lives in the request attributes, RequestContextHolder (a ThreadLocal, populated by RequestContextFilter/the servlet), and method parameters.
  • How would you debug "my controller is never reached"? — Enable logging.level.org.springframework.web=DEBUG (Spring 6 logs mappings and the chosen handler), check /actuator/mappings, verify no filter short-circuits (Security 401/403 happens before the servlet), and confirm the class is inside the scanned package.
  • Boot 2 vs 3 differences in this pipeline? — javax.servlet → jakarta.servlet (Servlet 6, Tomcat 10.1), PathPatternParser is the default matcher, trailing-slash matching is off, and 404s throw exceptions so ProblemDetail bodies can be produced.

Filters vs HandlerInterceptors vs AOP vs @ControllerAdvice: where each runs

Why interviewers ask: four ways to run "something before every request"; choosing the wrong layer produces bugs that are hard to explain (advice that never fires, a filter that runs twice, a header set after the response was committed). The probe is: do you know the nesting order?

Think of four concentric rings. Servlet Filter (Jakarta spec, outermost): sees raw request/response, can wrap streams, runs even for 404s and static files, has no idea which controller will handle the request. HandlerInterceptor (Spring MVC): inside the DispatcherServlet, knows the resolved handler (HandlerMethod, so it can read the controller's annotations), three hooks: preHandle (return false to stop), postHandle (after the method, before view rendering; not called for @ResponseBody after the body is already written, and not after exceptions), afterCompletion (always, with the exception). AOP @Around on the controller bean: innermost, sees Java arguments and return values, only for that bean's public methods. @ControllerAdvice is not a ring: it contributes @ExceptionHandler, @InitBinder, @ModelAttribute and ResponseBodyAdvice (mutate the body before conversion) to all controllers.

Ordering: filters by @Order/FilterRegistrationBean.setOrder() (Security's chain is at -100; lower = outer/earlier); a Filter bean is also auto-registered for all URLs, so use a FilterRegistrationBean to limit URL patterns or disable auto-registration (setEnabled(false)) when the filter belongs only to Security. OncePerRequestFilter guards against running twice in the same request on FORWARD/ERROR/async dispatches (the error page dispatch re-runs plain filters!). Interceptors are ordered by their registration order in WebMvcConfigurer.addInterceptors.

@Component @Order(10)
public class CorrelationIdFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        String id = Optional.ofNullable(req.getHeader("X-Correlation-Id")).orElse(UUID.randomUUID().toString());
        MDC.put("cid", id);
        try { res.setHeader("X-Correlation-Id", id); chain.doFilter(req, res); }
        finally { MDC.remove("cid"); }              // thread goes back to the pool: clean up!
    }
}

@Bean FilterRegistrationBean<AuditFilter> auditFilter(AuditFilter f) {
    var reg = new FilterRegistrationBean<>(f);
    reg.addUrlPatterns("/api/*"); reg.setOrder(20);   // scope + order, instead of "all URLs"
    return reg;
}

@Configuration class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    public void addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry r) {
        r.addInterceptor(new TimingInterceptor()).addPathPatterns("/api/**").excludePathPatterns("/api/health");
    }
}
FilterHandlerInterceptorAOP aspect@ControllerAdvice
LayerServlet containerDispatcherServletBean proxyMVC infrastructure
Knows the handler?NoYes (HandlerMethod)Yes (join point)Yes
Can wrap/replace request & responseYesNoNoBody only (ResponseBodyAdvice)
Exceptions go toContainer error page@ExceptionHandler@ExceptionHandleris the handler
Typical useAuth, CORS, logging, compression, MDCRate limit, locale, timing per handlerBusiness cross-cuts, audit of argsError format, binder config, global model

Pitfalls

  • A plain Filter runs again on the ERROR dispatch to /error; logging filters then double-log. Extend OncePerRequestFilter (and override shouldNotFilterErrorDispatch if needed).
  • Setting headers in postHandle for a @RestController is too late: the body has already been written and the response committed. Use a filter, ResponseBodyAdvice, or set them in the controller.
  • Forgetting to clear ThreadLocal/MDC in finally: the pooled thread leaks the previous user's context into the next request.
  • Registering a Security filter both as a @Component and in the SecurityFilterChain: it runs twice; disable auto-registration with a FilterRegistrationBean.
Interview questions
  • Filter vs interceptor: when would you choose which? — Filter when you need the raw request/response, must cover non-MVC paths, or must run before Security; interceptor when you need to know the target handler or its annotations, or want @ExceptionHandler to handle failures.
  • Why did my @ControllerAdvice not handle the JWT exception? — It was thrown in a Security filter, outside the DispatcherServlet; handle it with an AuthenticationEntryPoint/AccessDeniedHandler, or delegate from a filter to HandlerExceptionResolver (inject the handlerExceptionResolver bean and call resolveException).
  • What does OncePerRequestFilter actually guarantee? — It sets a request attribute the first time and skips on re-entry, so the filter runs once per request across FORWARD, INCLUDE, ERROR and async dispatches; plain filters may run several times.
  • How do you control filter order in Boot? — @Order on the Filter bean or FilterRegistrationBean.setOrder; lower values run first; Security's FilterChainProxy defaults to -100 (spring.security.filter.order); HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE for the correlation-ID filter is common.
  • Can an interceptor modify the response body? — No; by postHandle a @ResponseBody is already written. Use ResponseBodyAdvice<T> for envelope wrapping or a filter with ContentCachingResponseWrapper.
  • Is a Filter bean a Spring bean with full DI? — Yes in Boot: ServletContextInitializerBeans registers Filter beans with the embedded container, so constructor injection works; with an external WAR you would need DelegatingFilterProxy.
  • How would you implement per-endpoint rate limiting? — A HandlerInterceptor: cast the handler to HandlerMethod, read a custom @RateLimited annotation, check a bucket (Bucket4j/Redis), return false with 429 and Retry-After.
  • Boot 2 vs 3? — Filter API is jakarta.servlet.Filter; interceptors are unchanged; note that with PathPatternParser interceptor path patterns are also parsed by the new parser, so /api/**/x style patterns differ.

@Controller vs @RestController, mapping variants, Spring 6 path matching, content negotiation

Why interviewers ask: quick "do you know the API" screening, with one trap that bites real migrations: Spring 6 stopped matching /orders/ to /orders, and stopped supporting suffix patterns like /orders.json.

@RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody: every return value goes through an HttpMessageConverter instead of a ViewResolver. @RequestMapping is the general form; @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, @DeleteMapping are composed shortcuts. Narrowing attributes: params, headers, consumes (matched against Content-Type, else 415), produces (matched against Accept, else 406). When several mappings match, the most specific wins (literal segments beat variables beat wildcards).

Spring 6 / Boot 3 path matching: the default matcher is PathPatternParser (pre-parsed patterns, faster, ** only allowed at the end, {*path} captures the rest). Trailing-slash matching is off by default (/orders/ → 404 for a /orders mapping; the deprecated setUseTrailingSlashMatch(true) was removed in 6.1 — use a redirect filter or map both). Content negotiation uses the Accept header only by default; path-extension negotiation is gone, and the format query parameter is opt-in (spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.favor-parameter=true).

@RestController
@RequestMapping(path = "/api/v1/orders", produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
public class OrderController {
    @GetMapping("/{id}")                                         // literal beats {id}? no: /search below is literal, wins over /{id}
    OrderDto get(@PathVariable long id) { … }

    @GetMapping("/search")
    List<OrderDto> search(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page) { … }

    @GetMapping(path = "/{id}", produces = "application/vnd.shop.v2+json")   // versioning via media type
    OrderDtoV2 getV2(@PathVariable long id) { … }

    @PostMapping(consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    OrderDto create(@RequestBody @Valid CreateOrder body) { … }

    @GetMapping("/files/{*path}")                             // PathPatternParser: captures "a/b/c.txt"
    Resource file(@PathVariable String path) { … }
}
ConcernBoot 2.x / Spring 5Boot 3.x / Spring 6
Path matcherAntPathMatcherPathPatternParser (opt back with spring.mvc.pathmatch.matching-strategy=ant_path_matcher)
/orders/ matches /ordersYesNo (404)
Suffix /orders.jsonOff by default since 5.3, possibleRemoved
** in the middleAllowedOnly at the end; use {*rest}

Pitfalls

  • Returning a String from a @Controller method without @ResponseBody is a view name → "Could not resolve view" error, not text.
  • Two methods on the same path differing only by produces plus a client sending Accept: */*: the first registered one is chosen; make one the explicit default or use a version header.
  • @RequestMapping without a method matches all methods, including OPTIONS and HEAD, hiding CORS preflight problems.
Interview questions
  • Difference between @Controller and @RestController? — @RestController adds @ResponseBody at class level, so return values are serialised by message converters instead of resolved as view names.
  • What breaks in path matching when upgrading to Boot 3? — Trailing slashes no longer match, suffix patterns are gone, and ** is only valid at the end of a pattern; the fix is to add explicit mappings or a redirecting filter, not to disable the parser globally.
  • How is a 406 vs 415 produced? — 406 Not Acceptable: no converter can produce a type in Accept (or produces mismatch); 415 Unsupported Media Type: the request Content-Type does not match consumes or no converter can read it.
  • Can two handlers have the same path? — Yes if they differ by method, params, headers, consumes or produces; otherwise IllegalStateException: Ambiguous handler methods at startup.
  • How would you version a REST API? — URL prefix (/v1) is simplest and cache-friendly; header or media-type versioning keeps URLs stable; Spring 7 adds first-class API versioning, in Boot 3 use produces/headers attributes or a custom RequestCondition.
  • What does @ResponseStatus on a method do versus ResponseEntity? — Fixed status for the happy path (also on an exception class for a fixed error status); ResponseEntity lets you decide status and headers per call.

Argument binding, custom resolvers and Jackson configuration

Why interviewers ask: "why is my LocalDate serialised as an array?" and "how do I inject the current user into every controller without @AuthenticationPrincipal?" both come down to knowing which resolver/converter is doing the work and where Boot lets you customise it.

Each parameter is handled by the first HandlerMethodArgumentResolver that supportsParameter: @PathVariable (URI template, converted via the ConversionService), @RequestParam (query/form fields; a Map or MultiValueMap gets all of them; required by default → 400 MissingServletRequestParameterException), @RequestHeader, @CookieValue, @RequestBody (whole body via an HttpMessageConverter; missing body → 400 HttpMessageNotReadableException), @ModelAttribute (the default for non-simple types without annotations: bind query/form fields onto a bean via WebDataBinder using setters or a constructor, then validate). Plain HttpServletRequest, Principal, Locale are resolved without annotation. Type conversion for simple parameters uses Converter/Formatter beans (@DateTimeFormat); a custom resolver plus a custom annotation (e.g. @CurrentTenant) is registered through WebMvcConfigurer.addArgumentResolvers.

Jackson in Boot 3: JacksonAutoConfiguration builds one ObjectMapper through Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilder with JavaTimeModule, ParameterNamesModule and Jdk8Module registered, WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS disabled (ISO-8601 strings) and FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES disabled. Customise with spring.jackson.* properties, a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer bean, or Module beans; declaring your own @Bean ObjectMapper replaces Boot's and loses those defaults. Java records deserialise natively (Jackson 2.12+; canonical constructor, no setters needed). @JsonView on the handler method filters fields per view; MappingJacksonValue does it programmatically.

public record CreateOrder(@NotBlank String sku, @Positive int qty,
                          @JsonFormat(pattern = "yyyy-MM-dd") LocalDate deliverOn) {}

// custom resolver: @CurrentTenant String tenant  →  read from a header / JWT claim
@Component
class TenantArgumentResolver implements HandlerMethodArgumentResolver {
    public boolean supportsParameter(MethodParameter p) {
        return p.hasParameterAnnotation(CurrentTenant.class) && p.getParameterType() == String.class;
    }
    public Object resolveArgument(MethodParameter p, ModelAndViewContainer mav,
                                  NativeWebRequest req, WebDataBinderFactory f) {
        String t = req.getHeader("X-Tenant");
        if (t == null) throw new MissingRequestHeaderException("X-Tenant", p);   // → 400
        return t;
    }
}

@Bean
Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer jackson() {          // keeps Boot's defaults, adds yours
    return b -> b.serializationInclusion(JsonInclude.Include.NON_NULL)
                 .featuresToEnable(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES);
}
Interview angle: "A GET with a filter object of 8 optional fields: @RequestParam ×8 or one object?" Use a @ModelAttribute record/bean (?status=OPEN&from=2024-01-01 binds by field name); Spring 6.1 binds records via the constructor, so no setters are needed. @RequestBody on a GET is legal but rejected by many proxies and caches.

Pitfalls

  • Two @RequestBody parameters: the stream can be read only once → the second gets an empty body. Wrap both in one DTO.
  • @RequestParam Optional<String> x works, but @RequestParam int x with a missing value cannot be null → 400; use Integer or defaultValue.
  • A bean with a Boolean isActive getter named isActive(): Jackson names the property active, the JSON says isActive, silent mismatch (unknown properties are ignored by default in Boot!).
  • Relying on @JsonView without setting spring.jackson.mapper.default-view-inclusion=true: fields without a view annotation disappear.
Interview questions
  • @RequestParam vs @PathVariable vs @RequestBody vs @ModelAttribute? — Query/form field, URI template segment, entire body through a converter, and multi-field binding from request parameters onto an object (with validation) respectively.
  • How does Spring deserialise JSON into your DTO? — RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor picks a converter by Content-Type; MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter calls Boot's ObjectMapper.readValue; for a record it uses the canonical constructor with parameter names.
  • Why is my LocalDateTime serialised as [2024,1,15,10,0]? — Someone declared a bare new ObjectMapper() (bean or static), bypassing Boot's builder that disables WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS and registers JavaTimeModule; inject the Boot mapper or use a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer.
  • How do you write a custom argument resolver? — Implement HandlerMethodArgumentResolver (supportsParameter, resolveArgument), register in WebMvcConfigurer.addArgumentResolvers; custom resolvers run after the built-in ones, so they cannot override @RequestParam handling.
  • What happens with an unknown JSON property? — Ignored: Boot sets FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES=false; enable it (or @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown=false)) if strict contracts matter.
  • How do you expose different fields of the same DTO to admins and customers? — @JsonView(Views.Admin.class) on fields and handler methods, or separate DTOs/records (usually clearer), or a MappingJacksonValue with a FilterProvider.
  • Do records need @JsonCreator? — No with Jackson 2.12+ and Java 17: the canonical constructor is detected; you only need @JsonProperty when JSON names differ from component names.
  • Boot 2 vs 3? — Same Jackson 2.x line (2.15+ in Boot 3, with default string-length/nesting limits added in 2.15), ParameterNamesModule is auto-registered, and Boot 3.x uses -parameters so constructor binding works without extra annotations.

Validation: @Valid vs @Validated, groups, custom constraints, method validation

Why interviewers ask: two different machines produce validation errors in a Boot app and they throw different exceptions with different default statuses (400 vs 500). "Why is @Min on my @RequestParam ignored?" separates people who have read the stack trace from those who copy annotations.

Bean Validation 3.0 (jakarta.validation, implemented by Hibernate Validator 8; add spring-boot-starter-validation, it is no longer transitively included since Boot 2.3). @Valid (Jakarta) marks an object for cascaded validation; on a @RequestBody/@ModelAttribute parameter, the argument resolver runs the validator and, on failure, throws MethodArgumentNotValidException (@RequestBody) or BindException (@ModelAttribute) → 400 by default. Nested objects and collection elements need their own @Valid (List<@Valid Item>). @Validated (Spring) does two things: with groups it selects which constraints run, and on a class it turns on method validation through MethodValidationPostProcessor, which creates an AOP proxy and validates parameters and return values of every public method (@Min on a @RequestParam, on a service method…). Failures there are ConstraintViolationException → 500 unless you map it.

Spring 6.1 / Boot 3.2 change: controller method validation is built into the HandlerAdapter whenever a Bean Validation provider is present and a method parameter has a constraint; no @Validated on the class is needed, and failures throw HandlerMethodValidationException (400, handled by ResponseEntityExceptionHandler). If you still put @Validated on the controller, the older AOP path applies instead and you get ConstraintViolationException. Custom constraints: an annotation meta-annotated with @Constraint(validatedBy=…) and a ConstraintValidator<A, T>; validators are Spring beans, so you can inject a repository for uniqueness checks.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/orders")
class OrderController {
    private final OrderService service;
    OrderController(OrderService s) { this.service = s; }

    @PostMapping
    OrderDto create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrder body) {   // (A) body validation
        return service.create(body);
    }

    @GetMapping
    Page<OrderDto> list(@RequestParam @Min(0) int page,      // (B) parameter constraint
                        @RequestParam @Max(100) int size) {
        return service.list(page, size);
    }
}

@Service @Validated
class OrderService {
    OrderDto create(@Valid CreateOrder o) { … }               // (C) method validation via proxy
    @NotNull OrderDto find(@NotBlank String id) { … }
}

record CreateOrder(@NotBlank String sku, @Positive int qty, @Valid @NotNull Address ship) {}
  1. @Valid on the body: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor validates right after deserialisation and throws MethodArgumentNotValidException with a BindingResult.
  2. Cascade: ship is validated only because the record component carries @Valid; the same rule applies to List<@Valid Item>.
  3. Parameter constraints on a controller: in Spring 6.1+ the HandlerAdapter validates them itself and throws HandlerMethodValidationException (400).
  4. Same code in Boot 2.x, or with @Validated on the controller: the AOP interceptor throws ConstraintViolationException, which nobody maps → 500 unless your advice does.
  5. Service-level validation requires @Validated on the class so a proxy exists; self-invocation bypasses it, and the exception is ConstraintViolationException.
  6. Return values can be constrained too; a null from find fails after the method returns.
@Target({FIELD, PARAMETER}) @Retention(RUNTIME)
@Constraint(validatedBy = UniqueSkuValidator.class)
public @interface UniqueSku { String message() default "sku already exists";
                              Class<?>[] groups() default {}; Class<? extends Payload>[] payload() default {}; }

@Component   // validators are Spring beans → repository injection works
class UniqueSkuValidator implements ConstraintValidator<UniqueSku, String> {
    private final ProductRepository repo;
    UniqueSkuValidator(ProductRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }
    public boolean isValid(String sku, ConstraintValidatorContext ctx) {
        return sku == null || !repo.existsBySku(sku);   // null-safety belongs to @NotNull, not here
    }
}

// groups: create requires no id, update requires one
record ProductDto(@Null(groups = OnCreate.class) @NotNull(groups = OnUpdate.class) Long id,
                  @NotBlank String name) {}
@PutMapping("/{id}") void update(@Validated(OnUpdate.class) @RequestBody ProductDto p) { … }

Pitfalls

  • @Valid on List<CreateOrder> body: before Spring 6.1 elements were not validated; use List<@Valid CreateOrder> or a wrapper DTO. In 6.1+ container elements are validated through method validation.
  • Group-specific constraints run only when the group is requested; a constraint with groups={OnUpdate.class} is skipped by plain @Valid (which uses the Default group).
  • Forgetting spring-boot-starter-validation: annotations compile (API on classpath through other starters) but nothing validates.
  • A ConstraintValidator that is not thread-safe: one instance serves all threads.
Interview questions
  • @Valid vs @Validated? — @Valid is the Jakarta annotation for cascaded object validation; @Validated is Spring's, supports validation groups, and on a class enables AOP-based method validation of parameters and return values.
  • Why is @Min(0) on a @RequestParam ignored? — Before Boot 3.2 method-level constraints needed @Validated on the controller class (proxy); since Spring 6.1 they are validated by the handler adapter automatically.
  • MethodArgumentNotValidException vs ConstraintViolationException? — The first comes from @Valid on a @RequestBody in the argument resolver (400, has a BindingResult); the second from the method-validation proxy (500 by default; map it in an advice).
  • Validation annotations on nested objects are ignored. Why? — Cascading is opt-in: the field or collection element type must be annotated @Valid.
  • How do you validate "either A or B must be set"? — A class-level custom constraint (@Target(TYPE)) with a ConstraintValidator<Ann, Dto>, or a cross-field check in the service; use ctx.buildConstraintViolationWithTemplate(...).addPropertyNode("a") for a field-level error path.
  • Can a custom validator hit the database? — Yes, validators are Spring-managed in Boot, but keep it read-only and cheap, and remember validation runs before the transaction starts.
  • How do you return all field errors as JSON? — Handle MethodArgumentNotValidException in a @RestControllerAdvice, iterate ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors(), or extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler and build a ProblemDetail with an errors property.
  • Boot 2 vs 3? — javax.validation → jakarta.validation (Bean Validation 3.0, Hibernate Validator 8); Spring 6.1 built-in controller method validation with HandlerMethodValidationException; validation of @ConfigurationProperties still uses @Validated.

Exception handling: @ExceptionHandler, advices, ProblemDetail, BasicErrorController

Why interviewers ask: "your advice catches Exception, another catches NotFoundException; which one runs?", "why did the client get an HTML error page from a REST API?", and, for Boot 3, "what is RFC 7807 and how does Spring 6 support it?".

When a handler (or an interceptor/argument resolver) throws, DispatcherServlet.processHandlerException walks the HandlerExceptionResolver chain in order: (1) ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver: first looks for @ExceptionHandler methods in the throwing controller, then in @ControllerAdvice beans sorted by @Order (default lowest precedence, i.e. declaration order is undefined without @Order); within one class the method whose declared exception type is closest to the thrown type wins (ExceptionDepthComparator), not the first declared. Advices can be scoped with basePackages, assignableTypes or annotations. (2) ResponseStatusExceptionResolver: @ResponseStatus on the exception class, and ResponseStatusException. (3) DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver: Spring MVC's own exceptions (HttpMessageNotReadableException → 400, HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException → 405, …).

If nothing resolves it (or the exception was thrown in a filter), the servlet container performs an ERROR dispatch to /error, served by Boot's BasicErrorController: JSON (built from ErrorAttributes: timestamp, status, error, path; message and stack trace hidden unless server.error.include-message=always) for API clients, an HTML "Whitelabel" page for browsers (Accept: text/html). Spring 6 / Boot 3 adds first-class RFC 7807 (now RFC 9457) Problem Details: the ProblemDetail class (type, title, status, detail, instance + custom properties), rendered as application/problem+json. Extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler in a @RestControllerAdvice (it already maps all MVC exceptions to ProblemDetail), throw ErrorResponseException subclasses from your code, and set spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true to get problem details for framework exceptions without writing an advice.

@RestControllerAdvice
@Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)
public class ApiExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {   // MVC exceptions → ProblemDetail

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
    ProblemDetail notFound(OrderNotFoundException ex, HttpServletRequest req) {
        var pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
        pd.setType(URI.create("https://api.shop.com/problems/order-not-found"));
        pd.setTitle("Order not found");
        pd.setProperty("orderId", ex.orderId());
        return pd;                                    // rendered as application/problem+json
    }

    @Override                                         // field errors for @Valid @RequestBody
    protected ResponseEntity<Object> handleMethodArgumentNotValid(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex,
            HttpHeaders headers, HttpStatusCode status, WebRequest request) {
        var pd = ex.getBody();                        // Spring 6 already builds a ProblemDetail
        pd.setProperty("errors", ex.getFieldErrors().stream()
            .map(f -> Map.of("field", f.getField(), "message", String.valueOf(f.getDefaultMessage()))).toList());
        return ResponseEntity.status(status).headers(headers).body(pd);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(ConstraintViolationException.class)   // method validation → 400, not 500
    ProblemDetail constraint(ConstraintViolationException ex) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, ex.getMessage());
    }
}
Interview angle: "How do you keep error responses consistent across 30 microservices?" Ship a shared @RestControllerAdvice in a starter (auto-configured with @ConditionalOnMissingBean), standardise on RFC 9457 ProblemDetail with a type URI catalogue, include a correlation ID property, and never leak stack traces (server.error.include-stacktrace=never). Keep @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) at lowest precedence and log it at ERROR with the correlation ID.

Pitfalls

  • Extending ResponseEntityExceptionHandler and also declaring @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) in the same class does not break, but declaring a handler for a type the base class already handles (e.g. MethodArgumentNotValidException) throws "Ambiguous @ExceptionHandler method mapped" at startup: override the protected method instead.
  • Two advices handling the same exception without @Order: behaviour depends on bean registration order; it changes when you rename a class.
  • @ExceptionHandler in a controller catches only that controller's exceptions; a @ControllerAdvice bean applies globally unless scoped.
  • Throwing from inside an @ExceptionHandler is not re-resolved: you get the container error page.
  • Security 401/403 never reach advices; customise AuthenticationEntryPoint / AccessDeniedHandler, or in Boot 3 let them fall through to /error.
Interview questions
  • Order of exception resolution in Spring MVC? — Controller-local @ExceptionHandler → @ControllerAdvice beans by @Order (closest exception type within a class) → @ResponseStatus/ResponseStatusException → DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver for MVC's own exceptions → container error dispatch to /error.
  • Two advices, one catching Exception, one catching NotFoundException: which runs? — Whichever advice bean sorts first; within a single class the most specific type wins. Put both in one class or give the specific advice a lower @Order.
  • What is RFC 7807 / ProblemDetail? — A standard JSON error body (type, title, status, detail, instance, extensions) with media type application/problem+json; Spring 6 adds the ProblemDetail class, ErrorResponse/ErrorResponseException, and ResponseEntityExceptionHandler produces it for all MVC exceptions.
  • Why does a REST client sometimes receive HTML on error? — The error went through BasicErrorController with Accept: text/html (browser) → Whitelabel page; with Accept: application/json it returns the JSON error map. Fix the root cause: handle it in an advice or set an error-attributes bean.
  • How would you handle an exception thrown from a filter with the same JSON format? — Inject HandlerExceptionResolver (qualifier handlerExceptionResolver) into the filter and call resolveException(req, res, null, ex), or write the ProblemDetail directly with the ObjectMapper.
  • How do you hide the message and stack trace in prod but show them in dev? — server.error.include-message, include-binding-errors, include-stacktrace (never|always|on_param) per profile; ?trace=true works only with on_param.
  • Does @ExceptionHandler fire for exceptions thrown in a @Async method called by a controller? — No; the async thread's exception goes to AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler. For Callable/DeferredResult handlers it does, after the async dispatch.
  • Boot 2 vs 3? — Boot 3 (Spring 6) introduces ProblemDetail and spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled; ResponseEntityExceptionHandler now returns problem-detail bodies instead of empty ones; 404s are exceptions (NoResourceFoundException in 6.1) so they reach advices.

REST design: idempotency, PUT vs PATCH, status codes, pagination, ETags, CORS

Why interviewers ask: the design round for API teams. They want HTTP semantics used correctly and the Spring mechanism that implements each one, plus a clear explanation of the CORS preflight that "only fails in the browser".

Idempotency: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE (and OPTIONS) must be safe to retry; POST is not, so payment-style POSTs take an Idempotency-Key header stored with the response (Redis with TTL) and replayed on retry. PUT replaces the whole representation (client sends everything, missing fields become null/default); PATCH applies a partial change (application/merge-patch+json or JSON Patch application/json-patch+json; Spring has no built-in merge-patch, so bind to a Map/JsonNode or use Optional fields and ObjectMapper.readerForUpdating). Status codes that get asked: 200 vs 201 (+Location) vs 202 (accepted, async) vs 204; 400 (malformed/validation) vs 422 (semantically invalid, opinion); 401 (not authenticated) vs 403; 404 vs 410; 409 (conflict, optimistic lock); 412/428 (preconditions); 429 with Retry-After; 503 vs 504.

Pagination: Spring Data's Pageable is resolvable as a controller argument (?page=0&size=20&sort=createdAt,desc, spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size default 2000); return a DTO, not Page<Entity> (unstable JSON; Boot 3.3 warns and offers PagedModel via @EnableSpringDataWebSupport(pageSerializationMode = VIA_DTO)). Use keyset/cursor pagination for large offsets. HATEOAS: spring-boot-starter-hateoas, EntityModel/CollectionModel, linkTo(methodOn(...)); rarely used in practice, but say "Richardson Maturity Model level 3". ETags/caching: ResponseEntity.ok().eTag(version).cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(...)), then request.checkNotModified(etag) → 304; If-Match on PUT gives optimistic concurrency (412 on mismatch); ShallowEtagHeaderFilter computes a hash after the fact (saves bandwidth, not CPU). CORS: enforced by the browser; a cross-origin request with non-simple headers/methods triggers an OPTIONS preflight that must answer Access-Control-Allow-Origin/-Methods/-Headers. In Spring: @CrossOrigin per handler/class, global WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings, or (when Security is present, preferred) a CorsConfigurationSource bean + http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults()), so the CorsFilter runs before authentication and the preflight does not need credentials.

@GetMapping("/{id}")
ResponseEntity<OrderDto> get(@PathVariable long id, WebRequest req) {
    var order = service.get(id);
    String etag = "\"" + order.version() + "\"";
    if (req.checkNotModified(etag)) return null;      // Spring writes 304 Not Modified
    return ResponseEntity.ok().eTag(etag).cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofSeconds(30)).cachePrivate()).body(order);
}

@PutMapping("/{id}")
ResponseEntity<OrderDto> replace(@PathVariable long id, @RequestHeader("If-Match") String ifMatch,
                                @Valid @RequestBody OrderDto body) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(service.replace(id, body, parseVersion(ifMatch)));   // 412 on version mismatch
}

@PostMapping
ResponseEntity<OrderDto> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrder in,
                               @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key) {
    var dto = service.createIdempotent(key, in);
    return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/api/v1/orders/" + dto.id())).body(dto);   // 201 + Location
}

@Bean CorsConfigurationSource corsConfigurationSource() {          // global, runs in Security's CorsFilter
    var cfg = new CorsConfiguration();
    cfg.setAllowedOriginPatterns(List.of("https://*.shop.com"));  // patterns needed with allowCredentials
    cfg.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"));
    cfg.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("Authorization", "Content-Type", "Idempotency-Key"));
    cfg.setAllowCredentials(true); cfg.setMaxAge(3600L);           // cache the preflight for 1h
    var src = new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource(); src.registerCorsConfiguration("/api/**", cfg); return src;
}
QuestionPUTPATCHPOST
SemanticsReplace entire resource at known URIPartial modificationCreate subordinate / process
Idempotent?YesNot by definition (merge-patch usually is)No (use Idempotency-Key)
Typical success200 or 204; 201 if it created200/204201 + Location, 202 async
ConcurrencyIf-Match ETag → 412If-MatchIdempotency-Key replay

Pitfalls

  • @CrossOrigin("*") with allowCredentials=true: browsers reject * with credentials; use allowedOriginPatterns.
  • CORS configured only in MVC (addCorsMappings) while Spring Security rejects the unauthenticated OPTIONS preflight with 401/403 → "works in Postman, fails in browser".
  • Returning Page<Entity> directly: lazy-loading exceptions, JSON structure changes between Spring Data versions, and entity fields leak.
  • Using 200 with {"error":…} bodies: breaks clients, caches and observability; status codes are the contract.
Interview questions
  • Is PATCH idempotent? Is DELETE? — DELETE yes (second call returns 404 or 204, state is the same); PATCH is not guaranteed (a "increment by 1" patch is not), though a merge-patch of absolute values is.
  • How do you make a POST safe to retry? — Client-generated Idempotency-Key; server stores key → response (with TTL) atomically with the side effect, returns the stored response on replay, 409/422 if the same key arrives with a different payload.
  • Why does CORS fail only in the browser? — CORS is a browser-enforced policy; curl/Postman skip it. The browser sends an OPTIONS preflight; if it returns 401 (Security) or lacks the Access-Control-Allow-* headers, the real request is never sent.
  • @CrossOrigin vs global config vs Security's CORS? — Per-controller annotation for quick cases; addCorsMappings for MVC-wide; with Security use a CorsConfigurationSource so the CorsFilter is placed before the authentication filters and preflights succeed.
  • ETag vs Last-Modified; strong vs weak? — ETag is an opaque version (strong: byte-identical; weak W/"…": semantically equivalent); Last-Modified is one-second granular. Use ETag from a version column for both caching (If-None-Match → 304) and optimistic locking (If-Match → 412).
  • How do you paginate 50 million rows? — Keyset (cursor) pagination on an indexed sort key (WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY … LIMIT n), returning an opaque cursor; offset pagination (Pageable) degrades as offset grows and needs a COUNT. Spring Data provides Slice (no count) and 3.1+ ScrollPosition.keyset().
  • How do you version an API without breaking clients? — Additive changes only (new optional fields), tolerant readers on both sides; when a breaking change is unavoidable, bump the URL/media-type version, run both for a sunset window, and announce via Deprecation/Sunset headers.
  • What is HATEOAS and do you use it? — Hypermedia links in responses so clients discover actions; Spring HATEOAS provides EntityModel/linkTo. Honest answer: valuable for public APIs and workflows, rarely worth it for internal microservices with generated clients.

HTTP clients: RestTemplate vs WebClient vs RestClient (6.1) vs @HttpExchange, timeouts and pools

Why interviewers ask: "is RestTemplate deprecated?" (no, maintenance mode) and, more importantly, "what timeouts did you set?" Most production outages in this area come from a client with no timeouts and a default pool of 5 connections per route.

RestTemplate: synchronous, template-style (getForObject, exchange), in maintenance mode since Spring 5; build it via RestTemplateBuilder so Boot's converters, interceptors and spring.http.client.* apply. WebClient (spring-webflux): reactive, non-blocking, fluent; returns Mono/Flux; calling .block() from an MVC controller works but wastes the reactive machinery and must never happen on a Netty event-loop thread. RestClient (Spring 6.1 / Boot 3.2): the modern synchronous client with the WebClient fluent API, built on the same ClientHttpRequestFactory abstraction as RestTemplate; Boot 3.2 auto-configures a RestClient.Builder, and 3.4 adds RestClientCustomizer/spring.http.client.* properties for the factory, connect and read timeouts. Declarative HTTP interfaces (@HttpExchange, @GetExchange, Spring 6): a Java interface implemented by HttpServiceProxyFactory backed by any of the three (RestClientAdapter, WebClientAdapter, RestTemplateAdapter), Feign-style without Feign. Boot 3.x has no auto-registration of these interfaces (that arrives with Boot 4 / @ImportHttpServices); you create the proxy in a @Bean.

Timeouts and pools live in the request factory, not the client: SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory (JDK HttpURLConnection, no pool), JdkClientHttpRequestFactory (Java 11 HttpClient, HTTP/2, Boot 3.2 default when nothing else is present), Apache HttpClient 5 (HttpComponentsClientHttpRequestFactory, real pooling, preferred when the jar is on the classpath), Reactor Netty for WebClient. Set connect timeout (TCP handshake, 1–3 s), read/response timeout (per request, from the callee's SLO, 2–5 s), and for Apache also connection-request timeout (waiting for a pooled connection, the one people forget) with maxTotal/maxPerRoute (Apache defaults: 25/5, far too small under load). Add retries with jitter only for idempotent calls, and a circuit breaker (Resilience4j) for dependencies that can be down.

@Configuration
class HttpClients {
    @Bean RestClient inventoryClient(RestClient.Builder builder) {          // Boot auto-configured builder
        var cm = PoolingHttpClientConnectionManagerBuilder.create()
            .setMaxConnTotal(200).setMaxConnPerRoute(50)
            .setDefaultConnectionConfig(ConnectionConfig.custom()
                .setConnectTimeout(Timeout.ofSeconds(2)).setSocketTimeout(Timeout.ofSeconds(3)).build())
            .build();
        var http = HttpClientBuilder.create().setConnectionManager(cm)
            .setDefaultRequestConfig(RequestConfig.custom()
                .setConnectionRequestTimeout(Timeout.ofMillis(500)).build())   // waiting for a pooled conn
            .evictIdleConnections(TimeValue.ofSeconds(30)).build();
        return builder.baseUrl("http://inventory")
            .requestFactory(new HttpComponentsClientHttpRequestFactory(http))
            .defaultStatusHandler(HttpStatusCode::is5xxServerError,
                                  (req, res) -> { throw new InventoryUnavailable(res.getStatusCode()); })
            .build();
    }

    @HttpExchange("/stock")
    interface StockApi {                                     // declarative HTTP interface
        @GetExchange("/{sku}") Stock get(@PathVariable String sku);
        @PostExchange ResponseEntity<Void> reserve(@RequestBody Reservation r);
    }

    @Bean StockApi stockApi(RestClient inventoryClient) {
        return HttpServiceProxyFactory.builderFor(RestClientAdapter.create(inventoryClient)).build()
                                      .createClient(StockApi.class);
    }
}
// usage: inventoryClient.get().uri("/stock/{sku}", sku).retrieve().body(Stock.class);
RestTemplateRestClient (6.1)WebClient@HttpExchange
ModelSync, template methodsSync, fluentReactive, fluentInterface; delegates to any
ThreadsBlocks callerBlocks caller (virtual-thread friendly)Event loop, non-blockingDepends on adapter
Dependencyspring-webspring-webspring-webflux (+ Reactor Netty)spring-web
StatusMaintenanceRecommended for MVCRecommended for WebFlux / streamingRecommended facade

Pitfalls

  • new RestTemplate() in a field: no timeouts at all (infinite read timeout with the JDK factory) → one slow dependency exhausts the Tomcat pool.
  • Adding spring-boot-starter-webflux to an MVC app only to get WebClient: Boot still runs Tomcat/MVC, but you drag Reactor Netty in; in 3.2+ use RestClient.
  • Building a RestClient/WebClient per request: a new connection pool each time, no keep-alive, socket exhaustion (TIME_WAIT).
  • Retrying a POST without an idempotency key after a read timeout: the first call may have succeeded.
Interview questions
  • Which client would you pick for a new Boot 3.2+ MVC service and why? — RestClient (or an @HttpExchange interface over it): synchronous like the rest of the stack, fluent API, no Reactor dependency, works well with virtual threads; WebClient only for a reactive stack or true streaming.
  • Is RestTemplate deprecated? — No; it is in maintenance mode (bug fixes, no new features). Migrate opportunistically to RestClient, which shares the same underlying request factories and message converters.
  • Which timeouts exist and what values would you set? — Connect (TCP/TLS handshake, ~1–2 s), read/response (per request, below the caller's own deadline, 2–5 s), connection-request (pool wait, hundreds of ms), plus an overall budget/deadline propagated through the call chain; also a keep-alive/idle eviction so stale connections are dropped.
  • What happens if the pool is exhausted? — Apache: callers wait up to connectionRequestTimeout, then ConnectionRequestTimeoutException; with no such timeout they block forever and your Tomcat threads die with them.
  • How do you call WebClient from an MVC controller? — .block(timeout) on a Tomcat thread is acceptable; better, return the Mono directly (MVC supports reactive return types via async request processing) or use RestClient.
  • How do you test code that uses RestClient? — @RestClientTest with MockRestServiceServer (bound to the builder), or WireMock for integration; for HTTP interfaces mock the interface.
  • How would you add auth headers and tracing to every outbound call? — ClientHttpRequestInterceptor on the builder (or ExchangeFilterFunction for WebClient); Micrometer Observation is auto-applied when you use the Boot-provided builder, propagating traceparent.
  • Boot 2 vs 3? — Boot 3.2 introduced RestClient and its auto-configured builder, HTTP interfaces via RestClientAdapter, and the JDK HttpClient as a default factory; Apache HttpClient 4 support was dropped in favour of HttpClient 5.

Async & streaming in MVC: Callable, DeferredResult, SSE, @Async and Tomcat pool sizing

Why interviewers ask: "the API hangs at 200 concurrent users" is the classic capacity problem; the follow-up is whether you know how async request processing frees the container thread, what it does not fix, and how to size server.tomcat.threads.max.

Tomcat's pool (server.tomcat.threads.max, default 200; server.tomcat.accept-count 100 queued connections beyond that; max-connections 8192) is the hard concurrency limit of a blocking MVC app: request 201 waits in the accept queue, and the client eventually times out. Servlet 3 async processing lets a handler return early: returning a Callable<T> runs it on Spring's AsyncTaskExecutor (spring.task.execution.*, Boot's applicationTaskExecutor, default core 8 threads) and releases the Tomcat thread; when the value is ready Spring performs an async dispatch back into the container on another Tomcat thread to write the response. A DeferredResult<T> is the same idea with the completion driven by your code (a message listener, a callback, a CompletableFuture), so no thread is held at all while waiting. Returning CompletableFuture, Mono or ListenableFuture is adapted to DeferredResult automatically. spring.mvc.async.request-timeout bounds the wait (503 by default on timeout); interceptors implementing AsyncHandlerInterceptor get afterConcurrentHandlingStarted.

Streaming: ResponseBodyEmitter sends multiple objects through message converters as they become available; SseEmitter formats them as text/event-stream Server-Sent Events (one-way, auto-reconnect in browsers, works through plain HTTP; WebSocket only if you need bidirectional); StreamingResponseBody writes raw bytes on a separate thread (large file downloads). Long-lived emitters must be completed or timed out, or they leak. @Async is different: it moves a service call to another thread and returns immediately; in a controller it is used for fire-and-forget (audit, email) and needs @EnableAsync, a proxy (no self-invocation), and an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler. Analogy: Callable/DeferredResult is a restaurant pager: the waiter (Tomcat thread) goes back to serving others and you are called when the table is ready; @Async is sending your order to the kitchen and walking out.

@GetMapping("/stock/{sku}")
DeferredResult<Stock> stock(@PathVariable String sku) {
    var result = new DeferredResult<Stock>(2_000L, Stock.unknown(sku));   // per-request timeout + fallback
    inventory.getAsync(sku)                                  // CompletableFuture from an async client
             .whenComplete((s, ex) -> { if (ex != null) result.setErrorResult(ex); else result.setResult(s); });
    return result;                                            // Tomcat thread released here
}

@GetMapping(path = "/events", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
SseEmitter events() {
    var emitter = new SseEmitter(0L);                          // 0 = no timeout (manage lifecycle yourself)
    emitters.add(emitter);
    emitter.onCompletion(() -> emitters.remove(emitter));
    emitter.onTimeout(emitter::complete);
    return emitter;                                            // later: emitter.send(SseEmitter.event().name("order").data(dto));
}
server.tomcat.threads.max: 200          # blocking work: ~ cores × (1 + wait/compute); IO-bound APIs often 200–400
server.tomcat.threads.min-spare: 10
server.tomcat.accept-count: 100         # backlog beyond max threads
server.tomcat.max-connections: 8192
server.tomcat.connection-timeout: 20s
spring.mvc.async.request-timeout: 30s   # Callable / DeferredResult / SseEmitter default timeout
spring.task.execution.pool.core-size: 8 # Callable + @Async executor (applicationTaskExecutor)
spring.task.execution.pool.max-size: 8  # note: queue-capacity unbounded by default → max-size never reached

Pitfalls

  • Returning Callable for a blocking DB call: you traded 200 Tomcat threads for 8 executor threads; latency gets worse. Async only helps when the wait is event-driven.
  • @Async with Boot's default executor: queue-capacity is unbounded, so max-size never grows past core-size and bursts silently queue in memory.
  • ThreadLocal context (SecurityContextHolder, MDC, request scope) does not follow the request to the async thread; use DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor or a TaskDecorator.
  • Filters and Security run again on the async dispatch: OncePerRequestFilter handles it, plain filters do not; Security's chain must permit the dispatch (DispatcherType.ASYNC).
  • SSE through a proxy with response buffering (nginx proxy_buffering on) delivers nothing until the emitter completes.
Interview questions
  • Requests hang after roughly 200 concurrent users. First three things you check? — Thread dump: are all http-nio-*-exec threads in the same blocking call (outbound HTTP/DB/lock)? Metrics tomcat.threads.busy vs config.max; and the timeouts/pool size of that dependency. Fix the wait (timeouts, pool, circuit breaker) before raising thread counts.
  • Callable vs DeferredResult? — Both release the Tomcat thread; Callable hands the work to Spring's task executor (still a thread doing the work), DeferredResult is completed by any external event, holding no thread at all while waiting.
  • How is the response written after the handler already returned? — Servlet 3 AsyncContext.dispatch(): the container re-dispatches the request (type ASYNC) to the DispatcherServlet, which sees the concurrent result and runs the normal return-value handling on a pool thread.
  • Does @Async on a controller method make the request asynchronous? — No; the proxy returns immediately (void or a Future) so the client gets an empty 200 while work continues; for request-level async return Callable/DeferredResult/CompletableFuture instead.
  • How would you size Tomcat's thread pool? — For blocking IO-bound handlers, threads ≈ cores × (1 + wait time / compute time), capped by memory (~1 MB stack each) and by downstream capacity; measure tomcat.threads.busy under load; better still, remove the blocking or enable virtual threads.
  • SSE vs WebSocket vs long polling? — SSE: server → client stream over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, auto-reconnect, text only, simplest for notifications; WebSocket: full-duplex binary/text, needs upgrade support in proxies; long polling: fallback with highest overhead.
  • What happens on spring.mvc.async.request-timeout expiry? — DeferredResult uses its timeout result if given, otherwise an AsyncRequestTimeoutException → 503 (handled by ResponseEntityExceptionHandler); the emitter's onTimeout callback runs.
  • Boot 2 vs 3? — Same MVC async model; Boot 3.2 adds virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled) which make the blocking style scale without DeferredResult, and AsyncRequestNotUsableException (6.1) for client disconnects during async handling.

WebFlux vs MVC: event loop vs thread-per-request, backpressure, and Boot 3 virtual threads

Why interviewers ask: "should we rewrite in WebFlux?" is a real architecture decision; the strong answer explains what the event loop buys, what it costs (every blocking call becomes a bug), and why virtual threads in Boot 3.2 changed the default recommendation back to MVC for most teams.

MVC: thread-per-request on a platform-thread pool; blocking code is natural; concurrency ≤ pool size. WebFlux: a small number of event-loop threads (Reactor Netty, default = CPU cores) drive many connections; handlers return Mono<T> (0..1) / Flux<T> (0..n) pipelines that are assembled lazily and executed when subscribed (the framework subscribes). Backpressure: a Subscriber requests n elements (Reactive Streams request(n)), so a fast producer (DB cursor, Kafka) cannot overwhelm a slow consumer; strategies onBackpressureBuffer/Drop/Latest. The entire chain must be non-blocking: R2DBC instead of JDBC, WebClient instead of RestClient, reactive Redis/Mongo drivers. One blocking call on an event-loop thread (JDBC, Thread.sleep, block(), a synchronous logger appender) stalls every connection on that loop; if unavoidable, isolate it with Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) and detect it with BlockHound in tests.

Boot 3.2 virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true, Java 21): Tomcat's executor, applicationTaskExecutor, @Async, @Scheduled, Kafka/RabbitMQ listener containers all run on virtual threads; a blocking JDBC call parks the virtual thread cheaply (its stack lives on the heap), the carrier thread moves on, and you get event-loop-like scalability with plain sequential code, stack traces and debuggers. Caveats: pinning when blocking inside synchronized (fixed in JDK 24; use ReentrantLock in 21), no benefit for CPU-bound work, and downstream pools (HikariCP maximumPoolSize) become the real limit, so bound concurrency with a Semaphore rather than the thread count. Analogy: MVC is one waiter per table who waits by the kitchen; WebFlux is one waiter running between tables, never allowed to stand still; virtual threads are waiters who cost nothing while standing still.

// WebFlux handler: nothing here blocks; the framework subscribes
@GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
Mono<OrderView> get(@PathVariable String id) {
    return repo.findById(id)                                   // ReactiveCrudRepository (R2DBC)
        .zipWith(inventory.get().uri("/stock/{id}", id).retrieve().bodyToMono(Stock.class))
        .map(t -> OrderView.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2()))
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new OrderNotFound(id)));
}

// unavoidable blocking library inside WebFlux: isolate it
Mono<Report> report() {
    return Mono.fromCallable(legacy::renderPdf).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());
}

// Boot 3.2 + Java 21 alternative: keep MVC, flip a property
// spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true   → Tomcat, @Async, @Scheduled, listeners on virtual threads
MVC (platform threads)WebFluxMVC + virtual threads
Programming modelBlocking, sequentialReactive pipelines (Mono/Flux)Blocking, sequential
Scales waiting on IOUp to pool sizeVery wellVery well (memory-bound)
Needs reactive driversNoYes (R2DBC, WebClient, reactive Redis)No
BackpressureNo (queueing)Yes, end to endNo (bound with semaphores/pools)
DebuggabilityGoodHard (assembly vs execution, lost stack traces)Good
Best forMost CRUD servicesStreaming, very high fan-out gateways, SSE at scaleIO-heavy MVC services on Java 21

Pitfalls

  • Mixing starters: with both spring-boot-starter-web and -webflux on the classpath Boot picks MVC; your RouterFunctions silently do nothing unless spring.main.web-application-type=reactive.
  • Returning a Mono but forgetting that nothing runs until subscription: a Mono created and discarded (not returned/chained) never executes.
  • ThreadLocal-based code (MDC, SecurityContextHolder) breaks in WebFlux; use Reactor Context / ReactiveSecurityContextHolder; with virtual threads, ThreadLocal works but is expensive per thread (consider ScopedValue).
  • Virtual threads with synchronized-heavy libraries (older JDBC drivers, some loggers) pin carriers; check with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full (JDK 21) and upgrade drivers.
Interview questions
  • When would you choose WebFlux over MVC? — When the service is IO-bound with very high concurrency or streaming (SSE, large fan-out gateway, chat), the entire dependency chain has reactive drivers, and the team can debug reactive code; otherwise MVC, now with virtual threads for the scalability.
  • What happens if you block inside a WebFlux handler? — The event-loop thread stalls, so every other request multiplexed on it stalls; throughput collapses even though CPU is idle. Detect with BlockHound; offload with subscribeOn(boundedElastic()).
  • Explain backpressure in one sentence. — The consumer tells the producer how many items it can take (request(n)), so buffers stay bounded instead of the producer flooding memory.
