  • Mono vs Flux vs CompletableFuture? — Mono: 0..1 lazy; Flux: 0..n lazy with backpressure; CompletableFuture: exactly one eager result, no backpressure, no cancellation of the chain.
  • Do virtual threads make WebFlux obsolete? — For "scale blocking IO" they do for most teams; WebFlux still wins for backpressure, streaming semantics and composition of many async sources. Spring's own guidance in 6.1+ is that MVC with virtual threads is the default choice.
  • What changes with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true? — Boot 3.2 wires a VirtualThreadTaskExecutor into Tomcat/Jetty's protocol handler, applicationTaskExecutor, the scheduler, and messaging listener containers; nothing in your code changes, but pool-sized resources and synchronized sections become the new bottlenecks.
  • How do you cap concurrency on a virtual-thread service? — Not via thread count; use a Semaphore around the scarce resource, connection-pool limits (Hikari, HTTP client), and rate limiters; Tomcat's max-connections still applies.
  • Boot 2 vs 3? — WebFlux is the same Reactor 3 model; Boot 3.2 added the virtual-thread switch (Java 21) and made RestClient available so MVC apps no longer need WebFlux for a modern HTTP client.

File upload/download, multipart limits and large responses

Why interviewers ask: a practical screen: "how do you upload a 2 GB file without loading it in memory?" and "why do we get 413 or MaxUploadSizeExceededException?".

Uploads use multipart/form-data; the servlet container parses parts (Boot's MultipartAutoConfiguration + StandardServletMultipartResolver) and Spring exposes each as a MultipartFile (@RequestPart for a named part, also usable with a JSON part; @RequestParam works for simple file parts). Limits: spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size (1 MB default) and max-request-size (10 MB default), file-size-threshold (above which parts are written to a temp dir instead of memory, 0 by default). Exceeding them throws MaxUploadSizeExceededException (handled by ResponseEntityExceptionHandler → 413 in Spring 6.1+). For huge files, stream: read file.getInputStream() and copy to object storage in chunks, or bypass multipart with a raw InputStream body and a pre-signed upload URL (S3) so bytes never touch your service.

Downloads: return ResponseEntity<Resource> (InputStreamResource, FileSystemResource) with Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="…" (build it with ContentDisposition.attachment().filename(name, UTF_8)), Content-Type and Content-Length; ResourceRegion/Range headers give resumable downloads. For generated large payloads use StreamingResponseBody (writes on an executor thread, releases Tomcat's) or a ResponseBodyEmitter; for large JSON lists page them, or stream NDJSON with Flux/application/x-ndjson. Enable server.compression.enabled=true for text responses above min-response-size.

@PostMapping(path = "/docs", consumes = MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE)
ResponseEntity<Void> upload(@RequestPart("meta") @Valid DocMeta meta,          // JSON part
                            @RequestPart("file") MultipartFile file) throws IOException {
    if (!"application/pdf".equals(file.getContentType())) return ResponseEntity.status(415).build();
    try (var in = file.getInputStream()) {
        storage.put(meta.key(), in, file.getSize());     // stream, never file.getBytes() for large files
    }
    return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/docs/" + meta.key())).build();
}

@GetMapping("/docs/{key}")
ResponseEntity<StreamingResponseBody> download(@PathVariable String key) {
    var doc = storage.describe(key);
    return ResponseEntity.ok()
        .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PDF).contentLength(doc.size())
        .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION, ContentDisposition.attachment().filename(doc.name(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8).build().toString())
        .body(out -> storage.copyTo(key, out));            // written on the MVC async executor
}

Pitfalls

  • file.getBytes() or new String(file.getBytes()) on large uploads → heap exhaustion; stream instead.
  • Trusting getOriginalFilename(): path traversal (../../etc/passwd); sanitise or generate your own key.
  • A reverse proxy (nginx client_max_body_size, 1 MB default) returns 413 before Spring sees the request; the limits must agree at every hop.
  • Temp files under spring.servlet.multipart.location (default the container temp dir) pile up if the container dies mid-request; clean up on a schedule.
Interview questions
  • How do you upload a file together with JSON metadata? — Two parts in one multipart request: @RequestPart("meta") DocMeta (converted by Jackson because of its part content type) and @RequestPart("file") MultipartFile.
  • Where does a 50 MB upload live while the controller runs? — In a temp file once it exceeds file-size-threshold; below it, in memory. With the default threshold 0, in a temp file, deleted after the request.
  • How would you support 5 GB uploads? — Do not proxy them: pre-signed URL upload straight to S3/GCS, then a small POST with the key; if you must accept them, raise limits, stream to storage, and use multipart-upload APIs for resumability.
  • Why use StreamingResponseBody over writing to HttpServletResponse directly? — It runs on the async executor and frees the Tomcat thread for the duration of the slow write, and integrates with spring.mvc.async.request-timeout.
  • What does Content-Disposition do? — attachment forces a browser download with the given filename (use the RFC 5987 filename* form for non-ASCII, which ContentDisposition builds for you); inline renders in the browser.

Testing controllers: @WebMvcTest, MockMvc, MockMvcTester (6.2), WebTestClient

Why interviewers ask: "what does @WebMvcTest load and what does it not?" tells them whether you understand slices, and "MockMvc or a real server?" tells them whether you know what a test actually proves.

@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class) is a slice: it auto-configures only the MVC layer (controllers, @ControllerAdvice, Filters, WebMvcConfigurers, Jackson, Security's filter chain) and MockMvc; no @Service, no JPA, no DataSource. Collaborators must be mocked with @MockBean (deprecated in Boot 3.4 in favour of @MockitoBean from Spring Framework 6.2). MockMvc drives the DispatcherServlet directly without a server or real sockets: filters and the whole MVC pipeline run, but Tomcat, HTTP parsing and compression do not. Spring 6.2 adds MockMvcTester: the same engine with an AssertJ fluent API (assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/orders/1")).hasStatusOk().bodyJson().extractingPath("$.id").isEqualTo(1)) and no checked exceptions. @SpringBootTest + @AutoConfigureMockMvc gives MockMvc against the full context (real services). @SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT) starts real Tomcat; test with TestRestTemplate, RestClient, or WebTestClient (needs spring-webflux on the test classpath, fluent, works for MVC and WebFlux; it can also be bound to MockMvc without a server via MockMvcWebTestClient). WebFlux slices use @WebFluxTest + WebTestClient.

@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
@Import(ApiExceptionHandler.class)            // advices in the slice are picked up; explicit import is fine too
class OrderControllerTest {
    @Autowired MockMvcTester mvc;             // Spring 6.2 / Boot 3.4 (MockMvc also available)
    @MockitoBean OrderService service;        // Boot 3.4+; use @MockBean on 3.0–3.3

    @Test void returnsProblemDetailWhenNotFound() {
        when(service.get(42L)).thenThrow(new OrderNotFoundException(42L));
        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/api/v1/orders/{id}", 42).accept(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))
            .hasStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
            .hasContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON)
            .bodyJson().extractingPath("$.orderId").isEqualTo(42);
    }

    @Test @WithMockUser(roles = "ADMIN")      // Security filters are part of the slice
    void validatesBody() throws Exception {
        MockMvc classic = mvc.mockMvc();      // classic API when you need it (Boot 3.4 exposes both beans)
        classic.perform(post("/api/v1/orders").with(csrf())
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content("{\"sku\":\"\",\"qty\":-1}"))
               .andExpect(status().isBadRequest())
               .andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors.length()").value(2));
    }
}
ApproachContextServerProvesSpeed
@WebMvcTest + MockMvcMVC slice onlyNoneMapping, binding, validation, advice, security rulesFast
@SpringBootTest + @AutoConfigureMockMvcFullNoneWiring end to end, no HTTPMedium
@SpringBootTest(RANDOM_PORT) + WebTestClient/TestRestTemplateFullReal TomcatReal HTTP, compression, async, TLSSlow
@WebFluxTest + WebTestClientWebFlux sliceNoneReactive handlers/routersFast

Pitfalls

  • @WebMvcTest fails with "No qualifying bean of type X": the controller's dependency is not mocked, or a WebMvcConfigurer/filter in the slice depends on a service; mock it or exclude the config.
  • Security in the slice: every @WebMvcTest gets Boot's default security → 401/403 surprises; use @WithMockUser, csrf(), or @AutoConfigureMockMvc(addFilters=false) (which also disables your own filters).
  • Asserting on MockMvc for async handlers: you need asyncDispatch(mvcResult) after request().asyncStarted(); MockMvcTester and WebTestClient handle this for you.
  • @MockBean creates a new context per distinct mock set: many test classes with different mocks defeat context caching and slow the suite.
Interview questions
  • What does @WebMvcTest load? — Controllers (optionally filtered by class), advices, filters, converters, WebMvcConfigurers, Jackson, Security; not services, repositories or auto-configurations outside MVC; collaborators are mocked.
  • MockMvc vs a real server test: what does each prove? — MockMvc proves the MVC pipeline (mapping, validation, serialisation, advice) without sockets; a RANDOM_PORT test proves real HTTP behaviour (compression, async completion, actual status line, TLS) at higher cost. Use both, mostly the first.
  • What is MockMvcTester? — Spring 6.2's AssertJ-based front for MockMvc: fluent requests, assertions on status/headers/JSON via JSONPath, unchecked exceptions, and transparent async handling.
  • @MockBean vs @MockitoBean? — Same purpose (replace/insert a Mockito mock in the context); @MockitoBean is the Framework 6.2 version, @MockBean is deprecated in Boot 3.4; both invalidate the context cache per distinct mock configuration.
  • How do you test a filter or interceptor? — In a @WebMvcTest they are active by default; assert headers/side effects with MockMvc, or unit-test the filter with MockHttpServletRequest/MockFilterChain.
  • How do you test @ControllerAdvice alone? — MockMvcBuilders.standaloneSetup(controller).setControllerAdvice(advice) for a pure unit test, or include the advice in a @WebMvcTest.
  • Boot 2 vs 3? — MockMvcTester and @MockitoBean are new (Boot 3.4); @WebMvcTest and WebTestClient are unchanged; Security test support uses jakarta types.

A JWT validation filter throws InvalidTokenException. Your @RestControllerAdvice has an @ExceptionHandler(InvalidTokenException.class) returning a ProblemDetail. What does the client receive?

b. Filters run outside the DispatcherServlet; the HandlerExceptionResolver chain (where @ExceptionHandler lives) never sees the exception. The container performs an ERROR dispatch to /error, served by BasicErrorController. To reuse the advice, call HandlerExceptionResolver.resolveException from the filter.

In which order do these run for a normal request: (1) HandlerInterceptor.preHandle, (2) servlet Filter.doFilter, (3) @Around aspect on the controller, (4) HandlerMethodArgumentResolver?

c. Filters (container) → DispatcherServlet resolves the handler → preHandle → the HandlerAdapter resolves arguments → invokes the (proxied) controller, where the aspect wraps the actual method. Option d is wrong because arguments must exist before the proxy is invoked.

After upgrading to Boot 3, GET /api/orders/ (trailing slash) returns 404 while /api/orders works. Best production fix?

a. Spring 6 removed trailing-slash matching by design. b switches back to AntPathMatcher but does not restore trailing-slash matching in 6.1+ (the option was removed) and loses the parser's benefits; c makes everything ambiguous; d is unrelated (content negotiation).

record CreateOrder(@NotBlank String sku, List<Item> items) {} with record Item(@Positive int qty) {}. A request with qty=-5 passes @Valid @RequestBody CreateOrder validation. Why?

d. Bean Validation validates nested objects only where @Valid marks the field/element. Records support constraints fine (a); b and c are invented rules.

Boot 3.3 app, no @Validated on the controller. GET /orders?page=-1 hits list(@RequestParam @Min(0) int page). What happens?

b. Since Spring 6.1 (Boot 3.2) the handler adapter validates method parameter constraints itself and throws HandlerMethodValidationException, mapped to 400. a was Boot 2 behaviour without @Validated; c is what you get with @Validated on the class (AOP path); d is for @Valid on a body/model attribute.

Two advices: GlobalAdvice handles Exception, OrderAdvice handles OrderNotFoundException; neither has @Order. Controller throws OrderNotFoundException. Which handler runs?

c. Closest-type matching applies only within one advice class; across advices the first bean in @Order sequence that has any matching handler wins, and unordered advices share lowest precedence. Give the specific advice a lower order value or merge them.

A browser SPA on https://app.shop.com calls your API with an Authorization header; curl works, the browser shows a CORS error with a 401 on the OPTIONS request. Most likely cause?

a. Preflights carry no credentials, so the authentication filter returns 401 before any MVC CORS mapping is reached. Registering a CorsConfigurationSource bean and enabling http.cors() places CorsFilter before authentication. c is true but is a symptom, not the cause; d is false when Authorization is in allowedHeaders.

Handlers call a slow partner API (3 s) with RestClient. At 200 concurrent users the service hangs. Which change fixes the capacity problem rather than moving it?

d. The wait must stop costing an OS thread: virtual threads park cheaply, or a DeferredResult completed by an async client holds nothing. a moves the block to the 8-thread task executor (worse); b costs ~2 GB of stacks and still saturates; c returns immediately without a result.

In a WebFlux service a handler does Mono.just(jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(...)). What is the consequence?

b. Mono.just evaluates its argument eagerly on the calling (event-loop) thread. Nothing moves it automatically (d); the exception in c comes only from BlockHound in tests or from block() on a non-blocking thread. Use Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(boundedElastic()) or R2DBC.

Which statement about @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class) is correct?

c. It is a slice: no services, no repositories, no server; MockMvc talks to the DispatcherServlet directly. Security is included (d is wrong; that is why @WithMockUser is needed). a describes @SpringBootTest(RANDOM_PORT).

Practice

Scenario: the exception handler is never invoked

A team added a TenantFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter that throws MissingTenantException when the X-Tenant header is absent. Their @RestControllerAdvice maps that exception to a 400 ProblemDetail, and a @WebMvcTest that throws the exception from a controller passes. In production clients receive a 500 with {"timestamp":…,"status":500,"error":"Internal Server Error","path":"/api/orders"}. Explain the behaviour and give two fixes, stating which you would choose.

Tests: request lifecycle, filter vs DispatcherServlet, BasicErrorController
Hint 1
Where does ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver live, and does a filter's exception ever pass through it?
Hint 2
The JSON shape (timestamp/status/error/path) identifies the component that wrote it.
Reveal solution

Diagnosis: the filter runs in the servlet container, before the DispatcherServlet. Its exception propagates up the filter chain to Tomcat, which performs an ERROR dispatch to /error; Boot's BasicErrorController builds the body from DefaultErrorAttributes (hence the timestamp/status/error/path shape), and an unmapped exception is 500. The @ExceptionHandler chain only covers exceptions raised inside doDispatch (handlers, interceptors, argument resolvers), which is exactly what the test exercised.

Fix 1 (preferred): delegate to the MVC resolver from the filter.

@Component
class TenantFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    private final HandlerExceptionResolver resolver;
    TenantFilter(@Qualifier("handlerExceptionResolver") HandlerExceptionResolver resolver) { this.resolver = resolver; }

    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        String tenant = req.getHeader("X-Tenant");
        if (tenant == null) {
            resolver.resolveException(req, res, null, new MissingTenantException()); // runs your advice
            return;
        }
        TenantContext.set(tenant);
        try { chain.doFilter(req, res); } finally { TenantContext.clear(); }
    }
}

Fix 2: move the check to a HandlerInterceptor.preHandle (inside the dispatcher, so the advice applies naturally) or to a custom HandlerMethodArgumentResolver for a @CurrentTenant parameter. Choose this if tenant resolution is only needed for MVC handlers; keep the filter (fix 1) if Security or non-MVC endpoints also need the tenant. A third option, customising ErrorAttributes, fixes the body but not the status logic and duplicates the advice.

Fix the bug: validation ignored on nested and list fields

record Address(@NotBlank String street, @Pattern(regexp = "\\d{5}") String zip) {}
record Item(@NotBlank String sku, @Min(1) int qty) {}
record CreateOrder(@NotNull Address ship, @NotEmpty List<Item> items) {}

@RestController
class OrderController {
    @PostMapping("/orders")
    ResponseEntity<Void> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrder body) { … }

    @PostMapping("/orders/bulk")
    ResponseEntity<Void> bulk(@Valid @RequestBody List<CreateOrder> bodies) { … }
}

Requests with zip="abc", qty=0, and a bulk payload containing an order without ship all return 201. The app is Boot 3.1. Identify every reason and fix the code so each case returns 400.

Tests: cascading validation, container element constraints, method validation for list bodies
Hint 1
@NotNull and @NotEmpty check the container, not its contents.
Hint 2
For List<CreateOrder> as the top-level body, what does @Valid attach to, and which validation machinery understands a List?
Reveal solution
record CreateOrder(@NotNull @Valid Address ship, @NotEmpty List<@Valid Item> items) {}

@RestController
@Validated                        // Boot ≤ 3.1: enables method validation so List<@Valid …> works
class OrderController {
    @PostMapping("/orders")
    ResponseEntity<Void> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrder body) { … }

    @PostMapping("/orders/bulk")
    ResponseEntity<Void> bulk(@RequestBody List<@Valid CreateOrder> bodies) { … }
}

Reasons: (1) ship and items lacked @Valid, so their constraints were never cascaded. (2) For the bulk endpoint, @Valid on a List parameter validates the list object itself, which has no constraints; before Spring 6.1 the argument resolver does not iterate elements. Adding @Validated on the class routes the call through the method-validation proxy, which honours container element constraints (List<@Valid CreateOrder>); the failure is then a ConstraintViolationException, so map it to 400 in your advice. (3) On Boot 3.2+ the built-in method validation handles List<@Valid …> without @Validated and throws HandlerMethodValidationException (400 out of the box). A wrapper DTO (record Bulk(@NotEmpty List<@Valid CreateOrder> orders)) is the version-independent alternative.

Scenario: CORS preflight returns 403, only from the browser

The React app at https://app.shop.com calls PUT https://api.shop.com/api/v1/orders/7 with Authorization: Bearer … and Content-Type: application/json. Postman succeeds. The browser console shows "Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check" and the network tab shows OPTIONS /api/v1/orders/7 → 403. The controller has @CrossOrigin(origins = "https://app.shop.com") and the app uses Spring Security 6 with stateless JWT. Explain each step of what the browser is doing, why 403 occurs, and provide the correct configuration.

Tests: CORS preflight, filter ordering, Security vs MVC CORS, credentials
Hint 1
Which request methods and headers make a request "non-simple", and does the preflight carry the JWT?
Hint 2
Where in the filter chain is @CrossOrigin evaluated, and where is Security's CorsFilter when http.cors() is configured?
Reveal solution

What the browser does: PUT with a JSON content type and a custom Authorization header is not a "simple" request, so the browser first sends OPTIONS with Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT and Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization,content-type, and no credentials. Only if the response carries matching Access-Control-Allow-* headers does it send the real PUT. Postman never preflights.

Why 403: Spring Security's filter chain runs before the DispatcherServlet. Without http.cors(), the anonymous OPTIONS is authorised like any request: with anyRequest().authenticated() it fails (403 for anonymous in Security 6 with a bearer-token entry point, or 401 depending on configuration). @CrossOrigin is processed by the HandlerMapping's CORS interceptor inside MVC, which the preflight never reaches. Missing CSRF handling is not the issue for a stateless JWT chain if CSRF is disabled, but with CSRF enabled a PUT would also be rejected.

@Bean
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())                       // stateless bearer API
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())                    // adds CorsFilter before auth, uses the bean below
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
        .build();
}

@Bean
CorsConfigurationSource corsConfigurationSource() {
    var cfg = new CorsConfiguration();
    cfg.setAllowedOrigins(List.of("https://app.shop.com"));   // exact origins (or allowedOriginPatterns)
    cfg.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"));
    cfg.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("Authorization", "Content-Type", "Idempotency-Key"));
    cfg.setExposedHeaders(List.of("ETag", "Location"));       // headers JS may read from the response
    cfg.setAllowCredentials(true);                            // needed only for cookies; harmless with bearer
    cfg.setMaxAge(3600L);                                     // browser caches the preflight
    var source = new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
    source.registerCorsConfiguration("/api/**", cfg);
    return source;
}

Remove the @CrossOrigin annotations (a second CORS layer just adds confusion). With http.cors() Security's CorsFilter handles the preflight itself (responds 200 with the allow headers, without hitting authorisation) and adds the headers to actual responses. If a gateway (nginx, API Gateway) is in front, do CORS in exactly one place. Note the trap allowedOrigins("*") + allowCredentials(true): browsers reject it, and Spring throws at startup.

Scenario: the API hangs at 200 concurrent users

An order service (Boot 3.3, Java 21, MVC, 4 vCPU, default Tomcat settings) calls a pricing service through WebClient like this inside the handler:

@GetMapping("/orders/{id}/quote")
Quote quote(@PathVariable long id) {
    var order = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow();
    Price p = pricing.get().uri("/price/{sku}", order.sku()).retrieve().bodyToMono(Price.class).block();
    return Quote.of(order, p);
}

During a pricing-service incident (p99 latency 8 s, no errors), the order service stops responding to all endpoints, including /actuator/health, at roughly 200 concurrent users; Kubernetes restarts it; the cycle repeats. Explain the mechanism with numbers, list what you would look at in a thread dump and in metrics, and propose an immediate mitigation plus a proper fix.

Tests: Tomcat pool exhaustion, blocking client calls, timeouts, virtual threads vs async, resilience
Hint 1
Little's law: concurrency = throughput × latency. What is the max concurrency of default Tomcat, and what happens to the health endpoint when it is reached?
Hint 2
WebClient is non-blocking, but .block() with no timeout is a synchronous wait on a Tomcat thread. What is the default response timeout of Reactor Netty?
Reveal solution

Mechanism: server.tomcat.threads.max is 200. Each quote request holds its Tomcat thread inside block() for up to 8 s (Reactor Netty has no response timeout unless configured, so effectively unbounded). By Little's law, at 25 req/s × 8 s = 200 threads are permanently occupied; the 201st connection waits in the accept backlog (accept-count 100), then further connections are refused. The health probe is served by the same pool, so readiness/liveness time out, Kubernetes kills the pod, and on restart the same traffic refills the pool. Nothing "errored", so no circuit breaker (had there been one) would even open on error rate: the failure mode is slowness.

Evidence to collect: thread dump: ~200 http-nio-8080-exec-* threads in BlockingSingleSubscriber.blockingGet / CountDownLatch.await; metrics: tomcat.threads.busy == tomcat.threads.config.max, http.server.requests p99 climbing to the pricing latency, http.client.requests for /price showing the 8 s; reactor-netty connection pool (reactor.netty.connection.provider.*, default max 500 connections) not saturated, confirming the blockage is on the calling side.

Immediate mitigation (minutes): add a per-call timeout so requests fail fast (bodyToMono(Price.class).timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) or block(Duration.ofSeconds(1)), plus HttpClient.create().responseTimeout(...) on the connector), return a degraded quote or 503 with Retry-After. Move health to the management port (management.server.port=8081) so probes do not compete with traffic. Optionally raise threads.max as a stopgap, understanding it only buys a multiple.

Proper fix:

// 1) Timeouts + resilience on the client (bulkhead so pricing cannot consume every thread)
@Bean RestClient pricingClient(RestClient.Builder b, RestClientCustomizer c) { … connect 500 ms, read 1 s, pool 50/route … }

@Retry(name = "pricing") @CircuitBreaker(name = "pricing", fallbackMethod = "cachedPrice")
@Bulkhead(name = "pricing", type = Bulkhead.Type.SEMAPHORE)   // max 50 concurrent pricing calls
Price price(String sku) { return pricingClient.get().uri("/price/{sku}", sku).retrieve().body(Price.class); }

// 2) Stop paying an OS thread per wait: Java 21 + Boot 3.2+
// application.yml
// spring.threads.virtual.enabled: true
// management.server.port: 8081

// 3) Alternative without virtual threads: release the Tomcat thread while waiting
@GetMapping("/orders/{id}/quote")
CompletableFuture<Quote> quote(@PathVariable long id) {
    var order = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow();
    return pricing.get().uri("/price/{sku}", order.sku()).retrieve().bodyToMono(Price.class)
                  .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1)).map(p -> Quote.of(order, p)).toFuture();
}

With virtual threads the blocking style is fine: a parked virtual thread costs a few KB, so 5,000 in-flight quotes no longer exhaust anything, and the semaphore bulkhead plus timeout bound the damage. Without them, returning the Mono/CompletableFuture lets MVC use async request processing so no Tomcat thread waits. Either way, the timeout is the non-negotiable part: unbounded waits turn a dependency's latency incident into your outage.

⚡ Rapid-fire: Web MVC & REST

  • What is the DispatcherServlet? — Spring MVC's front controller: maps every request to a handler and coordinates interceptors, argument resolution, return-value handling and exception resolution.
  • HandlerMapping vs HandlerAdapter? — Mapping finds which handler; adapter knows how to invoke it.
  • Where does @RequestBody get deserialised? — In an argument resolver via an HttpMessageConverter (Jackson).
  • Filter vs interceptor in one line? — Filter: servlet-level, no handler knowledge, wraps streams; interceptor: MVC-level, knows the HandlerMethod.
  • Why OncePerRequestFilter? — Guarantees one execution across FORWARD/ERROR/ASYNC dispatches.
  • How to limit a filter to /api/*? — FilterRegistrationBean.addUrlPatterns.
  • Filter order? — @Order/setOrder, lower first; Security at -100.
  • @RestController? — @Controller + @ResponseBody.
  • Boot 3 path-matching gotchas? — PathPatternParser; no trailing-slash match; no suffix patterns; ** only at the end.
  • 406 vs 415? — Cannot produce what Accept wants vs cannot consume the Content-Type.
  • @RequestParam missing? — 400 MissingServletRequestParameterException unless required=false/defaultValue.
  • Unknown JSON field? — Ignored by default in Boot (FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES=false).
  • Why does declaring @Bean ObjectMapper break dates? — It replaces Boot's configured mapper; use Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer.
  • @Valid vs @Validated? — Jakarta cascade vs Spring groups + class-level method validation.
  • MethodArgumentNotValidException vs ConstraintViolationException? — Body validation (400) vs method-validation proxy (500 unless mapped).
  • Nested object not validated? — Missing @Valid on the field/element.
  • Exception resolution order? — Controller-local handler → advices by @Order → @ResponseStatus → default MVC resolver → /error.
  • What is ProblemDetail? — Spring 6's RFC 7807/9457 error body, application/problem+json.
  • Filter exception handling? — Not by advices; delegate to HandlerExceptionResolver or customise ErrorAttributes.
  • PUT vs PATCH? — Full replacement (idempotent) vs partial update.
  • Idempotent POST? — Idempotency-Key header with stored response.
  • 201 vs 202 vs 204? — Created (+Location) vs accepted for async processing vs success with no body.
  • ETag uses? — Conditional GET (304) and optimistic concurrency via If-Match (412).
  • CORS fails only in the browser? — Preflight OPTIONS blocked by Security; configure CorsConfigurationSource + http.cors().
  • RestTemplate status? — Maintenance mode; prefer RestClient (6.1) or WebClient for reactive.
  • Three timeouts to set on a client? — Connect, read/response, connection-request (pool wait).
  • @HttpExchange? — Declarative HTTP interface proxied by HttpServiceProxyFactory over RestClient/WebClient/RestTemplate.
  • Default Tomcat max threads? — 200 (server.tomcat.threads.max), accept-count 100.
  • Callable vs DeferredResult? — Executor-run task vs externally completed result; both release the Tomcat thread.
  • SSE in Spring MVC? — SseEmitter with text/event-stream.
  • Blocking inside WebFlux? — Stalls the event loop; offload to boundedElastic or go reactive end to end.
  • Backpressure? — Consumer-driven request(n) flow control in Reactive Streams.
  • Enable virtual threads in Boot? — spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true on Java 21 (Boot 3.2+).
  • Multipart default limits? — 1 MB per file, 10 MB per request.
  • @WebMvcTest loads? — MVC slice + Security, mocks for collaborators, no services/repos.
  • MockMvcTester? — Spring 6.2 AssertJ-style MockMvc.

4️⃣ AOP & Proxies

Almost every Spring annotation that "just works" — @Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable, @Retryable, @PreAuthorize — is really a proxy wrapped around your bean, and every one of them fails silently in exactly the same situations. Interviewers love this section because a candidate who can explain why this.save() skips the transaction understands the framework rather than memorising it. The path: AOP vocabulary → JDK vs CGLIB proxies → the self-invocation trap → writing aspects and ordering them → how the proxy is actually created → @Async, caching and retry internals → proxies vs @Configuration, equals and mocks → debugging a proxy.

AOP vocabulary & why Spring proxies instead of weaving

Why interviewers ask: the warm-up before the real question. They want the five terms used correctly, and the key fact that Spring AOP is a runtime proxy library, not a bytecode weaver.

A cross-cutting concern (logging, transactions, security, retries) touches many classes but belongs to none of them. An aspect is the module that holds it. A join point is a place in execution where the aspect could run; in Spring AOP that is only a public method call on a Spring bean (AspectJ also supports field access, constructors, static initialisers). A pointcut is an expression selecting join points; advice is the code that runs there (@Before, @After, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @Around). Weaving is how advice gets linked to the target: at compile time (AspectJ ajc), at load time (LTW with a Java agent) or at runtime by generating a proxy. Analogy: the aspect is airport security; the pointcut is "every international gate"; advice is the screening; weaving decides whether you rebuild the terminal (compile-time) or put a checkpoint in front of each gate (proxy).

Spring chose proxies because they need no special compiler or -javaagent, work on any JVM, and integrate naturally with the container: the ApplicationContext simply hands you the proxy instead of the raw object. The cost is the whole list of limitations in this section: only bean-to-bean, only public (CGLIB: non-private, non-final) methods, and no interception of self-calls. @EnableAspectJAutoProxy uses AspectJ's pointcut language and annotations but not its weaver; Boot auto-configures it whenever spring-boot-starter-aop (or anything that needs it, e.g. spring-tx) is on the classpath.

Spring AOP (proxy)AspectJ (weaving)
Join pointsPublic method execution on Spring beansMethods, constructors, field get/set, static init, any object
Self-invocationNot interceptedIntercepted
SetupZero: spring-boot-starter-aopajc compiler or -javaagent:aspectjweaver.jar (LTW)
PerformanceReflection/CGLIB call per advised method (negligible in practice)Inlined bytecode, fastest
Typical use99% of applications: @Transactional, @Cacheable, custom audit aspectsDomain objects created with new, field-level tracing, @Configurable

Pitfalls

  • Saying "Spring uses AspectJ": it borrows AspectJ's @Aspect annotations and expression parser (aspectjweaver.jar on the classpath), but weaves nothing.
  • Expecting advice on objects you created with new: only container-managed beans are proxied.
  • Advice types are not interchangeable: @After runs even on exception (like finally); @AfterReturning only on normal return; only @Around can change arguments, return value, or skip the call.
Interview questions
  • Define join point, pointcut and advice in one sentence each. — A join point is a point in execution (in Spring: a bean method call); a pointcut is a predicate selecting join points; advice is the code executed at matched join points, with a type saying whether it runs before, after or around.
  • Why doesn't Spring weave bytecode by default? — Proxies need no compiler plugin or agent and work with plain jars; the container already controls bean creation so wrapping is natural. Weaving is opt-in (@EnableSpringConfigured + LTW or ajc) for the cases proxies cannot cover.
  • What can Spring AOP not intercept? — Private methods, final methods/classes (CGLIB), internal this. calls, static methods, constructors, field access, and any object not managed by the container.
  • Which advice type would you use for timing a method and why? — @Around with ProceedingJoinPoint: it is the only type that sees both start and end of the call and can also capture the exception path.
  • What does @EnableAspectJAutoProxy actually register? — A single BeanPostProcessor, AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator, that scans for @Aspect beans and Advisors and wraps matching beans in proxies after initialisation.
  • Spring Boot 2 vs 3 differences here? — Mechanism unchanged; Boot 2.0+ and 3.x default to CGLIB (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true), and Spring 6 dropped some javax-based integrations; AOT/native images require proxies to be declared ahead of time (RuntimeHintsRegistrar / generated hints), which the auto-proxy creator handles for standard cases.

JDK dynamic proxies vs CGLIB: how the proxy object is built and what it looks like

Why interviewers ask: the deepest "how does it work" question in Spring. They probe whether you know the proxy is a different object from your bean, that Boot uses CGLIB subclasses by default, and what that means for final, constructors, getClass() and instanceof.

A JDK dynamic proxy (java.lang.reflect.Proxy) is a class generated at runtime that implements a list of interfaces and forwards every call to an InvocationHandler. It cannot be cast to the target's concrete class, so a bean injected as OrderServiceImpl would fail with BeanNotOfRequiredTypeException. A CGLIB proxy is a runtime-generated subclass of the target (OrderService$$SpringCGLIB$$0) that overrides each non-final, non-private method and routes it through a MethodInterceptor. Because it is a subclass, it needs a visible constructor and cannot override final methods; Spring uses Objenesis to instantiate the subclass without calling any constructor (so your constructor runs exactly once, for the real target). The proxy's fields are never initialised: it is a hollow shell holding a reference to the target.

Spring Framework's own default is "JDK if the bean implements an interface, else CGLIB"; Spring Boot flips it to spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true, so CGLIB is used everywhere and injecting by concrete class always works. Either way, getClass() on an injected bean returns the proxy class; instanceof YourInterface is true for both; instanceof YourClass is true only for CGLIB. Inside the proxy the call passes through a chain of MethodInterceptors (one per matching advisor — TransactionInterceptor, CacheInterceptor, your @Around…) via ReflectiveMethodInvocation.proceed(), and finally reaches the target method. Analogy: the JDK proxy is a receptionist who only knows the job titles on the door (interfaces); the CGLIB proxy is a body double who looks like you but hands every task to the real you behind the curtain.

@Service
public class OrderService {                       // no interface → CGLIB is the only option
    private final OrderRepository repo;
    public OrderService(OrderRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; } // runs ONCE, for the target

    @Transactional
    public Order place(Cart cart) { … }             // overridden in subclass → advised

    public final Order fastPath(Cart c) { … }      // final: CGLIB cannot override → NOT advised (WARN at startup)
    private void audit(Order o) { … }               // private: invisible to the subclass → never advised
}

// in a test or debugger:
OrderService s = ctx.getBean(OrderService.class);
s.getClass();                      // class com.acme.OrderService$$SpringCGLIB$$0
s instanceof OrderService;         // true (subclass)
AopUtils.isCglibProxy(s);          // true
AopProxyUtils.ultimateTargetClass(s); // class com.acme.OrderService
JDK dynamic proxyCGLIB proxy (Boot default)
Built fromInterfaces of the targetSubclass of the target class
RequirementsBean implements ≥1 interfaceClass not final; methods not final/private; no constructor call needed (Objenesis)
Inject asInterface onlyInterface or concrete class
getClass()jdk.proxy2.$Proxy42Foo$$SpringCGLIB$$0
InterceptsInterface methods (all public)Public, protected, package-private methods
Select withspring.aop.proxy-target-class=false=true (Boot default), or @EnableAspectJAutoProxy(proxyTargetClass=true)
LibraryJDKRepackaged in spring-core (org.springframework.cglib)
Interview angle: "You annotate a public final method with @Transactional; what happens?" Nothing at runtime: the subclass cannot override it, so calls go straight to the inherited method, no transaction. Spring 6 logs a warning at proxy creation ("Unable to proxy interface-implementing method … marked as final"). Kotlin classes are final by default, hence the kotlin-spring compiler plugin that opens annotated classes.

Pitfalls

  • Reading a field on the proxy via reflection (or a debugger watch) shows null; the state lives on the target. Always read through getters or unwrap with AopProxyUtils.getSingletonTarget.
  • Overriding equals/hashCode/toString: CGLIB proxies delegate toString but handle equals/hashCode specially (compares proxies); do not put proxies in identity-sensitive sets expecting target semantics.
  • A class with only a private constructor cannot be CGLIB-proxied; a protected/package one is fine.
  • JDK proxies plus @Autowired ConcreteClass is the #1 cause of "Bean named 'x' is expected to be of type … but was actually of type 'jdk.proxy2.$Proxy'".
Interview questions
  • What does Spring Boot use by default, JDK or CGLIB proxies, and why? — CGLIB (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true) so that beans can be injected by concrete type regardless of whether they implement an interface; plain Spring Framework defaults to JDK proxies when an interface exists.
  • How does CGLIB create the proxy if the class has a constructor with arguments? — It generates the subclass and instantiates it with Objenesis, which allocates the object without invoking any constructor; the real constructor runs only for the target instance.
  • Does @Transactional work on a protected method? — With CGLIB the method is overridable, but TransactionInterceptor's attribute source only considers public methods by default; Spring 6 lets you opt in to protected/package-private (AnnotationTransactionAttributeSource(false)), yet the safe answer in an interview is "public only, by design".
  • Why does getClass().getAnnotation(MyAnno.class) return null on an injected bean? — The injected object is the proxy subclass, which does not carry your class-level annotations; use AnnotationUtils.findAnnotation or AopUtils.getTargetClass(bean).
  • How would you detect at runtime whether an object is a proxy? — AopUtils.isAopProxy / isJdkDynamicProxy / isCglibProxy, or check bean instanceof Advised (every Spring proxy implements it, exposing getAdvisors() and getTargetSource()).
  • What happens if two aspects match the same method: two proxies? — No: one proxy with two advisors in its chain; AbstractAutoProxyCreator collects all eligible advisors per bean and builds a single proxy.
  • Spring 5/Boot 2 vs Spring 6/Boot 3 proxy differences? — Class name suffix changed from $$EnhancerBySpringCGLIB$$ to $$SpringCGLIB$$; JDK proxies are now in jdk.proxy2 packages (Java 16+); Spring 6 emits a warning for unproxiable final methods instead of silently ignoring them.

The self-invocation trap: this.method() bypasses the proxy

Why interviewers ask: the single most common Spring production bug. "My @Transactional did not roll back", "my @Cacheable never hits", "my @Async runs on the request thread" are all the same question, and they want the fix and the reason.

The proxy wraps the bean from the outside. Once the call has reached the target, this is the raw object, so any call to this.other(), an implicit other(), or a private helper goes straight to the target method: no interceptor chain, no transaction, no cache, no thread switch. The annotation is not "ignored"; it is never seen because nobody asked the proxy. Analogy: security checks visitors at the front desk; an employee walking from one office to the next inside the building is never re-screened.

Fixes, in order of preference: (1) move the method to another bean so the call crosses a proxy boundary — the design usually improves too; (2) self-inject the proxy: @Autowired @Lazy private OrderService self; or ObjectProvider<OrderService>, then call self.other() (Boot 2.6+ forbids plain circular self-injection unless spring.main.allow-circular-references=true, so the @Lazy or provider is required); (3) @EnableAspectJAutoProxy(exposeProxy = true) and ((OrderService) AopContext.currentProxy()).other() — ugly and only works when the outer call came through the proxy; (4) switch to AspectJ mode (@EnableTransactionManagement(mode = AdviceMode.ASPECTJ) plus LTW or ajc), which weaves the advice into the bytecode so self-calls are intercepted too.

@Service
public class ImportService {
    private final ImportService self;            // the PROXY, resolved lazily
    private final RowRepository repo;

    public ImportService(@Lazy ImportService self, RowRepository repo) {
        this.self = self; this.repo = repo;      // @Lazy → a lazy-resolution proxy, no circular-ref error
    }

    public ImportReport importAll(List<Row> rows) {
        int ok = 0;
        for (Row r : rows) {
            try { self.saveOne(r); ok++; }        // crosses the proxy → REQUIRES_NEW really starts
            catch (DataIntegrityViolationException e) { log.warn("skip {}", r.id()); }
        }
        return new ImportReport(ok, rows.size() - ok);
    }

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void saveOne(Row r) { repo.save(r); }
}
FixHowTrade-off
Split the beanMove the advised method into a separate @ServiceBest design; sometimes feels like over-splitting
Self-injection@Lazy constructor param or ObjectProvider<T>.getObject()Explicit but odd-looking; needs @Lazy to avoid Boot 2.6+ circular-reference failure
AopContext.currentProxy()exposeProxy = true; cast the resultTies code to Spring AOP; throws IllegalStateException if called outside a proxied invocation
AspectJ weavingAdviceMode.ASPECTJ + -javaagent / ajcBuild/runtime complexity; rarely worth it just for this

Pitfalls

  • Putting @Transactional on a private method: IntelliJ warns "Methods annotated with @Transactional must be overridable"; it is a no-op even when called from outside, because the proxy cannot override it.
  • @Cacheable on a method called from a @PostConstruct in the same class: the init method runs on the target before the proxy even exists; nothing is cached.
  • Lambdas and inner classes inside the bean still use the raw this; wrapping the call in a Runnable changes nothing.
Interview questions
  • A public method A (no annotation) calls public method B (@Transactional) on the same class; is B transactional? — No: A reaches the target through the proxy, but B is invoked on this, so no interceptor runs; B executes in whatever transaction A had (none).
  • And if A itself is @Transactional? — Then B simply runs inside A's transaction because it is the same thread and the same physical connection; B's own attributes (REQUIRES_NEW, noRollbackFor, timeout) are ignored.
  • How would you fix it without changing the class design? — Inject the bean into itself with @Lazy or ObjectProvider and call through that reference; or enable exposeProxy and use AopContext.currentProxy().
  • Why does Boot 2.6+ reject the naive @Autowired private OrderService self? — Circular references are prohibited by default (spring.main.allow-circular-references=false); @Lazy injects a resolution proxy that defers the lookup until first use, sidestepping the cycle.
  • How would you debug "transaction not rolled back"? — Enable logging.level.org.springframework.transaction.interceptor=TRACE and look for "Getting transaction for [ImportService.saveOne]"; if the line is absent for the inner call, it is self-invocation (or a private/final method, or a checked exception).
  • Does the problem exist with AspectJ? — No; compile-time or load-time weaving modifies the class itself so every call, including this.x(), executes the advice. That is the main reason teams enable AdviceMode.ASPECTJ.
  • Does @Async on an internal call block? — Yes, it runs synchronously on the caller's thread for exactly the same reason; the symptom is a fast endpoint that suddenly takes as long as the "background" job.

Writing aspects: pointcut expressions, @Around, and ordering vs @Transactional

Why interviewers ask: the hands-on check ("write an aspect that times every service method") and the follow-up that trips people: "does your aspect run inside or outside the transaction?"

An aspect is a @Component @Aspect bean. Pointcut designators you must know: execution(mod? ret pkg.Class.method(args)) for signatures (execution(public * com.acme..*Service.*(..))); within(com.acme.service..*) for a package/type; @annotation(com.acme.Audited) for methods carrying an annotation; @within/@target for class-level annotations; bean(*Service) for bean names; args(..) and this/target to bind runtime values into advice parameters. Combine with && || ! and name them with @Pointcut for reuse.

Ordering. When several advisors match one method, the chain order is determined by Ordered/@Order on the aspect class (lower value = outermost = runs first on the way in and last on the way out). Advisors without an order get Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE (Integer.MAX_VALUE). @EnableTransactionManagement(order = …) sets the transaction advisor's order and it also defaults to LOWEST_PRECEDENCE, so an un-ordered custom aspect and the transaction interceptor tie; ties are resolved by registration order, which you must not rely on. Give your aspect an explicit order: lower than the tx order to run outside the transaction (e.g. retry, metrics that must see the commit), higher to run inside (e.g. audit rows that must roll back with the business change). Within a single aspect, advice on the same join point runs @Around → @Before → method → @AfterReturning/@AfterThrowing → @After, with @Around "after" code last; two advices of the same type in one aspect have undefined order, so split them.

@Aspect @Component @Order(1)                         // outermost
public class TimingAspect {
    @Around("execution(* com.acme..*Service.*(..))")
    public Object time(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable {
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        try { return pjp.proceed(); }
        finally { Metrics.timer(pjp.getSignature().toShortString()).record(System.nanoTime() - t0); }
    }
}

@Aspect @Component @Order(Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE - 1)   // just outside tx? NO: see step 4
public class AuditAspect {
    @AfterReturning(pointcut = "@annotation(com.acme.Audited)", returning = "r")
    public void audit(JoinPoint jp, Object r) { auditRepo.save(new AuditRow(jp, r)); }
}

@Service
public class PaymentService {
    @Audited @Transactional
    public Receipt pay(Order o) { … }
}
  1. The proxy builds the chain for pay: Timing (1) → Audit (MAX−1) → Transaction (MAX). Timing is the outermost interceptor.
  2. t0 is captured before anything else; proceed() passes control down the chain.
  3. Audit is next but it is @AfterReturning: it does nothing on the way in and simply proceeds.
  4. The transaction begins after Audit has been entered. Because Audit's order is lower than the tx order, it is outside the transaction: its auditRepo.save will run after commit, in its own auto-commit (or in no transaction at all).
  5. Return path: tx commits, then audit() runs with the receipt. A failure here cannot roll back the payment: for atomic audit, give the aspect an order greater than the tx order (or set @EnableTransactionManagement(order = 100) and put audit at 200).
  6. Finally the timer records: because Timing is outermost, its measurement includes transaction begin/commit and the audit write, which is usually what you want for an endpoint-style metric.
@Aspect @Component @Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 10)   // outside tx: retries see rollback
public class RetryOnDeadlockAspect {
    @Pointcut("@annotation(com.acme.RetryOnDeadlock) && execution(public * *(..))")
    void retryable() {}

    @Around("retryable() && args(order,..)")               // binds first arg by type
    public Object retry(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, Order order) throws Throwable {
        for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
            try { return pjp.proceed(); }                       // proceed(new Object[]{...}) to change args
            catch (DeadlockLoserDataAccessException e) {
                if (attempt == 3) throw e;
                log.warn("deadlock on order {} attempt {}", order.id(), attempt);
            }
        }
    }
}

Pitfalls

  • @Order on the advice method is ignored; only the aspect class (or Ordered) counts.
  • Forgetting to return pjp.proceed()'s value from @Around: the caller silently gets null (or a NullPointerException on unboxing a primitive return).
  • Catching the exception in @Around and returning a default hides it from TransactionInterceptor only if you are inside the tx order; outside, the rollback has already happened.
  • execution(* *(..)) without a package matches every bean in the context, including Spring's own infrastructure; startup slows and internal beans get proxied.
Interview questions
  • Write a pointcut for all public methods of classes annotated @Service in com.acme. — @within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service) && execution(public * com.acme..*(..)).
  • Difference between @within and @target? — @within matches on the declared class's annotation (static); @target matches on the runtime object's class; with proxies and inheritance they can differ.
  • Your retry aspect never retries after a deadlock; why? — It is ordered inside the transaction (higher or unset order), so by the time the exception reaches it the transaction is already marked rollback-only; on retry the same dead transaction is reused and fails. Order retry outside the transaction.
  • How do you make an audit write roll back with the business transaction? — Ensure the audit advice is inside the tx: set @EnableTransactionManagement(order = 100) and @Order(200) on the audit aspect, or make the audit call part of the transactional method via a separate bean with REQUIRED.
  • Two @Before advices in the same aspect on the same method: which runs first? — Undefined in Spring AOP (reflection order); put them in separate ordered aspects if the sequence matters.
  • How would you unit-test an aspect? — Wrap the target manually: AspectJProxyFactory f = new AspectJProxyFactory(target); f.addAspect(new TimingAspect()); T proxy = f.getProxy();, then call the proxy without a Spring context.

How the proxy gets created: AbstractAutoProxyCreator as a BeanPostProcessor

Why interviewers ask: it links section 1 (bean lifecycle) to AOP. The give-away questions: "at which lifecycle step is the proxy made?", "why is there only one proxy even with five aspects?", and "what does not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors mean?"

@EnableAspectJAutoProxy (auto-configured by Boot's AopAutoConfiguration) registers one bean: AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator, a SmartInstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor. @EnableTransactionManagement, @EnableCaching and @EnableAsync register their own Advisor beans (BeanFactoryTransactionAttributeSourceAdvisor, BeanFactoryCacheOperationSourceAdvisor) and, if no AspectJ creator exists, an InfrastructureAdvisorAutoProxyCreator; Spring escalates so only one creator survives. In postProcessAfterInitialization (after @PostConstruct), the creator collects every Advisor whose pointcut matches the bean's class or any method (advisor matching, cached per class), and if the list is non-empty builds one proxy via ProxyFactory with all matching advisors sorted by order. Zero matches → the raw bean is returned untouched; that is why a class with no advised method costs nothing.

Because the creator is itself a bean, anything created before it, or needed by it, cannot be proxied: other BeanPostProcessors, their direct dependencies, and beans referenced from a BeanFactoryPostProcessor. Spring logs Bean 'x' of type [...] is not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors (for example: not eligible for auto-proxying). That info line is the reason a @Transactional bean injected into a custom BeanPostProcessor silently loses its transactions. Analogy: the security team that issues badges cannot issue its own badge on day one; anyone hired to set up the badge printer works without one too.

INFO  PostProcessorRegistrationDelegate$BeanPostProcessorChecker :
      Bean 'auditService' of type [com.acme.AuditService] is not eligible for getting processed
      by all BeanPostProcessors (for example: not eligible for auto-proxying)

// typical cause:
@Component
class MyBeanPostProcessor implements BeanPostProcessor {
    MyBeanPostProcessor(AuditService audit) { … }   // AuditService pulled in BEFORE the AOP creator → its @Transactional is lost
}
// fix: make the BPP static/@Bean static, take ObjectProvider<AuditService> and resolve lazily,
// or fetch the bean from BeanFactory inside postProcess*() rather than in the constructor.

Pitfalls

  • A circular reference between two singletons with AOP: Spring hands out an early reference (via getEarlyBeanReference, already proxied) so both sides see the proxy; but with Boot 2.6+ the cycle is refused anyway, so the fix is @Lazy.
  • Calling @Transactional methods from @PostConstruct, afterPropertiesSet, or a @Bean factory method body: the proxy does not exist yet; use ApplicationRunner / @EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent) instead.
  • Registering a @Bean BeanPostProcessor as a non-static method in a @Configuration drags the whole configuration class (and its dependencies) into early initialisation.
  • Two different auto-proxy creators cannot coexist; AopConfigUtils keeps the strongest (AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator) and merges proxyTargetClass/exposeProxy flags with OR semantics: one @EnableAsync(proxyTargetClass=true) flips CGLIB on globally.
Interview questions
  • At which point of the bean lifecycle does the proxy appear? — In BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization, after @PostConstruct; earlier only for beans involved in a circular reference (early reference hook).
  • Five aspects match one bean; how many proxy objects wrap it? — One: AbstractAutoProxyCreator gathers all applicable advisors and creates a single proxy whose chain contains all of them, sorted by order.
  • What does "not eligible for auto-proxying" mean and how do you fix it? — The bean was instantiated before the AOP post-processor was registered, usually because a BeanPostProcessor/BeanFactoryPostProcessor (or @Configuration hosting one) depends on it; break the early dependency with ObjectProvider, @Lazy, or a static @Bean method.
  • Why is my @Transactional repository call inside a @Bean method not transactional? — The @Bean method runs during creation, on the raw instance returned by the factory; the proxy is only wrapped around the returned object afterwards.
  • How does Spring decide whether to proxy a bean at all? — It evaluates every advisor's pointcut against the class and its methods (AopUtils.canApply); no match means the raw instance is returned, so unadvised beans pay nothing.
  • Can you get the raw target from a proxy? — Yes: cast to Advised and call getTargetSource().getTarget(), or AopProxyUtils.getSingletonTarget(bean); tests use AopTestUtils.getUltimateTargetObject.
  • Boot 2 vs Boot 3 in this area? — Same mechanism; Boot 3 (Spring 6) adds AOT processing that pre-generates CGLIB proxy classes for native images, so proxies must be determinable at build time (dynamic ProxyFactory usage at runtime needs hints).

@Async internals: executor resolution, return types, exceptions and context propagation

Why interviewers ask: everybody has used @Async; few know which pool it runs on, why the exception vanished, or why SecurityContextHolder and MDC are empty on the worker thread. Expect "the endpoint returns 200 but the email never sends; where do you look?".

@EnableAsync (auto-configured by Boot's TaskExecutionAutoConfiguration + AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor) registers an advisor whose AsyncExecutionInterceptor submits the method call to an executor and returns immediately. Executor resolution: the @Async("name") qualifier if given; else the single AsyncConfigurer.getAsyncExecutor(); else the unique TaskExecutor bean, or the bean named taskExecutor; Boot supplies applicationTaskExecutor (a ThreadPoolTaskExecutor, core 8, unbounded queue, threads task-1…) with alias taskExecutor. Only when nothing matches does Spring fall back to SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor, which creates a new thread per call and logs a warning. Boot 3.2+ can switch it to virtual threads with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true.

Return types must be void, Future, ListenableFuture (deprecated in 6) or CompletableFuture; anything else is an error. Return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(x) from inside the method: the interceptor unwraps it. Exceptions: for a Future return type they are stored in the future and surface on get()/join(); for void they go to the AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler (default SimpleAsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler: an ERROR log line and nothing else). Context: ThreadLocals do not cross threads, so SecurityContextHolder, MDC, RequestContextHolder and the current transaction are all absent in the worker; propagate with a TaskDecorator (copy MDC and security context into the task) or DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor. Analogy: handing a task to a courier: they leave right away (you get a receipt = Future), they do not carry your badge (security context), and if they trip on the way you only find out if you check the receipt.

@Configuration
@EnableAsync
public class AsyncConfig implements AsyncConfigurer {
    @Override public Executor getAsyncExecutor() {
        var ex = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        ex.setCorePoolSize(8); ex.setMaxPoolSize(32); ex.setQueueCapacity(500);   // bounded!
        ex.setThreadNamePrefix("async-");
        ex.setRejectedExecutionHandler(new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
        ex.setTaskDecorator(this::propagateContext);      // copy MDC + SecurityContext to the worker
        ex.initialize();
        return ex;
    }
    private Runnable propagateContext(Runnable task) {
        var mdc = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap(); var sec = SecurityContextHolder.getContext();
        return () -> {
            try { if (mdc != null) MDC.setContextMap(mdc); SecurityContextHolder.setContext(sec); task.run(); }
            finally { MDC.clear(); SecurityContextHolder.clearContext(); }
        };
    }
    @Override public AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler getAsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler() {
        return (ex, method, params) -> alerting.error("async %s failed".formatted(method.getName()), ex);
    }
}

@Service
public class ReceiptService {
    @Async
    public CompletableFuture<Void> sendReceipt(Order o) { mailer.send(o); return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null); }
}
Property (Boot)DefaultEffect
spring.task.execution.pool.core-size8Threads kept alive
spring.task.execution.pool.max-sizeInteger.MAX_VALUEOnly reached when the queue is full
spring.task.execution.pool.queue-capacityInteger.MAX_VALUEUnbounded queue → max-size never used, memory grows under load
spring.task.execution.thread-name-prefixtask-What you see in thread dumps
spring.threads.virtual.enabled (3.2+)falseReplaces the pool with a virtual-thread-per-task executor

Pitfalls

  • Queue capacity MAX_VALUE means the pool never grows past 8 threads: 8 slow tasks and everything else waits in memory; always bound the queue and pick a rejection policy.
  • @Async + @Transactional on the same method works (new tx on the worker thread) but the caller's transaction may not have committed yet: the worker can read stale or missing rows. Use @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) + @Async instead.
  • Returning a plain Order from an @Async method: the proxy returns null to the caller immediately (Spring 6 logs an error for non-void, non-Future returns).
  • Under a servlet filter that clears MDC at request end, a naive TaskDecorator that shares (not copies) the map leaks/clears the wrong values; copy it.
Interview questions
  • Which thread pool runs @Async by default in Spring Boot? — Boot's auto-configured applicationTaskExecutor (alias taskExecutor): a ThreadPoolTaskExecutor with 8 core threads and an unbounded queue; without Boot, Spring falls back to SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor (one new thread per call).
  • My @Async method runs synchronously; three possible causes? — Self-invocation; missing @EnableAsync (Boot adds it only via TaskExecutionAutoConfiguration if @EnableAsync is present somewhere — it is not enabled automatically); the executor is SyncTaskExecutor, or the method is private/final so it was never proxied.
  • Where does an exception from a void @Async method go? — To the AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler from your AsyncConfigurer; the default just logs. With a CompletableFuture return it completes exceptionally and the caller sees it on join().
  • Why is SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication() null inside @Async? — It is a ThreadLocal; the worker thread has its own. Use DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor, a TaskDecorator, or set SecurityContextHolder.setStrategyName(MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL) (works only for child threads created after the context was set, so not for pools).
  • How do you keep the trace/MDC id on the async thread? — A TaskDecorator that copies MDC.getCopyOfContextMap(); Micrometer Tracing's context-propagation library does this automatically for ThreadPoolTaskExecutor when ContextExecutorService.wrap is applied.
  • Can an @Async method be @Transactional? — Yes; the transaction starts on the worker thread, independent of the caller's. Risk: it may run before the caller commits, so prefer @TransactionalEventListener + @Async for after-commit side effects.
  • Boot 2 vs 3? — ListenableFuture deprecated in favour of CompletableFuture; Boot 3.2 adds spring.threads.virtual.enabled so @Async can use virtual threads; AsyncConfigurerSupport is deprecated in favour of default methods on AsyncConfigurer.

@Cacheable / @CachePut / @CacheEvict: keys, conditions, managers, and caching inside transactions

Why interviewers ask: caching is the second proxy feature on every résumé. They test key generation (the source of "cache never hits"), the sync/stampede story, and whether you know a cache write can leak an uncommitted value.

@EnableCaching registers CacheInterceptor behind the same auto-proxy creator. @Cacheable: compute the key (default SimpleKeyGenerator: all parameters, so Object params must implement equals/hashCode; or SpEL key = "#order.id", #root.methodName, #result in unless), look it up, and only call the method on a miss. @CachePut always calls the method and stores the result (update-through). @CacheEvict removes one key or allEntries = true, before or after the call (beforeInvocation). condition is evaluated before the call (can see args); unless after (can see #result). sync = true makes concurrent misses for the same key wait on one computation (Caffeine/Redis support it) to prevent a cache stampede.

Managers. Boot picks a CacheManager from the classpath: Caffeine (spring.cache.caffeine.spec=maximumSize=10000,expireAfterWrite=10m), Redis (spring.cache.redis.time-to-live, JSON serializer recommended over JDK), JCache, or the default ConcurrentMapCacheManager (no eviction, no TTL, never in production). Null values: Caffeine and ConcurrentMapCache store null as a sentinel by default (allowNullValues); Redis needs cache-null-values; if you do not want "not found" cached, add unless = "#result == null". Caching in a transaction is tricky: @Cacheable populates the cache immediately when the method returns, before the outer transaction commits; if it rolls back, other threads have already read a value that never existed in the DB. TransactionAwareCacheManagerProxy (or RedisCacheManager…transactionAware()) defers put/evict to after commit, which fixes evict-then-rollback but still cannot make reads "see" uncommitted writes.

@Service
public class ProductService {
    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "products", key = "#id", sync = true, unless = "#result == null")
    public Product byId(long id) { return repo.findById(id).orElse(null); }

    @Caching(put = @CachePut(cacheNames = "products", key = "#result.id()"),
             evict = @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "productsByCategory", allEntries = true))
    @Transactional
    public Product update(Product p) { return repo.save(p); }        // put happens on return; tx commits after

    @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "products", key = "#id", beforeInvocation = true)  // evict even if delete throws
    public void delete(long id) { repo.deleteById(id); }
}

@Configuration
class CacheConfig {
    @Bean CacheManager cacheManager(RedisConnectionFactory cf) {
        return RedisCacheManager.builder(cf)
            .cacheDefaults(RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig().entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
                .serializeValuesWith(SerializationPair.fromSerializer(new GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer())))
            .transactionAware()          // defer puts/evicts until the surrounding tx commits
            .build();
    }
}
AnnotationCalls the method?Writes cache?Typical use
@CacheableOnly on missOn miss, with the resultRead-mostly lookups
@CachePutAlwaysAlways, with the resultUpdate and refresh entry
@CacheEvictAlwaysRemoves key / allDelete, invalidate lists
@Caching—Groups several of the aboveMulti-cache updates

Pitfalls

  • Default key with a parameter lacking equals/hashCode (e.g. a hand-written DTO): every call misses and the cache grows unboundedly.
  • @Cacheable on a method that returns a mutable JPA entity: callers mutate the cached instance; with Caffeine that mutates the cache. Return immutable DTOs/records.
  • @Cacheable and @CachePut on the same method with the same key cancel out (Spring warns); use @CachePut alone for update paths.
  • Caching a lazily-loaded JPA entity in Redis serialises the proxy (LazyInitializationException or a Hibernate proxy in JSON); map to a DTO first.
Interview questions
  • @Cacheable never hits; list the causes you would check. — Self-invocation; missing @EnableCaching; a key that differs per call (mutable/param without equals, #root.args including a timestamp); condition/unless filtering everything; TTL of zero; a per-request CacheManager or a ConcurrentMapCacheManager on a different instance behind a load balancer.
  • What is the difference between condition and unless? — condition gates both lookup and store and is evaluated before the call (args only); unless vetoes only the store and is evaluated after (can reference #result).
  • How do you prevent a cache stampede on an expired hot key? — sync = true so only one thread computes while others block on that key; plus jittered TTLs or Caffeine refreshAfterWrite for background refresh.
  • What happens to the cache when a @Transactional @CacheEvict method rolls back? — With a plain manager the eviction already happened (harmless: next read reloads). With @CachePut the wrong value was stored; a transaction-aware manager defers put/evict until after commit and drops them on rollback.
  • Caffeine vs Redis cache in a multi-instance deployment? — Caffeine is in-process (nanosecond hits, no network, but per-instance and inconsistent across nodes); Redis is shared and survives restarts but costs a network hop and serialisation. Common pattern: Caffeine L1 with short TTL in front of Redis L2.
  • Are null results cached? — Depends on the cache: ConcurrentMapCache/Caffeine allow nulls by default; Redis requires spring.cache.redis.cache-null-values=true. Use unless="#result == null" to be explicit.
  • Boot 2 vs 3? — spring-boot-starter-cache unchanged; JCache moved to jakarta-neutral javax.cache (JSR-107 still uses javax.cache); Ehcache 3 via JCache; Redis cache serialisation now warns about the JDK serializer.

@Retryable/@Recover (spring-retry) vs Resilience4j, and their ordering against transactions

Why interviewers ask: resilience annotations are proxies too, and the ordering question ("does the retry re-run inside the failed transaction?") is a great discriminator.

spring-retry: @EnableRetry + @Retryable(retryFor = OptimisticLockingFailureException.class, maxAttempts = 3, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 200, multiplier = 2)) wraps the method in a RetryOperationsInterceptor; a @Recover method with the same return type and (exception, original args) signature is called after the last failure. Spring-retry 2.x (Boot 3) renamed value/include to retryFor. Resilience4j (resilience4j-spring-boot3) provides @Retry(name = "db", fallbackMethod = "…"), @CircuitBreaker, @RateLimiter, @Bulkhead, @TimeLimiter, configured in YAML and exposed via Actuator; its aspects have fixed relative order (Retry outermost by default: resilience4j.retry.retryAspectOrder). Spring Framework 7 / Boot 4 add a native @Retryable in spring-core, but for Boot 3 you choose between the two libraries.

Ordering rule. Retry must be outside the transaction: a retryable exception inside a transaction marks it rollback-only, and re-invoking the method through the same transaction just fails again. @EnableRetry's advisor defaults to Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE - 1, one notch higher precedence than @Transactional's default LOWEST_PRECEDENCE, so out of the box retry wraps the transaction. If you changed @EnableTransactionManagement(order = …), set @EnableRetry(order = …) lower. For Resilience4j, set retryAspectOrder lower than the tx order. Analogy: retry is the customer re-dialling after a dropped call; it must hang up (roll back) before dialling again, not shout into the dead line.

@Service
public class StockService {
    @Retryable(retryFor = OptimisticLockingFailureException.class,
               maxAttempts = 3, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 100, multiplier = 2, random = true))
    @Transactional                                    // retry is OUTSIDE: each attempt gets a fresh tx
    public void reserve(long sku, int qty) { … }

    @Recover
    public void reserveFallback(OptimisticLockingFailureException e, long sku, int qty) {
        outbox.enqueue(new ReserveLater(sku, qty));    // same return type, exception first, then args
    }
}
spring-retryResilience4j
ScopeRetry only (+ RetryTemplate programmatic)Retry, circuit breaker, rate limiter, bulkhead, time limiter
ConfigAnnotation attributes (SpEL allowed)YAML per instance name, Actuator metrics/events
Fallback@Recover method by signaturefallbackMethod = "name" with exception param
ReactiveNoYes (Reactor/RxJava operators)
StatusMaintenance; superseded by core @Retryable in Spring 7Actively developed; the usual choice for new Boot 3 services

Pitfalls

  • Retrying non-idempotent operations (payments, emails) without an idempotency key duplicates side effects.
  • Retrying DataIntegrityViolationException or validation errors: they never succeed; retry only transient exceptions (deadlock, optimistic lock, timeouts, 503).
  • Resilience4j @CircuitBreaker counts BusinessExceptions as failures unless ignoreExceptions is configured, opening the breaker on user errors.
  • Fixed backoff from 500 replicas at the same moment: use random = true / exponential jitter.
Interview questions
  • Where should retry sit relative to @Transactional and why? — Outside; the failed attempt's transaction must roll back completely before a new attempt opens a fresh one; retrying inside reuses a rollback-only transaction and fails on commit with UnexpectedRollbackException.
  • How does Spring know which method is the @Recover for a given @Retryable? — Same class, same return type, first parameter assignable from the thrown exception, remaining parameters matching the original method's (or recover = "name" explicitly since 1.3).
  • Retry vs circuit breaker? — Retry handles a transient blip on one call; a circuit breaker protects the downstream from a sustained outage by failing fast (open state) and probing (half-open). Combine: breaker outside retry so retries stop once the breaker opens.
  • Why did your Resilience4j fallback not run? — The fallback signature did not match (must take the exception as the last parameter and return the same type); the aspect was bypassed by self-invocation; or the exception is in ignoreExceptions.
  • Boot 2 vs 3 for spring-retry? — Boot 3 needs spring-retry 2.x: @Retryable(value=) became retryFor, exclude became noRetryFor, and spring-aspects or spring-boot-starter-aop must be on the classpath explicitly.

Proxies elsewhere: @Configuration classes, equals/hashCode, @MockBean and @SpyBean

Why interviewers ask: to see whether you recognise the same proxy machinery in three disguises: the CGLIB subclass of a @Configuration class, identity semantics of proxied beans, and how test mocks interact with (or replace) AOP proxies.

@Configuration proxies. A full-mode configuration class is CGLIB-subclassed by ConfigurationClassPostProcessor (a BeanFactoryPostProcessor, not the AOP creator) so that calling this.dataSource() from another @Bean method returns the container's singleton instead of a new object; see section 1 (card core-component-bean). proxyBeanMethods = false (used by every Boot auto-configuration) disables the subclass: faster startup, no CGLIB, but inter-bean calls become plain new. The rule is the same as here: a call that does not go through a proxy does not get the container's behaviour.

equals/hashCode. A CGLIB proxy's equals is intercepted: proxy.equals(other) compares the underlying advised configuration (same target, same advisors) rather than calling your method on the target, and hashCode is derived from the proxy class name and target source; with JDK proxies JdkDynamicAopProxy handles them similarly. proxy.equals(target) is therefore false even when your equals would say true. Beans in a Set or used as map keys behave by identity of the proxy, which is fine for singletons but surprising for scoped proxies. Tests. @MockBean replaces the bean definition with a Mockito mock, so no advisor applies: a mocked service has no transactions or caching, which is what you want. @SpyBean wraps the real bean in a Mockito spy; when the real bean is also an AOP proxy, Spring spies the proxy, so advice still runs, but verify() on a self-invoked method fails for the usual reason. To assert on the target, unwrap with AopTestUtils.getUltimateTargetObject(bean). Boot 3.4 deprecates @MockBean/@SpyBean in favour of Spring Framework 6.2's @MockitoBean/@MockitoSpyBean.

@SpringBootTest
class OrderServiceTest {
    @Autowired OrderService service;          // the CGLIB proxy (tx + audit advice)
    @MockBean PaymentGateway gateway;         // mock replaces the bean: no advice, no proxy chain
    @SpyBean  ReceiptService receipts;        // spy AROUND the async proxy

    @Test void placesOrder() {
        given(gateway.charge(any())).willReturn(Receipt.ok());
        service.place(cart());
        then(receipts).should().sendReceipt(any());     // works: called through the spy/proxy
        assertThat(AopUtils.isAopProxy(service)).isTrue();  // sanity: the advice really is applied
        OrderService raw = AopTestUtils.getUltimateTargetObject(service);   // for field assertions
    }
}

Pitfalls

  • @SpyBean on a JDK-proxied bean fails with "Cannot subclass final class $Proxy": switch that bean to CGLIB or spy the interface type.
  • Mockito's verify(service).save(...) when save was called via this.save(): the spy sees nothing, same as the proxy sees nothing.
  • Overriding equals on a service class and then comparing injected instances: you are comparing proxies; do not rely on it.
  • @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false) with inter-bean method calls creates duplicate objects silently (two connection pools, two schedulers).
Interview questions
