  • Which post-processor creates the @Configuration proxy, and is it the AOP one? — ConfigurationClassPostProcessor (a BeanFactoryPostProcessor), earlier than and independent of the AOP auto-proxy creator; it uses CGLIB with a different interceptor (BeanMethodInterceptor) that looks up the bean in the factory.
  • When would you set proxyBeanMethods = false? — When @Bean methods never call each other (they take dependencies as parameters instead); it saves the CGLIB subclass at startup and is mandatory for GraalVM-friendly configuration. All Boot auto-configurations use it.
  • Does @MockBean keep @Transactional behaviour of the mocked bean? — No; the bean definition is replaced by the mock, so no advisors match and no proxy is built. A test that relies on the mocked bean's transaction is testing nothing.
  • How do you assert internal state of a proxied bean in a test? — Unwrap: AopTestUtils.getTargetObject (one level) or getUltimateTargetObject (through nested proxies/spies), then read fields; never reflect on the proxy itself, its fields are null.
  • Is ctx.getBean(OrderService.class) == injectedOrderService? — Yes for a singleton: both are the same proxy instance stored in the singleton registry. It differs only for scoped proxies (proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS) whose target changes per request/session while the proxy stays the same.
  • Boot 2 vs 3 for test doubles? — Same annotations through Boot 3.3; Boot 3.4 deprecates @MockBean/@SpyBean for Spring's own @MockitoBean/@MockitoSpyBean, which also work in plain Spring TestContext tests.

Debugging proxies: AopUtils, Advised, properties, and reading a proxy stack trace

Why interviewers ask: "how would you prove the annotation is being applied?" separates people who guess from people who look. Knowing the frames in a proxy stack trace also makes production traces readable.

Toolbox: AopUtils.isAopProxy(bean), isJdkDynamicProxy, isCglibProxy; AopUtils.getTargetClass(bean) and AopProxyUtils.ultimateTargetClass(bean) (follows nested proxies); cast to Advised to list getAdvisors(), which shows exactly which interceptors (transaction, cache, async, your aspects) will run and in what order, and getTargetSource() for the raw object. Properties: spring.aop.proxy-target-class (CGLIB vs JDK), spring.aop.auto (disable the creator entirely), spring.main.allow-circular-references. Logging: org.springframework.aop=DEBUG logs "Creating implicit proxy for bean 'x' with 0 common interceptors and 2 specific interceptors" at startup: grep it for the bean you doubt; org.springframework.transaction.interceptor=TRACE shows "Getting transaction for" / "Completing transaction for" per call; org.springframework.cache=TRACE shows key computation and hits/misses.

Reading a stack trace. A CGLIB-proxied call shows, from the top: your target method → CglibAopProxy$CglibMethodInvocation.invokeJoinpoint → ReflectiveMethodInvocation.proceed → one frame per interceptor (TransactionInterceptor.invoke, CacheInterceptor.invoke, MethodInvocationProceedingJoinPoint.proceed ← your @Around) → CglibAopProxy$DynamicAdvisedInterceptor.intercept → OrderService$$SpringCGLIB$$0.place → the caller. For JDK proxies the bottom frames are JdkDynamicAopProxy.invoke and jdk.proxy2.$Proxy42.place. If the caller frame is immediately followed by your method with none of these frames in between, the call bypassed the proxy: that is the self-invocation fingerprint. Analogy: a stamped passport shows every checkpoint you passed; no stamps means you climbed the fence.

@Component
public class ProxyInspector implements ApplicationRunner {
    private final ApplicationContext ctx;
    ProxyInspector(ApplicationContext ctx) { this.ctx = ctx; }

    @Override public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {
        Object bean = ctx.getBean("orderService");
        System.out.println(AopUtils.isAopProxy(bean) + " " + AopUtils.isCglibProxy(bean));   // true true
        System.out.println(AopProxyUtils.ultimateTargetClass(bean));                          // class com.acme.OrderService
        if (bean instanceof Advised advised) {
            for (Advisor a : advised.getAdvisors()) System.out.println(a);   // BeanFactoryTransactionAttributeSourceAdvisor, TimingAspect.time…
        }
    }
}
at com.acme.OrderService.place(OrderService.java:42)                       ← target
at org.springframework.aop.framework.CglibAopProxy$CglibMethodInvocation.invokeJoinpoint(...)
at org.springframework.aop.framework.ReflectiveMethodInvocation.proceed(...)
at org.springframework.transaction.interceptor.TransactionInterceptor.invoke(...)   ← tx advice
at org.springframework.aop.framework.ReflectiveMethodInvocation.proceed(...)
at com.acme.TimingAspect.time(TimingAspect.java:15)                          ← your @Around
at org.springframework.aop.aspectj.AspectJAroundAdvice.invoke(...)
at org.springframework.aop.framework.CglibAopProxy$DynamicAdvisedInterceptor.intercept(...)
at com.acme.OrderService$$SpringCGLIB$$0.place(<generated>)                 ← proxy
at com.acme.OrderController.checkout(OrderController.java:30)                ← caller

Pitfalls

  • Debugger "evaluate expression" on service.repo shows null: you are looking at the proxy; step into a method or evaluate ((Advised) service).getTargetSource().getTarget().
  • spring.aop.proxy-target-class=false plus a @Autowired ConcreteClass injection fails at startup; the property is global and affects every proxy in the context.
  • Setting spring.aop.auto=false to "speed up startup" silently disables @Transactional, @Cacheable and all aspects.
  • Stack traces from @Async methods start at the executor; the calling request's frames are on another thread and are not in the trace unless you capture and attach them.
Interview questions
  • How do you verify that @Transactional is actually applied to a bean? — Check AopUtils.isAopProxy(bean) and inspect ((Advised) bean).getAdvisors() for BeanFactoryTransactionAttributeSourceAdvisor; at runtime enable TransactionInterceptor TRACE logging or call TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive() inside the method.
  • What does spring.aop.proxy-target-class control and what is the Boot default? — Whether the auto-proxy creator (and @EnableTransactionManagement/@EnableCaching/@EnableAsync) create CGLIB subclass proxies (true, the Boot default) or JDK interface proxies (false).
  • How do you tell from a stack trace that a call went through the proxy? — Frames such as CglibAopProxy$DynamicAdvisedInterceptor.intercept / JdkDynamicAopProxy.invoke and ReflectiveMethodInvocation.proceed between the caller and the target; their absence means self-invocation or a non-proxied object.
  • A bean is a proxy but your advice is not in the advisor list; what now? — The pointcut does not match: check the expression (package, return type, .. for sub-packages), that the aspect is a bean (@Component on the @Aspect class), and that the method is public and called externally.
  • Why does the proxy's class name change between runs? — CGLIB names include a hash of the generated class; do not persist or compare class names; use ultimateTargetClass.
  • Boot 2 vs 3? — The name suffix ($$EnhancerBySpringCGLIB$$ → $$SpringCGLIB$$), jdk.proxy2 package names on Java 17, and Spring 6's startup warning for un-proxiable final methods make diagnosis easier.

In a Spring Boot 3 app with default settings, @Service class OrderService (no interface) has a @Transactional method. What is ctx.getBean(OrderService.class).getClass()?

c. Boot sets spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true, so a CGLIB subclass is generated and that is the registered bean. a would mean no advice was applied. b requires an interface and JDK-proxy mode. d is the pre-CGLIB era; today only final classes fail.

How many times does OrderService's constructor run when the bean is CGLIB-proxied?

b. Spring uses Objenesis to allocate the subclass instance bypassing constructors; the target is built normally and the proxy holds a reference to it. That is why the proxy's own fields are null. a was true in very old Spring versions and is a classic outdated answer.

Public method importAll() (not annotated) loops and calls saveOne() on the same class, which is @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW). One row fails with a RuntimeException. What happened to the other rows?

d. saveOne() is called on this, bypassing the proxy, so REQUIRES_NEW is never seen; the JPA repository's own @Transactional (on SimpleJpaRepository.save) commits each row individually. a describes the intended behaviour, which needs a self-injected proxy or a separate bean. b would need an outer transaction on importAll.

Which fix for self-invocation is the safest under Boot 2.6+ defaults?

a. Both cross a proxy boundary; @Lazy avoids the circular-reference failure. b fails at startup (BeanCurrentlyInCreationException) unless spring.main.allow-circular-references=true. c makes it worse: private methods can never be advised. d throws IllegalStateException unless exposeProxy = true.

An @Aspect with no @Order has an @AfterReturning advice that writes an audit row for methods that are also @Transactional (default tx order). The audit insert throws. Does the business change roll back?

b. Unordered aspects and @EnableTransactionManagement both default to Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE; ties are broken by registration order, which can change between builds. Give the aspect an explicit order higher than the tx order to run inside the transaction (rollback together) or lower to run outside. c confuses advice type with chain position.

Startup logs: Bean 'auditService' … is not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors (for example: not eligible for auto-proxying). Most likely cause?

c. Post-processors and their dependency graphs are instantiated early, before AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator is registered, so they miss postProcessAfterInitialization. a produces a different error at proxy creation. b never happens: one proxy holds all advisors.

A void @Async method throws MailException. With Boot defaults, where does the exception end up?

d. For void methods there is no future to carry the exception, so the AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler is the only observer; configure your own via AsyncConfigurer. b applies only to Future/CompletableFuture return types when the caller calls get().

Boot's default applicationTaskExecutor has core size 8, max size Integer.MAX_VALUE and queue capacity Integer.MAX_VALUE. Under a burst of 10,000 @Async calls, what happens?

a. A ThreadPoolExecutor only creates threads beyond core size when the queue is full, and an unbounded queue is never full. That is why production configs bound queue-capacity and raise max-size. b would need a SynchronousQueue or small queue. d needs an explicit rejection handler.

@Cacheable("products") Product byId(long id) is called from a @PostConstruct warm-up in the same class and from a controller. Which calls are cached?

b. Initialisation callbacks execute before postProcessAfterInitialization creates the proxy, and they call this anyway. Warm caches from an ApplicationRunner that calls the injected (proxied) bean. d: primitives are boxed and work fine as keys.

Which statement about @MockBean and @SpyBean is correct?

c. The mock is a brand-new definition with no matching advisors; the spy is layered on the real bean instance from the context, proxy included. d is backwards: spying a JDK proxy fails because $Proxy classes are final, so CGLIB (the default) is what makes @SpyBean work.

Practice

Scenario: "@Transactional on the method, but nothing rolls back"

A batch endpoint imports rows. When one row's repo.save throws, the rows before it are still in the database. The team already "fixed" it twice. Find every reason it still does not roll back and rewrite it so that an exception in any row rolls back the whole batch.

@RestController
public class ImportController {
    private final ImportService service;
    ImportController(ImportService service) { this.service = service; }

    @PostMapping("/import")
    public int importRows(@RequestBody List<Row> rows) throws Exception { return service.importAll(rows); }
}

@Service
public class ImportService {
    private final RowRepository repo;
    ImportService(RowRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }

    public int importAll(List<Row> rows) throws Exception {
        int n = 0;
        for (Row r : rows) { persist(r); n++; }
        return n;
    }

    @Transactional
    private void persist(Row r) throws Exception {
        if (!r.valid()) throw new Exception("invalid row " + r.id());
        repo.save(r);
    }
}

Hints: count the ways the proxy is bypassed, then look at the exception type.

Hint 1Three separate problems: the visibility of persist, how it is called, and what it throws.
Hint 2Even after making it public and calling it through the proxy, a checked Exception does not trigger rollback by default; and one transaction per row still cannot roll back previous rows.
Solution

Why it fails. (1) persist is private: CGLIB cannot override it, so the annotation is never applied (Spring never even warns; IntelliJ does). (2) It is invoked via this from importAll, so even if it were public the proxy is bypassed. (3) It throws a checked Exception; the default rollback rule covers only RuntimeException and Error. (4) Design: a transaction per row can never undo earlier rows; the requirement is one transaction around the loop.

@Service
public class ImportService {
    private final RowRepository repo;
    ImportService(RowRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }

    @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)     // one tx for the whole batch, checked exceptions roll back too
    public int importAll(List<Row> rows) throws InvalidRowException {
        int n = 0;
        for (Row r : rows) {
            if (!r.valid()) throw new InvalidRowException(r.id());   // unchecked is simpler: extends RuntimeException
            repo.save(r); n++;
        }
        return n;
    }
}

Verification. logging.level.org.springframework.transaction.interceptor=TRACE should now show one "Getting transaction for [ImportService.importAll]" and, on failure, "Completing transaction … after exception … rolling back". A @SpringBootTest that posts a batch with a bad row in the middle and asserts repo.count() == 0 pins the behaviour. Mention to the interviewer that the controller-level call is what makes this work: the controller holds the proxy.

Scenario: the @Async notification makes the checkout endpoint slow

POST /checkout takes 3 seconds; profiling shows the time is spent in NotificationService.sendReceipt, which is annotated @Async. In a second environment the same code returns in 50 ms but receipts are sometimes sent twice and the log line for failures is never seen. Explain both environments and fix the code so it is fast, sends once, and reports failures.

@Service
public class CheckoutService {
    private final NotificationService notifications;
    CheckoutService(NotificationService n) { this.notifications = n; }

    @Transactional
    public Receipt checkout(Cart cart) {
        Receipt r = charge(cart);
        orders.save(r.toOrder());
        notifications.sendReceipt(r);       // "fire and forget"
        return r;
    }
}

@Service
public class NotificationService {
    @Async
    public void sendReceipt(Receipt r) { mailer.send(r); }
}

@SpringBootApplication
public class App { … }                       // no @EnableAsync anywhere in env 1; env 2 has it in a shared library config

Hints: what makes @Async active at all; what the worker thread can see; what happens on rollback.

Hint 1Boot does not enable @Async by itself. Without @EnableAsync no AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor exists, so the method is a plain synchronous call.
Hint 2In env 2 the send happens on a pool thread before checkout's transaction commits, and a retry at the HTTP layer resends. void + exception = swallowed by the default handler.
Solution

Env 1: no @EnableAsync → no async advisor → no proxy → synchronous 3 s call on the request thread (and inside the transaction, holding the connection). Env 2: async works, but (a) the mail is sent before the order transaction commits: if the commit fails the customer still gets a receipt, and if the client retries the request the receipt is sent again; (b) void return means MailException goes to SimpleAsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler, which logs at ERROR under the org.springframework.aop.interceptor logger, easily filtered out or on a logger nobody watches.

@Configuration @EnableAsync
class AsyncConfig implements AsyncConfigurer {
    @Override public Executor getAsyncExecutor() { /* bounded ThreadPoolTaskExecutor + TaskDecorator for MDC */ }
    @Override public AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler getAsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler() {
        return (ex, m, args) -> alerts.error("async " + m.getName() + " failed", ex);
    }
}

@Service
public class CheckoutService {
    @Transactional
    public Receipt checkout(Cart cart) {
        Receipt r = charge(cart);
        orders.save(r.toOrder());
        events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(r));      // ApplicationEventPublisher; nothing sent yet
        return r;
    }
}

@Component
public class ReceiptListener {
    @Async
    @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)   // only after the order is durable
    public void on(OrderPlaced e) { mailer.send(e.receipt()); }          // idempotency key = order id prevents duplicates
}

Reasoning. @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) defers the side effect until the data is committed; @Async on the listener moves it off the request thread (the listener is a separate bean, so no self-invocation). The custom AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler makes failures visible; an idempotency key (order id in the mail provider) makes duplicates harmless. For guaranteed delivery replace the listener with an outbox table polled by a scheduler.

Debug: @Cacheable never hits and Redis memory keeps growing

Metrics show a 0% hit rate on the prices cache while Redis key count grows by thousands per minute. Find the causes and fix them.

public class PriceQuery {                          // hand-written, no equals/hashCode
    public String sku; public String currency; public Instant asOf = Instant.now();
}

@Service
public class PriceService {
    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "prices")
    public Price price(PriceQuery q) { return pricingClient.fetch(q.sku, q.currency); }

    public Map<String, Price> prices(List<String> skus) {
        return skus.stream().collect(toMap(s -> s, s -> price(new PriceQuery(s))));   // hot path
    }
}

Hints: how is the key computed; where is price called from.

Hint 1SimpleKeyGenerator builds the key from the parameters using their equals/hashCode. What do two PriceQuery objects for the same sku compare as?
Hint 2Even with a good key, prices() calls price() on this.
Solution

Cause 1: key identity. PriceQuery has no equals/hashCode and, worse, contains asOf = Instant.now(); with a JSON-serialising Redis key every call produces a new key, hence 0% hits and unbounded growth (no TTL configured either). Cause 2: self-invocation. The bulk path calls price() internally, so it never reaches CacheInterceptor at all: the single-item endpoint populates keys the bulk path never reads.

public record PriceQuery(String sku, String currency) {}          // value semantics, no timestamp

@Service
public class PriceService {
    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "prices", key = "#q.sku() + ':' + #q.currency()", sync = true, unless = "#result == null")
    public Price price(PriceQuery q) { return pricingClient.fetch(q.sku(), q.currency()); }
}

@Service
public class BulkPriceService {                     // separate bean → calls cross the proxy
    private final PriceService prices;
    BulkPriceService(PriceService p) { this.prices = p; }
    public Map<String, Price> prices(List<String> skus, String ccy) {
        return skus.stream().collect(toMap(s -> s, s -> prices.price(new PriceQuery(s, ccy))));
    }
}

// application.yml
// spring.cache.redis.time-to-live: 5m
// spring.cache.redis.key-prefix: pricing:   (and enable-statistics for the hit-rate gauge)

Verification. logging.level.org.springframework.cache=TRACE prints "Computed cache key 'ABC:USD' for operation …" and "Cache entry for key … found in cache 'prices'". redis-cli --scan --pattern 'pricing:*' | wc -l should stabilise. For multi-key lookups at scale, replace N proxied calls with a single MGET through RedisTemplate or Caffeine's getAll; @Cacheable has no bulk mode.

Scenario: the retry aspect "fires but never recovers", and the metrics aspect fires twice

Two custom aspects and @Transactional apply to InventoryService.reserve. Under deadlock the logs show three "retrying" lines followed by UnexpectedRollbackException: Transaction silently rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only. Separately, the inventory.reserve timer records two samples per call. Predict the interceptor chain, explain both symptoms, and fix the configuration without changing business code.

@Aspect @Component
public class DeadlockRetryAspect {
    @Around("@annotation(com.acme.RetryOnDeadlock)")
    public Object retry(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable {
        for (int i = 1; ; i++) {
            try { return pjp.proceed(); }
            catch (CannotAcquireLockException e) { if (i == 3) throw e; log.warn("retrying {}", i); }
        }
    }
}

@Aspect @Component
public class MetricsAspect {
    @Around("execution(* com.acme..*Service.*(..))")
    public Object time(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable { … timer.record(...) … }

    @Around("within(com.acme.inventory..*)")
    public Object timeInventory(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable { … timer.record(...) … }
}

@Service
public class InventoryService {           // package com.acme.inventory
    @RetryOnDeadlock @Transactional
    public void reserve(long sku, int qty) { … }
}
@EnableTransactionManagement(order = 100)
@Configuration class TxConfig {}

Hints: sort the advisors by order; think about what "rollback-only" means for a re-invoked proceed().

Hint 1Neither aspect declares @Order, so both are LOWEST_PRECEDENCE (Integer.MAX_VALUE). The transaction advisor is 100. Which is outermost?
Hint 2Two advices in the same aspect with overlapping pointcuts both match the same method: two interceptors, two samples.
Solution

Chain prediction. Sorted ascending: TransactionInterceptor (100) is outermost; then retry and metrics (both MAX, undefined mutual order). So the sequence is: begin tx → retry advice → metrics advice(s) → method. Symptom 1. The deadlock exception passes through proceed() inside the transaction; JPA/Hibernate marks the transaction rollback-only on the first failure. The retry aspect catches it and calls proceed() again on the same doomed transaction and connection; each attempt fails similarly, and even a lucky success cannot commit: TransactionInterceptor finds the rollback-only flag and throws UnexpectedRollbackException. Symptom 2. time (execution(*Service.*)) and timeInventory (within(inventory..)) both match reserve: two @Around interceptors in the chain, each recording a sample.

@Aspect @Component
@Order(10)                                 // lower than tx (100) → OUTSIDE: each retry gets a fresh transaction
public class DeadlockRetryAspect { … unchanged … }

@Aspect @Component
@Order(1)                                  // outermost: measures retries + tx as one endpoint-level sample
public class MetricsAspect {
    @Around("execution(* com.acme..*Service.*(..)) && !within(com.acme.inventory..*)")
    public Object time(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable { … }

    @Around("within(com.acme.inventory..*)")          // pointcuts are now disjoint: one sample per call
    public Object timeInventory(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable { … }
}

Resulting chain: Metrics(1) → Retry(10) → Transaction(100) → target. On deadlock, the transaction interceptor rolls back and rethrows; retry catches a clean exception and the next proceed() starts a brand-new transaction. Verify with ((Advised) ctx.getBean(InventoryService.class)).getAdvisors(), which lists the advisors in chain order, and with TransactionInterceptor TRACE logging showing a new "Getting transaction" line per attempt. Note for the interviewer: if @EnableTransactionManagement had been left at its default (LOWEST_PRECEDENCE), the retry aspect and the transaction would have tied and the outcome would have varied by registration order; explicit orders are the fix, not luck.

⚡ Rapid-fire: AOP & proxies

  • Is Spring AOP proxy-based or weaving-based? — Proxy-based at runtime; AspectJ weaving is opt-in.
  • Only join point type in Spring AOP? — Method execution on a Spring bean.
  • Five advice types? — @Before, @After, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @Around.
  • Which advice can change the return value or skip the call? — Only @Around.
  • JDK proxy requirement? — At least one interface; the proxy implements the interfaces only.
  • CGLIB proxy requirement? — Non-final class; non-final, non-private methods; no constructor call needed thanks to Objenesis.
  • Boot's default proxy type? — CGLIB (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true).
  • Does @Transactional work on a private method? — No, never; it cannot be overridden or intercepted.
  • Does it work on a final public method? — No with CGLIB (warning at startup in Spring 6).
  • What is self-invocation? — Calling an advised method via this from inside the same bean; the proxy is bypassed.
  • Three fixes for self-invocation? — Split into another bean; @Lazy/ObjectProvider self-injection; AopContext.currentProxy() with exposeProxy=true (or AspectJ mode).
  • Which class creates AOP proxies? — AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator (an AbstractAutoProxyCreator BeanPostProcessor).
  • When in the lifecycle is the proxy created? — postProcessAfterInitialization, after @PostConstruct.
  • N aspects match one bean: how many proxies? — One proxy, N advisors in its chain.
  • "Not eligible for auto-proxying" means? — The bean was created before the AOP post-processor (it is a BPP or a BPP dependency).
  • How do you order aspects? — @Order/Ordered on the aspect class; lower value = outer; default LOWEST_PRECEDENCE.
  • Where should retry sit relative to @Transactional? — Outside (lower order), so each attempt gets a fresh transaction.
  • Default executor for @Async in Boot? — applicationTaskExecutor: ThreadPoolTaskExecutor, core 8, unbounded queue.
  • Allowed @Async return types? — void, Future, CompletableFuture (ListenableFuture deprecated).
  • Where does a void @Async exception go? — AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler; default only logs.
  • Is SecurityContext available inside @Async? — No; propagate via DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor or a TaskDecorator.
  • Does Boot enable @Async automatically? — No; you need @EnableAsync somewhere.
  • Default cache key? — SimpleKeyGenerator: all parameters (needs equals/hashCode).
  • condition vs unless? — Before the call on args vs after the call with #result.
  • @Cacheable vs @CachePut? — Skip the method on hit vs always run and store.
  • What does sync = true do? — One computation per key under concurrent misses (stampede protection).
  • Is @Configuration proxying done by the AOP creator? — No; by ConfigurationClassPostProcessor with CGLIB, for inter-@Bean calls.
  • Does @MockBean keep advice? — No; the mock replaces the bean definition.
  • How to detect a proxy at runtime? — AopUtils.isAopProxy, or bean instanceof Advised.
  • How to get the real class? — AopProxyUtils.ultimateTargetClass(bean).
  • Stack-trace fingerprint of a proxied call? — CglibAopProxy$DynamicAdvisedInterceptor.intercept / ReflectiveMethodInvocation.proceed frames between caller and target.

5️⃣ Data Access: JPA, Hibernate & Transactions

Most production incidents in a Spring Boot service trace back to this layer: a rollback that silently did not happen, a LazyInitializationException in a background thread, a request that fires 1,001 queries, a connection pool drained by open-in-view. Interviewers know it, so they probe transaction propagation, the persistence context and N+1 harder than any other Spring topic. The path: Spring's transaction abstraction → @Transactional semantics → isolation levels → the persistence context → Spring Data JPA → fetching & N+1 → mapping pitfalls → ID generation → pooling & performance → schema management → transactions across boundaries → testing the data layer.

Spring's transaction abstraction: PlatformTransactionManager, interceptor, thread-bound resources

Why interviewers ask: "what does @Transactional actually do?" separates candidates who can debug a missing rollback from those who only know the annotation exists.

PlatformTransactionManager is a three-method strategy interface: getTransaction(definition), commit(status), rollback(status). Boot auto-configures one implementation per technology: JpaTransactionManager when JPA is present (it also exposes the underlying JDBC connection so plain JdbcTemplate calls join the same transaction), DataSourceTransactionManager for JDBC-only apps, KafkaTransactionManager, JtaTransactionManager. Analogy: the manager is a bank teller; @Transactional is the form you fill in, and the teller decides whether to open a new account or add to the one you already have.

Declarative transactions are plain AOP: @EnableTransactionManagement (auto-applied by Boot) registers a BeanFactoryTransactionAttributeSourceAdvisor whose advice is TransactionInterceptor. Around every annotated public method it calls getTransaction, invokes the target, then commit or rollback according to the rollback rules. All proxy caveats (self-invocation, private methods, final classes) apply exactly as in section 4.

The state lives in TransactionSynchronizationManager: a set of ThreadLocals mapping the resource key (the DataSource / EntityManagerFactory) to the ConnectionHolder / EntityManagerHolder. That is why a transaction is thread-bound: a @Async method or a parallel stream runs on another thread, finds no holder, and gets its own connection (or none). DataSourceUtils.getConnection() and EntityManagerFactoryUtils are how JdbcTemplate and the shared EntityManager proxy find the current holder. TransactionTemplate is the programmatic twin: same manager, same propagation, no proxy, so it works for private methods, lambdas and self-invocation.

@Service
public class PayoutService {
    private final TransactionTemplate tx;         // built from the PlatformTransactionManager
    private final PayoutRepository repo;

    public PayoutService(PlatformTransactionManager tm, PayoutRepository repo) {
        this.tx = new TransactionTemplate(tm);
        this.tx.setPropagationBehavior(TransactionDefinition.PROPAGATION_REQUIRES_NEW);
        this.tx.setTimeout(5);
        this.repo = repo;
    }

    public void settle(List<Payout> batch) {
        for (Payout p : batch) {
            tx.executeWithoutResult(status -> {          // one short tx per item, no proxy needed
                repo.save(p.markSettled());
                if (p.amount().signum() < 0) status.setRollbackOnly();
            });
        }
        // diagnostics: which tx am I in?
        boolean active = TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive();
        String name = TransactionSynchronizationManager.getCurrentTransactionName();
    }
}
Interview angle: "We have JDBC batch inserts via JdbcTemplate and JPA writes in the same method; are they in one transaction?" Yes, if the manager is JpaTransactionManager and both use the same DataSource: the JPA manager binds the JDBC ConnectionHolder too. With two DataSources you need @Transactional(transactionManager = "…") per bean, and no atomicity across them without XA.

Pitfalls

  • Two DataSource beans and no @Primary: Boot refuses to auto-configure a transaction manager; every @Transactional then fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException at first call, not at startup.
  • Opening a thread pool inside a transaction and expecting workers to see uncommitted rows: they use different connections and see nothing until commit.
  • @Transactional on a @Bean of type JdbcTemplate-only app with spring-boot-starter-data-jpa on the classpath: you silently get JpaTransactionManager and an extra EntityManager per transaction.
Interview questions
  • What does @Transactional do under the hood? — A proxy runs TransactionInterceptor around the method; it asks the PlatformTransactionManager for a transaction (new or existing per propagation), binds the connection to the thread via TransactionSynchronizationManager, invokes the method, then commits or rolls back based on the exception type.
  • Why is a transaction thread-bound, and what breaks because of it? — Resources are stored in ThreadLocals keyed by the DataSource; @Async, CompletableFuture.supplyAsync, parallel streams and reactive pipelines run elsewhere and do not participate. Virtual threads still work because each has its own ThreadLocal map, but you must not pin them by holding the connection across blocking code you cannot control.
  • When would you use TransactionTemplate instead of the annotation? — Fine-grained scope (one tx per loop item), private or self-invoked methods, conditional propagation, or when I need TransactionStatus to set rollback-only programmatically.
  • Which transaction manager does Boot pick, and how do you override it? — JpaTransactionManager if JPA is present, else DataSourceTransactionManager; define your own PlatformTransactionManager bean or implement TransactionManagerCustomizer to tweak defaults such as defaultTimeout.
  • How would you debug "my write was not in a transaction"? — Set logging.level.org.springframework.transaction.interceptor=TRACE to see "Getting transaction for [Class.method]", check TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive() at the point of the write, and check whether the call went through the proxy.
  • Does @Transactional on an interface method work? — With CGLIB proxies (the Boot default), annotations on interface methods are not inherited by the class proxy for method-level lookups; put it on the implementation class or method.
  • Spring Boot 2 vs 3 here? — The abstraction is unchanged; javax.persistence became jakarta.persistence, Hibernate 6 is the default, and ChainedTransactionManager is deprecated.

@Transactional semantics: propagation, rollback rules, readOnly, timeout

Why interviewers ask: "inner method threw, outer caught it, why did the commit fail with UnexpectedRollbackException?" is a top-five Spring question. You need the propagation table and the rollback-only flag in your head.

Propagation answers "there may already be a transaction on this thread; what do I do?" REQUIRED (default): join it, or start one. REQUIRES_NEW: suspend the current one, open a second physical connection and a fully independent transaction. NESTED: same connection, but take a JDBC savepoint; an inner rollback returns to the savepoint while the outer continues (JDBC/DataSourceTransactionManager only; JpaTransactionManager rejects it unless nestedTransactionAllowed). SUPPORTS: join if present, else run non-transactionally. NOT_SUPPORTED: suspend any existing one. MANDATORY: throw IllegalTransactionStateException if none exists. NEVER: throw if one exists.

Rollback rules: by default the interceptor rolls back on RuntimeException and Error only; a checked exception commits (EJB heritage: checked exceptions were "business outcomes"). Override with rollbackFor = Exception.class or noRollbackFor. When a REQUIRED inner method throws a runtime exception, the interceptor for that inner call cannot roll back a transaction it did not start; it marks it rollback-only. If the outer method catches the exception and tries to commit, the manager throws UnexpectedRollbackException. Analogy: a co-signer on a shared contract crossed out a clause; you can keep writing, but the notary will refuse to stamp it at the end.

readOnly = true is a hint: JpaTransactionManager sets Hibernate's flush mode to MANUAL (no dirty checking, no flush, big CPU saving on large reads), sets Connection.setReadOnly(true) (Postgres then rejects writes; MySQL may route to a replica), and lets a routing DataSource pick a read replica. It does not make an entity immutable. timeout (seconds) is enforced by the manager as a deadline: Hibernate applies it as a JDBC statement query timeout per statement, so a method of many fast statements can exceed the wall-clock limit; it is not a hard kill.

@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Transactional                                       // REQUIRED
    public void place(Order o) {
        repo.save(o);
        audit.log(o);                                    // REQUIRES_NEW: survives our rollback
        try {
            stock.reserve(o);                            // REQUIRED → marks T1 rollback-only on failure
        } catch (StockException e) {                     // caught, but the damage is done
            o.setStatus(BACKORDERED);
        }
    }   // commit here → UnexpectedRollbackException: "Transaction silently rolled back"
}

@Service
public class StockService {
    @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class, timeout = 3)
    public void reserve(Order o) throws StockException { /* checked, now rolls back too */ }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)                      // FlushMode.MANUAL, no dirty check
    public List<Stock> report() { return repo.findAll(); }
}
PropagationExisting txNo txConnectionsInner failure affects outer?
REQUIREDJoinStart1Yes: rollback-only
REQUIRES_NEWSuspend, start newStart2 (held concurrently)No (independent)
NESTEDSavepointStart1No: rollback to savepoint
SUPPORTSJoinNone0–1Yes if joined
NOT_SUPPORTEDSuspendNone0 (outer parked)No
MANDATORYJoinIllegalTransactionStateException1Yes
NEVERIllegalTransactionStateExceptionNone0n/a
Interview angle: "Audit rows must persist even if the order fails" → REQUIRES_NEW on the audit method, and be ready to say the cost: a second pooled connection held while the first is suspended, so under load a pool of 10 can deadlock itself when 10 threads each hold one and wait for a second (HikariCP timeout after connection-timeout, 30 s by default).

Pitfalls

  • Catching an exception from a REQUIRED inner call and "handling" it: the outer transaction is already rollback-only. Fix: REQUIRES_NEW/NESTED on the inner, or noRollbackFor on the inner, or let it propagate.
  • @Transactional on a method that throws a checked exception (e.g. IOException) commits partial work; add rollbackFor = Exception.class or declare a global default via a custom TransactionAttributeSource.
  • readOnly = true and then repo.save(): Hibernate 6 silently skips the flush (nothing written, no error) unless the JDBC driver rejects writes on a read-only connection.
  • timeout does not interrupt Java code; a slow REST call inside the transaction will overrun it. Keep remote I/O outside transactions.
Interview questions
  • Inner REQUIRED method throws, outer catches and returns normally: what happens? — The inner interceptor marks the shared transaction rollback-only; at the outer commit the manager rolls back and throws UnexpectedRollbackException. Nothing from either method is persisted.
  • Why does a checked exception not roll back by default? — Spring inherited EJB semantics where checked exceptions represent expected business outcomes; only RuntimeException/Error trigger rollback. Use rollbackFor or make exceptions unchecked.
  • REQUIRES_NEW vs NESTED? — REQUIRES_NEW is a fully separate transaction on a second connection, commits independently, and can deadlock the pool; NESTED is a savepoint in the same transaction, commits only with the outer, and needs JDBC savepoint support (not JPA by default).
  • What does readOnly = true really do? — Hibernate flush mode MANUAL (skips dirty checking), Connection.setReadOnly(true) as a driver hint, and a routing key for read-replica DataSources; it is an optimisation, not a security boundary.
  • How would you debug "commit happened but the rows are missing"? — Check the method was called via the proxy, that the transaction manager targets the right DataSource, that readOnly is not set, and enable org.springframework.orm.jpa=DEBUG plus hibernate.SQL to see whether the flush emitted the statements.
  • Can you nest @Transactional on a private method? — The annotation is ignored (proxy cannot intercept); Spring 6 logs nothing, AspectJ mode would honour it. Use TransactionTemplate.
  • What is the cost of timeout and how does it work? — The manager computes a deadline; Hibernate sets Statement.setQueryTimeout on each statement with the remaining seconds, and the manager checks the deadline on the next resource access. Long Java-side work is not interrupted.
  • Spring Boot 2 vs 3 for @Transactional? — Same rules; Spring 6 adds @Transactional(label=…), honours jakarta.transaction.Transactional too, and Hibernate 6 treats the readOnly flag slightly more strictly (skipping the flush entirely).

Isolation levels & anomalies: dirty, non-repeatable, phantom, MVCC, when to lock instead

Why interviewers ask: "two users book the last seat at the same time" is the classic. They want you to name the anomaly (lost update), the DB default, and why raising isolation is usually the wrong first move.

The SQL standard defines anomalies and the levels that forbid them. Dirty read: seeing another transaction's uncommitted row. Non-repeatable read: the same row read twice returns different values because someone committed in between. Phantom read: the same range query returns new rows. READ_UNCOMMITTED allows all three, READ_COMMITTED forbids dirty reads, REPEATABLE_READ also forbids non-repeatable reads, SERIALIZABLE forbids everything by behaving as if transactions ran one after another. Lost update (two read-modify-write cycles, second overwrites first) is not in the standard table but is the one that costs money; READ_COMMITTED does not prevent it.

Defaults differ: PostgreSQL READ_COMMITTED, MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE_READ, Oracle READ_COMMITTED, SQL Server READ_COMMITTED (lock-based unless snapshot is on). Modern engines use MVCC: readers see a snapshot (per statement at READ_COMMITTED, per transaction at REPEATABLE_READ) instead of taking shared locks, so readers never block writers. Postgres's REPEATABLE_READ is actually snapshot isolation and also prevents phantoms; its SERIALIZABLE (SSI) detects write-skew and aborts with could not serialize access, which your code must retry. Analogy: MVCC hands each transaction a photocopy of the ledger taken when it started; locking makes everyone queue for the one original.

Spring's @Transactional(isolation = …) sets Connection.setTransactionIsolation for the tx and restores it on release; it only applies where the transaction starts (an inner REQUIRED call with a different level throws unless validateExistingTransaction is off, and then it is silently ignored). Rule of thumb: keep the DB default and handle the specific race with optimistic locking (@Version), pessimistic SELECT … FOR UPDATE (@Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)), or an atomic UPDATE … SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE qty > 0. Raise isolation to SERIALIZABLE only for short, retryable transactions where invariants span multiple rows (write skew).

LevelDirtyNon-repeatablePhantomLost updateTypical cost
READ_UNCOMMITTEDYesYesYesYesPostgres treats as READ_COMMITTED
READ_COMMITTEDNoYesYesYesStatement snapshot; cheapest
REPEATABLE_READNoNoStandard: yes; PG/InnoDB snapshot: mostly noPG: aborts; MySQL: yesTx snapshot; longer-held undo/WAL
SERIALIZABLENoNoNoNo (aborts)Retries required; throughput drops
Interview angle: "Would you set SERIALIZABLE for the booking service?" A strong answer: no; keep READ_COMMITTED, model the seat as a row with @Version or do an atomic conditional update, and reserve SERIALIZABLE for multi-row invariants ("at least one doctor on call") where write skew is the risk, with retry logic around it.

Pitfalls

  • Setting isolation on an inner REQUIRED method: with the default validateExistingTransaction=false it is silently ignored; the outer's level wins.
  • Relying on MySQL REPEATABLE_READ to stop lost updates: plain UPDATEs use the latest committed version (current-read), so both updates succeed.
  • Long-running REPEATABLE_READ transactions on Postgres bloat tables (vacuum cannot reclaim rows still visible to the old snapshot).
  • Using SELECT FOR UPDATE on rows read in a different order in two code paths: classic deadlock; order your locks.
Interview questions
  • Explain dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads. — Dirty: reading uncommitted data. Non-repeatable: the same row changes between two reads in one transaction. Phantom: a range query returns extra or fewer rows the second time because another transaction inserted or deleted.
  • What is the default isolation level in Postgres and MySQL, and does Spring change it? — Postgres READ_COMMITTED, MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE_READ. Spring's default Isolation.DEFAULT leaves the driver setting alone.
  • How does MVCC avoid readers blocking writers? — Each row version carries transaction ids; a reader sees the newest version committed before its snapshot, so no shared read locks are needed. Writers still take row locks against other writers.
  • How would you prevent double booking? — Prefer a @Version column (optimistic) for low contention, or @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) / SELECT FOR UPDATE for hot rows, or a single atomic conditional UPDATE whose affected-row count decides. Not a higher isolation level.
  • Why is SERIALIZABLE rarely used? — Throughput collapses under contention and, on Postgres, transactions can abort with serialization failures that the application must retry; most invariants can be enforced with row-level techniques.
  • What is write skew? — Two transactions read overlapping data, each writes a disjoint row based on what it read, and the combined result violates an invariant (two doctors both go off call). Only SERIALIZABLE (or an explicit lock on a guard row) prevents it.
  • How would you debug a suspected phantom in a report? — Reproduce with two psql sessions and explicit BEGIN; check the tx isolation in pg_stat_activity / SHOW transaction_isolation; fix by running the report in one REPEATABLE_READ transaction so all statements share one snapshot.

JPA core: EntityManager, persistence context, entity states, dirty checking, merge vs persist

Why interviewers ask: "you changed a field and never called save(), yet the row updated; why?" and "why did save() run a SELECT first?" are decided by the persistence context. Candidates who treat JPA as a DAO fail these.

The EntityManager (Hibernate Session) owns a persistence context: an identity map keyed by (entity class, id), also called the first-level cache. Within one context each row is represented by exactly one Java object, so find(User, 1) == find(User, 1) and a second find does not hit the DB. In Spring the context is transaction-scoped: the injected EntityManager is a shared proxy that resolves to the context bound to the current transaction (or a fresh one-shot context outside a transaction, or the request-scoped one when open-in-view is on).

Entity states: transient/new (just new-ed, unknown to any context), managed (in the context; its snapshot is kept for dirty checking), detached (was managed; the context closed or detach was called), removed (scheduled for DELETE). At flush time (before a query that might depend on pending changes under FlushModeType.AUTO, at commit, or on explicit flush()) Hibernate compares every managed entity with its snapshot and emits INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE in a fixed order: inserts, updates, collection deletes/updates/inserts, deletes. Analogy: the context is a shopping cart with a photo of every item as it came off the shelf; at checkout the cashier scans for differences and bills only those.

persist(e) makes a transient object managed (INSERT at flush; with IDENTITY ids, immediately). merge(e) copies the state of a detached (or transient) object onto a managed copy and returns that copy: the argument stays detached, which is the number-one merge bug. Spring Data's save() is isNew(e) ? persist : merge, where isNew checks id null / primitive 0 or Persistable.isNew(); so saving an entity with an assigned id triggers a SELECT via merge. saveAndFlush adds an immediate flush, useful to surface constraint violations at the call site. getReferenceById(id) returns a lazy proxy without a SELECT: ideal for setting a foreign key (order.setCustomer(repo.getReferenceById(cid))); touching any non-id field triggers the load, and a missing row surfaces as EntityNotFoundException only then.

@Transactional
public void rename(long id, String name, Address extra) {
    User u = em.find(User.class, id);          // SELECT; u is MANAGED, snapshot taken
    u.setName(name);                            // no SQL yet: just a field write
    User again = em.find(User.class, id);      // no SELECT: identity map hit, again == u
    List<User> all = em.createQuery("select u from User u", User.class)
                       .getResultList();       // AUTO flush: UPDATE fires BEFORE this query
    Address a = new Address("Delhi");          // TRANSIENT
    em.persist(a);                             // MANAGED (INSERT deferred, SEQUENCE id fetched now)
    em.detach(u);                              // DETACHED: later changes are ignored
    u.setName("ignored");
    User merged = em.merge(u);                 // copies state onto managed instance; merged != u
    merged.setName("final");
}                                              // commit: flush UPDATE name=final, INSERT address
  1. find issues a SELECT and registers the object in the identity map with a snapshot of its column values.
  2. Changing a field only changes the Java object. Nothing is sent to the DB; the snapshot still says old.
  3. A second find for the same key returns the very same instance. No query.
  4. A JPQL query on User under FlushMode.AUTO forces a flush first so the query sees the pending change; the snapshot is refreshed.
  5. persist needs an id to key the map: SEQUENCE ids are fetched now, the INSERT itself waits for flush (with IDENTITY the INSERT would run immediately).
  6. detach evicts the entry. u still exists as a Java object but no snapshot tracks it; the write of ignored will never be flushed.
  7. merge loads a fresh managed instance (SELECT), copies the detached state onto it and returns that object. Mutating u afterwards would be lost; mutate merged.
  8. Commit triggers the final flush: dirty check finds name=final, emits UPDATE, and the deferred INSERT runs. Then the context closes and every entity becomes detached.
CallInput stateReturnsSQL nowGotcha
persisttransientvoid; arg becomes managedid fetch (SEQUENCE) or INSERT (IDENTITY)Throws if id already assigned and entity is detached
mergedetached / transientmanaged copySELECT (unless in context)Arg stays detached; use the return value
Data JPA saveanymanaged instancepersist or merge as aboveAssigned ids always merge (extra SELECT)
saveAndFlushanymanaged instanceplus immediate flushOnly flushes; does not commit
getReferenceByIdidlazy proxynoneEntityNotFoundException on first access if missing
Interview angle: "A service loads 10,000 entities to export them and the JVM slows to a crawl." The context keeps every entity and its snapshot; each flush re-checks all 10,000. Answers: readOnly = true (no dirty checking), stream with em.clear() every n rows, DTO projections, or a StatelessSession.

Pitfalls

  • Calling repo.save(entity) on an already managed entity in the same transaction is harmless but redundant; dirty checking would have done it. Doing it in a loop with a merge-path entity costs a SELECT each.
  • Reading an entity outside a transaction (no open-in-view) gives a detached object; lazy collections then throw on access.
  • FlushModeType.COMMIT makes queries return stale results relative to pending changes; understand it before using it as a "performance fix".
  • Setting an id manually on a new entity with @GeneratedValue: persist throws PersistentObjectException: detached entity passed to persist.
Interview questions
  • What is the persistence context? — A per-EntityManager identity map of managed entities plus their snapshots; it guarantees one instance per row, caches lookups within the transaction and drives dirty checking at flush.
  • Why did the DB update without save()? — The entity was managed inside a transaction; at commit Hibernate flushed the dirty field. save() is only needed to attach new or detached objects.
  • persist vs merge? — persist attaches the very object you pass and only works on transient instances; merge copies state onto a managed instance (loading it if necessary) and returns the copy, working for detached objects.
  • When exactly is SQL executed? — At flush: automatically before a JPQL/Criteria query touching affected tables (AUTO), at commit, or on explicit flush(); the exception is IDENTITY inserts, which run at persist time.
  • What is the difference between findById and getReferenceById? — findById hits the DB (or the context) and returns Optional; getReferenceById returns an uninitialised proxy with only the id set, no query, and fails lazily if the row is absent.
  • How would you debug "field set but not persisted"? — Confirm a transaction was active (isActualTransactionActive), that the entity was managed (not the detached argument of merge), that the field is not @Transient/updatable=false, and that readOnly was not set.
  • What is the first-level cache vs the second-level cache? — First-level is the persistence context: mandatory, per transaction, not shared. Second-level is an optional, EntityManagerFactory-wide cache (Ehcache/Infinispan/Caffeine via JCache) of entity state by id.
  • Boot 2 vs 3: anything different? — getOne (Boot 2) was deprecated for getReferenceById; getById too. Hibernate 6 changed some flush and dirty-checking internals (bytecode enhancement is more capable) and the package is jakarta.persistence.

Spring Data JPA: repositories, queries, projections, Specification, paging, @Modifying, auditing

Why interviewers ask: everyone has used JpaRepository; the probing questions are "how does a method with no body execute?", "Page vs Slice", and "why did my @Modifying query leave stale entities?".

At startup @EnableJpaRepositories (auto-configured) scans interfaces extending Repository and creates a JDK proxy per interface backed by SimpleJpaRepository. A call is resolved in order: a custom-implementation fragment (UserRepositoryImpl), a @Query, a named query, then the derived-query parser which turns findTop3ByStatusAndCreatedAfterOrderByIdDesc into a Criteria query at startup (a typo fails the context, not the request). SimpleJpaRepository is annotated @Transactional(readOnly = true) at class level with @Transactional on save/delete, so repository calls always have a transaction; it also means calling findAll() from a non-transactional service opens and closes its own transaction and persistence context per call, detaching the results.

Projections avoid loading whole entities: an interface with getters (closed projection → only those columns selected; open projection with @Value("#{target.first + ' ' + target.last}") loads the entity), a record/class DTO via select new com.x.UserDto(u.id, u.name) or constructor-name matching, or a raw Tuple for ad-hoc native queries. Specification<T> composes Criteria predicates for dynamic filters (where(hasStatus(s)).and(nameLike(q))), the maintainable alternative to string-concatenated JPQL. Pageable → Page<T> runs the query plus a count(*); Slice<T> fetches size + 1 rows and only knows hasNext(), cheaper for infinite scroll. Keyset pagination (WHERE id > :last ORDER BY id, or Spring Data 3.1 ScrollPosition.keyset()) is what you propose for deep pages.

@Modifying marks a @Query as UPDATE/DELETE; it bypasses the persistence context entirely, so managed entities become stale. clearAutomatically = true clears the context after the query (losing unflushed changes unless flushAutomatically = true too). @EntityGraph declares which associations to fetch eagerly for that one query. Auditing: @EnableJpaAuditing, @CreatedDate/@LastModifiedDate/@CreatedBy/@LastModifiedBy on the entity (or a @MappedSuperclass) with @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class) and an AuditorAware<String> bean that reads the SecurityContext.

public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long>,
                                         JpaSpecificationExecutor<Order> {
    Slice<OrderSummary> findByCustomerIdAndStatus(long cid, Status s, Pageable p);  // derived + projection

    @Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.lines where o.id = :id")
    Optional<Order> findWithLines(@Param("id") long id);                           // JPQL, join fetch

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"lines", "customer"})
    List<Order> findByStatus(Status s);                                            // graph on a derived query

    @Modifying(clearAutomatically = true, flushAutomatically = true)
    @Query("update Order o set o.status = :to where o.status = :from and o.created < :cutoff")
    int expire(@Param("from") Status from, @Param("to") Status to, @Param("cutoff") Instant cutoff);
}

interface OrderSummary { Long getId(); Status getStatus(); BigDecimal getTotal(); }  // closed projection
  1. At startup the interface is turned into a proxy; every method is pre-parsed so a misspelt property (findByCustomrId) fails the context.
  2. The derived query becomes Criteria; the closed projection selects only three columns; Slice asks for one extra row instead of running count(*).
  3. join fetch initialises the collection in the same SELECT. Hibernate 6 de-duplicates the parent rows automatically (no distinct needed).
  4. @EntityGraph does the same declaratively; with two collections in the graph you would hit MultipleBagFetchException unless one is a Set.
  5. Bulk update: flushAutomatically pushes pending changes first so they are not lost, the UPDATE runs in SQL, clearAutomatically evicts everything so later reads are fresh.
  6. The projection instance has no lazy fields, so it can leave the transaction and be serialised without LazyInitializationException.
Interview angle: "The admin list page is slow at page 5,000." Page runs OFFSET 100000 plus a full count(*) on every request; propose Slice (drop the count), keyset pagination on an indexed sort column, and a projection instead of full entities.

Pitfalls

  • Native @Query with Pageable needs a countQuery; Spring Data cannot derive it reliably from arbitrary SQL.
  • @Modifying without a transaction throws TransactionRequiredException: the class-level readOnly=true does not cover custom queries, so annotate the repository method or the caller with @Transactional.
  • Open projections (@Value SpEL) load the whole entity; you lose the column-pruning benefit silently.
  • @EntityGraph on a paged query with a collection: Hibernate fetches everything in memory and paginates in Java (HHH90003004: firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch; applying in memory).
Interview questions
  • How does a repository interface execute without an implementation? — Spring Data registers a JDK proxy whose target is SimpleJpaRepository; derived method names are parsed into Criteria queries at startup and @Query strings are validated then.
  • Is a repository method transactional? — Yes: SimpleJpaRepository is @Transactional(readOnly=true) with read-write overrides on save/delete. Custom @Query methods inherit the read-only default, so @Modifying queries need their own @Transactional.
  • Page vs Slice? — Page issues an extra count query for total pages; Slice fetches size+1 rows and offers only hasNext(). For deep pages both suffer from OFFSET cost; use keyset pagination.
  • When do you use interface projections vs DTO projections? — Interface (closed) projections for simple column subsets with zero boilerplate; record DTOs via select new when you need computed values, nested structure, or want a plain class for serialisation and tests.
  • What does @Modifying(clearAutomatically = true) protect against? — Stale managed entities after a bulk JPQL update: the update goes straight to SQL, so entities loaded earlier still hold old values; clearing forces a reload. Pair with flushAutomatically to avoid losing pending writes.
  • How would you implement dynamic search filters? — JpaSpecificationExecutor with composable Specifications (or Querydsl), never string-built JPQL; add Pageable and a projection for the list view.
  • How do you populate created/modified audit columns? — @EnableJpaAuditing, AuditingEntityListener on a @MappedSuperclass, and an AuditorAware bean reading the current principal; dates come from a DateTimeProvider you can fix in tests.
  • Boot 2 vs 3 for Spring Data? — Spring Data 3 removed getOne/getById in favour of getReferenceById, introduced ListCrudRepository/ListPagingAndSortingRepository (CrudRepository.findAll now returns Iterable), added keyset scrolling (3.1) and requires Hibernate 6.

Fetching & N+1: LAZY vs EAGER, LazyInitializationException, JOIN FETCH, batch size, open-in-view

Why interviewers ask: N+1 is the most common JPA performance bug in production and open-in-view=true is the most common reason it goes unnoticed until the connection pool is exhausted. Expect "1 request = 1,001 queries: three ways to fix it".

JPA defaults: @ManyToOne and @OneToOne are EAGER, @OneToMany and @ManyToMany are LAZY. EAGER on a to-one is a trap: every query for the child also joins (or, for JPQL queries, issues a separate select per row) for the parent, whether you need it or not, and you cannot turn it off per query. Best practice: everything LAZY (@ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY)) and fetch what a use case needs explicitly. A lazy association is a proxy (to-one) or a PersistentBag/Set (collection) that loads on first access if the persistence context is still open; otherwise: LazyInitializationException: could not initialize proxy - no Session.

N+1: load N orders (1 query), then touch order.getLines() in a loop (N more). Fixes, from most targeted to most global: (1) JOIN FETCH / @EntityGraph for that query: one SQL; but only one collection ("bag" = List) per query or Hibernate throws MultipleBagFetchException (use Set, or fetch the second collection in a second query, which Hibernate merges via the identity map). (2) @BatchSize(size = 50) on the collection or entity, or globally spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50: when one lazy collection is touched, Hibernate loads it for up to 50 parents in the context with WHERE order_id IN (?, ?, …), turning N+1 into N/50+1. (3) @Fetch(SUBSELECT): one extra query re-running the original as a subselect. (4) DTO projections that never load entities. Analogy: N+1 is asking the librarian for each book's author one at a time; join fetch is bringing the authors on the same cart; batch size is asking for 50 authors per trip.

spring.jpa.open-in-view is true by default in Boot (it logs a warning at startup). It registers OpenEntityManagerInViewInterceptor, which opens the persistence context at the start of the web request and closes it after the view renders, so lazy loading works in controllers and Jackson serialisation. Costs: a DB connection is held for the entire request (including slow downstream calls), so the pool drains under load; N+1 in serialisation is hidden; the transaction boundary is blurred. Turn it off (spring.jpa.open-in-view=false) and load what the view needs inside the service transaction.

spring:
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false                       # Boot default is true; fail fast instead of holding a connection
    properties:
      hibernate:
        default_batch_fetch_size: 50          # N+1 → N/50+1 for every lazy association
        query.fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch: true   # Hibernate 6: refuse in-memory paging
TechniqueQueries for N parentsScopeWorks with pagingLimit
Lazy + loop (N+1)N + 1defaultYesSlow; throws when context closed
JOIN FETCH / @EntityGraph1per queryCollections: in memory onlyOne bag per query; row multiplication
@BatchSize / default_batch_fetch_size1 + ceil(N/size)global or per associationYesStill lazy; needs open context
@Fetch(SUBSELECT)2per associationYes (re-runs original query)Hibernate-specific
DTO projection1per queryYesNot an entity; no updates
Interview angle: "How do you catch N+1 before production?" Answer with tooling: hibernate.generate_statistics=true and assert getQueryExecutionCount() in a @DataJpaTest, datasource-proxy / p6spy query counting, or the Hypersistence Utils SQLStatementCountValidator; plus open-in-view=false so lazy access outside the transaction fails in tests.

Pitfalls

  • Returning entities from a controller with open-in-view=true: Jackson walks every lazy collection during serialisation, causing N+1 after the service returned and potentially infinite recursion on bidirectional mappings.
  • JOIN FETCH on a collection with Pageable: all rows are loaded and paged in memory; Hibernate 6 logs HHH90003004. Page on ids first, then fetch by id IN (…).
  • EAGER @ManyToOne everywhere: a JPQL query select o from Order o issues one extra SELECT per distinct customer because JPQL does not honour the EAGER join automatically.
  • Two List collections in one fetch graph: MultipleBagFetchException; switch to Set or split into two queries.
Interview questions
  • What is the N+1 problem and how do you detect it? — One query for the parents plus one per parent for a lazy association. Detect via SQL logging or Hibernate statistics in a test that asserts query counts, and via APM traces showing hundreds of identical statements per request.
  • Three ways to fix N+1? — JOIN FETCH/@EntityGraph for the specific query, @BatchSize/default_batch_fetch_size as a global mitigation, and DTO projections that skip entities; @Fetch(SUBSELECT) is a fourth.
  • Why does Boot warn about open-in-view? — It holds a persistence context and therefore a JDBC connection for the whole HTTP request, hiding lazy-loading problems and exhausting the pool under load; disable it and fetch inside the service transaction.
  • When does LazyInitializationException occur and how do you fix it properly? — Accessing a lazy proxy or collection after its persistence context closed (outside the transaction, in another thread, during JSON serialisation). Fix by fetching what is needed in the transaction (fetch join, entity graph, DTO), not by making the association EAGER or by enable_lazy_load_no_trans.
  • Why not simply use EAGER? — It fetches on every load, cannot be disabled per query, causes cartesian products with multiple collections and separate selects under JPQL; lazy plus explicit fetch plans keeps control per use case.
  • What is MultipleBagFetchException? — Hibernate refuses to fetch-join two List (bag) collections at once because the cartesian product cannot be de-duplicated without ordering; use Set, @OrderColumn, or separate queries.
  • How would you paginate orders with their lines efficiently? — Page the parent ids (or parents without the collection) with a normal query, then load lines for those ids with a second fetch-join or batch fetch; never fetch-join a collection with Pageable.
  • Boot 2 vs 3 differences here? — Same defaults for open-in-view; Hibernate 6 de-duplicates fetch-join results automatically (no distinct hack), uses a new SQM query engine, and adds the fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch setting.

Mapping pitfalls: equals/hashCode, owning side, cascades, enums, @Version, @Lock

Why interviewers ask: each of these has bitten every senior JPA developer at least once, so they are cheap to ask and expose whether you understand what Hibernate does with your objects.

Identity. Do not use Lombok @Data on entities. Field-based equals mutates with every setter and breaks a HashSet of managed entities; id-based equals fails for new entities (id null until flush) so two unsaved objects collide. The safe recipe: equals returns true only when both ids are non-null and equal (and classes match, unwrapping Hibernate proxies via Hibernate.getClass), while hashCode returns a constant (getClass().hashCode()) so the hash cannot change when the id is assigned; or use a client-assigned UUID / natural key.

Owning side. For a bidirectional @OneToMany/@ManyToOne the many side with the FK column is the owner; the collection side declares mappedBy and is ignored at flush. Adding to parent.getChildren() without setting child.setParent(parent) writes nothing. Sync helpers (addChild sets both sides) are the answer. A unidirectional @OneToMany with a @JoinColumn works but generates extra UPDATE statements and, without @JoinColumn, a join table. Cascade: CascadeType.REMOVE deletes children when the parent is removed; orphanRemoval = true additionally deletes a child that is merely removed from the collection (the child cannot exist without its parent). CascadeType.ALL on @ManyToMany is a classic bug: removing one author deletes shared books. Prefer a join entity (AuthorBook with its own columns like since) over @ManyToMany as soon as the relationship carries data or needs auditing.

Enums: the default @Enumerated(ORDINAL) stores the position, so reordering constants corrupts data; always EnumType.STRING (or a converter to a short code). @Version adds optimistic locking: every UPDATE gets WHERE id=? AND version=?; zero rows updated → OptimisticLockException, which Spring translates to ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException. It also works across requests when the version travels through the DTO (edit forms). @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) on a repository method emits SELECT … FOR UPDATE; pair it with @QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout", value = "3000")) so a waiter fails instead of hanging.

@Entity
public class Order {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "order_seq")
    @SequenceGenerator(name = "order_seq", sequenceName = "order_seq", allocationSize = 50)
    private Long id;

    @Version private long version;                         // optimistic lock column
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) private Status status;   // never ORDINAL

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();

    public void addLine(OrderLine l) { lines.add(l); l.setOrder(this); }   // keep both sides in sync
    public void removeLine(OrderLine l) { lines.remove(l); l.setOrder(null); } // orphanRemoval → DELETE

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof Order other)) return false;   // proxy-safe with instanceof
        return id != null && id.equals(other.id);
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Order.class.hashCode(); } // constant: stable across persist
}

public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {
    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
    @QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout", value = "3000"))
    Optional<Order> findWithLockById(Long id);            // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
}
ConcernWrongRight
EqualityLombok @Data, or Objects.hash(id)Id-based equals (null-safe), constant hashCode
Child deletionCascadeType.REMOVE onlyorphanRemoval=true when child cannot live alone
Many-to-many with attributes@ManyToMany + cascade=ALLJoin entity with two @ManyToOnes
Enum columnORDINAL (default)EnumType.STRING or AttributeConverter
Concurrent editsLast write wins@Version and surface 409 Conflict

Pitfalls

  • toString() including a lazy collection: LazyInitializationException from a log statement, or infinite recursion on bidirectional mappings.
  • Replacing an orphanRemoval collection (order.setLines(newList)) throws "A collection with cascade=all-delete-orphan was no longer referenced"; clear and re-add instead.
  • @ManyToMany with List: removing one element deletes all join rows and re-inserts the rest; use Set.
  • @Version on a DTO-less update flow: the version never leaves the server, so concurrent web edits still overwrite each other.
Interview questions
  • How should you implement equals/hashCode for an entity? — Compare ids only when both are non-null; return a constant hashCode so the entity can sit in a Set before and after its id is assigned; unwrap proxies with instanceof or Hibernate.getClass.
  • What is the owning side and why does it matter? — The side holding the FK (@ManyToOne) is what Hibernate writes; the mappedBy side is read-only for persistence. Forgetting to set the owning side leaves the FK null.
  • orphanRemoval vs CascadeType.REMOVE? — Both delete children when the parent is deleted; only orphanRemoval deletes a child that is disconnected from the parent's collection. Use it for true composition.
  • When do you replace @ManyToMany with an entity? — As soon as the link needs attributes, auditing, ordering or its own lifecycle; also to avoid cascade accidents and the delete-all-reinsert behaviour of bags.
  • How does @Version work and what exception do you get? — Hibernate appends AND version = ? to updates and increments it; a zero row count raises OptimisticLockException (Spring: ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException). Map it to HTTP 409 or retry idempotent work.
  • Optimistic vs pessimistic locking: how do you choose? — Optimistic for low contention and long user think-time (no locks held); pessimistic (PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) for hot rows with short transactions where retries would thrash, always with a lock timeout.
  • Why is EnumType.ORDINAL dangerous? — It persists the enum index; inserting or reordering constants silently remaps existing rows. STRING costs bytes but is self-describing.

ID generation: IDENTITY vs SEQUENCE (and why it decides batching), pooled optimizer, UUID, Hibernate 6

Why interviewers ask: "why are your inserts not batched?" has one answer most people miss: IDENTITY ids. It also tests whether you know what changed under Hibernate 6 in Boot 3.

IDENTITY (auto-increment) forces Hibernate to execute the INSERT immediately at persist to learn the id, which disables JDBC insert batching for that entity (hibernate.jdbc.batch_size is silently ignored). SEQUENCE fetches ids from a DB sequence before flush, so inserts stay deferred and batchable. With allocationSize = 50 (the default) and the pooled optimizer, Hibernate calls nextval once per 50 ids and hands out the range in memory: one round trip per 50 inserts, and other JVM instances simply get other ranges (gaps are harmless). pooled-lo is the variant to pick if legacy code also inserts directly with nextval. Create the sequence with INCREMENT BY 50 to match, or Hibernate's ddl-auto=validate complains about the mismatch (Hibernate 6 validates increment size). Analogy: IDENTITY is asking the receptionist for a ticket number one visitor at a time; SEQUENCE with pooled is taking a book of 50 tickets.

UUID ids (GenerationType.UUID, new in JPA 3.1 / Hibernate 6) are generated client-side, so they batch and can be assigned before persist (useful for idempotency keys and outbox events). Downsides: 16 bytes, random inserts fragment a B-tree primary key on MySQL (use UUIDv7/time-ordered or a BINARY(16) column; Postgres uuid type is fine). TABLE generation uses a row lock in a table and is slow; avoid. AUTO maps to SEQUENCE on Postgres/Oracle/H2 and, since Hibernate 5.x, to a global hibernate_sequence unless you name one, which is why explicit @SequenceGenerator per entity is standard practice.

Hibernate 6 changes in Boot 3: AUTO on MySQL/MariaDB now uses a sequence-like table per entity (<entity>_SEQ) instead of IDENTITY; the implicit sequence naming became <entity>_SEQ per entity instead of the shared hibernate_sequence, so migrated apps need hibernate.id.db_structure_naming_strategy=legacy (or explicit generators) to keep using the old sequence; allocationSize mismatch is validated; and @GenericGenerator is deprecated in favour of @IdGeneratorType.

@Entity
public class Event {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "event_seq")
    @SequenceGenerator(name = "event_seq", sequenceName = "event_seq", allocationSize = 50) // CREATE SEQUENCE event_seq INCREMENT BY 50
    private Long id;
}

@Entity
public class OutboxMessage {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.UUID)   // JPA 3.1: client-side, batchable, assignable
    private UUID id;
}
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size: 50
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_inserts: true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_updates: true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.id.optimizer.pooled.preferred: pooled-lo   # if others use nextval directly
StrategyId known atInsert batchingRound trips per 50 rowsNotes
IDENTITYafter INSERTNo50MySQL legacy default; simplest DDL
SEQUENCE + pooled(50)at persist (from range)Yes1 nextval + 1 batchPostgres/Oracle/H2 recommended
SEQUENCE, allocationSize=1at persistYes50 nextval + 1 batchHalves the benefit; avoid
UUIDbefore persistYes1 batchIndex fragmentation unless time-ordered
TABLEat persistYes1 row lock per rangeContention; avoid

Pitfalls

  • Migrating Boot 2 → 3 with GenerationType.AUTO and no explicit generator: Hibernate 6 looks for <Entity>_SEQ, the sequence does not exist, and inserts fail or ddl-auto creates new sequences starting at 1 → duplicate keys.
  • allocationSize=50 in Java but INCREMENT BY 1 in the DB: Hibernate hands out ids the sequence will later re-issue → DuplicateKeyException in another instance.
  • Random UUID v4 as a clustered primary key on MySQL InnoDB: page splits on every insert; prefer UUIDv7 or a surrogate bigint plus a UUID business key.
Interview questions
  • Why does IDENTITY prevent batch inserts? — Hibernate must run the INSERT at persist to obtain the generated key for the persistence context, so it cannot defer and group statements at flush.
  • What does allocationSize do and what happens on restart? — Hibernate reserves ids in blocks of that size from one nextval; an unused remainder is lost on restart, leaving gaps, which is acceptable for surrogate keys.
  • pooled vs hi/lo vs pooled-lo? — hi/lo multiplies the sequence value in Java (incompatible with raw SQL inserts); pooled stores the upper bound in the sequence; pooled-lo stores the lower bound and is safest when other clients call nextval too.
  • When would you choose UUID primary keys? — Multi-region or client-generated ids, idempotent retries, outbox/event ids, or when exposing ids publicly; mitigate index fragmentation with time-ordered UUIDs.
  • What broke with ids when upgrading to Spring Boot 3? — Hibernate 6 changed the implicit sequence name from the shared hibernate_sequence to <Entity>_SEQ and changed AUTO on MySQL; fix with explicit generators or hibernate.id.db_structure_naming_strategy=legacy.
  • How would you verify batching actually happens? — Enable hibernate.generate_statistics and check JDBC batches executed, or use datasource-proxy which logs batch:true, querySize:1, batchSize:50; show-sql cannot tell.

Connection pooling & performance: HikariCP sizing, leak detection, statement batching, SQL logging, second-level cache

Why interviewers ask: "requests hang after 200 concurrent users" is a connection-pool question in disguise; they want the sizing formula, the leak-detection flag, and an opinion on show-sql.

HikariCP is Boot's default pool (spring.datasource.hikari.*).
