Defaults: maximum-pool-size=10, minimum-idle = max, connection-timeout=30000 ms (then SQLTransientConnectionException: Connection is not available), max-lifetime=1800000, idle-timeout=600000. The sizing formula from the HikariCP wiki: connections ≈ cores × 2 + effective spindles, i.e. a small number like 10–20 per instance, because a database serving 500 connections thrashes; more connections do not add throughput once the DB CPU is saturated. Size for the DB, then bound concurrency in the app (Tomcat threads, bulkheads) so requests queue in the JVM rather than in the pool. leak-detection-threshold=20000 logs a stack trace for any connection held longer than 20 s, which finds open-in-view abuse and forgotten try-with-resources. Analogy: the pool is the number of checkout lanes; adding lanes beyond the number of cashiers (DB cores) just makes more people stand around.

Batching: hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50 groups INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE for the same table into one JDBC batch; order_inserts/order_updates=true reorder statements by entity so parents and children each form one batch instead of alternating; Postgres additionally needs reWriteBatchedInserts=true on the JDBC URL to turn the batch into a multi-row INSERT. Requires SEQUENCE or UUID ids. SQL logging: spring.jpa.show-sql=true writes to stdout, unparameterised, no timing: never in production. Use logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG plus org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE (Hibernate 6) in dev, or a proxy such as datasource-proxy/p6spy that logs real parameter values, execution time, and batch sizes, and can count queries in tests.

Second-level cache: an EntityManagerFactory-wide cache of entity state by id (@Cache/@Cacheable per entity, JCache provider such as Ehcache 3 or Caffeine, hibernate.cache.use_second_level_cache=true). Worth it only for read-mostly reference data (countries, product catalogue) accessed by id; in a multi-instance deployment it goes stale unless invalidated or backed by a distributed provider. The query cache caches result ids for a given query and is invalidated on any write to the involved tables: rarely a win. Most teams get more from Spring's @Cacheable at the service layer with Redis, which caches DTOs, not entities.

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop?reWriteBatchedInserts=true
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 16            # ~ cores*2 + spindles on the DB side; not "number of threads"
      minimum-idle: 4
      connection-timeout: 5000         # fail fast instead of piling up 30 s waits
      max-lifetime: 1500000            # below the DB / proxy idle kill (e.g. 30 min)
      leak-detection-threshold: 20000  # stack trace for connections held > 20 s
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false
    properties:
      hibernate:
        jdbc.batch_size: 50
        order_inserts: true
        order_updates: true
        generate_statistics: false     # true only in tests/profiling
logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL: DEBUG          # dev only; prod uses datasource-proxy with thresholds
Interview angle: "P99 latency spikes under load; DB CPU is at 40%." Walk it: check hikaricp.connections.pending and …acquire metrics (Micrometer exposes them); if threads wait for connections, look for long-held connections (open-in-view, REQUIRES_NEW holding two, remote calls inside transactions) before raising the pool size.

Pitfalls

  • Pool size 100 "to be safe": more context switching on the DB, lock contention, and Postgres process memory; the DB gets slower for everyone.
  • max-lifetime longer than the DB or load balancer idle timeout: connections are killed server-side and the first user gets a broken pipe; keep it a few minutes shorter.
  • REQUIRES_NEW inside a REQUIRED transaction under load: each request needs two connections; with a pool of 10 and 10 concurrent requests you deadlock the pool.
  • Second-level cache with ddl-auto and multiple instances: one instance updates a row, the others serve the cached copy until TTL.
Interview questions
  • How do you size a connection pool? — Start from the database: roughly cores × 2 plus spindles, so 10–20 per instance; measure pending waits and DB CPU; scale app instances, not pool size, and keep total connections across instances under the DB limit.
  • Requests hang after N concurrent users; where do you look? — Hikari metrics (active, pending, timeout), thread dumps showing HikariPool.getConnection, then find what holds connections long: open-in-view, external calls inside @Transactional, REQUIRES_NEW, or leaked connections (enable leak-detection-threshold).
  • Why not show-sql=true in production? — It prints to stdout bypassing the logging framework, shows ? placeholders without values or timings, and cannot be filtered; use a logging proxy with slow-query thresholds instead.
  • What is needed for Hibernate to batch inserts? — hibernate.jdbc.batch_size, non-IDENTITY ids, order_inserts for mixed entities, and on Postgres reWriteBatchedInserts=true; verify with statistics or datasource-proxy.
  • When is the second-level cache appropriate? — Read-mostly reference entities loaded by id in a single-instance or distributed-cache setup; not for frequently updated rows or query results. Many teams prefer service-level caching of DTOs.
  • How would you find a connection leak? — leak-detection-threshold logs the acquiring stack trace; also compare active connections over time and look for code that obtains a raw Connection from the DataSource outside try-with-resources.

Schema management: ddl-auto, Flyway vs Liquibase, spring.sql.init

Why interviewers ask: "how do schema changes reach production?" is a maturity check; ddl-auto=update in prod is a red flag they are listening for.

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto values: none (nothing), validate (compare mappings with the schema at startup; fail fast on a missing column, sequence or wrong type), update (add missing tables/columns; never drops or narrows, never renames, cannot express data migrations, and can create a different schema than your mappings intended), create (drop and create at startup), create-drop (also drop at shutdown). Boot defaults to create-drop for embedded databases (H2/HSQL/Derby) without a migration tool and none otherwise. In production: validate (or none) plus a migration tool.

Flyway: versioned SQL files (V3__add_order_status.sql, repeatable R__views.sql) on classpath:db/migration, applied in order at startup and recorded in flyway_schema_history with a checksum; editing an applied file fails validation (flyway repair fixes the checksum). Liquibase: changelog in XML/YAML/SQL with change sets, database-agnostic abstractions, rollback definitions, preconditions and contexts. Choose Flyway for SQL-first teams on one DB vendor; Liquibase when you must target several vendors or need declarative rollback. Both run before JPA initialises so validate sees the new schema. spring.sql.init (schema.sql/data.sql, spring.sql.init.mode=always|embedded|never) is for demos and tests; since Boot 2.5 it runs before Hibernate by default, so with ddl-auto=create your seed data would be dropped unless spring.jpa.defer-datasource-initialization=true.

-- src/main/resources/db/migration/V7__order_status_and_index.sql
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'NEW';
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_status_created ON orders (status, created_at);
-- Postgres: CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction → prefix the file name or set
-- spring.flyway.mixed=true / put it in its own migration with "-- flyway:executeInTransaction=false"
FlywayLiquibase
FormatPlain SQL (Java migrations possible)XML/YAML/JSON/SQL change sets
RollbackUndo migrations (paid) or write forward fixesDeclarative rollback per change set
Multi-vendorPer-vendor foldersAbstract change types
History tableflyway_schema_historydatabasechangelog + lock table
Boot propertyspring.flyway.*spring.liquibase.*

Pitfalls

  • ddl-auto=update in prod: no way to drop/rename, silently diverging schemas between environments, and locks on large tables at startup.
  • Two instances starting at once with Flyway: Flyway takes a DB lock so only one migrates; with long migrations the others block past their readiness probe.
  • Migration expands a column and the running old version still writes the narrow form: use expand/contract (add column → deploy code → backfill → drop old) for zero-downtime.
Interview questions
  • Why not ddl-auto=update in production? — It only adds, never removes or renames, cannot carry data migrations, produces types that may not match intent, and leaves no audit trail; use validate with Flyway/Liquibase.
  • Flyway or Liquibase? — Flyway for SQL-first simplicity on a single vendor; Liquibase for multi-vendor, declarative rollbacks and preconditions. Either is fine; consistency across services matters more.
  • How do you make a schema change with zero downtime? — Expand/contract: additive migration first, deploy code that handles both shapes, backfill in batches, then a later migration removes the old column; never a destructive change in the same deploy as the code.
  • What does validate catch? — Missing tables/columns/sequences and type mismatches between entity mappings and the DB at startup; it does not check indexes or constraints.
  • Why did my data.sql stop working after upgrading Boot? — Since 2.5 SQL init runs before Hibernate creates the schema; set spring.jpa.defer-datasource-initialization=true or move seed data to a migration.

Transactions across boundaries: @TransactionalEventListener, the dual-write problem, outbox, JTA/XA

Why interviewers ask: "you save the order and publish to Kafka in the same method; what can go wrong?" is the bridge between the Spring loop and the system-design loop. They want the dual-write failure modes and the outbox pattern by name.

The dual-write problem: a DB commit and a message send are two resources with no shared atomicity. Publish before commit → consumers see an order that later rolls back. Publish after commit → the process can die between the two and the event is lost. Wrapping both in one @Transactional changes nothing: the broker send is not enlisted in the JDBC transaction. Analogy: mailing a letter and updating your ledger are two actions; the post office does not take back the letter when you cross out the ledger entry.

@TransactionalEventListener binds a Spring event handler to the transaction that published it: phases BEFORE_COMMIT, AFTER_COMMIT (default), AFTER_ROLLBACK, AFTER_COMPLETION. It fixes the "consumer sees rolled-back data" half (the send happens only after commit) but not the lost-event half, and AFTER_COMMIT handlers run inside the completing transaction's synchronisation where the JDBC connection is still bound but the transaction is done: any write there is silently not committed unless you annotate the listener with @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW). Add @Async and the handler runs on another thread, where the lazy entities in the event are detached.

Transactional outbox: in the same DB transaction as the business write, insert a row into an outbox table (id, aggregate, type, JSON payload, created_at). A separate relay publishes rows to Kafka and marks/deletes them (polling with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, or CDC with Debezium reading the WAL). The guarantee is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent (dedup by event id). JTA/XA two-phase commit can enlist a JMS broker and a DB via Atomikos/Narayana, but Kafka is not XA, 2PC blocks on coordinator failure, and it is rarely used in cloud-native services. ChainedTransactionManager (commit in reverse order, best effort) was deprecated in Spring Data 2.5 precisely because people mistook it for atomicity.

@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Transactional
    public Order place(PlaceOrder cmd) {
        Order order = orderRepo.save(Order.from(cmd));
        outboxRepo.save(OutboxMessage.of("OrderPlaced", order.getId(), json.write(new OrderPlaced(order))));
        return order;                                   // single local transaction, no broker call
    }
}

@Component
public class OutboxRelay {
    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 500)
    @Transactional
    public void relay() {
        List<OutboxMessage> batch = outboxRepo.lockUnsent(100);   // ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
        for (OutboxMessage m : batch) {
            kafka.send("orders", m.aggregateId().toString(), m.payload()).join();  // sync: fail → row stays
            m.markSent(Instant.now());
        }
    }
}

// alternative for in-process side effects only:
@TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)   // needed if the listener writes to the DB
public void on(OrderPlaced e) { notifications.enqueue(e.orderId()); }
Interview angle: "Can we not just retry the Kafka send?" Retries fix transient broker errors, not the crash between commit and send. "Kafka transactions then?" They give atomicity across Kafka topics and consumer offsets, not across Kafka and Postgres. The outbox plus idempotent consumers is the standard answer; Debezium if you want zero polling.

Pitfalls

  • AFTER_COMMIT listener that calls repo.save() without REQUIRES_NEW: no exception, no row; the transaction is already committed and the synchronisation phase does not flush.
  • @Async @TransactionalEventListener receiving an entity: the entity is detached on the worker thread; pass ids or DTOs in events.
  • Publishing the event with ApplicationEventPublisher outside any transaction: a @TransactionalEventListener is not invoked at all by default (fallbackExecution=false).
  • Outbox relay with a single instance and no SKIP LOCKED: scaling the relay double-publishes; without ordering by aggregate key, consumers see events out of order.
Interview questions
  • Save to DB and publish to Kafka in one @Transactional method: what can go wrong? — The send is not part of the JDBC transaction: a later rollback leaves a phantom event, and if you send after commit a crash loses the event. Neither ordering is safe; you need the outbox pattern or CDC.
  • Explain the transactional outbox pattern. — Write the event to an outbox table in the same local transaction as the business data, then a relay (poller or Debezium) publishes it and marks it sent. Guarantees at-least-once delivery, so consumers deduplicate by event id.
  • What does @TransactionalEventListener give you over @EventListener? — Phase binding: the handler runs only after the publishing transaction commits (or on rollback), so side effects never act on data that is rolled back; it does not survive a crash, so it is not a substitute for the outbox.
  • Why is a DB write inside an AFTER_COMMIT listener lost? — The listener runs during the completed transaction's synchronisation with the old resources still bound; Hibernate will not flush a finished transaction. Use REQUIRES_NEW on the listener.
  • Why was ChainedTransactionManager deprecated? — It only orders commits and rollbacks across managers with no atomicity: if the second commit fails the first is already durable. Its name suggested a guarantee it could not provide.
  • When would you still use JTA/XA? — Legacy systems combining a JMS broker and a relational DB where both support XA and the operational cost of a coordinator is accepted; not with Kafka, and not for microservices where the outbox and sagas are the norm.
  • How do you make the consumer idempotent? — Store processed event ids (unique constraint on processed_events(event_id)) in the same transaction as the consumer's write, or design the operation to be naturally idempotent (upsert by business key).

Testing the data layer: @DataJpaTest, TestEntityManager, Testcontainers, @Sql

Why interviewers ask: "your JPA test passed but production failed with a constraint violation": the answer involves rollback-by-default, H2 vs Postgres, and the flush that never happened.

@DataJpaTest is a slice: it configures only JPA components (repositories, EntityManager, DataSource, Flyway/Liquibase if present), not @Service beans, and by default replaces your DataSource with an embedded H2 (@AutoConfigureTestDatabase); use @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE) to keep the real one. Each test method is @Transactional and rolled back at the end, so nothing is committed, and because the persistence context lives for the whole test, a save followed by findById hits the first-level cache and never runs SQL: bugs in mappings, constraints and queries stay invisible. Force the round trip with TestEntityManager.flush() and clear() (or saveAndFlush) before asserting. Use @Commit / @Rollback(false) when a test must persist.

Testcontainers runs the real database in Docker: @Testcontainers + @Container static PostgreSQLContainer<?> pg = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16"), and in Boot 3.1+ @ServiceConnection wires the URL/credentials automatically (before that: @DynamicPropertySource). A static container is shared across the test class; a singleton pattern (or testcontainers.reuse.enable=true) shares it across classes to keep the suite fast. @Sql("/fixtures/orders.sql") runs scripts before (or with executionPhase = AFTER_TEST_METHOD, after) a test method; @SqlGroup/@SqlMergeMode combine class- and method-level scripts. Prefer Flyway migrations for schema and @Sql only for fixture data.

@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)   // keep Postgres, not H2
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryTest {
    @Container @ServiceConnection                     // Boot 3.1+: url/user/password wired for you
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> pg = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16");

    @Autowired OrderRepository repo;
    @Autowired TestEntityManager em;

    @Test
    @Sql("/fixtures/customers.sql")
    void uniqueOrderNumberIsEnforced() {
        repo.save(Order.create("A-1", 7L));
        repo.save(Order.create("A-1", 7L));
        assertThrows(DataIntegrityViolationException.class, () -> em.flush());  // without flush: passes wrongly
    }

    @Test
    void findWithLinesFetchesInOneQuery() {
        Long id = em.persistAndGetId(Order.withLines(3), Long.class);
        em.flush(); em.clear();                          // leave the first-level cache behind
        Order o = repo.findWithLines(id).orElseThrow();
        assertTrue(Hibernate.isInitialized(o.getLines()));
    }
}
ApproachSpeedFidelityUse for
@DataJpaTest + H2FastLow (dialect, sequences, JSON, locks differ)Pure mapping smoke tests
@DataJpaTest + TestcontainersMedium (container reuse)HighRepositories, queries, constraints, migrations
@SpringBootTest + TestcontainersSlowHighestTransaction boundaries, listeners, outbox relay

Pitfalls

  • Testing REQUIRES_NEW or @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) inside a @Transactional test: the outer test transaction never commits, so the listener never fires; use TransactionTemplate in the test or drop @Transactional on it.
  • H2 in MODE=PostgreSQL is still not Postgres: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, jsonb, partial indexes and sequence increments behave differently.
  • A test that "passes" because the assertion reads from the first-level cache; always flush() and clear() before verifying query behaviour.
Interview questions
  • What does @DataJpaTest configure, and what does it not? — JPA repositories, EntityManager, a DataSource (embedded by default), migrations; not services, web layer or security. Each test is transactional and rolled back.
  • Why did a constraint violation not show in the test? — The insert was never flushed; the test rolled back before Hibernate sent the SQL. Call flush() (or saveAndFlush) so the statement executes.
  • Why Testcontainers instead of H2? — Dialect fidelity: sequences, locking syntax, JSON types, isolation behaviour and migration scripts are tested against the real engine; container reuse keeps it fast.
  • How would you test that a transaction rolls back on a specific exception? — A @SpringBootTest without @Transactional on the test, call the service through its proxy, catch the exception, then assert via the repository (or JdbcTemplate) that no row exists.
  • How do you test an AFTER_COMMIT listener? — Run the publishing code in a real committed transaction (TransactionTemplate or a non-transactional test) and await the side effect; alternatively use ApplicationEvents from @RecordApplicationEvents to assert publication.
  • Boot 2 vs 3 for data tests? — Boot 3.1 added @ServiceConnection and Testcontainers-at-development-time support (spring-boot-testcontainers, @RestartScope); before that @DynamicPropertySource was required.

outer() is @Transactional and calls inner() (also @Transactional, default propagation) on another bean. inner() throws IllegalStateException; outer() catches it and returns normally. Result?

c. Both share one REQUIRED transaction; inner()'s interceptor marks it rollback-only. At outer()'s commit the manager rolls back and throws UnexpectedRollbackException. a ignores the rollback-only flag; b would need REQUIRES_NEW on inner(); d is wrong because Spring refuses to hide a silent rollback.

A @Transactional method throws a checked IOException after a repo.save(). With no extra attributes, what happens?

b. The default rollback rule covers RuntimeException and Error. Use rollbackFor = Exception.class. c is irrelevant: the declaration does not change the rule; d is false.

Which propagation gives an audit record its own connection and lets it survive the caller's rollback?

d. REQUIRES_NEW suspends the outer transaction and commits independently on a second connection. a is a savepoint inside the same transaction, so it dies with the outer rollback; b and c join the existing transaction.

Two transactions each read seats_left = 1, then each runs UPDATE … SET seats_left = 0 and commits. Under Postgres's default isolation, what is this anomaly and does the level prevent it?

b. Both decisions were based on the same committed snapshot; READ_COMMITTED lets both updates succeed. Fix with @Version, SELECT FOR UPDATE or a conditional atomic update. No dirty data was read (a), no range query was involved (c).

Inside a transaction: User u = repo.findById(1).get(); u.setName("x"); User m = em.merge(u); m.setName("y"); u.setName("z"); What is the name after commit?

c. u was loaded in this context, so it is already managed; merge on a managed entity returns the same instance (m == u). The last write, "z", is flushed. d describes merge of a detached entity, where u would stay detached and the answer would be "y".

A service loads 200 Orders and the controller serialises each order's lazy lines. With open-in-view=true (Boot default) what do you observe?

a. Open-in-view keeps the persistence context (and its JDBC connection) open until the view is rendered, so each lazy collection loads with a separate SELECT: N+1 hidden in the serialiser. b happens only with open-in-view=false; c is wrong because default_batch_fetch_size is unset by default.

@Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.lines join fetch o.payments") where both are Lists. What happens?

d. Hibernate refuses to fetch two bags at once. Change one to a Set, or fetch the second collection in a separate query (the identity map merges them). a would be true if at most one collection were a bag.

You set hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50 but datasource-proxy shows 50 separate INSERTs. Most likely cause?

b. IDENTITY forces an immediate INSERT at persist to obtain the id, so nothing can be batched. a only matters when inserts of different entities interleave; c and d do not affect batching.

A @TransactionalEventListener (default phase) saves a notification row via a repository. No exception, but the row never appears. Why?

c. After commit the bound resources still exist but the transaction is complete; Hibernate does not flush. A new transaction on the listener fixes it. a describes BEFORE_COMMIT, which is not the default.

Which production configuration is correct?

a. Schema is verified but owned by versioned migrations, lazy loading fails fast, and the pool is sized for the database. b mutates the schema at startup and floods stdout; c destroys data; d has no audit trail or repeatability.

Practice

Scenario: inner REQUIRES_NEW committed, outer rolled back: what is in the database?

@Service class OrderService {
    @Transactional
    public void place(Order o) {
        orderRepo.save(o);                       // (1)
        audit.record("PLACE", o.getId());        // (2) AuditService.record is REQUIRES_NEW
        try { stock.reserve(o); }                // (3) StockService.reserve is REQUIRED, throws IllegalStateException
        catch (IllegalStateException e) { log.warn("no stock"); }
        orderRepo.save(o.withStatus(BACKORDERED)); // (4)
    }
}

A caller invokes place(o) via the proxy. Which rows exist afterwards, what does the caller see, and what would change if reserve were NESTED (on a DataSourceTransactionManager)?

Tests: propagation, rollback-only, savepoints
Hint 1
Who started the transaction that reserve() ran in, and what can its interceptor do when the method throws?
Hint 2
The audit transaction is already committed before step (3) even begins.
Reveal solution

Rows: only the audit row. It was written in its own transaction (REQUIRES_NEW) that committed when record() returned. The order insert (1) and the status update (4) are in the outer transaction, which reserve()'s interceptor marked rollback-only when the IllegalStateException crossed the proxy boundary. Catching it in place() does not clear that flag.

Caller sees: UnexpectedRollbackException: Transaction silently rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only, thrown by the outer commit. Step (4) executed in Java but its flush was discarded.

With NESTED (JDBC manager, nestedTransactionAllowed): reserve() runs after a savepoint; on the exception the interceptor rolls back to the savepoint only. The outer transaction stays healthy, steps (1) and (4) commit, and the caller gets a normal return. Note the audit row now references an order id that exists; in the first scenario it references an order that never existed, which is the classic REQUIRES_NEW-audit trap.

Alternatives: noRollbackFor = IllegalStateException.class on reserve, or have reserve return a result instead of throwing for an expected business outcome.

Scenario: LazyInitializationException only in the async listener

@Transactional
public Order place(PlaceOrder cmd) {
    Order order = repo.save(Order.from(cmd));
    events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(order));      // entity inside the event
    return order;
}

@Async
@TransactionalEventListener
public void onPlaced(OrderPlaced e) {
    for (OrderLine l : e.order().getLines())          // throws here, only in prod
        mailer.send(l.sku());
}

In tests (with @SpringBootTest) the listener works; in production it throws LazyInitializationException: could not initialize proxy - no Session. Explain and fix without switching to EAGER.

Tests: persistence context scope, threads, events
Hint 1
Which thread runs onPlaced, and which persistence context is bound to that thread?
Hint 2
Why might the test not reproduce it? Think about @Async being disabled without @EnableAsync, or the test using a synchronous executor, or open-in-view.
Reveal solution

Cause: @Async moves the listener to an executor thread. The persistence context that loaded order is bound to the request thread and is closed after commit. On the worker thread the entity is detached; getLines() is an uninitialised PersistentBag with no session. In the test the async executor was probably synchronous (no @EnableAsync, or a SyncTaskExecutor), so the listener ran on the publishing thread while the context was still open; with open-in-view=true in a web test the context would also survive.

Fixes (pick one, in order of preference):

  1. Put data, not entities, in the event: record OrderPlaced(long orderId, List<String> skus) built inside the transaction. Events crossing threads must be self-contained.
  2. Pass the id and reload in the listener inside its own transaction: @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW) plus repo.findWithLines(e.orderId()). Needed anyway if the listener writes to the DB.
  3. Initialise before publishing: Hibernate.initialize(order.getLines()) or load with join fetch; fragile because any new lazy access in the listener breaks again.

Do not set hibernate.enable_lazy_load_no_trans=true: it opens a temporary session per lazy access, hides N+1 and leaks connections.

Scenario: the checked exception did not roll back

@Service
public class ImportService {
    @Transactional
    public void importFile(Path p) throws IOException {
        for (String line : Files.readAllLines(p)) repo.save(parse(line));
        archive.move(p);                          // throws IOException when the archive volume is full
    }
}

After an IOException the rows from the file are in the table, yet the file was not archived and the job will re-import it. Explain, give two fixes, and name a third situation where the rollback would also not happen even with the fix.

Tests: rollback rules, proxy boundaries
Hint 1
Which exception types trigger rollback by default?
Reveal solution

Why: TransactionInterceptor rolls back only for RuntimeException and Error. IOException is checked, so the interceptor treats the method as a normal completion and commits the inserts.

Fix 1: @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class) (or rollbackFor = IOException.class). Fix 2: wrap in an unchecked exception (throw new UncheckedIOException(e)) or use a domain RuntimeException; many teams set a project-wide default via a custom TransactionAttributeSource or a meta-annotation @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class).

Still no rollback: when importFile is called from another method of the same class (self-invocation bypasses the proxy, see section 4), when the method is not public, or when importFile itself catches the exception and logs it. Also, if archive.move is a remote call, the rollback fixes the DB but not the partial remote side effect.

Scenario: 1 request = 1,001 queries: fix it three different ways

@Entity class Order {
    @Id Long id;
    @ManyToOne Customer customer;                          // EAGER by default
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order") List<OrderLine> lines;   // LAZY
}
@GetMapping("/orders")                                       // open-in-view = true
List<OrderView> list() {
    return repo.findByStatus(NEW).stream()                   // 1,000 orders
        .map(o -> new OrderView(o.getId(), o.getCustomer().getName(), o.getLines().size()))
        .toList();
}

datasource-proxy reports about 1,001 queries for this endpoint (sometimes ~2,000). Explain where every query comes from and give three different fixes with their trade-offs. Which one would you ship first?

Tests: N+1, fetch strategies, projections, open-in-view
Hint 1
Count separately: the main query, the lazy lines per order, and the EAGER customer for a JPQL/derived query.
Hint 2
Do you even need Order entities to produce OrderView?
Reveal solution

Where the queries come from: 1 for findByStatus; 1,000 for getLines().size() (each lazy bag initialises separately; the controller has a context only because open-in-view is on); and up to 1,000 more for customer: EAGER on a derived/JPQL query is satisfied with a secondary SELECT per distinct customer id not already in the context, which is why the count varies with customer cardinality.

Fix 1: fetch plan for this query. @Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.customer left join fetch o.lines where o.status = :s") or @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"customer","lines"}). 1 query. Trade-offs: row multiplication (1,000 × lines rows over the wire), only one bag per query, and no server-side pagination with the collection fetch.

Fix 2: batch fetching globally. spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50 (and @ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY) on customer). 1 + 20 + ~20 queries, all IN (…) lists. Trade-offs: still lazy, so still needs an open context; but it fixes every screen at once, works with paging, and is a one-line change.

Fix 3: do not load entities. @Query("select new com.x.OrderView(o.id, c.name, count(l)) from Order o join o.customer c left join o.lines l where o.status = :s group by o.id, c.name") or an interface projection. 1 query, minimal columns, no lazy state, and the result is safe to return with open-in-view=false. Trade-off: a read model per screen.

Ship first: Fix 2 (global batch size plus LAZY on to-one associations) as the safety net for the whole application, then Fix 3 for this hot endpoint, then set open-in-view=false so future regressions fail in tests instead of in production. Add a @DataJpaTest that asserts the query count via SessionFactory.getStatistics().

⚡ Rapid-fire: JPA, Hibernate & transactions

  • Default propagation? — REQUIRED: join the existing transaction or start one.
  • Default rollback rule? — Roll back on RuntimeException and Error; commit on checked exceptions.
  • What throws UnexpectedRollbackException? — Committing a transaction an inner REQUIRED call marked rollback-only.
  • REQUIRES_NEW cost? — A second pooled connection while the first is suspended; pool deadlock risk.
  • NESTED needs? — JDBC savepoints; DataSourceTransactionManager, not the JPA manager by default.
  • @Transactional on a private method? — Ignored; proxies intercept only external calls to public methods.
  • Where does Spring store the current transaction? — ThreadLocals in TransactionSynchronizationManager.
  • Does @Async join the caller's transaction? — No; different thread, no bound resources.
  • readOnly = true effect? — Hibernate flush mode MANUAL, connection read-only hint, possible replica routing.
  • Postgres vs MySQL default isolation? — READ_COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE_READ.
  • Phantom read? — A repeated range query returns rows another transaction inserted.
  • Lost update fix? — @Version, SELECT FOR UPDATE, or an atomic conditional UPDATE.
  • Persistence context? — Identity map of managed entities with snapshots; the first-level cache.
  • Entity states? — Transient, managed, detached, removed.
  • persist vs merge? — persist attaches the given object; merge returns a managed copy.
  • When does Hibernate flush? — Before queries under AUTO, at commit, on explicit flush().
  • save vs saveAndFlush? — Same, plus an immediate flush (not a commit).
  • getReferenceById? — Lazy proxy with only the id; no SELECT until a field is touched.
  • Default fetch types? — To-one EAGER, to-many LAZY; make everything LAZY.
  • N+1 fixes? — Fetch join / entity graph, batch size, subselect, DTO projection.
  • MultipleBagFetchException? — Fetch-joining two List collections; use Set or split queries.
  • open-in-view default and advice? — True in Boot; set it to false.
  • Page vs Slice? — Page runs a count query; Slice fetches size+1.
  • @Modifying(clearAutomatically=true)? — Clears the context after a bulk JPQL update to avoid stale entities.
  • Why not @Data on entities? — Mutable equals/hashCode and lazy toString recursion.
  • Owning side of @OneToMany? — The @ManyToOne side with the FK; mappedBy is read-only.
  • orphanRemoval vs CascadeType.REMOVE? — Orphan removal also deletes children removed from the collection.
  • IDENTITY vs SEQUENCE? — IDENTITY disables insert batching; SEQUENCE with pooled optimizer batches.
  • Hibernate 6 sequence change? — Implicit name became <Entity>_SEQ instead of hibernate_sequence.
  • HikariCP default pool size and timeout? — 10 connections, 30 s connection-timeout.
  • Pool sizing rule of thumb? — DB cores × 2 + spindles; small numbers win.
  • show-sql in prod? — No: stdout, no parameters, no timing; use datasource-proxy or p6spy.
  • ddl-auto in prod? — validate or none with Flyway/Liquibase.
  • Dual-write problem? — DB commit and broker send cannot be atomic; use the outbox pattern.
  • @TransactionalEventListener default phase? — AFTER_COMMIT; DB writes there need REQUIRES_NEW.
  • @DataJpaTest default behaviour? — Embedded DB, transactional, rolled back per test.
  • Why flush() in a repository test? — To force SQL and surface constraint violations before rollback.

6️⃣ Spring Security 6

Spring Security is where "framework magic" questions get sharpest: a request passes through fifteen filters before your controller sees it, a 401 and a 403 come from two different handlers, and one wrong requestMatchers order silently opens an endpoint. Interviewers use it to check that you can reason about a request before DispatcherServlet. The path: filter-chain architecture → the authentication model → authorization and method security → exception translation → JWT resource servers → OAuth2/OIDC roles → sessions vs stateless → CSRF and CORS → custom filters → hardening and testing → reactive and the 5→6 migration.

Architecture: DelegatingFilterProxy → FilterChainProxy → SecurityFilterChain(s) and filter order

Why interviewers ask: "walk me through what happens to a request before it reaches the controller" is the standard opener; it separates candidates who have read the filter list from those who have only copied a config from a blog.

Spring Security is a servlet filter, not an MVC concept. Boot registers one servlet filter named springSecurityFilterChain: a DelegatingFilterProxy whose only job is to look up a bean of the same name in the ApplicationContext (servlet filters are created by the container, so they cannot be Spring beans directly). That bean is a FilterChainProxy, which holds an ordered list of SecurityFilterChain beans. For each request it picks the first chain whose securityMatcher matches and runs that chain's filters; the other chains are ignored. Analogy: one airport entrance (the proxy) routes you to exactly one security lane (the chain) based on your ticket, and each lane has its own sequence of checks.

Since Spring Security 5.7 / 6.0 you no longer extend WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter; you declare SecurityFilterChain beans with the lambda DSL. The default chain contains roughly 15 filters in a fixed order (see the figure). The ones you must be able to name: SecurityContextHolderFilter (loads the context from the SecurityContextRepository, lazily), HeaderWriterFilter, CorsFilter, CsrfFilter, LogoutFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter (form login), BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter (JWT), BasicAuthenticationFilter, RequestCacheAwareFilter, AnonymousAuthenticationFilter, SessionManagementFilter, ExceptionTranslationFilter and finally AuthorizationFilter (replaces FilterSecurityInterceptor).

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean @Order(1)
    SecurityFilterChain apiChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.securityMatcher("/api/**")                    // this chain only for /api/**
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/public/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(rs -> rs.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable());
        return http.build();
    }

    @Bean @Order(2)
    SecurityFilterChain webChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/", "/login", "/css/**").permitAll()
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .logout(l -> l.logoutSuccessUrl("/"));
        return http.build();
    }
}
Interview angle: "How do you see the actual filter order in your app?" Set logging.level.org.springframework.security=TRACE; at startup the DefaultSecurityFilterChain log line lists every filter of every chain, and per request FilterChainProxy logs "Invoking X (3/15)". Also /actuator/beans shows the chain beans.

Pitfalls

  • Two chains, the general one registered first (lower @Order) → the specific chain never runs and its oauth2ResourceServer config is dead code. Symptom: 302 redirect to /login for an API call.
  • requestMatchers rules are evaluated top-down, first match wins; putting anyRequest().authenticated() before permitAll() rules throws at startup in 6.x ("Can't configure requestMatchers after anyRequest"), but a broad /** pattern before a narrow one silently wins.
  • With several servlets (e.g. an H2 console or Jersey) plain string patterns are ambiguous in 6.x; use MvcRequestMatcher / PathPatternRequestMatcher builders or securityMatcher with an explicit servlet path.
  • Filters are not Spring MVC interceptors: @ExceptionHandler, @RequestScope initialisation and HandlerInterceptors run later than every security filter.
Interview questions
  • What is DelegatingFilterProxy and why is it needed? — A servlet filter registered with the container that delegates to a Spring bean by name; needed because the servlet container instantiates filters itself and knows nothing about the ApplicationContext.
  • What does FilterChainProxy do when several SecurityFilterChain beans exist? — Evaluates them in order and runs only the first whose securityMatcher matches; unmatched chains are skipped entirely, so specific chains must have a lower @Order.
  • Name the filters in order that matter for a form-login app. — SecurityContextHolderFilter, HeaderWriterFilter, CorsFilter, CsrfFilter, LogoutFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, RequestCacheAwareFilter, SecurityContextHolderAwareRequestFilter, AnonymousAuthenticationFilter, SessionManagementFilter, ExceptionTranslationFilter, AuthorizationFilter.
  • Why did WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter get removed? — Inheritance forced one global config and hid defaults; component-based SecurityFilterChain beans compose, are testable, and allow multiple chains without @Order hacks on subclasses. Removed in 6.0 (deprecated 5.7).
  • What happens if no SecurityFilterChain bean is declared? — Boot's SpringBootWebSecurityConfiguration supplies a default: every request authenticated, form login + HTTP Basic, a generated password logged at startup for user user.
  • How would you debug "my endpoint returns 401 although I added permitAll"? — Turn on TRACE logging to see which chain was chosen and which rule matched; nine times out of ten a broader pattern earlier in the list, or a different chain, took the request.
  • Difference between securityMatcher and requestMatchers? — securityMatcher decides whether this chain handles the request at all; requestMatchers inside authorizeHttpRequests decides the authorization rule once the chain is chosen.

The authentication model: AuthenticationManager, UserDetailsService, PasswordEncoder, SecurityContextHolder

Why interviewers ask: "what exactly happens when a user submits the login form?" checks whether you know the objects by name and can explain why the password never leaves the provider, why the context is a ThreadLocal, and what changes for virtual threads and stateless APIs.

Authentication is both the request (principal = username, credentials = password, isAuthenticated()=false) and the result (principal = UserDetails, credentials erased, authorities filled). A filter builds the request token and hands it to the AuthenticationManager, whose standard implementation ProviderManager loops over AuthenticationProviders and uses the first one that supports() the token type. DaoAuthenticationProvider calls your UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername and compares via PasswordEncoder.matches; JwtAuthenticationProvider validates a token instead. On success the result is stored in the SecurityContextHolder, whose default strategy is MODE_THREADLOCAL; MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL copies it to child threads (dangerous with pooled threads, where it leaks), and MODE_GLOBAL is for desktop apps. Virtual threads support ThreadLocal but the JDK's ScopedValue is the intended future; Spring 6.x still uses ThreadLocal.

Boot's DelegatingPasswordEncoder stores hashes as {bcrypt}$2a$10$…: the prefix picks the algorithm at match time, so you can rotate from bcrypt to argon2 without a big-bang migration. BCrypt cost 10 (default) is ~100 ms; that slowness is the point. The SecurityContextRepository is the second half of the story: HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository persists the context in the session between requests; RequestAttributeSecurityContextRepository (the 6.x stateless default alongside session) keeps it for the current request only. Analogy: the provider is the bouncer checking your ID, the SecurityContextHolder is the wristband you wear for the rest of the night (this thread), and the repository is the guest list that lets you re-enter tomorrow (the session).

// UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.attemptAuthentication (simplified)
var request = UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.unauthenticated(user, pass);
Authentication result = authenticationManager.authenticate(request);

// ProviderManager.authenticate
for (AuthenticationProvider p : providers) {
    if (!p.supports(request.getClass())) continue;
    result = p.authenticate(request);            // DaoAuthenticationProvider
    if (result != null) break;
}

// DaoAuthenticationProvider
UserDetails ud = userDetailsService.loadUserByUsername(user);
if (!passwordEncoder.matches(pass, ud.getPassword()))
    throw new BadCredentialsException("Bad credentials");
result = UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.authenticated(ud, null, ud.getAuthorities());

// back in the filter: success handler
SecurityContext ctx = SecurityContextHolder.createEmptyContext();
ctx.setAuthentication(result);
SecurityContextHolder.setContext(ctx);           // ThreadLocal for this request
securityContextRepository.saveContext(ctx, req, res); // HttpSession for next request
  1. The filter only reacts to POST /login; every other request passes through untouched.
  2. ProviderManager also has a parent manager it falls back to, which is how Boot chains its global provider with per-chain ones.
  3. Unknown users are reported as BadCredentialsException (hideUserNotFoundExceptions=true) so attackers cannot enumerate accounts.
  4. Deliberately slow: bcrypt cost 10 keeps brute force at ~10 guesses/s per core. A missing user still runs a dummy hash so timing cannot leak existence.
  5. The result is a new immutable token; the password is dropped so it never sits in the session.
  6. Because it is a ThreadLocal, an @Async method or a parallel stream does not see it unless you propagate it (DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor).
  7. Next request: SecurityContextHolderFilter reads it back from the session. Stateless APIs skip this step and re-authenticate the bearer token every time.
@Bean
UserDetailsService users(UserRepository repo) {
    return username -> repo.findByEmail(username)
        .map(u -> User.withUsername(u.email())
                      .password(u.passwordHash())          // "{bcrypt}$2a$10$…"
                      .roles(u.roles().toArray(String[]::new))   // adds ROLE_ prefix
                      .build())
        .orElseThrow(() -> new UsernameNotFoundException(username));
}

@Bean
PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder(); // bcrypt default, {id} prefix
}
EncoderTypeCost knobWhen
BCryptPasswordEncoderAdaptive hash, 72-byte input limitstrength 4–31 (default 10)Default; universally supported
Argon2PasswordEncoderMemory-hard (needs Bouncy Castle)memory, iterations, parallelismNew systems; GPU-resistant
SCryptPasswordEncoderMemory-hardcpu/memory costAlternative to argon2
Pbkdf2PasswordEncoderIterated HMACiterationsFIPS environments
NoOpPasswordEncoderPlain text—Never; deprecated, tests only

Pitfalls

  • "There is no PasswordEncoder mapped for the id 'null'": the stored hash lacks the {id} prefix that DelegatingPasswordEncoder expects. Prefix legacy rows or set a default-for-matches encoder.
  • Reading SecurityContextHolder.getContext() inside @Async, CompletableFuture.supplyAsync or a Kafka listener returns an empty context; wrap the executor with DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor or pass the principal explicitly.
  • MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL with a thread pool: the first task's context is inherited by the pool thread at creation and reused for other users' tasks. A real, well-known leak.
  • Spring Security 6 no longer saves the context automatically on every request (SecurityContextPersistenceFilter → SecurityContextHolderFilter); a hand-rolled login endpoint must call securityContextRepository.saveContext(...) or the user is logged out on the next request.
Interview questions
  • Walk me through form login end to end. — UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter builds an unauthenticated token → ProviderManager → DaoAuthenticationProvider → UserDetailsService + PasswordEncoder.matches → authenticated token stored in SecurityContextHolder and saved to the session via SecurityContextRepository; success handler redirects to the cached request.
  • Why is SecurityContextHolder a ThreadLocal? — Servlet requests are thread-per-request, so it gives every filter, service and @PreAuthorize check the current user with no parameter passing. The cost: it does not cross thread boundaries and must be cleared at the end (the filter does it in finally).
  • What changes with virtual threads (Boot 3.2 spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true)? — ThreadLocal still works, and each request gets a fresh virtual thread so there is no pool leak; but millions of threads each holding a context is why the JDK is moving to ScopedValue. Avoid MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL.
  • How do you migrate password hashes from MD5 to bcrypt without forcing resets? — Configure DelegatingPasswordEncoder with an {MD5} legacy encoder, prefix existing rows, and on successful login re-hash with bcrypt (upgradeEncoding() hook on UserDetailsPasswordService) so hashes upgrade lazily.
  • Why does a wrong username and a wrong password give the same message? — User enumeration defence: hideUserNotFoundExceptions converts UsernameNotFoundException to BadCredentialsException, and the provider runs a dummy bcrypt to equalise timing.
  • How would you add a second authentication mechanism (e.g. API key) next to form login? — A custom AuthenticationProvider that supports(ApiKeyToken.class) plus a filter that creates that token; register the provider so ProviderManager tries it, or expose a separate SecurityFilterChain for the API paths.
  • Boot 2 vs 3: what changed in this model? — Explicit context saving (requireExplicitSave is true by default), SecurityContextHolderFilter loads lazily, AuthenticationManager is obtained from AuthenticationConfiguration instead of the adapter's authenticationManagerBean(), and User.withDefaultPasswordEncoder() is deprecated (demos only).

Authorization: AuthorizationManager, hasRole vs hasAuthority, method security

Why interviewers ask: "why does hasRole("ROLE_ADMIN") fail?" and "why is my @PreAuthorize ignored?" are two of the five most common Spring Security bugs; both have crisp mechanical explanations.

Spring Security 6 replaced the voter-based AccessDecisionManager/AccessDecisionVoter with a single functional interface: AuthorizationManager<T> with check(Supplier<Authentication>, T) → AuthorizationDecision. authorizeHttpRequests builds a RequestMatcherDelegatingAuthorizationManager (first matching rule wins), and method security builds PreAuthorizeAuthorizationManager etc. The Supplier is deliberate: the authentication is resolved lazily, so permitAll paths never touch the session.

Roles are authorities with a ROLE_ prefix. hasRole("ADMIN") is exactly hasAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN"); passing "ROLE_ADMIN" to hasRole throws in 6.x ("should not start with ROLE_"). JWT scopes become SCOPE_read authorities by default. A RoleHierarchy bean (ROLE_ADMIN > ROLE_USER) makes higher roles imply lower ones in both URL and method checks (6.x picks the bean up automatically). Method security is AOP: @EnableMethodSecurity (replaces @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity, and enables @PreAuthorize by default) registers advisors that wrap beans in proxies, so the same rules as @Transactional apply: public methods on Spring beans, called from outside the bean; a self-invocation bypasses the check entirely (see self-invocation). Analogy: the URL rules are the building's front desk; method security is a lock on each office door, but the lock only exists on the door, not on the wall you can walk through from the adjacent office.

@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity          // prePostEnabled = true by default; securedEnabled/jsr250Enabled opt-in
class MethodSecurityConfig {
    @Bean
    static RoleHierarchy roleHierarchy() {
        return RoleHierarchyImpl.fromHierarchy("ROLE_ADMIN > ROLE_MANAGER > ROLE_USER");
    }
}

@Service
public class AccountService {

    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('MANAGER') or #ownerId == authentication.name")
    public Account view(String ownerId) { … }

    @PostAuthorize("returnObject.owner == authentication.name")   // check after execution
    public Account load(long id) { … }

    @PreFilter("filterObject.amount < 10_000 or hasRole('ADMIN')")   // filters the argument collection
    public void bulkTransfer(List<Transfer> transfers) { … }

    @PreAuthorize("@accountGuard.canClose(#id, authentication)")     // delegate to a bean
    public void close(long id) { … }
}
AnnotationFamilySpELNotes
@PreAuthorize / @PostAuthorizeSpring (pre/post)Yes: #arg, authentication, principal, returnObject, @bean.method()Default-enabled in 6; use these
@PreFilter / @PostFilterSpring (pre/post)Yes: filterObjectFilters collections; O(n) SpEL, avoid on large results (filter in the query instead)
@Secured("ROLE_ADMIN")Spring legacyNoNeeds securedEnabled = true; exact authority strings
@RolesAllowed / @PermitAll / @DenyAllJSR-250 (jakarta.annotation.security)NoNeeds jsr250Enabled = true; portable to Jakarta EE
Interview angle: "URL security or method security?" Both: URL rules are the coarse perimeter (cheap, visible in one file), method security protects the service layer regardless of how it is reached (a second controller, a scheduler, a message listener). Domain-object rules (#ownerId == authentication.name) can only live at the method level.

Pitfalls

  • hasRole("ROLE_ADMIN") → IllegalArgumentException at startup in 6.x; hasAuthority("ADMIN") silently never matches when the stored authority is ROLE_ADMIN.
  • @PreAuthorize on a private method, on an interface default method with a JDK proxy, or on a method called via this: no proxy in the path, no check, no error.
  • #paramName in SpEL needs parameter names at runtime: compile with -parameters (Boot's plugins do) or the expression fails with "Failed to evaluate expression".
  • Boot 3 changed @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled = true) to @EnableMethodSecurity; the old annotation is deprecated and uses the legacy MethodSecurityInterceptor.
Interview questions
  • What is the difference between hasRole and hasAuthority? — None except the prefix: hasRole("X") checks for the authority ROLE_X. Authorities are the general concept (permissions, scopes); roles are a naming convention on top.
  • Why was AccessDecisionManager replaced? — Voters (affirmative/consensus/unanimous) were hard to reason about and eagerly required an Authentication; AuthorizationManager is one lambda-friendly interface, takes a Supplier so permitAll never loads the context, and works identically for requests, methods and messages.
  • Your @PreAuthorize on a service method is ignored when called from another method of the same class. Why? — Self-invocation bypasses the AOP proxy; the interceptor lives on the proxy, not on this. Fix: move the method to another bean, inject the proxy (ObjectProvider / @Lazy self), or use AspectJ mode.
  • How would you implement "a user can only edit their own orders"? — @PreAuthorize("@orderGuard.isOwner(#orderId, principal)") delegating to a bean that loads the order, or @PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerId == authentication.name"); for lists, filter in the repository query rather than @PostFilter.
  • What does @PostFilter cost on a 10,000-row result? — 10,000 SpEL evaluations after the full query ran, plus a mutable collection requirement; push the predicate into SQL/JPQL instead.
  • How does RoleHierarchy interact with JWT scopes? — It works on any authority string, so SCOPE_admin > SCOPE_read is valid; declare it as a bean and 6.x wires it into both authorizeHttpRequests and method security expressions.
  • Where is the authorization decision for a URL actually made? — In AuthorizationFilter (last filter), by calling the AuthorizationManager; denial throws AccessDeniedException, which ExceptionTranslationFilter turns into 401 or 403.

ExceptionTranslationFilter: 401 vs 403, AuthenticationEntryPoint vs AccessDeniedHandler

Why interviewers ask: "I wrote an @ExceptionHandler(AccessDeniedException.class) and it never fires" is a favourite; the answer requires knowing where in the pipeline the exception is thrown and caught.

ExceptionTranslationFilter sits just before AuthorizationFilter and wraps chain.doFilter in a try/catch. An AuthenticationException, or an AccessDeniedException thrown while the user is anonymous, means "we do not know who you are": the filter clears the context, saves the request in the RequestCache and invokes the AuthenticationEntryPoint to start authentication: a 302 to /login for form login, a 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer for a resource server (BearerTokenAuthenticationEntryPoint). An AccessDeniedException for an already-authenticated user means "we know you and you may not": the AccessDeniedHandler returns 403.

Because the exception is thrown by AuthorizationFilter (or by the method-security interceptor inside the controller call and then propagated up through DispatcherServlet), whether @ControllerAdvice sees it depends on where it happened: a URL rule failure never reaches MVC; a @PreAuthorize failure inside a controller or service does pass through DispatcherServlet, so an @ExceptionHandler(AccessDeniedException.class) catches it first and the filter never sees it. Since Boot 3, with spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true, Spring MVC has no built-in mapping for these; you write one or leave it to the filter.

http.exceptionHandling(ex -> ex
        .authenticationEntryPoint((req, res, e) -> {          // 401: who are you?
            res.setStatus(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED.value());
            res.setHeader(HttpHeaders.WWW_AUTHENTICATE, "Bearer");
            res.setContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON_VALUE);
            res.getWriter().write("{\"title\":\"Unauthorized\",\"status\":401}");
        })
        .accessDeniedHandler((req, res, e) -> {               // 403: you may not
            res.setStatus(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN.value());
            res.setContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON_VALUE);
            res.getWriter().write("{\"title\":\"Forbidden\",\"status\":403}");
        }));

Pitfalls

  • A catch-all @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) returning 500 swallows AccessDeniedException from method security; add a specific handler that rethrows or maps to 403.
  • Returning 403 for missing credentials on an API: clients cannot tell "log in" from "not allowed". Bearer APIs should keep the 401 + WWW-Authenticate contract.
  • For form login the entry point is a redirect to /login; if an SPA calls a session-secured API without a cookie it gets a 302 + HTML, which looks like a CORS failure in the browser console.
Interview questions
  • When does Spring Security return 401 vs 403? — 401 (AuthenticationEntryPoint) when the user is anonymous or credentials are invalid; 403 (AccessDeniedHandler) when the user is authenticated but lacks the authority. An anonymous AccessDeniedException is upgraded to the entry point on purpose.
  • Why does my @ControllerAdvice not handle authentication failures? — They occur in filters, before DispatcherServlet; MVC exception resolvers only see exceptions thrown inside handler execution. Customise exceptionHandling() instead.
  • How would you return RFC 7807 ProblemDetail bodies for 401/403? — Custom entry point / denied handler writing application/problem+json; or delegate to a HandlerExceptionResolver from the entry point so one advice handles both filter and MVC paths.
  • What is RequestCache for? — Saves the original request when an anonymous user is bounced to login so the success handler can redirect back; disable it for APIs (requestCache(c -> c.disable())) to avoid unnecessary sessions.
  • Where does BearerTokenAuthenticationEntryPoint put the error details? — In the WWW-Authenticate header (error="invalid_token", error_description="Jwt expired at …"), not the body, per RFC 6750.

JWT resource server: NimbusJwtDecoder, JWK sets, claims → authorities, audience and clock skew

Why interviewers ask: nearly every microservice at a large company is a resource server. The probes: how the signature is verified without a shared secret, what is validated by default (and what is not: audience), and where custom roles come from.

Add spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server and set spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri. At startup Boot fetches {issuer}/.well-known/openid-configuration, reads jwks_uri, and builds a NimbusJwtDecoder that downloads the JWK set (public keys) and caches it, re-fetching when it meets an unknown kid header (key rotation). Alternatively set jwk-set-uri directly (no startup call to the issuer) or a public-key-location. The decoder verifies the signature (RS256 by default; HS256 needs a shared SecretKey), then runs OAuth2TokenValidators: JwtTimestampValidator (exp/nbf with 60 s default clock skew) and JwtIssuerValidator. Audience is not validated by default; add JwtClaimValidator("aud", …) via JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer + DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator, or 6.x's audiences property (Boot 3.1+, spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.audiences).

The result is a Jwt principal wrapped in a JwtAuthenticationToken. JwtAuthenticationConverter maps claims to authorities: default is the scope/scp claim with a SCOPE_ prefix. For Keycloak-style realm_access.roles or a custom roles claim you plug a JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter (or a lambda) that emits ROLE_…. Opaque tokens (random strings) are handled by opaqueToken(): each request calls the authorization server's introspection endpoint (RFC 7662) — instantly revocable, but one network hop per request, so cache. Analogy: a JWT is a passport: anyone with the issuing country's public seal can verify it offline, but a stolen one stays valid until it expires; an opaque token is a hotel key card: meaningless alone, the front desk (introspection) is asked every time.

@Bean
JwtDecoder jwtDecoder(@Value("${spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri}") String issuer) {
    NimbusJwtDecoder decoder = JwtDecoders.fromIssuerLocation(issuer);      // discovery + JWKS
    OAuth2TokenValidator<Jwt> withIssuer = JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer(issuer);
    OAuth2TokenValidator<Jwt> audience = new JwtClaimValidator<List<String>>(
            "aud", aud -> aud != null && aud.contains("orders-api"));
    decoder.setJwtValidator(new DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator<>(withIssuer, audience));
    return decoder;
}

@Bean
JwtAuthenticationConverter jwtAuthenticationConverter() {
    var scopes = new JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter();               // SCOPE_ from "scope"
    var converter = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
    converter.setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter(jwt -> {
        Collection<GrantedAuthority> out = new ArrayList<>(scopes.convert(jwt));
        Map<String, Object> realm = jwt.getClaimAsMap("realm_access");   // Keycloak style
        if (realm != null && realm.get("roles") instanceof List<?> roles)
            roles.forEach(r -> out.add(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_" + r.toString().toUpperCase())));
        return out;
    });
    converter.setPrincipalClaimName("preferred_username");             // authentication.getName()
    return converter;
}
// http.oauth2ResourceServer(rs -> rs.jwt(j -> j.jwtAuthenticationConverter(jwtAuthenticationConverter())))
JWT (jwt())Opaque (opaqueToken())
ValidationLocal: signature + claims, no network after JWKS cacheRemote introspection call per request (cache it)
RevocationImpossible before exp (keep tokens short, 5–15 min, use refresh tokens)Immediate
PayloadReadable by anyone (base64, not encrypted; never put PII/secrets in it)Nothing leaks
SizeHundreds of bytes to KBs (header bloat)Small
Principal typeJwt in JwtAuthenticationTokenOAuth2AuthenticatedPrincipal in BearerTokenAuthentication

Pitfalls

  • issuer-uri makes Boot call the IdP at startup; if the IdP is down the app fails to start. Prefer jwk-set-uri (lazy) plus an explicit issuer validator, or make the decoder lazy.
  • Using HS256 with a secret shared across services: any service can mint tokens for all others. Use asymmetric keys; keep the private key on the authorization server only.
  • Forgetting audience validation in a multi-API estate: a token for billing-api is accepted by orders-api.
  • Claims mapped to ROLE_ but the check uses hasAuthority("admin"); or roles arrive lower-case and hasRole("ADMIN") compares exact strings.
Interview questions
  • How does the resource server verify a JWT without calling the auth server on every request? — Asymmetric signatures: the auth server signs with a private key, publishes public keys at the JWKS URL; NimbusJwtDecoder caches them and verifies locally, refetching only for an unknown kid.
  • What does Spring validate by default on a JWT? — Signature, exp/nbf (60 s skew) and iss when configured via issuer-uri. Not aud, not sub, not scopes; add validators or the audiences property.
  • How do you revoke a JWT? — You cannot; you mitigate: short lifetimes with refresh tokens, a deny-list of jti checked in a custom validator (reintroduces a lookup), or switch to opaque tokens with introspection for high-risk operations.
  • How would you map Keycloak realm roles to Spring roles? — A custom Converter<Jwt, Collection<GrantedAuthority>> reading realm_access.roles (or resource_access.{client}.roles), prefixing ROLE_, set on JwtAuthenticationConverter.
  • Where should a JWT be validated in a microservice architecture: gateway or each service? — Both: the gateway rejects garbage early, but each service must validate too (zero-trust; internal callers can bypass the gateway). Propagate the original token, or exchange it (token exchange RFC 8693) for service-scoped tokens.
  • How do you handle key rotation? — Publish the new key in the JWKS alongside the old, start signing with the new kid, remove the old key after the longest token lifetime; decoders pick it up via kid miss-refetch.
  • Access token in the Authorization header vs cookie? — Header: immune to CSRF, but JS-accessible storage is XSS-exposed; HttpOnly cookie: XSS-safe but needs CSRF protection and SameSite. Spring supports a custom BearerTokenResolver to read from a cookie.
  • How do you test a resource server without a running IdP? — @WebMvcTest + SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.jwt().jwt(j -> j.claim("scope","orders:read")); the decoder is mocked (@MockBean JwtDecoder) so no keys are needed.

OAuth2 / OIDC roles: resource server vs client vs authorization server, auth code + PKCE, client credentials

Why interviewers ask: candidates mix up "login with Google" (OIDC client) with "protect my API" (resource server); the interviewer wants the four roles, the flow arrows, and which Spring starter implements which.

OAuth2 has four roles: resource owner (the user), client (your web app or SPA that wants to act for the user), authorization server (issues tokens: Keycloak, Okta, Entra, Spring Authorization Server) and resource server (your API, validates tokens). OAuth2 is about delegated access; OIDC adds an id_token (a JWT about the user) and /userinfo so the client can log the user in. In Spring: spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client gives oauth2Login() (OIDC login: the user's session principal becomes an OidcUser) and oauth2Client() (obtain access tokens to call APIs without logging the user in that way); spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server gives oauth2ResourceServer(); spring-security-oauth2-authorization-server lets you be the issuer.

The authorization code flow with PKCE is the only recommended browser flow (implicit and password grants are gone in OAuth 2.1). The client redirects the user to the auth server with a code_challenge; the user logs in and consents; the auth server redirects back with a short-lived code; the client's backend exchanges code + code_verifier (+ client secret for confidential clients) for access_token, refresh_token, id_token. Tokens never transit the browser URL. Client credentials is for service-to-service with no user: Spring's OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager fetches and caches the token and refreshes it before expiry; plug it into RestClient/WebClient via OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor (6.4+) or ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction. Analogy: a hotel: the guest (user) asks reception (auth server) for a key card (token) that lets the valet (client) fetch the car from the garage (resource server) without ever knowing the guest's room password.

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      client:
        registration:
          keycloak:                          # user login (OIDC)
            client-id: web-app
            client-secret: ${KC_SECRET}
            authorization-grant-type: authorization_code
            scope: openid, profile, orders:read
          billing-svc:                       # service-to-service
            client-id: orders-service
            client-secret: ${BILLING_SECRET}
            authorization-grant-type: client_credentials
            provider: keycloak
        provider:
          keycloak:
            issuer-uri: https://idp.example.com/realms/shop
@Bean
RestClient billingClient(OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager manager) {
    var interceptor = new OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor(manager);   // Spring Security 6.4+
    interceptor.setClientRegistrationIdResolver(req -> "billing-svc");
    return RestClient.builder().baseUrl("https://billing")
            .requestInterceptor(interceptor)                 // fetches/refreshes client_credentials token
            .build();
}
GrantWhoUser present?Spring piece
Authorization code + PKCEWeb apps, SPAs, mobileYes (browser redirect)oauth2Login() / oauth2Client()
Client credentialsService → serviceNoOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager + interceptor
Refresh tokenAny client holding oneNoAutomatic via the manager
Device codeTVs, CLIsYes, on another deviceCustom provider; SAS supports it
Implicit / password——Removed in OAuth 2.1; not supported for new apps

Pitfalls

  • Using oauth2Login() when you only needed oauth2Client(): your app now creates sessions and OIDC principals for a backend that just calls another API.
  • In-memory OAuth2AuthorizedClientService behind a load balancer: token found on node A, missing on node B → re-login loops. Use JdbcOAuth2AuthorizedClientService or a sticky session.
  • Storing client-secret in Git; missing state check disabled "for testing" → login CSRF. Spring enforces state; never turn it off.
  • Refresh token in a browser SPA: prefer the BFF pattern (backend holds tokens, browser gets an HttpOnly session cookie) over storing tokens in localStorage.
Interview questions
  • Resource server vs client vs authorization server in Spring terms? — Resource server validates bearer tokens on incoming requests (oauth2ResourceServer()); client obtains tokens to log users in (oauth2Login()) or call APIs (oauth2Client()); authorization server issues tokens (Spring Authorization Server). One app can be several.
  • Why PKCE if you already have a client secret? — It binds the code to the party that started the flow, defeating code interception on mobile/SPA where a secret cannot be kept, and OAuth 2.1 recommends it for all clients; Spring enables it automatically for public clients and via OAuth2AuthorizationRequestCustomizers.withPkce() for confidential ones.
  • What is the difference between an access token and an ID token? — Access token: for the API (audience = resource server), opaque to the client, may not be a JWT. ID token: for the client (audience = client_id), always a JWT describing the authenticated user; never send it to APIs.
  • How does service A call service B securely with no user involved? — Client credentials grant: A authenticates to the auth server with its own client id/secret (or mTLS/private_key_jwt), gets a token with A's scopes, B validates it as a resource server. Spring's OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager handles caching and refresh.
  • Where do refresh tokens live and how are they rotated? — Server-side in the client app (OAuth2AuthorizedClientService), never in the browser. Good auth servers rotate them on each use and revoke the family on reuse detection.
  • How does oauth2Login() populate authorities? — From scopes (SCOPE_…) plus OIDC_USER/OAUTH2_USER; customise with a GrantedAuthoritiesMapper or a custom OidcUserService reading a roles claim.
  • When would you run Spring Authorization Server instead of Keycloak/Okta? — When you need a lightweight, code-configured issuer inside your estate (custom grants, token customisers via OAuth2TokenCustomizer, embedded in tests) and do not need an admin UI or federation out of the box.

Stateless vs session authentication: SessionCreationPolicy, fixation, concurrency, remember-me, where to keep the JWT

Why interviewers ask: "should the API be stateless?" is a design question with a mechanical follow-up: what exactly does STATELESS change in the chain, and what do you lose (logout, revocation, concurrency limits)?

SessionCreationPolicy: ALWAYS, IF_REQUIRED (default: a session is created when something needs storing, e.g. after login or by the RequestCache), NEVER (never creates but uses an existing one) and STATELESS (never creates, never reads: the SecurityContextRepository becomes NullSecurityContextRepository, no JSESSIONID, every request must carry its credentials). Stateless is the norm for bearer-token APIs; sessions remain right for browser apps with form or OIDC login, and Spring Session (Redis/JDBC) makes them cluster-safe.

Session-based defences the framework gives you for free: session fixation protection (changeSessionId by default in Servlet 3.1+: a new id is issued at login so an attacker who planted a session id before login gains nothing), concurrent session control (maximumSessions(1) + maxSessionsPreventsLogin, requiring a HttpSessionEventPublisher and, in clusters, Spring Session's SessionRegistry) and remember-me (a signed cookie: hash-based TokenBasedRememberMeServices or the safer persistent-token variant with a PersistentTokenRepository). A JWT in the browser has the same choice as any credential: Authorization header from JS memory (no CSRF, but XSS-readable and lost on refresh) or an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax cookie (XSS-safe, survives refresh, but now CSRF applies and you must enable csrf() again). Analogy: a session is a coat-check ticket, the state is in the cloakroom; a JWT is carrying your coat everywhere: nothing to look up, but you cannot make the coat disappear until it wears out.

http.sessionManagement(s -> s
        .sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.IF_REQUIRED)
        .sessionFixation(f -> f.changeSessionId())        // default; alternatives: migrateSession, newSession
        .maximumSessions(1).maxSessionsPreventsLogin(false) // second login kicks the first
        .expiredUrl("/login?expired"))
    .rememberMe(r -> r.key("rotate-me-in-vault").tokenValiditySeconds(14 * 24 * 3600))
    .logout(l -> l.deleteCookies("JSESSIONID").invalidateHttpSession(true));

@Bean HttpSessionEventPublisher sessionEventPublisher() { return new HttpSessionEventPublisher(); }

// Stateless API chain: no session at all
http.sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
    .requestCache(c -> c.disable())
    .csrf(c -> c.disable());
Session cookie (server state)JWT in headerJWT in HttpOnly cookie
Revocation / logoutImmediate (invalidate)Only by expiryOnly by expiry
CSRF neededYesNoYes
XSS exposureCookie unreadableToken readable by injected JSCookie unreadable
Horizontal scalingNeeds Spring Session / stickyFreeFree
Best forBrowser apps, BFFService-to-service, mobileSPA with BFF-less API

Pitfalls

  • STATELESS on a chain that still has formLogin(): login succeeds and the next request is anonymous, because nothing persisted the context.
  • Concurrent session control without HttpSessionEventPublisher: expired sessions are never removed from the SessionRegistry and users get locked out after the limit.
  • JSESSIONID without Secure/SameSite behind a TLS-terminating proxy: set server.servlet.session.cookie.secure=true and server.forward-headers-strategy=framework so Boot knows the request was HTTPS.
  • "Stateless" APIs that still call request.getSession() in a controller or via RequestCache, silently creating sessions and memory per request.
Interview questions
  • What does SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS actually change? — Spring Security stops reading/writing the HttpSession: NullSecurityContextRepository, no JSESSIONID, no RequestCache save. It does not stop your code from creating sessions.
  • What is session fixation and how does Spring prevent it? — Attacker gets the victim to log in under a session id the attacker already knows. Spring issues a new session id at authentication (changeSessionId), so the pre-login id is worthless.
  • How do you limit a user to one concurrent login across a cluster? — maximumSessions(1) backed by a shared SessionRegistry (SpringSessionBackedSessionRegistry with Redis) and HttpSessionEventPublisher so logouts/expiries update it.
  • Where should an SPA store a JWT? — Prefer not at all: use a BFF with an HttpOnly session cookie. If the SPA must hold it, an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite cookie plus CSRF protection beats localStorage, which any XSS can read.
  • How do you implement "logout" with JWTs? — Short access tokens plus revocable refresh tokens at the auth server; client discards the token; optionally a jti deny-list checked by a custom OAuth2TokenValidator until expiry.
  • Is remember-me safe? — Hash-based tokens are vulnerable if the key leaks and cannot be revoked per device; persistent tokens (series + token) detect theft and can be revoked. Keep validity short and never use remember-me for admin roles.
  • Boot 2 vs 3 for sessions? — requireExplicitSave(true) is the default (the context is saved only when a filter/your code calls saveContext), and SecurityContextHolderFilter no longer eagerly creates sessions, reducing accidental session creation.

CSRF and CORS: when each matters, SPA setup in Security 6, why CORS must be configured in Security

Why interviewers ask: the "JWT works in Postman but fails in the browser" scenario is a top-three production incident, and it is always one of these two. They also want to hear that CSRF is a cookie problem, not a "web app" problem.

CSRF exploits credentials the browser attaches automatically: cookies (session, JWT-in-cookie) and HTTP Basic. A bearer token in a header set by your JS is never attached by a foreign site, so CSRF protection is unnecessary and csrf().disable() is correct for pure bearer APIs.
