For cookie-based auth keep it on: CsrfFilter requires a token on every non-safe method (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE), compared against the one stored server-side (HttpSessionCsrfTokenRepository) or in a readable XSRF-TOKEN cookie (CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse()) that JS echoes in the X-XSRF-TOKEN header (Angular/Axios do this automatically). Security 6 changed two things: the token is deferred (not loaded until something reads it, so the cookie only appears once a request touches CsrfToken; add a OncePerRequestFilter calling csrfToken.getToken() or a controller endpoint), and the default XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler masks the token per response (BREACH mitigation), which breaks SPAs that compare raw values; the documented fix is a handler that uses CsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler for header-submitted tokens and the Xor one for form params (6.1+ ships SpaCsrfTokenRequestHandler in the docs).

CORS is a browser rule: a page on app.example.com calling api.example.com triggers a preflight OPTIONS with no credentials. If Spring Security answers that preflight with 401 (the anonymous OPTIONS hits authenticated()), the browser never sends the real request. That is why http.cors(...) must be configured in Security: it registers CorsFilter early in the chain, before authentication, using a CorsConfigurationSource bean. A WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings or @CrossOrigin alone runs inside DispatcherServlet, which the rejected preflight never reaches. Analogy: CSRF is someone forging your signature on a cheque your bank auto-honours; CORS is the bank's rule about which branches may phone in a transfer on your behalf, decided at the switchboard, not at the teller.

@Bean
CorsConfigurationSource corsConfigurationSource() {
    var cfg = new CorsConfiguration();
    cfg.setAllowedOrigins(List.of("https://app.example.com"));  // no "*" with credentials
    cfg.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"));
    cfg.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("Authorization", "Content-Type", "X-XSRF-TOKEN"));
    cfg.setAllowCredentials(true);
    cfg.setMaxAge(Duration.ofHours(1));
    var source = new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
    source.registerCorsConfiguration("/api/**", cfg);
    return source;
}

// SPA with cookie session: keep CSRF, cookie repository, header-friendly handler
http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults())                 // picks up the bean → CorsFilter in the chain
    .csrf(csrf -> csrf
        .csrfTokenRepository(CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse())
        .csrfTokenRequestHandler(new SpaCsrfTokenRequestHandler()))   // raw header, Xor for form params
    .addFilterAfter(new CsrfCookieFilter(), BasicAuthenticationFilter.class); // forces csrfToken.getToken()

// Pure bearer API: CSRF off is correct
http.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable());
Auth styleCSRF protectionCORS
Session cookie / JWT cookieRequiredIf cross-origin, with allowCredentials=true and explicit origins
Bearer header (JS-set)DisableRequired for cross-origin; Authorization in allowed headers
HTTP Basic from browserRequired (browser auto-attaches)Same as cookie
Service-to-serviceIrrelevant (no browser)Irrelevant

Pitfalls

  • allowedOrigins("*") with allowCredentials(true): the browser rejects the response; use allowedOriginPatterns or explicit origins.
  • Disabling CSRF "because it is a REST API" while authentication is a session cookie set by formLogin/oauth2Login: the API is now CSRF-able.
  • Security 6: the XSRF-TOKEN cookie never appears because nothing read the deferred token; add the small filter that calls getToken().
  • Preflight blocked by an authenticated() rule: either http.cors() (preferred) or requestMatchers(HttpMethod.OPTIONS, "/**").permitAll().
Interview questions
  • When is it safe to disable CSRF? — When no credential is attached automatically by the browser: bearer tokens in the Authorization header set by JS, or non-browser clients. Cookie or Basic auth needs it.
  • JWT works in Postman, 403 in the browser. What do you check? — Network tab: is it the OPTIONS preflight failing (CORS not configured in Security, missing Authorization in allowed headers, wildcard origin with credentials)? Or a POST with a cookie session and no CSRF token? Postman sends neither preflight nor foreign-origin headers.
  • Why configure CORS in Spring Security rather than WebMvcConfigurer? — The security chain runs before DispatcherServlet; an unauthenticated preflight is rejected before MVC's CORS handling. http.cors() inserts CorsFilter ahead of authentication.
  • How does the double-submit cookie CSRF pattern work in Spring? — CookieCsrfTokenRepository writes a readable XSRF-TOKEN cookie; the SPA sends it back as X-XSRF-TOKEN; CsrfFilter compares the two. A foreign origin cannot read the cookie so it cannot forge the header.
  • What broke SPAs when upgrading to Spring Security 6 CSRF? — Deferred token loading (cookie not issued until read) and the Xor masking handler (header value no longer equals the cookie). Fix with the documented SPA request handler and a filter that touches the token.
  • Does SameSite=Lax make CSRF protection unnecessary? — It blocks most cross-site POSTs but not all (same-site subdomains, older browsers, top-level GET side effects); treat it as defence in depth, keep the token.
  • What does the CSRF token protect against that CORS does not? — CORS only restricts reading cross-origin responses; a simple form POST is sent regardless. CSRF tokens stop the action from being accepted.

Custom filters: OncePerRequestFilter, addFilterBefore/After, the "registered twice" trap, shouldNotFilter

Why interviewers ask: "write an API-key filter" is a common hands-on question, and the follow-up "why does it run twice?" or "why does it run on /actuator/health?" checks whether you understand that the servlet container and the security chain are two separate registries.

Extend OncePerRequestFilter (guarantees one execution per request even across forwards/async dispatch, and offers shouldNotFilter(request) and shouldNotFilterAsyncDispatch()). Place it in the chain relative to a known filter: addFilterBefore(f, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class) for something that authenticates, addFilterAfter(f, BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter.class) for something that needs the principal (MDC user id), addFilterAt to run alongside (not replace) a filter's position. The filter's job pattern: extract credential → build an Authentication → call the AuthenticationManager (or validate directly) → SecurityContextHolder.setContext → chain.doFilter; on failure either continue anonymously (let AuthorizationFilter deny) or invoke the entry point.

The trap: if the filter is a @Component, Boot's ServletContextInitializer registers every Filter bean with the servlet container, so it runs on all URLs of all chains once outside security, and then again inside the chain where you added it, with OncePerRequestFilter's guard preventing the second body execution (its alreadyFiltered attribute) but the container registration still applying to permitAll and non-secured paths. Fix: do not make it a bean (new ApiKeyFilter(...) in the config), or register a FilterRegistrationBean<ApiKeyFilter> with setEnabled(false) to suppress the container registration. Analogy: giving the same guard both a post at the building entrance and a post inside the security lane; visitors get checked in the lobby even when they were heading for the public café.

public class ApiKeyFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {         // NOT a @Component
    private final ApiKeyService keys;
    ApiKeyFilter(ApiKeyService keys) { this.keys = keys; }

    @Override
    protected boolean shouldNotFilter(HttpServletRequest req) {
        return !req.getServletPath().startsWith("/api/partner/");  // skip everything else
    }

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        String key = req.getHeader("X-Api-Key");
        if (key != null) {
            Optional<Partner> p = keys.lookup(key);
            if (p.isEmpty()) { res.sendError(401, "invalid api key"); return; }
            var auth = new PreAuthenticatedAuthenticationToken(p.get(), key, p.get().authorities());
            SecurityContext ctx = SecurityContextHolder.createEmptyContext();
            ctx.setAuthentication(auth);
            SecurityContextHolder.setContext(ctx);          // AnonymousAuthenticationFilter now skips
        }
        chain.doFilter(req, res);                                   // no key → stays anonymous → 401 later
    }
}

// in the SecurityFilterChain bean:
http.addFilterBefore(new ApiKeyFilter(keys), UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class);

// if it MUST be a bean (for injection), stop the container registration:
@Bean FilterRegistrationBean<ApiKeyFilter> apiKeyReg(ApiKeyFilter f) {
    var reg = new FilterRegistrationBean<>(f); reg.setEnabled(false); return reg;
}

Pitfalls

  • Writing to the response and not returning: the chain continues and the controller writes too → IllegalStateException: response already committed.
  • Not clearing the context: the security chain's SecurityContextHolderFilter clears it in finally, but a container-registered copy running outside the chain leaks the context onto the pooled thread.
  • addFilterBefore(f, SomeFilter.class) where SomeFilter is not in this chain (e.g. UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter with no formLogin()) → IllegalArgumentException at startup; anchor to a filter that exists, like AuthorizationFilter.
  • Throwing an AuthenticationException from a filter placed before ExceptionTranslationFilter: nothing catches it → 500. Either handle it locally or place the filter after ExceptionTranslationFilter.
Interview questions
  • Why does my custom filter execute twice? — It is a @Component: Boot registers every Filter bean with the servlet container, and you also added it to the security chain. Remove the bean, or disable the container registration with FilterRegistrationBean.setEnabled(false).
  • Why does it run on permitAll and non-matching paths? — Same cause (container registration is global), or the filter is in a chain whose securityMatcher is broader than you think. Use shouldNotFilter for path exclusions and check the chain order.
  • OncePerRequestFilter vs GenericFilterBean vs plain Filter? — OncePerRequestFilter adds the once-per-request guard (forwards, includes, error dispatch, async) and typed HttpServletRequest; GenericFilterBean only gives Spring lifecycle; prefer OncePerRequestFilter.
  • Where do you put a filter that needs the authenticated user (MDC, audit)? — After the authenticating filter and before AuthorizationFilter: addFilterAfter(f, BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter.class), or simply addFilterBefore(f, AuthorizationFilter.class).
  • Should the filter call the AuthenticationManager or validate itself? — Prefer a custom AuthenticationProvider plus a thin filter: providers are reusable, testable, and ProviderManager handles events and credential erasure.
  • How do you unit-test a filter? — Instantiate it, use MockHttpServletRequest/Response and a MockFilterChain, assert on SecurityContextHolder and the chain's getRequest(); clear the holder in @AfterEach.

Hardening and testing: headers, secrets, login rate limiting, audit events, @WithMockUser / jwt()

Why interviewers ask: after the flow questions come the "senior" ones: what does the framework harden by default, how do you keep credentials out of Git and logs, how do you slow down a brute-force attack, and how do you test all of this without a running IdP.

Headers: HeaderWriterFilter writes Cache-Control: no-store, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, X-XSS-Protection: 0 and, on HTTPS, Strict-Transport-Security by default; add contentSecurityPolicy, referrerPolicy and permissionsPolicy yourself. Secrets: @Value("${db.password}") is fine as a mechanism; the problem is where the value lives. Keep it out of the repo (env vars, Kubernetes secrets, Spring Cloud Vault / AWS Secrets Manager via ConfigDataLoader), never log Environment dumps (/actuator/env masks keys matching password|secret|key|token|credentials; set management.endpoint.env.show-values=never in prod), and give toString()-less holders for passwords (char[] or a record that redacts). Rate limiting login is not built in: use Bucket4j / a Redis counter keyed by username+IP in a filter before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, or lock the account via an AuthenticationFailureBadCredentialsEvent listener; also UserDetails.isAccountNonLocked() feeds LockedException.

Audit: ProviderManager publishes AuthenticationSuccessEvent / AbstractAuthenticationFailureEvent; 6.x adds AuthorizationDeniedEvent when you register an AuthorizationEventPublisher bean (SpringAuthorizationEventPublisher). Boot Actuator's AuditEventRepository (/actuator/auditevents) records them in memory; ship them to your SIEM from a listener. Testing: @WithMockUser(roles="ADMIN") fabricates a principal (no UserDetailsService), @WithUserDetails("alice") loads a real one through your service, @WithSecurityContext builds custom tokens. For MockMvc, SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors: .with(jwt().jwt(j -> j.claim("scope","orders:read")).authorities(...)), .with(user("bob")), .with(csrf()), .with(oidcLogin()), .with(opaqueToken()). @WebMvcTest loads your SecurityFilterChain beans automatically (import the config class if it lives elsewhere) and needs a @MockBean JwtDecoder for resource servers.

@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
@Import(SecurityConfig.class)
class OrderControllerSecurityTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    @MockBean JwtDecoder jwtDecoder;              // resource server: never contacts the IdP
    @MockBean OrderService orders;

    @Test void anonymousGets401() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/api/orders")).andExpect(status().isUnauthorized());
    }

    @Test void wrongScopeGets403() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/api/orders").with(jwt().authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_billing"))))
           .andExpect(status().isForbidden());
    }

    @Test @WithMockUser(username = "alice", roles = "ADMIN")
    void adminCanDelete() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(delete("/api/orders/7").with(csrf()))   // csrf() only if CSRF is enabled
           .andExpect(status().isNoContent());
    }
}

@Component
class LoginAudit {
    @EventListener
    void onFailure(AuthenticationFailureBadCredentialsEvent e) {
        log.warn("login failed user={} ip={}", e.getAuthentication().getName(), clientIp(e)); // never log the password
    }
}
Test helperGoes throughUse when
@WithMockUserNothing (fake principal in context)Authorization rules on roles/authorities
@WithUserDetailsYour UserDetailsServiceCustom UserDetails fields matter
jwt() / opaqueToken() / oidcLogin()Sets the resulting Authentication directlyResource server / OAuth2 client controllers
Real token via httpBasic() / form postWhole chain incl. providersTesting the login mechanism itself; @SpringBootTest + Testcontainers Keycloak

Pitfalls

  • @WithMockUser(authorities="ADMIN") vs roles="ADMIN": only the latter adds ROLE_; hasRole("ADMIN") fails with the former.
  • Testing @PreAuthorize on a service with a plain unit test: no proxy, no security; use @SpringBootTest or @Import of the service plus @EnableMethodSecurity config.
  • Account lockout without a decay: an attacker can lock out any user by spamming wrong passwords (denial of service). Rate-limit per IP+user with a sliding window instead, and alert.
  • Logging the full Authentication object or the request headers at DEBUG in production: bearer tokens and Basic credentials end up in log aggregation.
Interview questions
  • Which security headers does Spring Security set by default? — Cache-Control/Pragma/Expires no-store, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, X-XSS-Protection: 0, HSTS on secure requests. CSP and Referrer-Policy are opt-in.
  • How do you keep a DB password out of source control in Boot? — Reference it as ${DB_PASSWORD} from an environment variable or mounted secret, or use Spring Cloud Vault / cloud secret managers as a ConfigData source; rotate, and restrict /actuator/env.
  • How would you stop credential-stuffing on the login endpoint? — Per-IP and per-account rate limits (Bucket4j/Redis) in a filter before the auth filter, progressive delays, CAPTCHA after N failures, alerts from AuthenticationFailureBadCredentialsEvent, and MFA for privileged users; avoid hard lockouts that enable DoS.
  • How do you audit "who accessed what"? — Listen to Spring Security's authentication/authorization events, add an AuthorizationEventPublisher for denials, correlate via MDC (user, request id) and ship to a SIEM; Actuator's AuditEventRepository is for local inspection, not retention.
  • Difference between @WithMockUser and @WithUserDetails? — Mock builds a User in the context with no lookup; @WithUserDetails calls your UserDetailsService (needs that bean and the user in the test DB) so custom principal types are correct.
  • How do you test a JWT-secured controller without an issuer? — @WebMvcTest + @MockBean JwtDecoder + SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.jwt() with the claims/authorities under test; for end-to-end, Testcontainers with Keycloak and real tokens.
  • Why does a POST in a test return 403 while GET works? — CSRF is enabled and the test did not add .with(csrf()); a 403 with an empty body on write methods is the classic symptom.

Reactive security basics: SecurityWebFilterChain and ReactiveSecurityContextHolder

Why interviewers ask: Spring Cloud Gateway and WebFlux services use the reactive stack; the question is whether you know that the servlet filter chain and the ThreadLocal context simply do not exist there.

Same concepts, different types: @EnableWebFluxSecurity, a SecurityWebFilterChain bean built from ServerHttpSecurity (authorizeExchange(ex -> ex.pathMatchers(...).hasRole(...))), ReactiveAuthenticationManager, ReactiveUserDetailsService returning Mono<UserDetails>, ReactiveJwtDecoder. There is no ThreadLocal: the principal lives in the Reactor Context and is read with ReactiveSecurityContextHolder.getContext() (a Mono), or injected as Mono<Principal> / @AuthenticationPrincipal in handlers. Method security is @EnableReactiveMethodSecurity and the annotated method must return Mono/Flux. Session state uses WebSession (NoOpServerSecurityContextRepository for stateless). Boot picks the reactive auto-configuration when spring-boot-starter-webflux is on the classpath and spring-webmvc is not.

@Bean
SecurityWebFilterChain apiChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
    return http
        .csrf(ServerHttpSecurity.CsrfSpec::disable)
        .authorizeExchange(ex -> ex
            .pathMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()
            .pathMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
            .anyExchange().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(rs -> rs.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
        .securityContextRepository(NoOpServerSecurityContextRepository.getInstance())
        .build();
}

// reading the user inside a reactive pipeline
Mono<String> current = ReactiveSecurityContextHolder.getContext()
        .map(ctx -> ctx.getAuthentication().getName());
Interview questions
  • Why does SecurityContextHolder.getContext() return empty in a WebFlux handler? — WebFlux hops threads; the context is in the Reactor subscriber context, so use ReactiveSecurityContextHolder or inject the principal.
  • Servlet vs reactive security: what maps to what? — SecurityFilterChain→SecurityWebFilterChain, HttpSecurity→ServerHttpSecurity, authorizeHttpRequests→authorizeExchange, AuthenticationManager→ReactiveAuthenticationManager, ThreadLocal→Reactor context.
  • Where does Spring Cloud Gateway validate tokens? — It is a WebFlux app: a SecurityWebFilterChain with oauth2ResourceServer (or oauth2Login + TokenRelay filter to forward the access token downstream).
  • Can you mix MVC and WebFlux security in one app? — No; Boot chooses one web stack. A servlet app calling WebClient still uses servlet security (ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction).

Spring Security 5 → 6 migration: what was removed and what replaced it

Why interviewers ask: most teams did this migration in 2023–2024; asking "what broke when you moved to Boot 3?" is a quick way to check hands-on experience versus tutorial knowledge.

The headline removals: WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter (→ SecurityFilterChain bean; WebSecurityCustomizer bean for web.ignoring(), though ignoring is discouraged: prefer permitAll so headers still apply), antMatchers/mvcMatchers/regexMatchers (→ requestMatchers), authorizeRequests (→ authorizeHttpRequests with AuthorizationManager), @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity (→ @EnableMethodSecurity, pre/post on by default), the non-lambda chained DSL with .and() (removed in 7, deprecated in 6.1: use lambdas everywhere), javax.servlet → jakarta.servlet, SecurityContextPersistenceFilter → SecurityContextHolderFilter with explicit saving, FilterSecurityInterceptor → AuthorizationFilter, the spring-security-oauth2 legacy project → the new resource-server/client/authorization-server modules, and hasRole("ROLE_X") now throws. Behavioural changes: authorization runs once per request (not on forwards/errors) unless shouldFilterAllDispatcherTypes(true); permitAll no longer touches the session; CSRF token handling is deferred and masked; default password encoder ids unchanged.

// Spring Security 5 (Boot 2)
public class OldConfig extends WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter {
    @Override protected void configure(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.authorizeRequests()
                .antMatchers("/public/**").permitAll()
                .anyRequest().authenticated()
            .and().httpBasic();
    }
}

// Spring Security 6 (Boot 3)
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
            .requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults());
    return http.build();
}
Security 5 / Boot 2Security 6 / Boot 3
extends WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter@Bean SecurityFilterChain
authorizeRequests().antMatchers()authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.requestMatchers())
@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled=true)@EnableMethodSecurity
authenticationManagerBean()AuthenticationConfiguration.getAuthenticationManager()
AccessDecisionManager / votersAuthorizationManager
Context auto-saved every requestrequireExplicitSave(true)
javax.servlet.Filterjakarta.servlet.Filter
Interview questions
  • What replaced WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter and why is it better? — SecurityFilterChain beans: composable, multiple chains without subclass ordering tricks, no hidden inherited defaults, easier to test in isolation.
  • antMatchers vs requestMatchers: is it just a rename? — Mostly: requestMatchers(String...) uses MvcRequestMatcher when Spring MVC is present (path-pattern semantics, trailing-slash handling) and falls back to Ant; with multiple servlets you must disambiguate.
  • What silently changed behaviour in the upgrade? — Explicit context save (custom login endpoints log users out), CSRF deferred/masked tokens (SPAs break), authorization no longer applied to FORWARD/ERROR dispatches by default, hasRole("ROLE_…") throwing.
  • How do you migrate incrementally? — Upgrade to Security 5.8 first (it backports the 6 APIs with deprecations), fix every deprecation warning, then jump to 6 with the jakarta package rename via OpenRewrite recipes.
  • What about the legacy spring-security-oauth2 (@EnableAuthorizationServer)? — End of life; replace with Spring Authorization Server for issuing tokens, and the resource-server / client starters for consuming them.

Two SecurityFilterChain beans: chain A (@Order(1)) has no securityMatcher and uses formLogin(); chain B (@Order(2)) has securityMatcher("/api/**") with JWT. A request to /api/orders with a valid bearer token arrives. What happens?

b. FilterChainProxy picks the first chain whose matcher accepts the request; a chain with no securityMatcher matches everything, so A wins and B is dead code. Specificity (c) is not considered and overlap is legal (d). Fix: give the specific chain the lower order.

Which filter turns an AccessDeniedException thrown for an anonymous user into a 401 / redirect to login rather than a 403?

c. ExceptionTranslationFilter catches the exception; if the current authentication is anonymous it invokes the AuthenticationEntryPoint (start authentication), otherwise the AccessDeniedHandler. AuthorizationFilter (a) throws, it does not handle; @ControllerAdvice (d) never sees filter-level exceptions.

In a stateless resource server, which of these is not validated by default after spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri is set?

d. Audience validation must be added (JwtClaimValidator or the audiences property). Signature, timestamps (60 s skew) and issuer are the defaults; forgetting aud lets tokens minted for another API of the same issuer through.

A JWT contains "scope": "orders:read" and no roles claim. With the default converter, which rule permits the request?

a. JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter prefixes scopes with SCOPE_. b looks for ROLE_orders:read, c lacks the prefix, and d throws in 6.x because hasRole arguments must not carry a prefix (and would look for ROLE_SCOPE_… anyway).

The form login works but the user is anonymous on the very next request. The team wrote a custom /login controller that calls AuthenticationManager.authenticate and sets SecurityContextHolder. Most likely cause in Spring Security 6?

c. SecurityContextHolderFilter no longer persists the context automatically (requireExplicitSave=true); the standard filters call saveContext, a hand-rolled controller must too. The default policy is IF_REQUIRED (d), and the anonymous filter (b) only fills an empty context.

@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") is on OrderService.cancelAll(). OrderService.nightly() calls this.cancelAll(). A USER triggers nightly(). Result?

b. Method security is proxy-based AOP; this.cancelAll() never passes through the proxy, so the interceptor never runs. proxyTargetClass (d) changes JDK vs CGLIB proxies, not self-invocation. See self-invocation.

An SPA on https://app.example.com calls https://api.example.com/api/orders with a bearer header. The browser console shows a CORS error although @CrossOrigin is on the controller. Why?

d. Preflights carry no credentials; authenticated() denies them inside the filter chain, which runs before DispatcherServlet. http.cors() with a CorsConfigurationSource bean inserts CorsFilter ahead of authentication. c would be a 401 on the real request, not a CORS error.

In the authorization-code flow with PKCE, what does the client send to the token endpoint that proves it started the flow?

a. PKCE binds the code to the original requester. state (c) protects the client's callback against CSRF, not the token exchange; the id_token (b) is a result of the exchange; the password (d) never reaches the client.

A custom OncePerRequestFilter annotated @Component is also added with addFilterBefore. Logs show it running for /actuator/health, which is in a separate permitAll chain. Best fix?

c. Boot registers every Filter bean with Tomcat, globally, outside the security chains. web.ignoring() (b) removes security from actuator but the container filter still runs; ordering (a) and the base class (d) do not change where it is registered.

Which statement about JWT vs opaque tokens on a resource server is correct?

b. Introspection (RFC 7662) trades a network call per request for instant revocation. JWTs are base64-encoded, not encrypted (c), and the JWK set holds keys, not tokens (d); removing a key invalidates every token signed with it, not one user's.

Practice

Scenario: /actuator/health returns 401 after adding Spring Security

Kubernetes liveness probes started failing the moment spring-boot-starter-security was added. The only config is:

@Bean
SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
            .requestMatchers("/api/**").authenticated()
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(rs -> rs.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));
    return http.build();
}

Explain the 401 and fix it so that health/info are open, other actuator endpoints need ROLE_OPS, and the app stays stateless.

Tests: rule ordering, actuator matchers, entry point behaviour
Hint 1
Rules are first-match; both rules say authenticated(), and the probe carries no token, so ExceptionTranslationFilter hands the anonymous request to the bearer entry point.
Hint 2
Boot ships EndpointRequest.to(...) / EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint() matchers that follow management.endpoints.web.base-path and a separate management port.
Reveal solution
http.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
        .requestMatchers(EndpointRequest.to(HealthEndpoint.class, InfoEndpoint.class)).permitAll()
        .requestMatchers(EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint()).hasRole("OPS")
        .requestMatchers("/api/**").authenticated()
        .anyRequest().denyAll())                       // explicit is safer than authenticated()
    .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
    .csrf(c -> c.disable())
    .oauth2ResourceServer(rs -> rs.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));

Why 401 and not 403: the probe is anonymous, so the AccessDeniedException from AuthorizationFilter is routed to the AuthenticationEntryPoint, which for a resource server answers 401 + WWW-Authenticate: Bearer. Why EndpointRequest: it survives a changed base path or management.server.port, where a string "/actuator/health" would silently stop matching. Also set management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized so the open probe does not leak component details. Do not use web.ignoring(): that removes security headers and the anonymous context from those requests.

Scenario: @PreAuthorize ignored on an internal call (and on a private method)

@Service
public class PayoutService {

    public void runMonthEnd() {
        for (var acct : accounts()) approve(acct.id());   // called by a USER via a scheduler endpoint
    }

    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('FINANCE_ADMIN')")
    public void approve(long accountId) { ... }

    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('AUDITOR')")
    private List<Account> accounts() { ... }
}

A user with only ROLE_USER calls the endpoint that invokes runMonthEnd(). Every payout is approved. Explain both failures and give two fixes, stating which you would ship.

Tests: proxy-based method security, self-invocation, private methods, design of authorization boundaries
Hint 1
Where does the @PreAuthorize interceptor live: on the object, or on the proxy the caller holds?
Hint 2
CGLIB subclasses cannot override private methods; JDK proxies only see interface methods.
Reveal solution

Failure 1, self-invocation: the controller holds the CGLIB proxy and calls runMonthEnd(), which is not annotated, so the proxy delegates straight to the target. Inside, approve() is invoked on this, the raw target; no proxy, no AuthorizationManager check. Failure 2, private method: accounts() can never be advised: CGLIB cannot override it and Spring silently ignores the annotation (see self-invocation).

Fix A (ship this): put the check on the entry point that is actually crossed. Annotate runMonthEnd() with @PreAuthorize("hasRole('FINANCE_ADMIN')") and make accounts() package-private or move data access to a repository. Authorization belongs on the boundary the caller crosses, not on helpers.

Fix B: split the class: PayoutApprover.approve() in its own bean, injected into PayoutService, so every call goes through a proxy. Self-injection via ObjectProvider<PayoutService> or @Lazy works too but reads as a hack.

Fix C (rarely): AspectJ compile/load-time weaving (@EnableMethodSecurity(mode = AdviceMode.ASPECTJ)) advises the bytecode itself so this calls and private methods are covered; heavier build setup, worth it only if the codebase is full of internal calls.

Add a test: @SpringBootTest with @WithMockUser(roles = "USER") asserting assertThrows(AccessDeniedException.class, () -> service.runMonthEnd()); a plain unit test would have passed because there was no proxy.

Scenario: JWT works in Postman, browser gets 403 on POST (and a CORS error on OPTIONS)

An SPA on https://shop.example.com calls https://api.example.com. GETs succeed from the browser. POSTs fail; the console shows a CORS error on the preflight, and after adding @CrossOrigin the POST itself now returns 403 with an empty body. Postman succeeds for everything. Config:

http.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.anyRequest().authenticated())
    .oauth2Login(Customizer.withDefaults())          // used by the admin UI
    .oauth2ResourceServer(rs -> rs.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));

Diagnose both symptoms and propose the production configuration.

Tests: preflight vs security chain, CSRF with mixed session + bearer, chain separation
Hint 1
Postman sends no Origin, no preflight and no cookies from another site. The browser does all three.
Hint 2
oauth2Login() keeps CSRF enabled and creates a session. A 403 with an empty body on a write method, while GET works, is the signature of CsrfFilter.
Reveal solution

Symptom 1, CORS: the OPTIONS preflight is anonymous and hits anyRequest().authenticated() inside the filter chain; @CrossOrigin lives in MVC, which never runs. Configure http.cors() with a CorsConfigurationSource bean (explicit origin, Authorization and Content-Type in allowed headers, allowCredentials only if cookies are used).

Symptom 2, 403 on POST: the single chain mixes oauth2Login() (session cookie, CSRF on) with the bearer API. CsrfFilter runs before authentication and rejects any non-GET without a token, regardless of the bearer header. Postman never triggered it because CSRF checks are about the token, not the origin, and the team's Postman collection happened to use GETs or an older build.

Production fix: two chains.

@Bean @Order(1)
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http, CorsConfigurationSource cors) throws Exception {
    http.securityMatcher("/api/**")
        .cors(c -> c.configurationSource(cors))
        .csrf(c -> c.disable())                      // bearer header: no auto-attached credential
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(rs -> rs.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));
    return http.build();
}

@Bean @Order(2)
SecurityFilterChain adminUi(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2Login(Customizer.withDefaults());       // session + CSRF stay on here
    return http.build();
}

If the SPA must send the JWT in a cookie instead, keep CSRF enabled on the API chain with CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse() and the SPA request handler. Verify with the browser Network tab: preflight 200 with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, then the POST with 2xx.

Scenario: custom auth filter runs twice, runs on permitAll paths, and sometimes leaks a user

@Component
public class TenantHeaderAuthFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        String tenant = req.getHeader("X-Tenant");
        if (tenant != null) {
            var auth = new PreAuthenticatedAuthenticationToken(tenant, "n/a", List.of(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_TENANT")));
            SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(auth);
        }
        chain.doFilter(req, res);
    }
}

// SecurityConfig
http.addFilterBefore(tenantHeaderAuthFilter, AuthorizationFilter.class);

Observed: (1) DEBUG logs show the filter class twice per request; (2) it runs for /public/**, which is permitAll in another chain; (3) under load, a request without X-Tenant occasionally executes as a tenant. Explain all three and rewrite it.

Tests: container vs security registration, context lifecycle on pooled threads, thread safety of the holder
Hint 1
Boot registers every Filter bean with the servlet container. That instance runs outside the security chain, so who clears the ThreadLocal afterwards?
Hint 2
SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(...) mutates a context object that may be shared; the documented pattern is createEmptyContext() + setContext().
Reveal solution

(1) Twice: @Component → Boot's ServletContextInitializer registers it with Tomcat for /*; the same instance is also inserted into the security chain. OncePerRequestFilter prevents the body from running twice (request attribute …FILTERED), but both registrations are invoked and logged. (2) permitAll paths: the container registration is global and ignores securityMatcher. (3) Leak: the container-registered execution happens before SecurityContextHolderFilter, which is the thing that clears the ThreadLocal in its finally. On a permitAll path in the other chain the context is set by the outer copy and, if that chain's holder filter is bypassed for any reason (e.g. web.ignoring() paths, error dispatch), the pooled Tomcat thread keeps the tenant for the next unrelated request. Mutating the shared context object rather than installing a fresh one makes the window worse.

public class TenantHeaderAuthFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {   // no @Component
    private final AuthenticationManager authManager;                  // provider validates the header
    TenantHeaderAuthFilter(AuthenticationManager m) { this.authManager = m; }

    @Override protected boolean shouldNotFilter(HttpServletRequest req) {
        return req.getHeader("X-Tenant") == null;                     // cheap early exit
    }

    @Override protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        try {
            Authentication result = authManager.authenticate(
                    new PreAuthenticatedAuthenticationToken(req.getHeader("X-Tenant"), "n/a"));
            SecurityContext ctx = SecurityContextHolder.createEmptyContext();
            ctx.setAuthentication(result);
            SecurityContextHolder.setContext(ctx);                    // fresh context, never mutate shared
        } catch (AuthenticationException e) {
            SecurityContextHolder.clearContext();                     // stay anonymous; AuthorizationFilter decides
        }
        chain.doFilter(req, res);
    }
}

// config: create it here, position it after ExceptionTranslationFilter so auth failures are translated
http.addFilterBefore(new TenantHeaderAuthFilter(authManager), AuthorizationFilter.class);

If injection forces it to be a bean, add FilterRegistrationBean<TenantHeaderAuthFilter> with setEnabled(false). Verify: TRACE logging lists the filter once, inside the intended chain only; a load test with alternating tenant/no-tenant requests never returns cross-tenant data. Longer term, prefer a real AuthenticationProvider that verifies the header is signed or issued by the gateway; a bare header is trivially forgeable.

⚡ Rapid-fire: Spring Security

  • What is springSecurityFilterChain? — The FilterChainProxy bean that DelegatingFilterProxy forwards every request to.
  • Authentication vs authorization in one line? — Who you are (filters + AuthenticationManager) vs what you may do (AuthorizationManager).
  • Last filter in the default chain? — AuthorizationFilter.
  • Which filter is responsible for 401/403 responses? — ExceptionTranslationFilter via entry point / denied handler.
  • What replaced WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter? — @Bean SecurityFilterChain with the lambda DSL.
  • antMatchers in Security 6? — Gone; use requestMatchers.
  • hasRole("USER") checks which authority? — ROLE_USER.
  • Default authority for JWT scope read? — SCOPE_read.
  • Default SecurityContextHolder strategy? — MODE_THREADLOCAL.
  • Why is the context empty in @Async? — ThreadLocal does not propagate; use DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor.
  • Default PasswordEncoder in Boot? — DelegatingPasswordEncoder with bcrypt ({bcrypt} prefix).
  • What does {noop} mean in a stored password? — Plain text; test data only.
  • Where is form-login handled? — UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter on POST /login.
  • Bean that loads users from your DB? — UserDetailsService.
  • Which provider handles username/password? — DaoAuthenticationProvider.
  • Which provider handles JWTs? — JwtAuthenticationProvider using a JwtDecoder.
  • Does Spring validate JWT aud by default? — No; add a validator or the audiences property.
  • Default JWT clock skew? — 60 seconds.
  • Starter for "protect my API with tokens"? — spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server.
  • Starter for "login with Google" or calling APIs on behalf of users? — spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client.
  • oauth2Login() vs oauth2Client()? — Login authenticates the user (OIDC session); client only obtains tokens for outbound calls.
  • Grant for service-to-service? — Client credentials.
  • Recommended browser grant? — Authorization code with PKCE.
  • Access token vs ID token? — API audience vs client audience; never send the ID token to APIs.
  • When can CSRF be disabled? — Bearer token in a header set by JS, or non-browser clients.
  • Why configure CORS in Security? — Preflights are rejected by the chain before MVC sees them.
  • What does SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS do? — Security never reads or writes the HttpSession.
  • Default session-fixation protection? — changeSessionId.
  • Annotation to enable @PreAuthorize in 6? — @EnableMethodSecurity.
  • Why is @PreAuthorize skipped on this.method()? — Proxy-based AOP; self-invocation bypasses the proxy.
  • Custom filter base class? — OncePerRequestFilter.
  • Why does a @Component filter run twice? — Registered by the servlet container and by the security chain.
  • Test annotation for a fake principal? — @WithMockUser; jwt() post-processor for resource servers.
  • Reactive equivalent of SecurityFilterChain? — SecurityWebFilterChain.

7️⃣ Messaging, Async & Resilience

Once a service talks to more than one other service, the interview moves from "does it work" to "what happens when the broker is slow, the consumer dies mid-batch, or the downstream is on fire". This section covers Spring Kafka end to end (producer → partitions → consumer group → offsets → retries → DLT), the JMS/RabbitMQ alternatives, transactional messaging and why it is not atomic with your database, scheduling across multiple pods, and the Resilience4j toolbox (circuit breaker, retry, bulkhead, timeouts) that stops one failure becoming an outage. Learn it in that order: every later topic assumes you can explain a rebalance and a duplicate delivery.

Spring Kafka basics: KafkaTemplate, @KafkaListener, partitions & consumer groups

Why interviewers ask: "you have 3 pods and 6 partitions, how many threads consume?" and "what does acks=all actually guarantee?" separate people who wired a listener once from people who ran Kafka in production.

A topic is split into partitions; each partition is an append-only, ordered log. The producer picks the partition from the record key (murmur2(key) % partitions; null key → sticky round-robin per batch), so all events for the same key land on the same partition in order. A consumer group (group.id) divides the partitions among its members: each partition is owned by exactly one consumer in the group at a time, so more consumers than partitions means idle consumers. Analogy: partitions are checkout lanes, a consumer group is one team of cashiers; a shopper (key) always joins the same lane, and a lane never has two cashiers.

In Spring, KafkaTemplate<K,V> wraps a Producer built by a ProducerFactory (Boot auto-configures both from spring.kafka.producer.*). @KafkaListener methods are turned into ConcurrentMessageListenerContainers by a ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory; its concurrency=n starts n KafkaConsumer instances (threads) in that JVM, each a member of the group. Effective parallelism = min(total consumers across pods, partitions).

Producer knobs that matter: acks (0 fire-and-forget, 1 leader wrote it, all/-1 all in-sync replicas wrote it, paired with broker min.insync.replicas=2 for real durability); enable.idempotence=true (default since Kafka 3.0 clients: producer id + sequence numbers let the broker drop retried duplicates, gives exactly-once per partition per producer session); retries/delivery.timeout.ms; linger.ms and batch.size (wait up to linger.ms to fill a batch → fewer, larger requests, higher throughput, +latency); compression.type.

@Configuration
class KafkaConfig {
    @Bean
    ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<String, OrderEvent> orderFactory(
            ConsumerFactory<String, OrderEvent> cf) {
        var f = new ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<String, OrderEvent>();
        f.setConsumerFactory(cf);
        f.setConcurrency(3);                       // 3 KafkaConsumer threads in this JVM
        f.getContainerProperties().setAckMode(ContainerProperties.AckMode.BATCH);
        return f;
    }
}

@Service
class OrderPublisher {
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderEvent> template;
    OrderPublisher(KafkaTemplate<String, OrderEvent> template) { this.template = template; }

    CompletableFuture<SendResult<String, OrderEvent>> publish(OrderEvent e) {
        return template.send("orders", e.customerId(), e)     // key = customerId → ordering per customer
                       .whenComplete((r, ex) -> { if (ex != null) log.error("send failed", ex); });
    }
}

@Component
class OrderListener {
    @KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "billing", containerFactory = "orderFactory")
    void on(OrderEvent event, @Header(KafkaHeaders.RECEIVED_PARTITION) int partition) { … }
}
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: kafka-1:9092,kafka-2:9092
    producer:
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonSerializer
      acks: all
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
        linger.ms: 20
        batch.size: 65536
    consumer:
      group-id: billing
      auto-offset-reset: earliest          # only applies when the group has NO committed offset
      value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonDeserializer
      properties:
        spring.json.trusted.packages: com.acme.events
        spring.json.value.default.type: com.acme.events.OrderEvent
Serialization detail interviewers like: JsonSerializer adds a __TypeId__ header with the producer's class name; JsonDeserializer uses it unless you set spring.json.use.type.headers=false plus a default type or a TypeMapper. Cross-language or cross-repo consumers should not rely on the header (package names differ), so map type ids explicitly or use Avro/Protobuf with a schema registry.
KnobEffectProduction default to say
acksHow many replicas must persist before ackall + broker min.insync.replicas=2, RF 3
enable.idempotenceBroker dedups producer retries by sequence numbertrue (forces acks=all, max.in.flight ≤ 5)
linger.ms / batch.sizeTrade latency for throughput5–50 ms / 64 KB for event streams; 0 for request-like traffic
concurrencyConsumer threads per JVM≤ partitions / pods
auto.offset.resetWhere a new group startsearliest for replayable data, latest for live metrics

Pitfalls

  • Ordering is per partition; a listener with concurrency=3 on one partition still gets one thread. Do not "fix" order with a synchronized block; fix the key.
  • KafkaTemplate.send is asynchronous and buffers; calling .get() on every send throws away batching. Use the future callback or flush() at shutdown.
  • auto-offset-reset only applies when there is no committed offset for the group; changing it on an existing group does nothing.
  • Hot keys (one big customer) make one partition hot; no amount of consumers helps. Consider a composite key or key salting where ordering allows.
Interview questions
  • 3 pods, concurrency 4, topic has 6 partitions: how many threads do work? — 12 consumers join the group, only 6 get a partition; 6 threads are idle. Either cut concurrency to 2 or add partitions.
  • How does Kafka guarantee ordering? — Only within a partition; the producer routes by key hash, so choose the key as the entity whose events must be ordered (order id, customer id), never a random UUID.
  • What does acks=all guarantee without min.insync.replicas? — Only that all in-sync replicas wrote it; if the ISR shrinks to the leader alone, that is one copy. Set min.insync.replicas=2 so the broker rejects writes (NotEnoughReplicasException) instead of silently accepting them.
  • What does the idempotent producer prevent and what does it not? — Duplicates caused by the producer's own retries within a session on one partition. It does not dedupe two application-level send() calls or survive a producer restart.
  • Why would you set linger.ms above 0? — To let batches fill: fewer requests, better compression, higher throughput at the cost of a few ms of latency; 0 means each record can go alone.
  • How do you consume the same topic twice for two purposes? — Two different group.ids; each group tracks its own offsets. Same group would split, not duplicate, the stream.
  • How would you debug "listener receives nothing"? — Check the group's committed offset and lag (kafka-consumer-groups --describe), whether the container started (KafkaListenerEndpointRegistry, autoStartup), deserialization errors in logs, and that the topic names/partition assignment are what you expect.
  • Spring Boot 2 vs 3 for Kafka? — Boot 3 ships Spring Kafka 3.x: KafkaTemplate.send returns CompletableFuture instead of ListenableFuture, ContainerProperties.AckMode nesting, @RetryableTopic is GA, and Micrometer observation is built in.

Consumer semantics: poll loop, rebalances, ack modes, at-least/at-most/exactly-once

Why interviewers ask: every "we saw a duplicate charge" story comes down to when the offset was committed relative to the side effect. They want you to trace one record through poll → process → commit and say exactly where a crash creates a duplicate or a loss.

A KafkaConsumer is single-threaded: the container loops poll(timeout) → hand records to your listener → commit offsets. poll() also sends heartbeats' companion signal: if the thread does not call poll() again within max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 min) the coordinator assumes the consumer is dead, evicts it and rebalances its partitions to the others. Slow processing of a batch of max.poll.records (default 500) is the classic cause: 500 records × 1 s each = 8 min > 5 min → eviction → the partition moves, the same 500 records are re-delivered elsewhere, that consumer also times out … the rebalance storm. (Heartbeats themselves come from a background thread every heartbeat.interval.ms; session.timeout.ms catches a crashed process, max.poll.interval.ms catches a stuck one.)

Spring's ack modes decide when the container commits: BATCH (default: after the listener has processed everything from the last poll), RECORD (after each record), TIME/COUNT, MANUAL (you call ack.acknowledge(), commit happens after the batch), MANUAL_IMMEDIATE (commit right when you call it). Boot disables the client's own enable.auto.commit so the container is in charge. Analogy: the offset is a bookmark; commit after reading the page and a crash costs you a re-read (duplicate), commit before and a crash loses the page.

That gives the three guarantees. At-least-once: process then commit (Spring default) — duplicates on crash, never loss; make the consumer idempotent (unique constraint on event id, processed_events table in the same DB transaction, or versioned upserts). At-most-once: commit first, process later — no duplicates, possible loss. Exactly-once: only within Kafka via transactions: consumed offsets and produced records are committed atomically by a transactional producer, and downstream consumers with isolation.level=read_committed never see aborted output. It does not extend to your database or an HTTP call.

@KafkaListener(topics = "payments", groupId = "ledger", containerFactory = "manualAckFactory")
@Transactional                                   // DB transaction, NOT a Kafka transaction
public void on(ConsumerRecord<String, PaymentEvent> rec, Acknowledgment ack) {
    var e = rec.value();
    if (processedRepo.existsById(e.eventId())) { ack.acknowledge(); return; }   // idempotent
    ledgerRepo.save(Ledger.from(e));
    processedRepo.save(new ProcessedEvent(e.eventId(), Instant.now()));       // same tx as the write
    ack.acknowledge();       // MANUAL_IMMEDIATE: commit offset rec.offset()+1 now
}
// factory: f.getContainerProperties().setAckMode(AckMode.MANUAL_IMMEDIATE);
// consumer props: max.poll.records=100, max.poll.interval.ms=600000
GuaranteeOrder of operationsFailure outcomeHow in Spring
At-most-oncecommit → processLossCommit early (MANUAL_IMMEDIATE before the work) — rarely wanted
At-least-onceprocess → commitDuplicateDefault BATCH/RECORD/MANUAL* + idempotent handler
Exactly-once (Kafka→Kafka)consume + produce + offset in one Kafka txAborted tx invisible to read_committedKafkaTransactionManager, transaction-id-prefix, isolation.level=read_committed

Pitfalls

  • max.poll.interval.ms is about processing time, not network health. Raising session.timeout.ms does nothing for a slow handler.
  • Calling KafkaConsumer methods from another thread throws ConcurrentModificationException; hand work to a pool only with pause()/resume() handling (or use @RetryableTopic/async patterns).
  • @Transactional on the listener with a JPA transaction manager: the offset commit is not part of that transaction; a crash between DB commit and Kafka commit replays the record.
  • Default eager rebalance stops all consumers in the group; Boot 3 clients default to CooperativeStickyAssignor via partition.assignment.strategy only if you configure it, so set it explicitly for large groups.
Interview questions
  • Heartbeat is fine but the consumer still got kicked out. Why? — Heartbeats run on a background thread; liveness for the coordinator also requires poll() within max.poll.interval.ms. A long-running handler violates that, not the heartbeat.
  • Where exactly does a duplicate come from with the default settings? — Spring commits after the batch; a crash, eviction or exception after the side effect but before that commit means the next owner replays from the old offset.
  • Is "exactly-once" with a database possible? — Not via Kafka transactions. Get the effect by an idempotent consumer: store the event id (or offset per partition) in the same DB transaction as the business write, and skip when already present.
  • MANUAL vs MANUAL_IMMEDIATE? — Both require ack.acknowledge(); MANUAL batches the commits until the poll's records are done, MANUAL_IMMEDIATE commits synchronously on the call (safer replay window, more commit traffic).
  • What is isolation.level=read_committed for? — Consumers skip records from aborted Kafka transactions and stop at the last stable offset; required for the downstream half of exactly-once streaming.
  • How would you handle a handler that legitimately takes minutes? — Lower max.poll.records, raise max.poll.interval.ms, or pause the container, process asynchronously and resume; and make the result idempotent because a replay is still possible.
  • What happens to offsets when you deploy a new version of the consumer? — Nothing; offsets belong to the group, so the new pods resume where the old ones committed. Pods stopped ungracefully mid-batch replay their uncommitted records — a common source of "duplicates after deploy".
  • What is a cooperative rebalance? — CooperativeStickyAssignor revokes only the partitions that actually move, so the other consumers keep processing instead of the whole group stopping ("stop-the-world" eager rebalance).

Error handling: DefaultErrorHandler, DLT, @RetryableTopic, poison pills

Why interviewers ask: "a message throws every time — what happens to the partition?" The naive answer ("it retries") hides a stuck partition, a flood of duplicates, or lost ordering. They want the blocking vs non-blocking retry trade-off and where deserialization errors go.

Since Spring Kafka 2.8 the container's default error handler is DefaultErrorHandler: on an exception it seeks back to the failed record's offset and re-polls it, retrying with a BackOff (default 9 retries, no delay — always replace it with ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries or FixedBackOff(1000L, 3)). This is blocking retry: the partition does not advance until the record succeeds or retries are exhausted, then the recoverer runs — usually a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer that publishes the record to <topic>.DLT (same partition by default) with exception headers and lets the partition move on. Exceptions listed via addNotRetryableExceptions(…) (deserialization, conversion, MethodArgumentResolution are pre-registered) go straight to the recoverer.

@RetryableTopic implements non-blocking retry: failures are forwarded to orders-retry-0, orders-retry-1… topics with growing back-off, consumed by auto-created listeners, and finally to orders-dlt (a @DltHandler method receives them). The main partition keeps flowing at the cost of ordering: the retried record is now behind newer records for the same key. Analogy: blocking retry is a stuck car in a single lane; retry topics tow it to a side road so traffic moves, but it will arrive after cars that left later.

A poison pill is a record that fails before your code: bad JSON, unknown type header. The plain JsonDeserializer throws inside poll(), the container has no record to skip, and it loops forever on the same offset. Wrap deserializers in ErrorHandlingDeserializer: it returns a record whose value is null plus a DeserializationException header, so the error handler can recover (DLT) and advance.

@Bean
DefaultErrorHandler kafkaErrorHandler(KafkaTemplate<Object, Object> template) {
    var recoverer = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template,
        (rec, ex) -> new TopicPartition(rec.topic() + ".DLT", rec.partition()));
    var backOff = new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(4);      // 4 retries
    backOff.setInitialInterval(500); backOff.setMultiplier(2.0); backOff.setMaxInterval(8_000);
    var handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer, backOff);
    handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(ValidationException.class);  // straight to DLT
    return handler;      // Boot auto-wires a CommonErrorHandler bean into the default factory
}

// Non-blocking alternative
@RetryableTopic(attempts = "4", backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 3),
                exclude = ValidationException.class, dltStrategy = DltStrategy.FAIL_ON_ERROR)
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "billing")
void on(OrderEvent e) { … }

@DltHandler
void dlt(OrderEvent e, @Header(KafkaHeaders.EXCEPTION_MESSAGE) String why) { alerts.raise(e, why); }
spring.kafka.consumer:
  key-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.ErrorHandlingDeserializer
  value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.ErrorHandlingDeserializer
  properties:
    spring.deserializer.key.delegate.class: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
    spring.deserializer.value.delegate.class: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonDeserializer
Blocking retry (DefaultErrorHandler)Non-blocking (@RetryableTopic)
Partition while retryingStalled (seek back)Keeps flowing
Per-key orderingPreservedLost for the retried key
Extra topicsOnly the DLTOne per retry level (or SINGLE_TOPIC strategy)
Long back-offsRisk max.poll.interval.ms (handler pauses the container to avoid it)Fine; partition is paused until due
Use whenOrder matters, short transient failuresThroughput matters, failures are per-record, or delays are long

Pitfalls

  • @Transactional + DefaultErrorHandler: the retry re-invokes the whole listener, so a non-transactional side effect (email, HTTP POST) happens on every attempt.
  • Batch listeners: an exception in the middle of a batch retries the whole batch unless you throw BatchListenerFailedException(msg, index) to say which record failed.
  • A DLT record carries the original value bytes; if the failure was deserialization, the DLT consumer must read it as byte[].
  • Retry topics multiply partitions and consumers; with 10 topics × 3 levels you now run 40 listener containers per pod.
Interview questions
  • A record throws on every attempt. With defaults, what happens? — DefaultErrorHandler retries it 10 times back-to-back (seek + re-poll), then logs and skips it (default recoverer just logs) — you lose the record unless you configured a DLT recoverer.
  • Why does a corrupt message block the partition forever? — The exception is thrown inside poll() before the container has a record to skip; ErrorHandlingDeserializer converts it into a record with a failure header so the normal error path (DLT) applies.
  • When would you not use @RetryableTopic? — When per-key ordering is a business invariant (account balance events): the retried record would be applied after later ones. Use blocking retry with short back-off, or re-key/version the events.
  • How do you avoid retrying a validation error 10 times? — addNotRetryableExceptions / exclude so it goes straight to the DLT; retries only make sense for transient faults.
  • What headers do you get in the DLT? — kafka_dlt-original-topic/-partition/-offset/-timestamp, kafka_dlt-exception-fqcn/-message/-stacktrace; enough to trace and replay.
  • How do you replay a DLT? — A dedicated (usually paused) listener or a CLI job that republishes to the original topic after the fix, ideally keeping the original key so partition ordering is restored going forward.
  • Spring Kafka 2.x vs 3.x error handling? — SeekToCurrentErrorHandler/RecoveringBatchErrorHandler were replaced by the single DefaultErrorHandler implementing CommonErrorHandler; @RetryableTopic moved from experimental to GA.

Kafka Streams & Spring Cloud Stream in one card

Why interviewers ask: to check you know when a plain listener stops being enough (joins, windows, aggregations) and that "Cloud Stream" is a binder abstraction, not another broker.

Kafka Streams is a client library (no cluster) for topology processing: KStream (event stream), KTable (changelog → latest value per key), GlobalKTable, windowed aggregations, stream-table joins, with state stored locally in RocksDB and backed up to changelog topics so a restarted instance rebuilds it. Exactly-once is one property: processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2. Boot auto-configures a StreamsBuilder when you add @EnableKafkaStreams and spring.kafka.streams.application-id.

Spring Cloud Stream hides the broker behind a binder (Kafka, RabbitMQ, Kafka Streams, Pulsar…) and a functional model: a Supplier<T> bean is a source, Function<A,B> a processor, Consumer<T> a sink; bindings are named <bean>-in-0/-out-0 and wired to destinations in YAML. StreamBridge sends imperatively. Use it when you want broker-portable code or consistent retry/DLQ config across many services; use Spring Kafka directly when you need Kafka-specific control (manual acks, rebalance listeners, headers).

@Bean
public Function<KStream<String, OrderEvent>, KStream<String, Long>> ordersPerCustomer() {
    return orders -> orders
        .groupByKey()
        .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeWithNoGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(5)))
        .count()
        .toStream()
        .map((w, c) -> KeyValue.pair(w.key(), c));
}
// spring.cloud.stream.bindings.ordersPerCustomer-in-0.destination=orders
// spring.cloud.stream.bindings.ordersPerCustomer-out-0.destination=orders-per-customer
Spring KafkaSpring Cloud StreamKafka Streams
AbstractionKafka client wrapperBroker-agnostic binderStateful stream topology
State / joins / windowsNo (do it in your DB)Via Kafka Streams binderYes, local RocksDB + changelog
Control over acks/rebalanceFullLimited (properties)Managed by the library
Interview questions
  • Where does Kafka Streams keep state and what happens when a pod dies? — Locally in RocksDB, mirrored to a changelog topic; the partition's task moves to another instance which replays the changelog (standby replicas shorten the gap).
  • KStream vs KTable? — Stream = every event; table = latest value per key (an upsert view); a join of an order stream with a customer table enriches events.
  • Why choose Spring Cloud Stream? — Same code and retry/DLQ properties across Kafka and RabbitMQ, functional beans, test binder; the price is less broker-specific control.
  • How does Cloud Stream name bindings? — <functionBeanName>-in-<index> / -out-<index>; multiple functions are enabled with spring.cloud.function.definition=a;b.

JMS & RabbitMQ: @JmsListener, @RabbitListener, DLQ/DLX, and choosing a broker

Why interviewers ask: "why Kafka and not RabbitMQ here?" is a design question in disguise: it checks you understand a log (retained, replayable, consumer-tracked offsets) versus a queue (message deleted on ack, broker-tracked, per-message routing).

JMS (jakarta.jms in Boot 3) is an API: brokers such as ActiveMQ Artemis or IBM MQ implement it. Boot auto-configures a ConnectionFactory, JmsTemplate and a DefaultJmsListenerContainerFactory; @JmsListener(destination="orders") consumes from a queue (competing consumers, one delivery) or a topic (pub/sub, durable subscriptions). Ack modes: AUTO (after the listener returns without exception), CLIENT (you ack), DUPS_OK, or sessionTransacted=true so ack rolls back with your transaction. After maxRedeliveries the broker moves the message to its DLQ (Artemis: DLQ address).

RabbitMQ speaks AMQP 0-9-1: producers publish to an exchange (direct, topic, fanout, headers) which routes by routing key to bound queues. RabbitTemplate.convertAndSend(exchange, routingKey, obj); @RabbitListener(queues="orders.q") with AcknowledgeMode.AUTO (container acks after success, nacks-and-requeues on exception — a poison message loops unless you throw AmqpRejectAndDontRequeueException or set default-requeue-rejected=false) or MANUAL (channel.basicAck). A dead-letter exchange (x-dead-letter-exchange queue argument) receives rejected/expired messages; delayed retry is built by a wait queue with x-message-ttl dead-lettering back. Prefetch (prefetch=250 default in Spring AMQP) bounds unacked messages per consumer. Analogy: RabbitMQ is a post office that routes each letter to the right mailbox and shreds it once you sign; Kafka is a newspaper archive where every subscriber keeps their own bookmark.

@Configuration
class RabbitTopology {
    @Bean Queue ordersQ() {
        return QueueBuilder.durable("orders.q")
            .deadLetterExchange("orders.dlx").deadLetterRoutingKey("orders.dead").build();
    }
    @Bean TopicExchange ordersX() { return new TopicExchange("orders.x"); }
    @Bean Binding ordersB() { return BindingBuilder.bind(ordersQ()).to(ordersX()).with("order.#"); }
}

@RabbitListener(queues = "orders.q", ackMode = "AUTO", concurrency = "3-6")
void on(OrderEvent e) {
    if (!valid(e)) throw new AmqpRejectAndDontRequeueException("invalid");   // → DLX, not requeue loop
    …
}

@JmsListener(destination = "orders", containerFactory = "jmsFactory")       // Artemis queue
void onJms(OrderEvent e) { … }  // factory.setSessionTransacted(true) → ack rolls back with the tx
KafkaRabbitMQJMS broker (Artemis/IBM MQ)
ModelPartitioned log, consumer keeps offsetExchange → queues, broker tracks acksQueues + topics per JMS API
Retention / replayTime/size based, replay by seekingDeleted on ackDeleted on ack
RoutingBy partition key onlyRich (topic patterns, headers, fanout)Selectors on headers
OrderingPer partitionPer queue with single consumerPer queue with single consumer / message groups
Per-message retry/delay/priorityAwkward (retry topics)Native (TTL, DLX, priority queues)Native (redelivery policy, scheduled delivery)
FitEvent streaming, high volume, multiple readers, audit/replayTask queues, RPC-style, fan-out to many small consumersEnterprise integration, XA transactions, legacy

Pitfalls

  • RabbitMQ default requeue on exception: a message that always throws is redelivered instantly and forever, pinning a consumer at 100 % CPU.
  • Unlimited prefetch or a huge prefetch with slow consumers starves other consumers: one consumer hoards 250 messages while others sit idle.
  • JMS AUTO ack with an async handoff to a thread pool acks before the work is done (at-most-once by accident).
  • Boot 3 moved JMS to jakarta.jms; ActiveMQ "Classic" 5.x needed the 5.18+ client for Jakarta, Artemis was ready first.
Interview questions
  • When would you pick RabbitMQ over Kafka? — Work distribution with per-message acks, priorities, delays and complex routing at moderate volume; no need to replay; many short-lived consumers. Kafka when you need retention, replay, ordering by key, very high throughput, or several independent consumer groups on the same stream.
  • How does a consumer group differ from competing consumers on a queue? — Queue: broker hands each message to one consumer, any number of consumers, no ordering. Kafka: parallelism capped by partitions, ordering within a partition, offsets per group.
  • How do you implement delayed retry in RabbitMQ? — Reject to a DLX bound to a wait queue with x-message-ttl and its own DLX pointing back to the work exchange, or use the delayed-message plugin.
  • What does sessionTransacted buy you in JMS? — The receive is acked only when the session commits; with Spring's JmsTransactionManager a listener exception rolls the message back for redelivery.
  • Can you get exactly-once with RabbitMQ? — No; publisher confirms + consumer acks give at-least-once, so dedupe on message id in the consumer.
  • How would you debug messages "disappearing" in RabbitMQ? — Check unroutable publishes (no binding → dropped unless mandatory=true with a return callback), queue TTL/expiry, DLX, and a consumer with AUTO ack that dies after receipt.

Transactional messaging: Kafka transactions, consume-transform-produce, and why DB + Kafka in one @Transactional is not atomic

Why interviewers ask: the "dual write" question. Candidates who say "I put @Transactional on it" fail; the strong answer names the exact window in which the DB commits and the Kafka send is lost (or vice versa) and reaches for the outbox pattern.

A Kafka transaction spans Kafka only: a producer configured with transactional.id (Boot: spring.kafka.producer.transaction-id-prefix) does beginTransaction → send to any topics → sendOffsetsToTransaction(consumedOffsets, groupMetadata) → commitTransaction. Output records and the consumed offsets become visible atomically, and consumers with isolation.level=read_committed never see aborted output. That is consume-transform-produce, the only true exactly-once shape. The transactional.id also provides zombie fencing: a producer epoch bumps on restart, so a stalled old instance's late commit is rejected.

In Spring, configuring the prefix makes Boot create a KafkaTransactionManager; a listener with a KafkaTemplate send inside runs the whole handler in a Kafka transaction and the container sends offsets to it (EOSMode.V2). kafkaTemplate.executeInTransaction(ops -> …) does it locally. ChainedKafkaTransactionManager (commit DB then Kafka in sequence) is deprecated since 2.7 because it was never atomic — it merely ordered two commits. The replacement guidance: put a @Transactional("dbTm") DB transaction inside a Kafka-transactional listener (Kafka tx begins → DB tx commits → Kafka tx commits) so a Kafka failure after the DB commit is at most a replay (handled by idempotency), never a lost DB write — or avoid the problem with the outbox pattern. Analogy: two safes with two keys; you can lock them one after the other, but there is no single key that locks both at once.

@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Transactional                                    // JpaTransactionManager only
    public void place(OrderRequest req) {
        Order o = orderRepo.save(Order.from(req));    // (1) INSERT inside DB tx
        kafka.send("orders", o.id(), new OrderPlaced(o)); // (2) async send, buffered
        auditRepo.save(Audit.of(o));                  // (3) may throw!
    }                                                 // (4) commit DB tx here (proxy)
}
// producer: acks=all, buffered until batch/linger; broker may be down
  1. The transactional proxy starts a database transaction. There is no Kafka transaction; KafkaTemplate is not a transactional resource of JpaTransactionManager.
  2. The order row exists only inside the open transaction.
  3. send() is asynchronous and unrelated to the DB transaction. Depending on linger.ms the event may hit the broker now, before the DB commit.
  4. Case A: step (3) throws. The proxy rolls back the DB; the event is already on the topic. Downstream ships an order that was never placed. A phantom event.
  5. Case B: no exception, DB commits at (4), but the broker was unreachable or the pod was killed before the producer flushed. Order exists, nobody hears about it. A lost event.
  6. Fixes, weakest to strongest: @TransactionalEventListener(phase=AFTER_COMMIT) removes phantoms only; nested Kafka/DB transactions bound the damage to replays; the outbox writes the event into the same DB transaction and a relay publishes it, making the pair atomic (see section 5).
// consume-transform-produce, exactly-once within Kafka
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "enricher")     // container uses KafkaTransactionManager
public void enrich(OrderEvent in) {
    var out = in.withPrice(pricing.priceFor(in));
    template.send("orders-priced", in.customerId(), out);   // same Kafka tx as the offset commit
}
// application.yml
// spring.kafka.producer.transaction-id-prefix: enricher-tx-
// spring.kafka.consumer.isolation-level: read_committed
// spring.kafka.consumer.properties.isolation.level: read_committed   (downstream consumers too)

Pitfalls

  • Setting transaction-id-prefix makes every KafkaTemplate.send outside a transaction throw IllegalStateException: No transaction is in process; use executeInTransaction or @Transactional("kafkaTransactionManager") for producer-only paths, or a second non-transactional template.
  • Two PlatformTransactionManager beans (JPA + Kafka) make plain @Transactional ambiguous: mark one @Primary or always qualify.
  • Transactions add latency (commit markers, transaction.timeout.ms) and cap throughput; do not turn them on "for safety" on a fire-and-forget metrics topic.
  • read_committed consumers lag behind read_uncommitted ones by up to one transaction; a hung producer blocks the last stable offset until transaction.timeout.ms (default 60 s).
Interview questions
  • I annotate a method that saves to Postgres and sends to Kafka with @Transactional. Is it atomic? — No. Only the JPA resource enlists; the send is an independent async operation that can succeed before a DB rollback (phantom event) or fail after the DB commit (lost event).
  • Why was ChainedKafkaTransactionManager deprecated? — It only ordered commits; a crash between the two still diverges. Spring's guidance is nested transactions with the Kafka one outermost, or the outbox.
  • What does exactly-once in Kafka actually cover? — Read from topic A, write to topic B, commit offsets of A — atomically, within the Kafka cluster. Anything outside (DB, HTTP) is out of scope.
  • What is zombie fencing? — Each transactional.id has an epoch; when a new producer instance initialises, older instances with the same id are fenced (ProducerFencedException) so a stalled pod cannot commit stale work.
  • How would you implement the outbox with Spring? — Insert the event row in the same JPA transaction; a relay (Debezium CDC or a @Scheduled poller with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) publishes and marks it sent; consumers stay idempotent because the relay is at-least-once.
  • Kafka transactions vs idempotent producer? — Idempotence dedupes retries of one producer on one partition; transactions make multi-partition writes plus offset commits atomic and add fencing. Transactions imply idempotence.

Scheduling: @Scheduled (fixedRate vs fixedDelay vs cron), the single thread, and running on many pods

Why interviewers ask: two production classics: "the nightly job ran three times" (three pods) and "the 5-minute job stopped running" (another job hogs the one scheduler thread). Both are about defaults nobody reads.

@EnableScheduling registers ScheduledAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, which turns every @Scheduled method into a task on a TaskScheduler. Boot auto-configures a ThreadPoolTaskScheduler with pool size 1 (spring.task.scheduling.pool-size), so all scheduled methods in the app share one thread: a long job delays every other one. fixedRate = start every N ms regardless of duration (but runs never overlap on one thread; missed ticks queue up and fire back-to-back), fixedDelay = N ms after the previous run finished, cron = wall-clock expression (6 fields with seconds; zone attribute; Spring 5.3+ macros like @daily and L/# support). initialDelay avoids running during startup. Since Spring 6 you can use timeUnit and string durations like "PT30S".

With N replicas each pod runs its own scheduler, so the job runs N times. Options: ShedLock (@SchedulerLock(name, lockAtMostFor, lockAtLeastFor) takes a lock row in the DB/Redis before running; lockAtMostFor guards against a dead holder), a DB advisory lock (pg_try_advisory_lock) or SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on a job table so instances share the work rather than exclude each other, a leader election (Spring Integration LockRegistryLeaderInitiator, Kubernetes lease), or a full scheduler like Quartz in clustered JDBC mode. Combining @Scheduled with @Async hands the body to the async executor so the scheduler thread is free — allowed, but then overlapping runs become possible.

@Configuration
@EnableScheduling
@EnableSchedulerLock(defaultLockAtMostFor = "PT10M")
class SchedulingConfig {
    @Bean LockProvider lockProvider(DataSource ds) { return new JdbcTemplateLockProvider(ds); }
}
// spring.task.scheduling.pool-size=4     ← otherwise ONE thread for all jobs

@Component
class Jobs {
    @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * *", zone = "UTC")
    @SchedulerLock(name = "nightlyReconcile", lockAtLeastFor = "PT1M", lockAtMostFor = "PT30M")
    void reconcile() { … }                     // runs on exactly one pod

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 30, timeUnit = TimeUnit.SECONDS, initialDelay = 60)
    void pollOutbox() { … }                    // 30 s after the previous run ends

    @Scheduled(fixedRate = 5_000) @Async        // do not block the scheduler thread
    void heartbeat() { … }                     // may overlap if a run takes > 5 s
}
AttributeNext runOverlap on one thread?Use for
fixedRateEvery N from the previous startNo, but backlog catches upMetrics, heartbeats
fixedDelayN after the previous endNo, no backlogPollers, cleanup
cronWall clock (seconds first, 6 fields)Missed ticks are skippedReports, batch windows

Pitfalls

  • @Scheduled on a method of a bean that is also proxied lazily or is a prototype: the post-processor needs a singleton; prototypes are not scheduled.
  • An exception in a scheduled method is logged by the ErrorHandler and the schedule continues; an Error or an infinite loop kills the schedule silently — add a metric per job.
