  • Spring's cron is 6 fields (seconds first); copying a 5-field Unix cron shifts everything.
  • ShedLock only prevents concurrent runs; it does not guarantee a run happens if all pods are down at that second — use a persistent scheduler (Quartz) for "must run once, eventually".
Interview questions
  • A @Scheduled(fixedRate=60000) job stopped running. The other job in the app takes 20 minutes. Why? — Default scheduler pool size is 1; the long job occupies it. Increase spring.task.scheduling.pool-size, move heavy work to @Async, or split the app.
  • Three replicas, a nightly job ran three times. Fix? — Distributed lock (ShedLock with lockAtMostFor), DB advisory lock, leader election, or clustered Quartz; or redesign so the work is partitioned and each instance takes a slice.
  • fixedRate with a job that takes longer than the rate? — Runs never overlap on the same thread; they queue and run back-to-back until caught up (a burst after a slow run). With @Async they do overlap.
  • How do you test a scheduled method? — Call it directly in a unit test; verify the cron with CronExpression.parse(...).next(now); disable scheduling in slices by not importing the config or using a profile.
  • What does lockAtMostFor protect against? — A pod that dies while holding the lock; after that duration the lock expires and another pod can run the job. Set it above the longest realistic run.
  • Spring 5/Boot 2 vs 6/Boot 3 scheduling changes? — Spring 6 added timeUnit, string durations, @Scheduled on reactive/Kotlin suspend methods, and Boot 3.2 can use virtual threads for the scheduler (spring.threads.virtual.enabled).

Resilience4j: circuit breaker state machine, retry with jitter, rate limiter, bulkhead, time limiter

Why interviewers ask: "explain the circuit breaker" is table stakes; the depth questions are the thresholds (how many failures, over what window, when does it probe again), the order the annotations apply in, and why a fallback that is also slow makes things worse.

A circuit breaker protects the caller from a failing dependency. CLOSED: calls pass, outcomes are recorded in a sliding window (slidingWindowType=COUNT_BASED of slidingWindowSize calls, or TIME_BASED seconds). Once at least minimumNumberOfCalls are recorded and the failure rate ≥ failureRateThreshold (default 50 %) — or the slow call rate ≥ slowCallRateThreshold with calls over slowCallDurationThreshold — it trips to OPEN: calls fail immediately with CallNotPermittedException (no waiting on a dead service). After waitDurationInOpenState it moves to HALF_OPEN and lets permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState probe calls through; if their failure rate is below the threshold → CLOSED, else → OPEN again. Analogy: an electrical breaker; the half-open state is you flipping it back on once to see whether the wiring still sparks.

The rest of the toolbox: Retry (maxAttempts, waitDuration, enableExponentialBackoff + enableRandomizedWait/jitter so 1 000 clients do not retry in lockstep, retryExceptions/ignoreExceptions: never retry 4xx or non-idempotent writes); RateLimiter (limitForPeriod per limitRefreshPeriod, callers wait up to timeoutDuration); Bulkhead (SEMAPHORE: max concurrent calls on the caller's thread; THREADPOOL: separate pool + queue, isolates and adds a timeout hook, returns CompletableFuture); TimeLimiter (bounds a CompletableFuture/reactive call; needs a cancellable future, not a blocking method). With resilience4j-spring-boot3 these are annotations on proxied beans, and the aspect order by default is Retry ( CircuitBreaker ( RateLimiter ( TimeLimiter ( Bulkhead ( method ))))) — outermost first — configurable via resilience4j.*.*Aspect-order. Fallback methods must match the signature plus a trailing exception parameter; the most specific exception type wins.

@Service
class PricingClient {
    private final RestClient rest;
    PricingClient(RestClient.Builder b) { this.rest = b.baseUrl("http://pricing").build(); }

    @CircuitBreaker(name = "pricing", fallbackMethod = "cachedPrice")   // applied inside Retry
    @Retry(name = "pricing")                                            // outermost by default
    @Bulkhead(name = "pricing", type = Bulkhead.Type.SEMAPHORE)
    public Price price(String sku) {
        return rest.get().uri("/prices/{sku}", sku).retrieve().body(Price.class);
    }
    Price cachedPrice(String sku, CallNotPermittedException ex) { return cache.get(sku); }  // breaker open
    Price cachedPrice(String sku, Exception ex) { return Price.unknown(); }               // anything else
}
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      pricing:
        slidingWindowType: COUNT_BASED
        slidingWindowSize: 20
        minimumNumberOfCalls: 10
        failureRateThreshold: 50
        slowCallDurationThreshold: 2s
        slowCallRateThreshold: 80
        waitDurationInOpenState: 10s
        permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 3
        registerHealthIndicator: true          # /actuator/health shows CB state
        ignoreExceptions: [com.acme.NotFoundException]   # 404 is not a failure
  retry:
    instances:
      pricing:
        maxAttempts: 3
        waitDuration: 200ms
        enableExponentialBackoff: true
        exponentialBackoffMultiplier: 2
        enableRandomizedWait: true             # jitter
        retryExceptions: [java.io.IOException, org.springframework.web.client.HttpServerErrorException]
management.health.circuitbreakers.enabled: true
PatternProtects againstKey settingsTrap
Circuit breakerHammering a dead dependency; latency pile-upwindow, thresholds, wait, half-open permitsCounting 4xx as failures; slow fallback
RetryTransient blipsattempts, backoff, jitter, which exceptionsRetrying non-idempotent POSTs; retry storms
Rate limiterExceeding a partner's quotalimitForPeriod, refresh, timeoutPer-instance limit × N pods
BulkheadOne slow dependency eating all threadsmaxConcurrentCalls (semaphore) / pool + queueThread-pool type on a blocking call wrapped in a future for no reason
Time limiterUnbounded waitstimeoutDuration, cancelRunningFutureDoes nothing for a blocking method; set client timeouts instead

Pitfalls

  • Fallback method not found: it must be in the same class, same parameters plus one Throwable param, same return type; and the annotated method must be called through the proxy (self-invocation bypasses it, see section 4).
  • Breaker never opens because minimumNumberOfCalls is never reached on a low-traffic endpoint, or because the exceptions are caught inside the method and turned into a return value.
  • Retry outside the breaker (default) means the breaker sees each attempt as a call — fine; the reverse order (breaker outside) means an OPEN breaker's rejections get retried — configure retryAspectOrder/circuitBreakerAspectOrder consciously.
  • Feign: with spring-cloud-starter-openfeign set spring.cloud.openfeign.circuitbreaker.enabled=true and use a fallback class; Resilience4j annotations on the Feign interface itself are ignored.
Interview questions
  • Explain the three states and the transitions with numbers. — CLOSED records outcomes in a sliding window; when ≥ minimumNumberOfCalls and failure (or slow-call) rate ≥ threshold → OPEN, calls are rejected for waitDurationInOpenState; then HALF_OPEN lets N probes through; below threshold → CLOSED, else → OPEN.
  • Our breaker never opens even though the service is down. Why? — Usually: not enough calls to reach minimumNumberOfCalls; the exception is swallowed inside the method; the exception type is in ignoreExceptions; the annotated method is self-invoked so the aspect never runs; or the failure is a timeout longer than the caller's own timeout so it is counted elsewhere.
  • Why add jitter to retry backoff? — Without it every client that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment and re-creates the spike (thundering herd); randomised waits spread the load.
  • Semaphore vs thread-pool bulkhead? — Semaphore caps concurrent calls on the caller thread (cheap, works with blocking clients); thread-pool isolates into its own threads and queue and pairs with a TimeLimiter, at the cost of context switches and losing the caller's thread-locals (security context, MDC).
  • In which order do @Retry, @CircuitBreaker, @RateLimiter, @TimeLimiter, @Bulkhead apply? — Default outer to inner: Retry → CircuitBreaker → RateLimiter → TimeLimiter → Bulkhead → method; each configurable with *AspectOrder.
  • What should a fallback do? — Return a degraded but safe result from local data (cache, default, feature off) or fail fast with a typed error; never make another network call that can also hang.
  • How do you see breaker state in production? — /actuator/health (with registerHealthIndicator; OPEN reports DOWN unless you map it to a custom status), /actuator/circuitbreakers and /actuator/circuitbreakerevents, and Micrometer metrics resilience4j.circuitbreaker.*.
  • Hystrix vs Resilience4j? — Hystrix is in maintenance since 2018 and thread-pool based; Resilience4j is lightweight, functional, semaphore-first, Java 17/Boot 3 ready via resilience4j-spring-boot3, and integrates with Spring Cloud CircuitBreaker abstraction.

Timeouts everywhere: connect / read / pool for RestClient, WebClient, JDBC, Kafka — and retry budgets

Why interviewers ask: the classic outage postmortem: one slow dependency, no read timeout, every Tomcat thread stuck, health check fails, the whole tier restarts. They want you to enumerate the timeouts and their defaults, not just say "add timeouts".

Three timeouts exist on every client: connect (TCP handshake; short, 1–2 s), read/response (time waiting for bytes; bounded by your SLA, e.g. 2–5 s), and pool acquisition (waiting for a free connection; must be short so a slow pool fails fast). A missing read timeout is the killer: RestTemplate/RestClient with the JDK HttpURLConnection factory defaults to infinite, HikariCP's connectionTimeout defaults to 30 s, JDBC statements default to no queryTimeout, Kafka's producer waits delivery.timeout.ms = 120 s before giving up and max.block.ms = 60 s just to get metadata/buffer space. Analogy: a restaurant where waiters wait indefinitely at a slow kitchen window: soon every waiter is standing there and no table is served.

Timeouts must nest: caller timeout > callee timeout, and the sum of retries × per-try timeout must fit inside the caller's budget, or the caller gives up while you are still retrying. A retry storm is 3 services each retrying 3 times = 27× load on the leaf when it is already struggling; the cure is retries only at one layer, exponential backoff with jitter, a retry budget (retries ≤ 10 % of requests, as Envoy/Finagle do), and a circuit breaker so retries stop entirely once the dependency is declared down.

@Bean
RestClient pricingClient(RestClient.Builder builder) {
    var settings = ClientHttpRequestFactorySettings.DEFAULTS
        .withConnectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
        .withReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3));            // never leave this unbounded
    return builder.baseUrl("http://pricing")
        .requestFactory(ClientHttpRequestFactories.get(settings))
        .build();
}

@Bean
WebClient inventoryClient(WebClient.Builder b) {
    var http = HttpClient.create()
        .option(ChannelOption.CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS, 1_000)
        .responseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
        .doOnConnected(c -> c.addHandlerLast(new ReadTimeoutHandler(3)));
    return b.clientConnector(new ReactorClientHttpConnector(http)).build();
}
spring:
  datasource.hikari:
    connection-timeout: 3000        # ms to wait for a pooled connection (default 30000)
    validation-timeout: 1000
    max-lifetime: 1800000
  jpa.properties.jakarta.persistence.query.timeout: 5000   # ms, per JPA query
  kafka:
    producer.properties:
      delivery.timeout.ms: 30000    # total time incl. retries (default 120000)
      request.timeout.ms: 10000
      max.block.ms: 5000            # send() blocking on metadata/buffer (default 60000)
    consumer.properties:
      default.api.timeout.ms: 30000
server.tomcat.connection-timeout: 20s   # idle client connections
LayerSettingDefaultSane starting point
RestClient / RestTemplate (JDK factory)connect / readnone / none1 s / 2–5 s
WebClient (Reactor Netty)CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS, responseTimeout30 s / none1 s / 3 s
HikariCPconnectionTimeout30 s2–5 s (fail fast, size the pool right)
JDBC / JPAqueryTimeout / jakarta.persistence.query.timeoutnonePer query class; plus DB-side statement_timeout
Kafka producerdelivery.timeout.ms, max.block.ms120 s / 60 s≤ request SLA if send is on the request path; else default
@Transactionaltimeout-1 (none)Bound long transactions to protect the pool

Pitfalls

  • @Transactional(timeout=5) applies to statements via the JDBC driver; time spent in an HTTP call inside the transaction is not interrupted.
  • Apache HttpClient's connectionRequestTimeout (pool wait) is separate from connect timeout; leaving it default on a pool of 20 is another infinite wait.
  • A timeout does not cancel the remote work: the callee still runs the query. Combine with idempotency so the retry is safe.
  • Setting the Kafka producer max.block.ms low on a request thread is right, but then handle the TimeoutException — do not let it bubble as a 500 for something that could be queued.
Interview questions
  • Walk me through how one slow downstream took down the service. — No read timeout → each request thread blocks → Tomcat's 200 threads exhaust → new requests queue in the acceptor → liveness probe times out → pod restarts → traffic shifts to the other pods, which now also exhaust. Fix: timeouts, bulkhead per dependency, breaker, and a health check that does not depend on the downstream.
  • How do you choose a timeout value? — From the dependency's p99 plus margin, inside the caller's budget: if my SLA is 1 s and I call two things sequentially, each gets ~400 ms including retries.
  • Where should retries live in a 4-hop call chain? — At one layer, usually the edge or the layer closest to the flaky dependency, with a budget; nested retries multiply load.
  • What is a retry budget? — A cap on retries as a ratio of live requests (e.g. 10 %) so retries cannot exceed a fraction of normal traffic during an incident.
  • What does Hikari's connectionTimeout 30 s cost you? — Under pool exhaustion each request waits 30 s and then fails; with 2 s it fails fast and the thread returns, and the metric tells you to size the pool or fix slow queries.
  • Boot 2 vs 3 client config? — Boot 3.1+ gives RestClient and ClientHttpRequestFactorySettings for timeouts; Boot 3.4 added spring.http.client.connect-timeout/read-timeout properties for the auto-configured builder.

Backpressure & load shedding: bounded queues, rejection policies, the CallerRunsPolicy trap, graceful shutdown

Why interviewers ask: "what happens to the 201st task when the pool is full?" and "how does a pod stop without losing in-flight messages?" are the questions that decide whether your async design survives a deploy under load.

Boot's default ThreadPoolTaskExecutor (applicationTaskExecutor, used by @Async) has core=8, max=Integer.MAX_VALUE, queue-capacity=Integer.MAX_VALUE: an unbounded queue, so under load it silently grows until OOM, and because the queue never fills, the pool never grows past core either. Set spring.task.execution.pool.queue-capacity (e.g. 200) and max-size; then a full queue triggers the RejectedExecutionHandler: AbortPolicy (default, throws TaskRejectedException — fail fast, the honest load-shedding answer), DiscardPolicy/DiscardOldestPolicy (silent loss), CallerRunsPolicy (the submitting thread runs the task itself). Analogy: a full waiting room; you either turn people away at the door (abort), or the receptionist starts treating patients (caller runs) and nobody is left at the desk.

The CallerRunsPolicy trap: it looks like backpressure, but the caller is a Tomcat request thread or a Kafka consumer thread; running the task there stalls request handling (or stops poll() → rebalance), and the "backpressure" propagates into the wrong place. Prefer bounded queue + abort + 429/503 upstream, or a real backpressure protocol (Reactive Streams request(n), Kafka consumer pause()/resume(), RabbitMQ prefetch). Graceful shutdown: server.shutdown=graceful stops accepting new requests and waits up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase (default 30 s) for in-flight ones; the same phase machinery (SmartLifecycle phases) stops the Kafka listener containers, which finish the current batch, commit, and leave the group (so a rebalance happens once, cleanly, and no records are replayed). Executors created via TaskExecutorBuilder get waitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown and awaitTerminationSeconds from spring.task.execution.shutdown.*. Kubernetes must give the pod at least that long (terminationGracePeriodSeconds > phase timeout) and a preStop sleep lets the endpoint be removed from the Service before SIGTERM.

spring:
  task:
    execution:
      pool: { core-size: 8, max-size: 32, queue-capacity: 200 }     # bounded!
      shutdown: { await-termination: true, await-termination-period: 20s }
    scheduling.pool.size: 4
  lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 25s
  kafka.listener.immediate-stop: false        # finish the current batch before stopping
server.shutdown: graceful
# k8s: terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 40, preStop: sleep 5
@Bean("ioExecutor")
ThreadPoolTaskExecutor ioExecutor() {
    var ex = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
    ex.setCorePoolSize(16); ex.setMaxPoolSize(64); ex.setQueueCapacity(500);
    ex.setRejectedExecutionHandler(new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());   // shed, don't CallerRuns
    ex.setThreadNamePrefix("io-"); ex.setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true);
    ex.setAwaitTerminationSeconds(20);
    ex.setTaskDecorator(r -> { var ctx = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap(); return () -> { MDC.setContextMap(ctx); r.run(); }; });
    return ex;
}

@RestControllerAdvice class Shed {
    @ExceptionHandler(TaskRejectedException.class)
    ResponseEntity<Void> full() { return ResponseEntity.status(503).header("Retry-After", "2").build(); }
}
PolicyWhen queue is fullEffect under overloadVerdict
AbortPolicyThrowsFast 503, threads stay freeDefault choice with a handler
CallerRunsPolicyCaller executesRequest/consumer thread blocked; hides overload; may trigger Kafka rebalanceOnly for batch jobs with an idle caller
DiscardPolicyDrops silentlyData loss with no signalNever for business work
DiscardOldestPolicyDrops the headLoses the oldest waiting taskOnly for superseded values (latest-wins)

Pitfalls

  • Because the pool grows only when the queue is full, an unbounded queue means max-size is decorative; people "add threads" and see no change.
  • Graceful shutdown waits for requests, but a request blocked on a missing timeout waits the full phase and is then killed anyway; timeouts and graceful shutdown are one design.
  • A @PreDestroy that closes the DataSource can run before the executor has drained if bean dependencies are not declared (@DependsOn or SmartLifecycle phases fix ordering).
  • Virtual threads (Boot 3.2 spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true) remove the pool but not the need for limits: use a Semaphore or bulkhead to bound concurrency to downstreams.
Interview questions
  • Why is CallerRunsPolicy dangerous in a web app? — The Tomcat thread that submitted the task now runs it, so it stops serving; under load every request thread becomes a worker, latency explodes and the overload is invisible in queue metrics.
  • What does server.shutdown=graceful do exactly? — On SIGTERM the connector stops accepting connections, in-flight requests get up to timeout-per-shutdown-phase to finish, then the context closes; requests arriving during the window get a connection refused, so a preStop delay for endpoint removal matters.
  • How does a Kafka listener stop gracefully? — The container is a SmartLifecycle; on stop it finishes the current poll's records (unless immediate-stop), commits offsets, closes the consumer which sends LeaveGroup, so partitions move without replay.
  • How would you implement backpressure from a Kafka consumer to a slow DB? — Bounded in-process buffer; when full, container.pause() (poll keeps running so no rebalance) and resume() when drained; or simply process synchronously with smaller max.poll.records.
  • How do you shed load at the edge? — Bounded executor + 503 with Retry-After, rate limiter per client, concurrency limit (bulkhead) per endpoint, and priority for health checks so the pod is not killed while shedding.
  • Boot 2 vs 3 here? — Graceful shutdown arrived in 2.3; Boot 3.2 added virtual threads for Tomcat, @Async and Kafka listeners; Boot 3.x uses SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor with virtual threads when enabled, so queue settings no longer apply.

Event-driven design questions: choreography vs orchestration, sagas, idempotency keys, schema evolution

Why interviewers ask: after the Kafka mechanics, the system-design layer: how services coordinate without a distributed transaction, and how you change an event's shape without breaking 12 consumers.

Choreography: each service reacts to events and emits its own (Order placed → Payment charged → Inventory reserved); no central brain, loose coupling, but the flow is implicit and compensations are scattered. Orchestration: a coordinator (a saga orchestrator, Temporal, Camunda, a state machine in the order service) tells each participant what to do and tracks state; explicit, debuggable, but a central dependency. A saga is the sequence of local transactions with compensating actions (refund, release stock) replacing the ACID rollback you no longer have; the design trade-offs are covered in the System Design guide.

Because delivery is at-least-once, every consumer needs an idempotency key (event id, or business key + version) stored with the effect; for commands over HTTP the client sends Idempotency-Key and the server stores the response. Versioning: an event envelope (id, type, version, occurredAt, producer, traceId, payload) plus a schema registry (Confluent/Apicurio with Avro/Protobuf/JSON Schema) enforcing compatibility: BACKWARD (new schema reads old data: you may delete fields or add optional ones — consumers upgrade first), FORWARD (old readers can read new data — producers upgrade first), FULL. Breaking changes go to a new topic (orders.v2) with a migration period, never in place.

ChoreographyOrchestration
CouplingLow (events only)Participants depend on the orchestrator's commands
Visibility of the flowEmergent; needs tracing to seeExplicit state machine, easy to query "where is order 42"
Adding a stepNew subscriber, no change to othersChange the orchestrator
CompensationEach service listens for failure eventsOrchestrator issues compensations in reverse
Fits2–4 steps, independent teamsLong flows, strict ordering, SLAs, audits
Interview questions
  • Order → payment → inventory across three services: how do you keep them consistent? — Saga: local transactions plus compensations, events published through an outbox, idempotent consumers, and an orchestrator if the flow needs visibility and timeouts.
  • How do you make a payment consumer safe against redelivery? — Store the event id (or an idempotency key) in the same transaction as the ledger write with a unique constraint; on conflict, treat as already processed and ack.
  • How do you add a required field to an event? — You do not; add it optional with a default (backward compatible), or publish v2 to a new topic and run both until consumers migrate.
  • What belongs in an event envelope? — Event id, type and version, timestamp, producer, correlation/trace id, aggregate id, and the payload; keys and headers carry the routing and tracing parts.
  • Event notification vs event-carried state transfer? — Notification: "order 42 changed", consumer calls back for details (small, coupled to the API). State transfer: the event carries the data (decoupled, larger, consumers keep local copies).
  • Why not a distributed transaction (2PC/XA) across services? — Locks held across network calls, coordinator as a single point of failure, no Kafka/HTTP participants; sagas trade atomicity for availability and explicit compensation.

Observability for messaging: Micrometer observations, trace propagation through Kafka, consumer lag

Why interviewers ask: "how do you trace a request that becomes an event and is consumed 3 seconds later on another pod?" — the answer is headers, and Boot 3 does most of it if you turn it on.

Boot 3 replaced Spring Cloud Sleuth with Micrometer Tracing and the Observation API. Spring Kafka can observe both sides: KafkaTemplate.setObservationEnabled(true) (spring.kafka.template.observation-enabled) creates a producer span and injects W3C traceparent (or B3) headers into the record; ContainerProperties.setObservationEnabled(true) (spring.kafka.listener.observation-enabled) extracts them so the listener span is a child of the original request. The same goes for RabbitMQ (spring.rabbitmq.template/listener.observation-enabled) and @Scheduled (@Observed or a manual observation). Logs get traceId/spanId in MDC automatically; for a manual @Async hop you need a TaskDecorator that propagates context (ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator with context-propagation on the classpath).

Metrics that matter: consumer lag per partition (kafka.consumer.fetch.manager.records.lag.max via Micrometer's Kafka binder, or Burrow/kafka-exporter), spring.kafka.listener timer (duration, exception tags), producer record-error-rate and request-latency-avg, DLT topic size, Resilience4j breaker state, executor queue depth (executor.queued), and the scheduler's last-success timestamp per job.

spring:
  kafka:
    template.observation-enabled: true
    listener.observation-enabled: true
management:
  tracing:
    sampling.probability: 0.1
    propagation.type: w3c          # traceparent header; add b3 for legacy peers
  metrics.tags.application: ${spring.application.name}
logging.pattern.level: "%5p [${spring.application.name},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}]"
Interview questions
  • How does the trace id get from the HTTP request to the Kafka consumer? — The producer observation writes traceparent into record headers; the listener observation reads it and starts a child span, so Zipkin/Tempo shows request → send → consume as one trace.
  • Which metric tells you the consumer is falling behind? — Consumer lag (latest offset minus committed offset) per partition; alert on lag growth rate, not just absolute lag.
  • Logs from the listener have no trace id. Why? — Listener observation not enabled, or the producer did not inject headers (older client), or work was handed to a thread pool without context propagation.
  • Sleuth vs Micrometer Tracing? — Sleuth is Boot 2 only; Boot 3 uses Micrometer Tracing bridges (Brave or OpenTelemetry) with the Observation API so metrics and traces come from the same instrumentation.
  • What would you put on the messaging dashboard? — Lag per group/partition, listener duration p99 and error rate, DLT throughput, rebalance count, producer errors and batch size, breaker states, executor queue depth.

A topic has 4 partitions. You run 2 pods, each with a @KafkaListener whose factory has concurrency=4. How many consumer threads actively process records?

A partition is owned by exactly one consumer in a group. 8 consumers join, only 4 get a partition. Option (a) is wrong because partitions are never shared inside a group; that is what a second group would do.

A listener uses the default ack mode and processes a batch of 200 records at 2 s each. After ~5 minutes the logs show a rebalance and downstream reports duplicates. Root cause?

Heartbeats run on their own thread, so (a) is not it; the poll-interval check is the one a slow handler violates. Offsets are committed after the batch in BATCH mode, so the new owner starts from the old committed offset and re-processes. (d) only applies when there is no committed offset at all.

Which statement about enable.idempotence=true on the producer is correct?

Idempotence works with a producer id + sequence numbers per partition; the broker drops a retried batch it already has. It knows nothing about your application calling send() twice (c) and nothing about consumers (b). Transactions imply idempotence, not the reverse (d).

With DefaultErrorHandler and no custom recoverer, a record throws a NullPointerException on every attempt. What is the eventual outcome with default settings?

The default BackOff is 9 retries with no delay and the default recoverer only logs. A DLT (a) requires configuring DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer. (b) describes a deserialization failure without ErrorHandlingDeserializer, which happens inside poll().

You add @RetryableTopic to a listener on a topic keyed by account id where events must apply in order. What is the main risk?

Non-blocking retry means the main partition keeps going; that is its purpose and its cost. Blocking retry via DefaultErrorHandler (option a describes it) is what preserves order.

A service method annotated with a JPA @Transactional saves an order and then calls kafkaTemplate.send(...). A later statement in the same method throws and the transaction rolls back. What can downstream consumers observe?

KafkaTemplate is not a resource of JpaTransactionManager; the send is buffered and flushed independently. Only a Kafka transaction (or @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT), or the outbox) prevents the phantom event. Fencing (d) is about duplicate transactional producers.

Circuit breaker config: slidingWindowSize=10, minimumNumberOfCalls=10, failureRateThreshold=50. The dependency is completely down but the endpoint gets 4 calls per minute. When does the breaker open?

The failure rate is not evaluated until minimumNumberOfCalls outcomes exist, regardless of how bad the rate looks earlier. For low-traffic endpoints lower that number or use a TIME_BASED window. (c) forgets the minimum-calls gate.

With Resilience4j Spring Boot defaults, a method has @Retry(maxAttempts=3) and @CircuitBreaker. The breaker is OPEN. What happens on a call?

Default aspect order is Retry → CircuitBreaker → RateLimiter → TimeLimiter → Bulkhead → method. Rejections are cheap but pointless; either ignore CallNotPermittedException in the retry config or reorder the aspects. (b) is the reverse order, which you can configure but is not the default.

A ThreadPoolTaskExecutor is configured with core 8, max 64 and the default queue capacity. Under load, what do you observe?

ThreadPoolExecutor adds threads beyond core only when offer() to the queue fails; an Integer.MAX_VALUE queue never refuses, so max is never reached. Bound the queue to make max-size and the rejection policy meaningful.

A @Scheduled(cron="0 */5 * * * *") job silently stops firing after a deploy that added a second @Scheduled method which runs for 40 minutes. Best fix?

Both jobs share the single scheduler thread; cron ticks that occur while it is busy are skipped. ShedLock (d) solves the multi-instance problem, not thread starvation.

Practice

Scenario: the consumer group rebalances every ~5 minutes and throughput is near zero

Group enrichment (3 pods, concurrency=2, topic with 6 partitions) shows in logs: Member … sending LeaveGroup request due to consumer poll timeout has expired, then Attempt to heartbeat failed since group is rebalancing, every 5 minutes on every pod. Lag climbs. The handler calls an external API (p99 = 4 s) per record and uses the defaults below. Explain the loop and propose the fix set, in priority order.

spring.kafka.consumer:
  max-poll-records: 500            # default
  properties:
    max.poll.interval.ms: 300000   # default 5 min
spring.kafka.listener.ack-mode: batch   # default
Tests: poll loop, rebalance mechanics, replay, sizing
Hint 1
500 records × up to 4 s. How long can a single poll's batch take? What is the coordinator's deadline?
Hint 2
When the member is evicted, which offset does the new owner start from, and how long will it take to get through the same records?
Reveal solution

The loop. Each poll returns up to 500 records; at 1–4 s each the batch takes far more than 300 s. The consumer never calls poll() in time, so the coordinator evicts it (the log line is literally the poll timeout). Its partitions move to a peer, which starts from the last committed offset (nothing was committed in BATCH mode) and hits the same wall five minutes later. Meanwhile the evicted consumer rejoins, triggers another rebalance, and the group spends its life re-processing the same few hundred records: near-zero progress plus duplicate API calls.

Fix set, in order.

  1. Make the poll fit the deadline: max.poll.records=20 (20 × 4 s = 80 s < 300 s) and/or max.poll.interval.ms=900000. Compute it from the handler's p99, not by guessing.
  2. Bound the handler: a read timeout on the API client (3–5 s) and a circuit breaker so a slow API cannot stretch record time unboundedly.
  3. Commit more often: ack-mode: record or MANUAL_IMMEDIATE so a future eviction replays one record, not 500.
  4. Idempotency: store the event id with the result; replays after the fix are then harmless.
  5. Reduce rebalance blast radius: partition.assignment.strategy=org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor so a single member's exit does not stop all six consumers; optionally a group.instance.id per pod (static membership) so restarts do not trigger rebalances at all within session.timeout.ms.
  6. Throughput: if the API is the bottleneck, parallelism comes from partitions: 6 partitions cap you at 6 in-flight calls across the group; raise partitions (with the ordering caveat) or batch the API calls.

What not to do: raise session.timeout.ms (irrelevant to poll timing), or hand records to an unbounded thread pool inside the listener and return immediately (offsets commit before the work is done: at-most-once).

Debug: one payment was processed twice right after a deploy — where did the duplicate come from?

The ledger service consumes payments with the listener below. During a rolling deploy at 14:02:10 the old pod was terminated. Records with offsets 8 811 and 8 812 on partition 3 appear twice in the ledger table (two rows each, 6 seconds apart). The producer uses enable.idempotence=true and the event ids are unique. Explain the exact sequence and list what to change (three things).

@KafkaListener(topics = "payments", groupId = "ledger")   // default BATCH ack mode
@Transactional
public void on(List<PaymentEvent> batch) {
    for (var e : batch) ledgerRepo.save(Ledger.from(e));
}
// pod spec: terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 5
// application.yml: server.shutdown: immediate (default)
Tests: at-least-once, offset commit timing, graceful shutdown, idempotent consumer
Hint 1
Order of events on SIGTERM: does the JPA transaction commit before the container commits the offsets? What happens if the JVM is killed between the two?
Hint 2
Which of the three defenses (producer idempotence, unique event id, consumer idempotency check) actually exist in this code?
Reveal solution

Sequence. (1) Old pod polls a batch containing 8 811–8 812. (2) The JPA transaction commits the ledger rows. (3) Before the container can commit the offsets for the batch (BATCH mode commits after the listener returns and the container loops back), SIGTERM arrives; with a 5 s grace period and immediate shutdown the JVM is killed, or the consumer closes without a final commit. (4) The group rebalances; the new pod takes partition 3 from the last committed offset (8 810) and processes 8 811–8 812 again 6 seconds later. Producer idempotence is irrelevant: the duplicate was created on the consumer side by replay after a DB commit without an offset commit. "Unique event ids" mean nothing unless something checks them.

Changes.

  1. Idempotent consumer: a processed_event(event_id PRIMARY KEY) insert in the same transaction as the ledger write (or a unique constraint on ledger.event_id); on a duplicate, skip and ack. This is the only change that removes the class of bug.
  2. Graceful shutdown: server.shutdown=graceful, spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s, terminationGracePeriodSeconds ≥ 40, so the container finishes the batch, commits offsets and leaves the group cleanly. Replay windows shrink from "whole batch" to "crash only".
  3. Tighter commits: MANUAL_IMMEDIATE with per-record acknowledgement, or RECORD mode with a per-record transaction, so at most one record is in the replay window.

Bonus point: @Transactional here is the JPA manager; it does not include the offset commit. Kafka transactions would not help either, since the effect is in Postgres. The senior phrasing is "at-least-once delivery is a given; exactly-once effect is the consumer's job".

Debug: the circuit breaker never opens while the pricing service is down

During an incident the pricing service returned 503 for 20 minutes. Latency on /checkout went to 6 s, but /actuator/circuitbreakers showed pricing: CLOSED the whole time and the fallback never ran. Find every reason in the code and config below.

@Service
public class CheckoutService {
    private final PricingClient pricing;   // this class, not a separate bean
    …
    public Quote quote(Cart c) { return this.priced(c); }          // (A)

    @CircuitBreaker(name = "pricing", fallbackMethod = "fallback")
    public Quote priced(Cart c) {
        try {
            return rest.get().uri("/price").retrieve().body(Quote.class);   // (B) RestClient, JDK factory
        } catch (RestClientException ex) {
            log.warn("pricing failed", ex);
            return Quote.EMPTY;                                           // (C)
        }
    }
    private Quote fallback(Cart c, Throwable t) { return cache.lastQuote(c); }
}
resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.pricing:
  slidingWindowSize: 100
  minimumNumberOfCalls: 100
  failureRateThreshold: 50
  ignoreExceptions: [org.springframework.web.client.RestClientException]   # (D)
Tests: proxy self-invocation, exception handling vs breaker, thresholds, timeouts
Hint 1
Which object does this.priced(c) go through? Which object carries the Resilience4j aspect?
Hint 2
Even if the aspect ran: does the method ever throw? Would the exception count?
Reveal solution
  1. (A) Self-invocation. quote() calls this.priced(), bypassing the proxy; the @CircuitBreaker aspect never runs. Fix: move priced into its own bean (PricingClient) or inject a self-reference (ObjectProvider<CheckoutService>). Same rule as @Transactional/@Async.
  2. (C) Swallowed exception. Catching and returning Quote.EMPTY makes every call a success in the breaker's window. Either let the exception propagate (the fallback handles it) or record it explicitly with recordExceptions/a recordResultPredicate that treats Quote.EMPTY as a failure.
  3. (D) Ignored exception. RestClientException is the supertype of HttpServerErrorException; ignoring it means 503s are neither successes nor failures. Ignore only the client-side (4xx) subtypes, e.g. HttpClientErrorException.
  4. (B) No read timeout. The 6 s latency is the downstream's; with the JDK factory and no timeout, a hang would be unbounded. Add a 2 s read timeout so a slow call is recorded as a failure (or as a slow call via slowCallDurationThreshold=1s, slowCallRateThreshold=80).
  5. Thresholds. minimumNumberOfCalls=100 means the first 99 failures cannot trip anything; for a checkout endpoint use e.g. window 20 / minimum 10, or a TIME_BASED window of 30 s.

Verification: after the fixes, /actuator/circuitbreakerevents/pricing should show ERROR events followed by a STATE_TRANSITION CLOSED→OPEN, and the health endpoint should reflect it if registerHealthIndicator=true.

Scenario: the nightly report ran on all 3 pods, and the 5-minute cleanup never runs anymore

Two symptoms after scaling from 1 to 3 replicas and adding a new job:

@Component
public class Jobs {
    @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 1 * * *")
    public void nightlyReport() { … 45 minutes, emails the CFO … }   // sent 3 emails last night

    @Scheduled(fixedRate = 300_000)
    public void cleanupTemp() { … }                                   // no longer logs anything at 01:00–01:45,
                                                                      // and now runs 9 times in a row at 01:45
}

Explain both symptoms and give a configuration that fixes them without a full scheduler product.

Tests: scheduler thread pool, fixedRate backlog, distributed lock semantics
Hint 1
How many threads does Boot's default TaskScheduler have? What does fixedRate do with the ticks it missed?
Hint 2
Each pod has its own scheduler and its own clock at 01:00. What must be shared between pods to make one run?
Reveal solution

Three emails: each replica has its own ThreadPoolTaskScheduler and fires the cron independently; there is no cluster awareness in @Scheduled. Cleanup silent, then bursts: the scheduler pool defaults to one thread; while nightlyReport occupies it for 45 minutes, cleanupTemp cannot run. fixedRate schedules from the previous planned start, so the 9 missed ticks are executed back-to-back once the thread frees up (with fixedDelay there would be a single run; with cron the ticks would be skipped).

@Configuration
@EnableScheduling
@EnableSchedulerLock(defaultLockAtMostFor = "PT2H")
class SchedulingConfig {
    @Bean LockProvider lockProvider(DataSource ds) {
        return new JdbcTemplateLockProvider(JdbcTemplateLockProvider.Configuration.builder()
            .withJdbcTemplate(new JdbcTemplate(ds)).usingDbTime().build());   // broker-free, uses DB clock
    }
}

@Component
public class Jobs {
    @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 1 * * *", zone = "UTC")
    @SchedulerLock(name = "nightlyReport", lockAtLeastFor = "PT5M", lockAtMostFor = "PT2H")
    public void nightlyReport() { … }

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 300_000)          // no catch-up burst
    @SchedulerLock(name = "cleanupTemp", lockAtMostFor = "PT4M")
    public void cleanupTemp() { … }
}
// application.yml
// spring.task.scheduling.pool-size: 4
  • pool-size: 4 gives each job its own thread; the long job no longer starves the short one.
  • ShedLock takes a row lock in a shedlock table before running; the other two pods see the lock and skip. lockAtLeastFor covers clock skew between pods (a fast pod finishing in 10 s must not let a slow pod's 01:00 tick run it again); lockAtMostFor releases the lock if the holder dies, so size it above the worst-case runtime.
  • Switching cleanup to fixedDelay removes the backlog behaviour entirely; if you keep fixedRate, the extra thread already prevents the queueing.
  • Alternatives without a library: SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on a job_run row, or Postgres pg_try_advisory_lock(hash); Quartz with JDBC job store if you also need "must run eventually even if all pods were down at 01:00".

⚡ Rapid-fire: messaging, async & resilience

  • What decides which partition a record goes to? — Hash of the key modulo partitions; null key → sticky partitioner per batch.
  • Ordering guarantee in Kafka? — Per partition only.
  • Max useful consumers in a group? — Number of partitions.
  • concurrency in the listener factory means? — Number of KafkaConsumer threads per JVM in that group.
  • acks=all + ? — min.insync.replicas=2 on the broker for real durability.
  • What does the idempotent producer dedupe? — Its own retries per partition per session.
  • Default Spring ack mode? — BATCH: commit after the poll's records are processed.
  • Consumer killed for not polling: which setting? — max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 min), not the heartbeat.
  • At-least-once vs at-most-once in one line? — Commit after processing vs commit before.
  • Exactly-once scope? — Kafka-to-Kafka with transactions and read_committed; never DB or HTTP.
  • How do you make a consumer idempotent? — Store the event id with the effect in the same transaction, unique constraint, skip on conflict.
  • Default error handler and its default? — DefaultErrorHandler, 10 attempts no back-off, then log and skip.
  • Poison pill fix? — ErrorHandlingDeserializer wrapping the real deserializer + DLT recoverer.
  • Blocking vs non-blocking retry? — DefaultErrorHandler seeks back (keeps order, stalls partition) vs @RetryableTopic (retry topics, loses per-key order).
  • auto.offset.reset applies when? — Only when the group has no committed offset.
  • Rebalance that does not stop everyone? — CooperativeStickyAssignor; static membership via group.instance.id avoids it on restarts.
  • Kafka vs RabbitMQ in one line? — Replayable partitioned log with consumer-held offsets vs routed queues with broker-held acks and delete-on-ack.
  • RabbitMQ message that always throws? — Requeued forever by default; throw AmqpRejectAndDontRequeueException or set default-requeue-rejected=false with a DLX.
  • Is DB write + Kafka send in one @Transactional atomic? — No; use the outbox pattern.
  • Why is ChainedKafkaTransactionManager deprecated? — It only sequenced commits; not atomic.
  • Setting transaction-id-prefix side effect? — Every send must be inside a transaction or it throws.
  • Default scheduler threads? — One; set spring.task.scheduling.pool-size.
  • fixedRate vs fixedDelay? — From previous start (backlog catches up) vs from previous end.
  • Spring cron fields? — Six, seconds first.
  • Job runs on every pod: fix? — ShedLock / DB lock / leader election / clustered Quartz.
  • Circuit breaker states? — CLOSED → OPEN (rate ≥ threshold after min calls) → HALF_OPEN (probes) → CLOSED or OPEN.
  • Why doesn't it open on the first failures? — minimumNumberOfCalls not reached.
  • Default Resilience4j aspect order? — Retry → CircuitBreaker → RateLimiter → TimeLimiter → Bulkhead.
  • Fallback signature rule? — Same params plus a trailing Throwable, same return type, same class, most specific exception wins.
  • Why jitter on retries? — Prevents synchronized retry storms.
  • Semaphore vs thread-pool bulkhead? — Caller-thread concurrency cap vs isolated pool (needs futures, loses thread-locals).
  • The one timeout people forget? — Read/response timeout (JDK client default is unbounded); also Hikari connectionTimeout 30 s.
  • Default executor queue capacity? — Unbounded; pool never grows past core, memory grows instead.
  • CallerRunsPolicy in a web app? — Blocks request threads; hidden overload. Prefer abort + 503.
  • Graceful shutdown properties? — server.shutdown=graceful, spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase; k8s grace period must exceed it.
  • Trace id through Kafka? — traceparent header injected by template observation, extracted by listener observation.
  • Metric that says the consumer is behind? — Consumer lag per partition.
  • Schema change rule? — Additive with defaults (backward compatible); breaking → new topic version.

8️⃣ Microservices, Observability & Interview Scenarios

This is where the interview stops being about one JVM and becomes about a fleet: how services find each other, share configuration, trace a request across hops and survive a rolling deploy. The path: the Spring Cloud landscape today → discovery and load balancing → gateway → externalized config → inter-service calls → tracing and metrics → logging → Kubernetes probes → containers → secrets and 12-factor → data patterns → production troubleshooting — ending with a bank of design/debug scenarios and a whole-guide rapid-fire.

Spring Cloud in the Boot 3 era: what is alive, what is dead

Why interviewers ask: half the tutorials online still teach Hystrix and Zuul. Naming a dead project as your resilience plan is an instant seniority downgrade; knowing the replacements (and the Kubernetes-native alternatives) is the fastest credibility win in a microservices round.

Still first-class (release train 2023.x/2024.x for Boot 3.x): Spring Cloud Config (central config server), Spring Cloud Gateway (reactive edge router), OpenFeign (declarative HTTP clients), Spring Cloud LoadBalancer (client-side LB, replaced Ribbon), the Circuit Breaker abstraction (facade whose main implementation is Resilience4j — see section 7), and Spring Cloud Stream (binder abstraction over Kafka/Rabbit, section 7).

Dead or maintenance-only: Hystrix → Resilience4j; Ribbon → Spring Cloud LoadBalancer; Zuul 1 → Spring Cloud Gateway; Sleuth → Micrometer Tracing (Sleuth does not support Boot 3 at all); Eureka is the one Netflix survivor still maintained. Analogy: the Netflix OSS stack is a classic car — historically important, parts still on the road, but you would not buy one for a new commute.

On Kubernetes much of the stack becomes optional: Service + DNS replaces Eureka, ConfigMaps/Secrets replace Config Server, Ingress/Gateway API can replace Spring Cloud Gateway at the edge, and a service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) can move retries, mTLS and traffic-splitting out of the application entirely. The senior answer is "the platform provides discovery and config; I keep business-aware concerns — auth, per-client rate limits, circuit breakers — in the app or gateway".

ConcernNetflix eraBoot 3 eraKubernetes-native
DiscoveryEurekaEureka (still fine)Service + DNS
Client LBRibbonSpring Cloud LoadBalancerkube-proxy / mesh
Circuit breakingHystrixResilience4j via CB abstractionmesh outlier detection
Edge routingZuul 1Spring Cloud GatewayIngress / Gateway API
TracingSleuth + ZipkinMicrometer Tracing + OTLPsame (app-level)
ConfigConfig Server (Archaius)Config Server / VaultConfigMap / Secret
Interview angle: "You're migrating a Boot 2 Netflix-stack system to Boot 3 — what breaks?" Sleuth must be swapped for Micrometer Tracing (different packages, same B3/W3C wire formats), Hystrix/Ribbon dependencies simply have no Boot 3 artifacts, and every javax.* import becomes jakarta.*.

Pitfalls

  • Adding spring-cloud-starter-sleuth to a Boot 3 app: it fails fast at startup — the replacement is micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave (or -otel) plus an exporter.
  • Version drift: Spring Cloud has its own release train BOM (spring-cloud-dependencies); pairing the wrong train with your Boot version causes cryptic NoSuchMethodErrors at startup.
  • Running Eureka inside Kubernetes: two discovery systems disagree during rollouts; pick one source of truth.
Interview questions
  • What replaced Hystrix, Ribbon, Zuul and Sleuth? — Resilience4j (behind the Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker facade), Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, Spring Cloud Gateway, and Micrometer Tracing respectively.
  • Do you still need Spring Cloud on Kubernetes? — Not for discovery/config (DNS + ConfigMaps cover it), but Gateway, OpenFeign, Resilience4j and Stream still add value because they are business-logic-aware, which the platform is not.
  • Why did Zuul 1 lose to Spring Cloud Gateway? — Zuul 1 is servlet-based, thread-per-request; Gateway is built on WebFlux/Netty so a few event-loop threads proxy thousands of concurrent connections.
  • What is the Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker abstraction for? — A CircuitBreakerFactory facade so code doesn't bind to Resilience4j APIs directly; you can swap implementations (e.g. Sentinel) via dependencies alone.
  • How do you keep Boot and Spring Cloud versions compatible? — Import the spring-cloud-dependencies BOM for the release train matched to the Boot line (the project publishes a compatibility table) and let it manage all cloud artifact versions.
  • Boot 2 vs 3 here? — Boot 3 requires the 2022.0+ ("Kilburn") trains: Sleuth is gone, Netflix modules except Eureka are gone, and tracing/metrics unify under Micrometer.

Service discovery & client-side load balancing

Why interviewers ask: "how does service A find service B?" is the canonical microservices opener, and the follow-up — "what happens when an instance dies?" — separates people who have run this in production from people who read a blog.

Two models. Registry-based (Eureka): each instance registers itself and heartbeats every 30s; clients fetch the registry, cache it, and pick an instance themselves (client-side load balancing). Failure detection is eventual — a dead instance lingers until heartbeats lapse (up to ~90s with default eviction, worse with self-preservation mode). Platform-based (Kubernetes): a Service gives a stable DNS name; the endpoints list is maintained by the kubelet's readiness probes, and kube-proxy or the client library spreads load. Analogy: Eureka is a phone book everyone photocopies every 30 seconds; Kubernetes DNS is a receptionist who always knows who is at their desk right now.

In Spring, annotating a builder with @LoadBalanced decorates the client so URLs like http://order-service/api/orders resolve the hostname through DiscoveryClient + Spring Cloud LoadBalancer (round-robin by default) instead of DNS. Health-aware routing comes from combining the registry's status with per-instance stats; on Kubernetes you instead rely on readiness gating (probes card).

@Configuration
class ClientConfig {
    @Bean @LoadBalanced   // resolves http://order-service/ via the registry
    RestClient.Builder loadBalancedRestClientBuilder() { return RestClient.builder(); }
}

@Service
class CartService {
    private final RestClient rest;
    CartService(RestClient.Builder lb) { this.rest = lb.build(); }

    OrderSummary summary(String id) {
        return rest.get().uri("http://order-service/api/orders/{id}", id)
                   .retrieve().body(OrderSummary.class);
    }
}

Pitfalls

  • Injecting a plain (non-@LoadBalanced) builder and calling http://order-service/…: UnknownHostException — the name only exists in the registry, not in DNS.
  • Eureka self-preservation mode: when many heartbeats disappear at once (network blip), Eureka stops evicting anything, so clients keep dead instances longer than expected.
  • Long-lived HTTP/2 or keep-alive connections pin you to one pod behind a Kubernetes Service; use a client-side LB or mesh if per-request spreading matters.
Interview questions
  • Client-side vs server-side load balancing? — Client-side: caller holds the instance list and picks (no extra hop, but every client needs the logic and a fresh cache). Server-side: a proxy/VIP picks (simple clients, extra hop, proxy must scale).
  • What happens between an instance dying and traffic healing? — A stale-cache window: registry eviction (heartbeat timeouts) plus client cache refresh; you cover it with retries against other instances and connection timeouts, not by pretending discovery is instant.
  • How does @LoadBalanced actually work? — It is a @Qualifier; an auto-configured customizer adds an interceptor/filter to those builders that resolves the host through LoadBalancerClient before the request goes out.
  • Why is Eureka AP rather than CP? — It prefers availability: peers replicate asynchronously and clients work from cache even if Eureka is unreachable; a slightly stale list beats refusing to route.
  • Do you need Eureka on Kubernetes? — No: a Service gives DNS + readiness-gated endpoints. Keep Eureka only for hybrid (VM + k8s) estates or when you need its metadata/zone features outside the platform.

API Gateway: Spring Cloud Gateway routes, predicates, filters

Why interviewers ask: the gateway is where cross-cutting edge concerns live (auth, rate limiting, routing), and "what belongs in the gateway vs in each service?" is a favorite design probe.

Spring Cloud Gateway is a reactive (WebFlux/Netty) proxy configured as a list of routes. Each route = an id, a destination uri (can be lb://order-service for load-balanced discovery), a set of predicates (match on path, method, header, host, time, weight…) and a chain of filters (rewrite path, add headers, rate-limit, retry, circuit-break, call auth). Analogy: a hotel front desk — one entrance, checks your reservation (predicate), applies house rules (filters), then directs you to the right room (route).

Standard edge duties: authentication — validate the JWT once at the edge (resource-server style, see section 6) and forward identity claims downstream in headers; rate limiting — the built-in RequestRateLimiter filter uses a Redis token bucket (replenishRate, burstCapacity) keyed by a KeyResolver (user id, API key, IP); resilience — per-route timeouts, retries and circuit breakers so one slow backend cannot camp on the edge. Versus Kong/NGINX/Envoy: those are more performant general-purpose proxies, but Spring Cloud Gateway wins when your filters are JVM business logic (custom auth, request enrichment from a Java library, shared code with services).

spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: orders
          uri: lb://order-service            # via discovery + LoadBalancer
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/orders/**
          filters:
            - StripPrefix=1
            - name: RequestRateLimiter          # Redis token bucket
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 10   # tokens/sec steady
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 20   # bucket size
                key-resolver: "#{@userKeyResolver}"
            - name: CircuitBreaker
              args: { name: ordersCb, fallbackUri: forward:/fallback/orders }
Interview angle: "Where do you rate-limit — gateway or service?" Both, differently: coarse per-client fairness at the edge (Redis bucket, cheap rejection with 429 before work is done), plus bulkheads/semaphores inside services to protect specific resources. A limit only inside the service still lets the flood consume gateway threads and network.

Pitfalls

  • Blocking calls (JDBC, RestTemplate) inside a gateway filter freeze Netty event-loop threads — the whole edge stalls at low CPU. Gateway code must stay reactive.
  • RequestRateLimiter without Redis configured silently lets everything through (no limiter bean → not applied); always test the 429 path.
  • Forwarding the raw Authorization header everywhere: downstream services replaying tokens to third parties. Exchange it at the edge for an internal identity header (signed) or use token exchange.
Interview questions
  • Route, predicate, filter — define each. — Route: mapping to a backend URI; predicates: conditions deciding if the route matches a request; filters: request/response transformations and policies applied around the proxying, plus global filters that run for every route.
  • Why is Spring Cloud Gateway reactive? — A proxy is 99% waiting on I/O; event loops let a handful of threads hold tens of thousands of in-flight connections, where thread-per-request Zuul 1 needed a thread each.
  • How does the Redis rate limiter work? — Token bucket per key evaluated by an atomic Lua script in Redis: bucket refills at replenishRate/sec up to burstCapacity; a request that finds no token gets 429. Redis makes the count shared across gateway replicas.
  • Gateway vs Kong/NGINX — when each? — Kong/NGINX/Envoy for raw throughput, TLS termination and polyglot estates; Spring Cloud Gateway when edge logic is Java-shaped and evolves with your services (shared DTOs, custom filters, Spring Security integration).
  • How do you avoid the gateway becoming a single point of failure? — It is stateless: run N replicas behind an L4 balancer; shared state (rate-limit counters, sessions if any) lives in Redis.
  • What would you NOT put in the gateway? — Business logic and orchestration (aggregating N calls with rules): that becomes an accidental monolith. Keep the edge to auth, routing, limiting, observability.

Externalized config: Config Server, Vault, ConfigMaps & @RefreshScope

Why interviewers ask: "change a config value without redeploying 40 services" is a real ops task, and @RefreshScope is a beautiful trap: most candidates cannot explain how a running singleton's field can change.

Spring Cloud Config Server serves properties from a Git repo (or Vault) over HTTP: /{app}/{profile}/{label}. A Boot 3 client opts in with spring.config.import=configserver:http://config:8888 (Boot 2's bootstrap.yml phase is legacy — the import mechanism replaced it). Precedence merges with local config per the rules in section 2. Secrets belong in Vault (dynamic DB credentials, leases) or Kubernetes Secrets; plain ConfigMaps handle non-secret config, mounted as files or env vars, with spring-cloud-kubernetes optionally watching them.

Why is @RefreshScope a proxy? A singleton's fields are set once at creation; other beans hold a direct reference, so you cannot swap it under them. A refresh-scoped bean is registered as a CGLIB proxy; the proxy forwards each call to a target held in the scope's cache. POST /actuator/refresh re-fetches the Environment, works out which keys changed, and clears the cache — the next method call lazily creates a new target from the new values. Nobody's reference changed; the object behind it did. Analogy: everyone dials the same desk extension (proxy); a refresh quietly seats a new employee at the desk. Fan-out to a fleet uses Spring Cloud Bus (/actuator/busrefresh broadcast over Kafka/Rabbit) — or, on Kubernetes, a rolling restart, which is often simpler and more honest.

# application.yml (Boot 3 style — no bootstrap.yml)
spring:
  application.name: order-service
  config.import: "configserver:http://config:8888", "vault://secret/order-service"
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,refresh

Pitfalls

  • @RefreshScope on a bean holding state (connection pool, cache): refresh destroys and rebuilds it mid-flight — in-flight work can hit a closing resource. Refresh only cheap config holders; @ConfigurationProperties beans are re-bound on refresh without needing the scope.
  • Config Server down at startup: with spring.config.import=configserver: the app fails fast by default; use configserver:?optional=true (or spring.cloud.config.fail-fast tuning) deliberately, not accidentally.
  • Secrets in Git behind Config Server "because it's encrypted" — {cipher} values are decryptable by anyone with the server key; Vault gives leases, rotation and audit.
  • Calling /actuator/refresh on one pod of twenty and wondering why behavior is inconsistent — refresh is per-instance; use Bus or restart the Deployment.
Interview questions
  • How can a singleton's config change at runtime? — It can't; @RefreshScope beans are proxies. Refresh clears the scope cache and the next call re-creates the target from the new Environment — holders keep the same proxy reference.
  • What does POST /actuator/refresh return? — The set of property keys whose values changed; it also re-binds @ConfigurationProperties and destroys changed refresh-scoped beans.
  • bootstrap.yml in Boot 3? — Replaced by spring.config.import=configserver: in normal config processing; the legacy bootstrap context needs an explicit opt-in dependency and is discouraged.
  • ConfigMap vs Config Server? — ConfigMap: platform-native, versioned with the Deployment, no extra service to run, but no Git history semantics across apps and a restart (or a watcher) to pick up changes. Config Server: central Git audit trail, per-profile composition, works off-Kubernetes.
  • Where do DB passwords live? — Vault (dynamic credentials with TTL, rotation, audit) or sealed Kubernetes Secrets with RBAC; never in the image, never in plain Git.
  • How do you refresh 40 instances at once? — Spring Cloud Bus /actuator/busrefresh broadcasting over Kafka/Rabbit — or trigger a rolling restart, which also exercises your deploy path instead of a special-case code path.

Inter-service communication: Feign vs RestClient vs HTTP interfaces, sync vs async

Why interviewers ask: every microservices design ends up at "how do these two talk, and what happens when the callee is slow?" — the answer reveals whether you think in failure modes or happy paths.

Three synchronous client styles in Boot 3. OpenFeign: annotate an interface with @FeignClient("order-service") — declarative, discovery/LB integrated, mature ecosystem, but a Spring Cloud dependency and its own config dialect. RestClient (Boot 3.2+): the modern fluent blocking client, successor to RestTemplate (see section 3). HTTP interfaces (@HttpExchange + HttpServiceProxyFactory): Feign-like declarative interfaces from Spring Framework itself, backed by RestClient/WebClient — the direction Spring is pointing for new code.

Sync vs async: a synchronous call chain couples availability (A is down while B is down) and latency (they add up), but is simple and read-your-own-write. Messaging (section 7) decouples availability and absorbs bursts at the cost of eventual consistency and harder debugging. Rule of thumb: queries the user is waiting on → sync; state changes other services react to → events. Every sync hop needs a timeout budget: if the edge promises 2s, allocate inward (gateway 1900ms → service A 1500ms → service B 800ms) so inner calls always time out before outer ones — detailed mechanics in section 7.

Keeping callers and callees compatible: consumer-driven contract testing (Spring Cloud Contract: consumer expectations become a stub jar the consumer tests against and generated tests the producer must pass), and API versioning — additive changes by default (tolerant reader), URL major versions (/v2/orders) or media-type versioning when you must break, never silently changing field semantics.

// HTTP interface (Spring 6): declarative like Feign, no Spring Cloud needed
public interface OrderApi {
    @GetExchange("/api/orders/{id}")
    OrderSummary get(@PathVariable String id);
}

@Configuration
class OrderApiConfig {
    @Bean OrderApi orderApi(RestClient.Builder lb) {
        RestClient rc = lb.baseUrl("http://order-service")
            .requestFactory(ClientHttpRequestFactories.get(
                ClientHttpRequestFactorySettings.DEFAULTS
                    .withConnectTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(300))   // always set both
                    .withReadTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(800))))
            .build();
        return HttpServiceProxyFactory.builderFor(RestClientAdapter.create(rc))
                                      .build().createClient(OrderApi.class);
    }
}
OpenFeignRestClientHTTP interface
StyleDeclarative interfaceFluent builder callsDeclarative interface
Comes fromSpring CloudSpring Framework 6.1Spring Framework 6.0
Discovery/LBBuilt-inVia @LoadBalanced builderVia the underlying client
Best forExisting Cloud estatesAd-hoc calls, full controlNew declarative clients

Pitfalls

  • Default timeouts are effectively infinite on several client stacks: one hung downstream call can pin threads until the pool starves. Explicit connect + read timeouts on every client, no exceptions.
  • Retrying non-idempotent POSTs on timeout: the first request may have succeeded — pair retries with idempotency keys (data patterns).
  • Versioning by "we deploy both sides together" — works until team B has an incident freeze; contracts + tolerant readers keep deploys independent.
Interview questions
  • When sync, when async between services? — Sync for user-facing queries needing an immediate answer; async events for state propagation and side effects. Deciding factor: does the caller need the result to respond, and can it tolerate the callee being down?
  • What is a timeout budget? — The end-to-end SLA split across hops so each inner timeout is strictly smaller than its caller's remaining time; otherwise the outer layer gives up while inner work continues, wasting capacity and duplicating retries.
  • Feign vs HTTP interfaces? — Same declarative shape; HTTP interfaces are core Spring (no Cloud dependency), ride on RestClient/WebClient, and are the recommended path for new Boot 3 code; Feign remains fine where already established.
  • How does Spring Cloud Contract prevent breaking a consumer? — Consumers publish contracts; the producer's build generates tests from them that fail if the API drifts, and consumers test against generated stubs instead of a live producer.
  • How do you version a REST API without breaking clients? — Prefer additive/tolerant-reader evolution; when breaking is unavoidable, run /v1 and /v2 side by side and retire v1 on telemetry, not hope.
  • Why did retries make an outage worse? — Retry storms: N layers each retrying 3× multiplies load 3^N onto an already-sick service. Cap with budgets, jittered backoff and circuit breakers (section 7).

Distributed tracing & observability: Micrometer Observation, traceparent, metrics

Why interviewers ask: "a request is slow somewhere across six services — find it" is the defining ops question of microservices. They probe whether you know how context actually propagates and how to keep metrics from blowing up cardinality.

Boot 3 unified metrics and tracing under the Micrometer Observation API: one Observation around a piece of work produces both a timer metric and a trace span. Spring instruments MVC, RestClient/WebClient, Kafka listeners etc. automatically; you add your own with @Observed (needs ObservedAspect) or Observation.createNotStarted("checkout", registry).observe(...).

Propagation: a trace is a tree of spans sharing a traceId. Context crosses process boundaries in headers — W3C traceparent: 00-<traceId>-<parentSpanId>-<flags> (default) or Zipkin's B3 (b3: traceId-spanId-sampled) — injected by the instrumented client, extracted by the instrumented server. Spans export via OTLP to a backend (Tempo, Jaeger) or Zipkin format; sampling (e.g. management.tracing.sampling.probability=0.1) keeps volume sane. Log correlation: the tracer puts traceId/spanId into SLF4J MDC, so log lines join across services by grepping one id.

Metrics discipline: Prometheus scrapes /actuator/prometheus; every unique tag combination is a separate time series, so tags must be low-cardinality (status, method, outcome — never userId, orderId or raw URI with path variables). Dashboards follow RED per service (Rate, Errors, Duration) and USE per resource (Utilization, Saturation, Errors); SLOs ("99.9% of checkouts under 500ms over 30 days") turn them into error budgets that gate release pace.

management:
  tracing:
    sampling.probability: 0.1        # sample 10% of traces
  otlp.tracing.endpoint: http://tempo:4318/v1/traces
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,prometheus,metrics
logging.pattern.correlation: "[${spring.application.name:},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}] "

Pitfalls

  • Tagging metrics with unbounded values (userId, full URI): millions of series, Prometheus OOM. Use bucketed/low-cardinality tags; put high-cardinality detail in traces and logs.
  • Trace context dies at manual thread hops: submitting to your own ExecutorService loses MDC and the span. Wrap executors with context propagation (ContextExecutorService / Micrometer context-propagation) or use instrumented ones.
  • Sampling at 100% in prod "temporarily": span export volume can rival business traffic. Prefer probabilistic + always-sample-on-error (tail sampling in the collector).
  • Boot 2 habit: expecting Sleuth properties (spring.sleuth.*) to work — they are ignored in Boot 3; everything moved under management.tracing.*.
Interview questions
  • How does a traceId physically travel between services? — In HTTP headers: W3C traceparent (version-traceId-parentSpanId-flags) by default, or B3 headers; for Kafka it rides in record headers. Instrumented clients inject, instrumented servers extract and continue the trace.
  • Trace vs span? — A trace is the whole request tree identified by one traceId; a span is one timed operation within it, with a parent span forming the hierarchy.
  • What does the Observation API give over raw tracing? — One instrumentation point emits metrics and spans with consistent names/tags, so timers and traces can't drift apart; conventions are pluggable via ObservationConvention.
  • How do you correlate logs with traces? — The tracer writes traceId/spanId into MDC; the log pattern (or structured logging) prints them, and the log platform links to the trace backend by id.
  • Why is metric cardinality dangerous, and where does per-user detail go? — Each tag combination is a stored time series; unbounded tags multiply storage and query cost until the TSDB falls over. Per-entity detail belongs in traces/logs (exemplars can bridge metrics → traces).
  • What are RED and USE? — RED for services: Rate, Errors, Duration; USE for resources: Utilization, Saturation, Errors. Together they cover "is it slow/broken" and "what is it starving on".
  • What is an SLO and an error budget? — A target ("99.9% of requests < 500ms per 30 days"); the allowed 0.1% failure is the budget — burn it and you slow releases and fix reliability instead of shipping features.

Structured logging, Logback & changing levels at runtime

Why interviewers ask: "how would you find one user's failed request across five services?" and "can you turn on DEBUG in prod without a restart?" are quick tests of real operational habits.

Grep-able text lines don't survive aggregation; log platforms want JSON. Since Boot 3.4 structured logging is built in: logging.structured.format.console=ecs (Elastic Common Schema), logstash or gelf — no more hand-rolled logstash-logback-encoder config for the common case (that library is still the tool for custom shapes). Each line becomes a JSON object with timestamp, level, logger, message, MDC keys (so traceId lands as a field, joining logs to traces from the tracing card).

Runtime levels: the actuator loggers endpoint reads and writes levels live — POST /actuator/loggers/com.acme.checkout {"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"} — per instance, reversible, no restart. MDC caveats: MDC is a ThreadLocal, so it does not follow work across your own executors or @Async boundaries; with virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true) each request still gets its own thread so MDC works per-request, but millions of short-lived threads make inheritable/copied MDC and context propagation wrappers the correct pattern, not manual copying. Async appenders (AsyncAppender/Loki push) keep logging off the hot path — but bounded queues can drop under burst; know your appender's policy.

logging:
  structured.format.console: ecs      # Boot 3.4+: JSON logs out of the box
  level:
    com.acme: info
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,loggers
# runtime: POST /actuator/loggers/com.acme.checkout  {"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}
# revert:  {"configuredLevel": null}   → back to inherited level

Pitfalls

  • Logging at DEBUG fleet-wide "for a few minutes": log volume can 100× and take the aggregator (and disk/network) with it. Target one logger on one instance.
  • Building expensive log messages eagerly: use parameterized logging (log.debug("state {}", obj)) so formatting only happens if the level is enabled.
  • MDC leaking between requests on pooled threads: always clear (try/finally or filter) — a stale userId on a reused thread misattributes logs, a subtle security issue.
  • Logging full payloads: PII in logs is a compliance incident; mask at the encoder level, not by hoping developers remember.
Interview questions
  • How do you enable JSON logs in Boot? — Boot 3.4+: logging.structured.format.console=ecs|logstash|gelf; earlier: logstash-logback-encoder in logback-spring.xml. JSON makes fields queryable in ELK/Loki.
  • Change a log level in prod without restart? — POST /actuator/loggers/<logger> with a configuredLevel; secure the endpoint, and remember it is per-instance and reverts on restart.
  • Why can MDC values vanish in async code? — MDC is thread-local; a task on another executor thread starts with an empty (or stale) MDC. Use context-propagating wrappers or a TaskDecorator that copies the map.
  • Does virtual threads break logging? — No — each request gets its own virtual thread and MDC; the trap is pooling assumptions (ThreadLocal caches sized "per thread" now mean per-request) and synchronized appenders becoming pinning points (pre-Java 24).
  • logback-spring.xml vs logback.xml? — The -spring variant is processed by Boot, enabling <springProfile> and <springProperty> (reading from the Environment); plain logback.xml loads before Spring and can't use those.

Health, readiness/liveness & zero-downtime rolling deploys

Why interviewers ask: "how do you deploy without dropping requests?" is pure production seniority. The wrong answer (liveness = readiness = /health) causes both dropped traffic and restart storms — and they know it.

Boot exposes Kubernetes-shaped probes automatically when it detects k8s (or via management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true): /actuator/health/liveness — "is this process broken beyond recovery? if so restart it" — and /actuator/health/readiness — "can it take traffic right now?". They are backed by in-process ApplicationAvailability state; your code can flip it by publishing AvailabilityChangeEvent.publish(ctx, ReadinessState.REFUSING_TRAFFIC) (e.g. when a critical dependency is gone). Crucial asymmetry: a broken external dependency (DB down) may fail readiness but must not fail liveness — restarting you won't fix the DB, and cascading restarts turn one outage into two.

Zero-downtime rolling deploy = readiness gating + graceful shutdown. Boot 3 defaults to server.shutdown=graceful: on SIGTERM the server stops accepting new requests but finishes in-flight ones within spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase (default 30s). The race to know: Kubernetes removes the pod from endpoints asynchronously with sending SIGTERM, so for a moment traffic still arrives at a terminating pod — the standard fix is a preStop sleep (5–10s) so endpoint propagation wins, with terminationGracePeriodSeconds > preStop + shutdown timeout so the kubelet doesn't SIGKILL mid-flight. Analogy: a cashier closing their lane switches off the lane light (readiness), waits a beat for approaching carts to divert (preStop), serves whoever is already in line (graceful shutdown), then leaves.

# application.yml
server.shutdown: graceful                       # Boot 3 default
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 25s
management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled: true
management.health.readinessstate.enabled: true

# deployment.yaml (the k8s half)
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 } }
livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness,  port: 8080 } }
lifecycle: { preStop: { exec: { command: ["sh","-c","sleep 8"] } } }
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 40   # > preStop 8s + shutdown 25s

Pitfalls

  • Wiring the DB health indicator into liveness: DB blips → kubelet restarts every pod → thundering-herd reconnects on recovery. External dependencies belong (carefully) in readiness only.
  • No preStop: 502/connection-reset spikes on every deploy as traffic races SIGTERM — often misdiagnosed as "flaky network".
  • terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30) smaller than preStop + graceful timeout: kubelet SIGKILLs mid-request, defeating the whole setup.
  • Slow-starting apps failing liveness during startup: use a startupProbe (or generous initialDelaySeconds) instead of loosening liveness forever.
Interview questions
  • Liveness vs readiness — and what does each failure trigger? — Liveness "process is wedged" → container restart; readiness "can't take traffic now" → removed from endpoints, no restart. Confusing them causes restart storms or traffic to dead pods.
  • Should /actuator/health include the database? — In readiness possibly (if the pod truly can't serve without it), in liveness never; a restart cannot heal an external outage, and mass restarts amplify it.
  • How does Boot's graceful shutdown work? — On SIGTERM the web server stops accepting new connections and the lifecycle waits up to timeout-per-shutdown-phase for active requests, then continues the normal context close (smart lifecycles in reverse phase order).
  • Why the preStop sleep? — Endpoint removal is eventually consistent; sleeping keeps the app fully serving while kube-proxy/ingress converge, so no request meets a closed socket.
