  • What is ApplicationAvailability? — Boot's in-process liveness/readiness state machine; you can publish AvailabilityChangeEvents to flip states (e.g. refuse traffic during a critical cache rebuild) and probes reflect it.
  • Boot 2 vs 3? — Same probe model (since 2.3); Boot 3 turns graceful shutdown on by default and its probes are auto-enabled on Kubernetes detection.

Containerizing Boot: images, JVM-in-container sizing, CDS/AOT/native

Why interviewers ask: "your pod keeps getting OOMKilled but the heap looks fine" is a classic senior screen — it tests whether you know a JVM is much more than its heap, and that CPU limits silently resize every thread pool you own.

Building the image: hand-written multi-stage Dockerfile (full control) vs Cloud Native Buildpacks (mvn spring-boot:build-image — curated JVM, memory calculator, no Dockerfile to maintain). Either way, exploit layered jars: java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers splits dependencies / spring-boot-loader / snapshot-deps / application into separate image layers, so a one-line code change re-pushes kilobytes, not a 300MB fat jar.

Memory: container RSS = heap + Metaspace + thread stacks (1MB × threads) + code cache + direct buffers + GC/JIT overhead. The JVM is container-aware (cgroup limits since JDK 10): size the heap with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60-75 rather than a fixed -Xmx, and leave real headroom — a 1GiB limit with a 900MiB heap is an OOMKill scheduled for later. CPU: the JVM derives availableProcessors() from CPU quota, and that number sizes GC threads, ForkJoinPool, and many defaults — a 500m CPU limit means 1 processor, so parallel streams and GC ergonomics collapse; latency-sensitive pods often set requests=limits or drop CPU limits entirely.

Startup: JVM Boot apps start in seconds; shrink it with CDS/AppCDS (class-data sharing archive, ~30–50% faster start, Boot 3.3+ has first-class support), Spring's AOT processing, or go all the way to GraalVM native image: tens-of-milliseconds startup and low RSS, at the cost of build time, closed-world reflection (hints needed), and no JIT peak throughput. Native suits scale-to-zero/serverless and CLIs; long-running high-throughput services usually stay on the JVM (Project Leyden/ahead-of-time caches are closing the gap).

# Multi-stage Dockerfile with layered jar
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre AS builder
COPY target/app.jar app.jar
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers --destination extracted

FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre
COPY --from=builder extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=builder extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder extracted/application/ ./          # only this layer changes often
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
ENTRYPOINT ["java","org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]
JVM (JIT)JVM + CDS/AOTGraalVM native
Startup3–10s~2–5s50–200ms
Peak throughputBest (JIT)BestLower (no JIT)
Memory (RSS)HighHighLow
Constraints—same JVM/classpath for archiveclosed world: reflection/proxies need hints; long builds

Pitfalls

  • OOMKilled (exit 137) with a healthy heap: native memory (threads, direct buffers, Metaspace) blew past the cgroup limit — -Xmx only caps one region. Measure with Native Memory Tracking (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary + jcmd VM.native_memory).
  • Running as root on a JDK (not JRE) base image with shell tools: bigger attack surface and image; use slim JRE or distroless, non-root user.
  • 200 Tomcat threads × 1MB stacks in a 512MiB container: the stacks alone can evict you; right-size pools to CPU and workload, not defaults.
  • Native image passing all unit tests but failing at runtime on ClassNotFoundException-style reflection errors: exercise real paths in tests, ship reachability hints (@RegisterReflectionForBinding / runtime hints).
Interview questions
  • Pod OOMKilled but heap dumps show 40% heap use — what's eating memory? — Non-heap native memory: thread stacks, Metaspace, direct ByteBuffers, JIT code cache, GC structures, glibc arenas. Turn on NMT, count threads, check direct buffer pools; then lower MaxRAMPercentage or raise the limit.
  • Why prefer MaxRAMPercentage over -Xmx in containers? — The heap then scales with the cgroup limit, so one image works across sizes and resizing memory is a manifest change, not a rebuild.
  • What do CPU limits do to a JVM? — Quota → availableProcessors() → sizes GC/JIT/ForkJoin/common pools. Tiny limits mean single-threaded GC and throttling; check with Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() in the actual pod.
  • Dockerfile vs buildpacks? — Buildpacks: zero Dockerfile, patched base images, built-in memory calculator — great default. Dockerfile: full control (custom base, agents, distroless) at the price of owning JVM ergonomics yourself.
  • When native image, when not? — Native for cold-start-critical (serverless, scale-to-zero, CLI) and memory-dense fleets; JVM for peak throughput and heavy-reflection stacks. CDS + AOT is the low-risk middle.
  • Why layered jars? — Docker caches per layer; separating rarely-changing dependencies from your classes makes rebuild/push/pull incremental and registries cheaper.

12-factor config, secrets hygiene & feature flags

Why interviewers ask: a quick culture check — "same artifact through all environments" and "flags decouple deploy from release" are sentences they want to hear verbatim.

The 12-factor rule for config: strict separation of config from code — one immutable image promoted dev → staging → prod, with everything environment-specific injected from outside (env vars, mounted files, config service). Boot makes this natural: relaxed binding maps SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL onto spring.datasource.url, and the property-source precedence (section 2) lets the environment override packaged defaults. Baking a profile into the image ("the prod build") breaks the promotion guarantee — what you tested is no longer what you run.

Secrets hygiene: never in the image, never in Git, never in plain env dumps if avoidable (env vars leak via /proc, crash dumps, child processes) — prefer mounted Secret files or Vault (config card), rotate regularly, and scrub actuator /env output (Boot sanitizes obvious key names, and since 3.x shows values only when explicitly configured). Feature flags separate deploy (code reaches prod, dark) from release (flag flips traffic on): start with @ConfigurationProperties booleans + refresh, graduate to Togglz/Unleash/LaunchDarkly for percentage rollouts and kill switches. Flags are also the cheap rollback: flipping a boolean beats redeploying under incident pressure.

Pitfalls

  • Long-lived flags become configuration forks nobody dares remove — put an owner and expiry on every flag; stale flags are how you get two untested code paths in prod.
  • @Profile("prod") beans for behavior differences: environment-specific code paths escape testing; keep profiles for wiring (which DB), flags for behavior.
  • Kill switch that itself needs a deploy to flip — the switch must be runtime config (flag service, refreshable property), or it is not a switch.
Interview questions
  • What does "config in the environment" buy you? — One tested artifact runs everywhere; promotion is a config change, secrets stay out of VCS, and rebuilds aren't needed to change endpoints.
  • Deploy vs release? — Deploy ships code; release exposes it. Flags let you deploy continuously and release deliberately (canary %, cohorts), and roll back in milliseconds.
  • Env var vs mounted secret file? — Files can be updated without pod restart, don't leak into process listings/inherited environments, and map to Vault agent/CSI patterns; env vars are simpler but more exposed.
  • How does Boot map SPRING_JPA_OPEN_IN_VIEW=false? — Relaxed binding: upper-case + underscores translates to spring.jpa.open-in-view; the env var property source outranks packaged files.
  • How would you do a 5% rollout of new pricing logic? — Flag evaluated per request (stable hash of user id → bucket), metrics tagged by flag state to compare cohorts, automatic kill on error-budget burn.

Data in microservices: DB-per-service, sagas, idempotency

Why interviewers ask: "order service and payment service must both commit — how?" is the microservices question. Saying "distributed transaction" without flinching, or joining two services' tables, ends the interview early.

Database per service: each service owns its schema; others get data only through its API or events. This buys independent deploys/scaling and technology freedom, and costs you joins and ACID across services. 2PC/XA is not the answer in this world — it holds locks across networks, couples availability to a coordinator, and popular infra (many cloud DBs, Kafka) won't play. Instead: sagas — a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions for rollback (reserve stock → charge card → on failure: release stock). Choreography: services react to each other's events — loose coupling, but the flow lives nowhere and is hard to reason about past ~4 steps. Orchestration: a coordinator (state machine, Temporal, or a plain orchestrator service) drives steps explicitly — visible flow, one more component. Full walkthroughs live in the System Design guide.

The glue that makes sagas safe: the transactional outbox (event write commits atomically with state, relayed to Kafka afterwards — mechanics in section 7) and idempotent APIs — retries and redeliveries are guaranteed, so consumers dedupe by business key and POSTs accept an Idempotency-Key header stored with the result (unique constraint = the enforcement). CQRS separates the write model from read models projected from events — the cure for "I need a join across three services" (build a read-side projection) — at the cost of eventual consistency in reads.

// Idempotent create: the DB unique constraint is the real guard
@PostMapping("/payments")
ResponseEntity<Payment> pay(@RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key,
                            @RequestBody PaymentRequest req) {
    return repo.findByIdempotencyKey(key)
        .map(existing -> ResponseEntity.ok(existing))          // replay → same result
        .orElseGet(() -> {
            try {
                Payment p = repo.save(Payment.of(key, req));   // unique(key) column
                return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(p);
            } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException race) {   // concurrent retry lost
                return ResponseEntity.ok(repo.findByIdempotencyKey(key).orElseThrow());
            }
        });
}

Pitfalls

  • "Database per service" implemented as separate schemas that services still cross-query "just for reporting" — the coupling returns invisibly; give reporting its own projection or warehouse.
  • Compensations that can fail with nowhere to go: design them to be idempotent and retryable, and alert into a dead-letter/manual queue — a saga stuck half-done is a business incident.
  • Dedupe cache in memory: two pods, or a restart, and the duplicate walks through. The dedupe store must share the consumer's transaction (a table) or be durable.
  • Reading your own write through a CQRS read model and "losing" data: reads are eventually consistent; return the write result directly or read-your-writes from the write model.
Interview questions
  • Why not 2PC across services? — It holds locks while waiting on network round-trips, the coordinator is a single point of failure, blocked participants can't proceed on coordinator loss, and modern brokers/DBs often lack XA — you trade availability for a consistency you can get more cheaply with sagas + idempotency.
  • Choreography vs orchestration — pick one for a 6-step order flow. — Orchestration: at 6 steps with compensations, an explicit state machine is debuggable and evolvable; choreography's implicit flow becomes archaeology.
  • How do you make a consumer idempotent? — Natural business key or event id recorded in the same local transaction as the state change (unique constraint); replays hit the constraint and are acknowledged without effect. See also exactly-once discussion in section 7.
  • What problem does the outbox solve? — The dual-write: DB commit succeeds but the broker publish fails (or vice versa). Writing the event into an outbox table inside the same transaction makes publish-eventually atomic with state.
  • When is CQRS worth it? — When read and write shapes/scales diverge hard (search, dashboards, cross-service views). Not as a default — two models and a projector are real ongoing cost.
  • A saga fails at step 3 of 5 — what happens? — Compensating transactions run for steps 2 and 1 in reverse order (release reservation, refund); the saga ends in a semantically-rolled-back state, and unrecoverable compensation failures page a human.

Production troubleshooting: thread dumps, heap dumps, pool exhaustion, GC

Why interviewers ask: anyone can build a service; seniors can debug one at 3 a.m. "Walk me through diagnosing a hung service" tests whether you have a method — symptoms → hypothesis → evidence — or just restart and pray.

The toolbox: actuator gives /actuator/threaddump and /actuator/heapdump (an .hprof you open in Eclipse MAT — protect these endpoints, a heap dump contains your secrets); on the box, jcmd <pid> Thread.print, jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump file.hprof, jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary, plus jstat -gcutil for GC pressure at a glance. Metrics to keep on a dashboard: Hikari (hikaricp.connections.active/pending), Tomcat threads (tomcat.threads.busy), GC pause time, heap after full GC.

Pattern recognition: requests hang + hikaricp.connections.pending climbing → pool exhaustion (leaked connections, transactions held across slow external calls, or a genuinely slow query downstream — enable Hikari leakDetectionThreshold=60000 to get creation stack traces of leakers). p99 spikes with CPU bursts and sawtooth heap → GC pauses (check pause logs: -Xlog:gc*; old-gen occupancy rising after every full GC → memory leak). Classic leak sources: unbounded caches/maps, listeners never deregistered, and ThreadLocal on pooled threads — value outlives the request because the thread never dies (with the bonus classloader leak on redeploy). Slow queries: N+1, missing index, lock waits — find them in pg_stat_activity/slow-query log, correlate with traces (tracing card).

Thread-dump reading: take 3 dumps ~10s apart; a thread parked in the same stack in all three is stuck, not busy. Look for many threads in WAITING on the same lock/pool (HikariPool.getConnection, a synchronized monitor, an Object.wait on an HTTP client pool) — the shared choke point names the culprit.

> kubectl top pod order-7f9c            # CPU 3%  MEM 61%  ← low CPU, not compute
> curl -s app:8080/actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.pending \
    | jq .measurements                  # value: 47  ← 47 requests queued for a connection
> curl -s app:8080/actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.active \
    | jq .measurements                  # value: 10  ← pool max (10) all checked out
> kubectl exec order-7f9c -- jcmd 1 Thread.print > td1.txt   # dump 1 of 3
> grep -c "HikariPool.getConnection" td1.txt                 # 47 threads waiting
> grep -B2 -A8 "http-nio-8080-exec-3" td1.txt   # what are the 10 holders doing?
#   at java.net.SocketInputStream.socketRead0   ← blocked on HTTP to tax-service
#   at c.a.tax.TaxClient.quote(TaxClient.java:41)
#   at c.a.order.OrderService.place(OrderService.java:88)  @Transactional
> curl -s app:8080/actuator/metrics/http.client.requests?tag=uri:/tax/quote \
    | jq '.measurements'                 # max: 119.7s  ← no read timeout!
  1. Triage: low CPU + hanging requests = threads blocked, not overloaded. GC and compute are off the suspect list.
  2. Hikari metrics: the pool (max 10) is fully checked out with 47 waiters — pool exhaustion confirmed. Question becomes: who holds the 10, and why so long?
  3. Three thread dumps, 10s apart. 47 threads wait in getConnection in all of them — matching connections.pending exactly.
  4. The 10 holder threads share one stack: a blocking HTTP read to tax-service — inside @Transactional place(), so each holds its DB connection while waiting on the network.
  5. Client metrics: tax calls up to 119s — the client has no read timeout. tax-service degraded, and every order thread now camps on a connection until the socket gives up.
  6. Root cause: an unbounded external call inside a transaction. Fixes in order: set connect/read timeouts + circuit breaker (section 7), move the HTTP call outside the transaction boundary (section 5), alert on connections.pending > 0.
Interview angle: narrate exactly this order — symptoms (CPU/mem/latency shape) → shared choke point (metrics) → thread dumps ×3 → holder stacks → root cause → fix + regression guard. Naming leakDetectionThreshold, jcmd, and "external call inside a transaction" is what "has done this before" sounds like.

Pitfalls

  • Taking one thread dump and reading tea leaves: busy threads look identical to stuck ones in a single snapshot; always compare several.
  • /actuator/heapdump on a 12GB heap in prod: seconds-long pause and a 12GB file through your ingress — prefer jcmd GC.heap_dump to local disk, and dump a pod already out of rotation.
  • Fixing pool exhaustion by raising maximumPoolSize to 100: you just moved the queue into the database, which now dies for everyone. Fix the hold time, not the pool size.
  • ThreadLocal "cleared at the end of the request" — until one exception path skips the finally, or an @Async hop runs on another pool. Prefer try/finally in a filter, or request-scoped beans.
Interview questions
  • Service hangs, CPU near zero — first three moves? — Check thread-pool and connection-pool metrics for saturation, take 3 thread dumps 10s apart, find the common stack of waiters and of holders; the shared resource in those stacks is the culprit.
  • How do you find a connection leak? — Hikari leakDetectionThreshold logs the acquisition stack of any connection held too long; also diff active vs actual in-flight requests, and audit code paths that acquire outside @Transactional/try-with-resources.
  • OOM: how do you find what filled the heap? — -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError, open the hprof in MAT, look at dominator tree / "biggest retained set"; a leak shows one root (cache, static map, ThreadLocal map) retaining an outsized graph.
  • Why is ThreadLocal a leak on pooled threads? — Pool threads never die, so per-thread map entries persist after the request; with value types from a redeployed webapp classloader, they also pin the whole classloader (Metaspace leak).
  • p99 is 2s, p50 is 40ms — GC or downstream? — Check GC logs first (pauses correlate across all endpoints simultaneously); downstream slowness clusters on endpoints calling that dependency — traces split the two in minutes.
  • What does jcmd give you that actuator doesn't? — Works when HTTP is wedged (the exact failure mode you're debugging), plus NMT, VM flags, GC.run, JFR start/stop — all through the local attach mechanism.

🎯 Interview scenarios: design & debug

Why interviewers ask: senior loops end with open scenarios — no single right answer, but a right method: clarify, hypothesize from symptoms, name the evidence you'd collect, fix, then prevent. Practice saying these out loud.

Each scenario below is a realistic prompt followed by the skeleton of a strong answer. Cover the method, not just the punchline — interviewers score the path.

1. "Order service p99 jumped 80ms → 2s after a deploy; nothing in the logs. Walk me through it."
  • Confirm scope: p50 vs p99 (p50 flat + p99 spiked = a subset or queueing, not everything), all endpoints or some, all pods or some.
  • Diff the deploy: code, dependency bumps, config, JVM flags — git diff the release and the manifests before touching the service.
  • Traces first (nothing in logs ≠ nothing happened): compare a slow trace vs a fast one — which span grew? self-time vs downstream call?
  • Usual suspects for "logs clean, p99 up": a lost index / changed query plan (JPA query changed), N+1 introduced, connection/thread pool queueing (pending metrics), GC change, a new sync call added on the hot path.
  • Check GC pauses and pool saturation dashboards over the deploy boundary — queueing shows as flat p50, exploding tail.
  • Mitigate now: roll back (deploys must be reversible), confirm p99 recovers — that proves causality while you analyze offline.
  • Prevent: perf smoke test in the pipeline on the key endpoint, SLO burn alert, always-canary deploys with automatic rollback on latency regression.
2. "Your pod gets OOMKilled every few hours, but heap usage looks fine in Grafana. Diagnose."
  • Distinguish killers: OOMKilled (exit 137) = cgroup limit breached by total RSS — not necessarily heap; a Java OutOfMemoryError would show in logs instead.
  • RSS = heap + Metaspace + thread stacks + direct buffers + code cache + GC overhead + native libs; "heap fine" only clears the first term.
  • Enable Native Memory Tracking (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary) and diff jcmd VM.native_memory over hours — see which category grows.
  • Count threads over time (each ~1MB stack): a leaked executor per request is a classic. Check direct buffer metrics (Netty, big file I/O).
  • Check the math: memory limit vs MaxRAMPercentage — a 75% heap on a 1GiB limit leaves ~250MiB for everything else; often the whole bug is under-provisioned headroom.
  • Fix: cap the real growth source (bounded pools/buffers), right-size limit vs heap percentage, add -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError so real heap OOMs restart cleanly.
  • Prevent: alert on container RSS at 90% of limit and on thread count growth, not only on heap.
3. "A list endpoint is fast in staging, 8s in prod. DBA says 'you send thousands of tiny queries'. What happened and what do you do?"
  • Classic N+1: a collection is LAZY, staging has 10 rows so 11 queries; prod has 2000 rows so 2001 queries — the pattern hides at small scale.
  • Prove it: enable SQL logging locally / check APM query counts per request; the trace shows one query fanning into thousands of identical ones with different ids.
  • Fix options in order: join fetch in the JPQL for this use case, @EntityGraph on the repository method, or @BatchSize/batch fetching to turn N queries into N/size.
  • If the endpoint only needs a few columns: switch to a DTO projection — no entities, no lazy graph at all.
  • Beware fixing by EAGER: it "fixes" this endpoint by breaking every other one that loads the entity.
  • Prevent: a test asserting query count on key endpoints (e.g. Hibernate statistics), review rule that lists rendering collections must state their fetch plan. (Deep dive: section 5.)
4. "The same Kafka payment event was processed twice and a customer was charged twice. Find the hole and close it."
  • Duplicates are normal in at-least-once delivery: rebalance after processing but before commit, retry after a timeout, or a producer retry creating two records — the bug is that processing wasn't idempotent, not that Kafka misbehaved.
  • Reconstruct: find both processings' traces/log lines — same offset (redelivery) or two different offsets (producer duplicate)? That splits the fix.
  • Same offset: consumer committed too late/early around a rebalance — check for long processing beyond max.poll.interval.ms and the deploy/rebalance timeline.
  • Different offsets: enable producer idempotence (default on modern clients) to kill retry duplicates within a session; cross-session duplicates still need consumer-side dedupe.
  • Real fix: idempotent consumer — record the payment id in the same DB transaction as the charge (unique constraint); replays hit the constraint and ack without effect.
  • For money specifically: an idempotency key on the charge call to the PSP, so even your own bug can't double-charge.
  • Prevent: chaos-test redelivery in integration tests (kill consumer mid-batch), alert on dedupe-hit rate. (Semantics: section 7.)
5. "Ops needs a config value changed in prod NOW, but the next deploy window is tomorrow. Options?"
  • First question: is it a Spring property, a feature flag, or a secret? Each has a different safe path.
  • If the value is refresh-scoped / @ConfigurationProperties behind Config Server: change Git, POST /actuator/busrefresh (or per-pod refresh) — no restart, audited by the Git commit.
  • On Kubernetes with mounted ConfigMap: kubectl edit configmap + rolling restart of the Deployment — a restart is a deploy of config only, usually allowed even in freeze windows.
  • If it's a flag in a flag service: flip it — that is exactly what flags are for; verify with metrics tagged by flag state.
  • What NOT to do: kubectl exec and edit files in a running container (unaudited, lost on restart, drift between pods).
  • Log-level-only change: POST /actuator/loggers/... per instance, no restart at all.
  • Afterwards: make whatever was hard about this easy — values ops may need to change at 2 a.m. belong in runtime config with an audit trail.
6. "You must rename a column (or change its type) on a table serving live traffic. Zero downtime. Plan it."
  • Rule: never a breaking change in one step — expand/contract (parallel change), because during a rolling deploy old and new code run simultaneously against one schema.
  • Expand: add the new column nullable (or new table); deploy code that writes both old and new, still reads old.
  • Backfill: batched background migration copying old → new (throttled, resumable, off-peak); verify counts/checksums.
  • Flip reads: deploy code reading the new column (write both still); watch error rates and data-diff metrics.
  • Contract: stop writing old; after a soak period + backup, drop the old column in a final migration.
  • Each step is independently deployable and reversible; Flyway migrations stay additive per step (section 5).
  • Gotchas to name: long ALTER TABLE locks (use online DDL / pg_repack), ORMs validating schema (ddl-auto=validate must tolerate the extra column — it does), and triggers as an alternative backfill-sync mechanism.
7. "A new internal service exposes payroll data to two consumer services. Secure it — what do you actually set up?"
  • Authentication service-to-service: OAuth2 client-credentials flow — each consumer gets a client id/secret from the IdP, calls with a JWT; payroll validates as a resource server (issuer-uri, JWKS) — no passwords between services. (section 6.)
  • Authorization: scopes/roles per consumer (payroll.read vs payroll.admin) enforced with @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_payroll.read')") at the method level, not just URL patterns.
  • Network layer: mTLS (mesh or manual) + NetworkPolicy so only the two consumers can even reach the pod — defense in depth under the token check.
  • Data minimization: separate endpoints/DTOs per consumer need; no "give me everything" endpoint for convenience.
  • Secrets: client credentials in Vault/Secrets with rotation, never in Git or images.
  • Audit + rate limits: who asked for whose payroll, when; per-client limits at the gateway.
  • Non-negotiables to say out loud: actuator endpoints locked down, TLS everywhere, and the payroll DB reachable only from the payroll service.
8. "Every request waits ~30s then fails with 'connection is not available (timeout)'. It started gradually. Go."
  • The 30s is Hikari's connectionTimeout default: threads queue for a pooled connection and give up — pool exhaustion; "gradually" suggests a slow leak, not a sudden downstream outage.
  • Metrics: hikaricp.connections.active pinned at max, pending growing; compare active connections vs actual concurrent requests — a widening gap = leak.
  • Enable leakDetectionThreshold=60000: Hikari logs the stack trace that acquired each over-held connection — usually names the exact method.
  • Typical roots: connection acquired outside try-with-resources on an exception path, @Transactional method doing slow external I/O while holding the connection, or a stuck query (check pg_stat_activity for idle-in-transaction).
  • Thread dumps ×3 confirm: many waiters in getConnection, holders' stacks show the offending code (see the walkthrough above).
  • Fix the hold, don't inflate the pool: bound the external call, shrink the transaction, close in finally; then alert on pending > 0 for early warning.
9. "Startup takes 4 minutes; Kubernetes keeps killing the pod before it's ready. Fix both the symptom and the cause."
  • Stop the killing first: add a startupProbe (e.g. 30 × 10s) so liveness doesn't run until startup succeeds — no code change, ends the crash loop today.
  • Measure where the 4 minutes go: ApplicationStartup with BufferingApplicationStartup + /actuator/startup shows per-bean timings; also check CPU throttling — a 500m CPU limit makes JIT + context init crawl (raise the limit or use a startup CPU boost).
  • Common causes: eager cache warming / data preloading in @PostConstruct, scanning huge classpaths, connecting to slow external systems serially, ddl-auto=validate against a huge schema, retry loops for unavailable dependencies at boot.
  • Move warm-up out of the critical path: do it async after startup and gate readiness (ApplicationAvailability) on completion — pod alive, just not receiving traffic yet.
  • Structural: lazy-init for rarely used beans (spring.main.lazy-initialization=true selectively), CDS/AOT for JVM-side startup cost.
  • Prevent: track startup time as a CI metric; probes reviewed with every new blocking init added.
10. "A service doing almost no traffic sits at 90% CPU. Nothing in the logs. What's burning it?"
  • Profile before guessing: async-profiler/JFR flame graph for 60s tells you in one look whether it's GC, a spinning loop, or a library.
  • GC death spiral: heap nearly full → back-to-back full GCs at 100% CPU with no OOM yet — jstat -gcutil 1s shows old gen pinned high and GC time climbing; the fix is the leak/heap size, not CPU.
  • Busy-wait loops: a poll loop with no sleep/backoff (queue consumer with 0 timeout, retry-without-delay against a dead dependency) — thread dump shows the same RUNNABLE stack constantly.
  • Accidental workload: a @Scheduled job misconfigured (fixedDelay=0 or an aggressive cron), or a retry storm from a broken circuit config, or regex/JSON parsing pathologically on some poisoned input.
  • Also check it's really your process: kubectl top vs in-container top — sidecars/agents count against the pod.
  • Fix the specific loop, then add backoff-by-default policy for all polling/retry code and an alert on CPU-vs-traffic mismatch.
11. "Your integration tests pass locally, fail ~20% of runs in CI. The team retries the pipeline. Make them actually reliable."
  • Ban blind retries first culturally: a flaky test is a race you shipped; quarantine (tag + track) instead of retrying into the void.
  • Classify the flakes from CI history: timing (fixed Thread.sleep vs slower CI), ordering (tests sharing state/context), resources (ports, Docker startup), external calls (real networks in tests).
  • Kill sleeps: replace Thread.sleep with Awaitility (await().atMost(...).untilAsserted(...)) for async assertions — the #1 flake source in Kafka/async tests.
  • Isolate state: Testcontainers per class (or reused with cleanup between tests), unique topics/queues per test, no shared static mutable state; watch @DirtiesContext cost vs correctness.
  • Pin the environment: fixed container image tags, dynamic ports (webEnvironment=RANDOM_PORT, mapped container ports) — never hardcoded 8080.
  • Replace real external calls with WireMock/contract stubs (contract testing) — the network is not part of your unit of test.
  • Then make flakiness visible: fail the build on newly-flaky tests, dashboard the quarantine list, fix or delete within a sprint.
12. "Checkout must tell inventory, payments and email about a new order. Sync calls, or events? Defend your choice."
  • Split by what checkout needs to answer the user: payment authorization is required to confirm the order → sync (with timeout budget + circuit breaker); inventory reservation likely too (or optimistic with compensation); email is pure side effect → event, always.
  • Sync costs: availability coupling (checkout down whenever payments is), latency addition, retry complexity. Event costs: eventual consistency, duplicate handling, harder debugging (need tracing through the broker).
  • So: minimal synchronous core (payment), then persist the order and emit OrderPlaced via the outbox — inventory-sync, email, analytics all subscribe; new consumers appear without touching checkout.
  • Name the failure modes of each: sync → timeout budget, breaker, idempotency keys on retries; async → outbox for atomicity, idempotent consumers, DLT + alerting for poison events.
  • State the wrong answers too: all-sync (checkout's availability = product of four services) and all-async (user confirmed an order whose payment later failed — now you're sending apology emails).
  • Close with the test: "would the user notice if this step happened 5 seconds later?" No → event.
Interview questions
  • What's the universal debugging order? — Scope the symptom (who/where/when), form hypotheses from the shape (CPU vs latency vs errors), gather cheap evidence first (dashboards, traces), then expensive (dumps, profilers); mitigate (rollback/flag) before root-causing at leisure; end with a prevention.
  • Rollback or roll-forward during an incident? — Rollback by default: it's tested, fast and reversible; roll-forward only when rollback is impossible (schema contracted, data written in new format) — which is why expand/contract exists.
  • What do you say when you don't know? — Name the evidence that would decide it: "I'd confirm with a flame graph / the trace / NMT" beats guessing; interviewers score the method.

1. A Boot 2 app uses Sleuth, Hystrix and Ribbon. Migrating to Boot 3, what is the correct replacement set?

Sleuth has no Boot 3 support (→ Micrometer Tracing), Hystrix and Ribbon are dead Netflix projects (→ Resilience4j and Spring Cloud LoadBalancer). (b) keeps Hystrix, which has no Boot 3 artifacts, and confuses Ribbon (client LB) with Zuul (edge). (d) is wrong: the OTel agent is an option but Spring's own Micrometer stack is first-class.

2. A bean annotated @RefreshScope changed behavior after POST /actuator/refresh even though other beans hold references to it. How?

Refresh-scoped beans are CGLIB proxies delegating to a cached target; refresh evicts the target and the next invocation rebuilds it — references never change. (a) would break final fields and invariants; (c) would drop all state and in-flight work; (d) is impossible — Spring cannot rewrite arbitrary references already handed out.

3. Which trace header does Boot 3's Micrometer Tracing propagate by default, and what does it carry?

Default propagation is W3C Trace Context: 00-<traceId>-<parentSpanId>-<flags>; B3 remains available for Zipkin compatibility. (a) regenerating per hop is exactly what tracing avoids; (d) the header carries only the parent linkage — the backend assembles the tree from exported spans.

4. Which metric tag would blow up Prometheus cardinality?

Every distinct tag value combination creates a stored time series; customerId is unbounded (millions of series). Status, method and outcome have a handful of values each. Per-customer detail belongs in traces and logs, not metric tags.

5. The database goes down for 2 minutes. Your health setup wires the DB indicator into both probes. What happens on Kubernetes?

DB in liveness turns an external outage into fleet-wide restarts — and all pods reconnect at once when the DB returns. Readiness-only (a) is the acceptable half; (d) is fiction — unready pods just receive no traffic, requests fail or go elsewhere.

6. During rolling deploys users see sporadic connection resets from terminating pods, despite server.shutdown=graceful. Best fix?

Endpoint removal and SIGTERM race; graceful shutdown can't help with requests that arrive after the server stopped accepting. A short preStop keeps the app serving while routing converges. (a) lengthens an unrelated deadline; (d) makes it worse by killing in-flight requests.

7. A pod with a 1GiB memory limit and -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 is OOMKilled while heap dashboards show 60% heap usage. Most likely explanation?

A 750MiB max heap leaves only ~250MiB for stacks, Metaspace, code cache and buffers — easily exceeded. The kernel kills on total RSS, not heap. (a) is outdated (container awareness since JDK 10); (b) possible but far less likely than the arithmetic; (d) is not how cgroup OOM works.

8. Order and inventory are separate services with separate databases. The PM asks for "order placement and stock decrement to be atomic". Best production answer?

Sagas trade brief eventual consistency for availability and loose coupling — the accepted microservices answer. (a) holds locks across the network and many modern stores refuse XA; (c) destroys service ownership; (d) is the classic trap — @Transactional governs the local DB connection only, HTTP calls are never rolled back.

9. All requests hang; CPU is 3%; hikaricp.connections.active = max and pending is climbing. Thread dumps show the 10 holders blocked in SocketInputStream.socketRead0 inside a @Transactional method. Root cause?

socketRead0 is a network read, not SQL — the transaction pins the connection while the thread waits indefinitely on a sick downstream. (a) a bigger pool just queues more threads at the same wall; (b) would show stacks in JDBC/DB waits; (d) contradicts 3% CPU and dumps full of network waits.

10. Your gateway's Redis-backed RequestRateLimiter has replenishRate=10, burstCapacity=20. A quiet client suddenly sends 25 requests in one second. What happens?

Token bucket: an idle client's bucket is full at burstCapacity (20), so ~20 requests consume tokens and ~5 are rejected with 429; refill continues at 10 tokens/s. (c) inverts the parameters' meaning; (d) describes shaping/queueing, which this filter does not do — it rejects.

Practice

Scenario: the feature flag flipped in Git, half the pods still run the old behavior

A team stores features.new-pricing=true in the Config Server's Git repo, bound via @ConfigurationProperties(prefix="features") into a @RefreshScope bean. After merging the change they ran POST /actuator/refresh against pricing-service.internal (the Service DNS name) three times "to be safe". An hour later, roughly half of the 6 pods apply new pricing and half don't. Explain what happened and give two correct ways to do this.

Concepts: refresh scope per instance · load-balanced actuator calls · Spring Cloud Bus

Hint 1
Where does an HTTP request to a Kubernetes Service DNS name actually land? How many distinct pods did three POSTs hit?
Hint 2
/actuator/refresh affects exactly one JVM's Environment and scope cache. What broadcasts the refresh, and what non-Spring mechanism achieves the same end state?
Solution

What happened: refresh is per-instance — it re-fetches config and clears the refresh scope in the JVM that received the request. The Service DNS load-balanced the three POSTs to (at most) three of the six pods; those pods now serve new pricing, the others still hold the old target beans. The fleet is split-brained by the deployment's own load balancing.

Correct options:

  • Spring Cloud Bus: add the bus (Kafka/Rabbit) and call POST /actuator/busrefresh once — the event is broadcast and every instance refreshes itself.
  • Rolling restart: kubectl rollout restart deployment/pricing-service — every new pod boots against current config; slower but uses the ordinary, well-tested deploy path and needs no bus infrastructure.
  • (Also acceptable: loop over pod IPs from the Endpoints and POST to each — works, but is hand-rolled bus.)

Deeper point for the interview: a flag that must flip atomically across a fleet shouldn't live in per-instance-refreshed config at all — a flag service (or a shared store checked per request) gives one source of truth with no propagation skew.

Debug: the trace goes dark between order-service and its async worker

A checkout trace shows gateway → order-service spans, but the expensive fraud check — submitted like this — appears as a separate one-span trace with a different traceId, and its log lines carry no traceId at all:

private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);

public void place(Order o) {
    repo.save(o);
    pool.submit(() -> fraudService.check(o));   // shows up as an orphan trace
}

Why does the trace break, and what are two idiomatic fixes in a Boot 3 app?

Concepts: context propagation · ThreadLocal trace context · MDC · instrumented executors

Hint 1
Where does the current span live between instrumentation points? What does a brand-new pool thread know about it?
Hint 2
Micrometer's context-propagation library can wrap an ExecutorService; Spring can also do this for its own task executors.
Solution

Why: trace context (and MDC) is thread-local. A hand-built ExecutorService knows nothing about Micrometer: the submitted lambda runs on a thread with empty context, so instrumentation inside fraudService.check (an HTTP client, @Observed…) starts a fresh trace, and logging has no MDC to print.

Fixes:

  • Wrap the executor with Micrometer context-propagation: ContextExecutorService.wrap(pool, ContextSnapshotFactory.builder().build()::captureAll) — the snapshot of trace context + MDC is captured at submit and restored on the worker thread.
  • Use Spring-managed async: @Async on the fraud call with Boot's auto-configured TaskExecutor and spring.task.execution/context-propagation enabled (or a TaskDecorator that captures/restores the snapshot) — Spring's own executors are instrumentable, hand-rolled statics are invisible.

Verify: the fraud span now appears as a child in the checkout trace, and worker log lines carry the original traceId. Bonus point: the same reasoning explains "lost" security context and MDC in async code — same ThreadLocal, same cure (see the logging card).

Scenario: after moving to Kubernetes, every deploy causes a 5-minute p99 latency spike

A JVM Boot service was moved from VMs to Kubernetes. Deploys now cause ~5 minutes of elevated p99 (but no errors). The manifest: replicas: 4, rolling update maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0, readiness probe on /actuator/health/readiness with initialDelaySeconds: 5, CPU requests: 250m, limits: 500m. The team says "the app is ready in 6 seconds, we checked the logs". Explain the spike and propose fixes, cheapest first.

Concepts: JIT warm-up · CPU throttling · readiness ≠ warmed · probe design

Hint 1
"Started in 6 seconds" means the context is up. What state is the JIT compiler in, and what does a 500m CPU limit do to compilation and the first minutes of traffic?
Hint 2
Readiness gates traffic. What could readiness wait for besides "the web server responds"?
Solution

What's happening: each new pod starts cold: everything runs interpreted until the JIT compiles hot paths — and JIT compilation itself needs CPU, but the 500m limit throttles it hard (1 effective processor shared between serving and compiling). Readiness only checks that the app answers, so Kubernetes routes 25% of traffic to a pod that is functionally up but 5–10× slower, pod by pod through the rollout ≈ your 5 minutes of degraded p99. On VMs this was masked by abundant CPU and rare restarts.

Fixes, cheapest first:

  • Raise/remove the CPU limit (keep requests): startup CPU is bursty; throttling warm-up is the single biggest lever. Even limits: 2 shortens warm-up dramatically.
  • Warm up before receiving traffic: exercise hot endpoints in-process at startup (self-calls / warm-up runner priming caches, JPA metamodel, serializers), gating readiness on completion via ApplicationAvailability — pods join the Service already warm.
  • CDS/AOT (Boot 3.3+ CDS support): cuts class-loading/startup cost, modestly helps time-to-warm.
  • Slow the rollout (maxSurge: 1 is fine; add minReadySeconds) so only one cold pod is in rotation at a time — spreads, not removes, the cost.
  • Structural options if p99 SLO is strict: native image (no JIT warm-up, trading peak throughput) or traffic ramping via mesh (send a cold pod 1% → 100% over 2 minutes).

Interview point: "ready" (accepting traffic) and "warmed" (meeting latency SLO) are different states; production-grade readiness encodes the second, not the first.

⚡ Rapid-fire: whole-guide warm-up

Why interviewers ask: the first ten minutes of any Spring loop is exactly this list — instant answers here buy you credibility for the deep questions. Spanning all eight sections; if one stalls you, its section is the link.

  • Constructor vs field injection — why constructor? — Explicit, final/immutable, testable with new, circular deps fail fast.
  • Bean lifecycle in one breath? — Definition → instantiation → populate → Aware callbacks → BeanPostProcessor before → @PostConstruct/afterPropertiesSet → BPP after (proxies here) → in use → @PreDestroy.
  • Singleton with a prototype dependency — what's wrong? — Injected once, so the "prototype" is effectively singleton; fix with ObjectProvider, @Lookup or scoped proxy.
  • BeanFactoryPostProcessor vs BeanPostProcessor? — BFPP edits bean definitions before creation; BPP wraps bean instances during creation.
  • How does Boot 2.6+ treat circular references? — Refused by default; break the cycle (redesign, @Lazy, setter) rather than re-enabling the escape hatch.
  • How does auto-configuration actually work? — @EnableAutoConfiguration imports candidates listed in AutoConfiguration.imports, each gated by @ConditionalOn*; user beans win via @ConditionalOnMissingBean and back-off.
  • What does a starter contain? — No code: a curated dependency set (auto-config + libraries + versions from the Boot BOM).
  • Property precedence, roughly? — Command line > env vars > profile-specific files > application.yml > defaults; later profile files override earlier.
  • @ConfigurationProperties vs @Value? — Typed, validated, relaxed-bound groups vs single-expression injection; prefer the former for anything structured.
  • How do you see why an auto-config backed off? — --debug condition evaluation report, or /actuator/conditions.
  • DispatcherServlet in one sentence? — Front controller mapping requests via HandlerMapping to a controller, invoking it through argument resolvers, then rendering via message converters or a view.
  • @RestController vs @Controller? — @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody: return values go through HttpMessageConverters, not view resolution.
  • Filter vs interceptor? — Servlet filter wraps everything before Spring (security, logging); HandlerInterceptor runs inside MVC with handler knowledge; filters see raw request, interceptors see the chosen controller.
  • Where do you handle exceptions globally? — @RestControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler, returning ProblemDetail (RFC 7807) in Boot 3.
  • @Valid fails — what error? — 400 with MethodArgumentNotValidException (body) or ConstraintViolationException (params, needs @Validated on the class).
  • MVC vs WebFlux in one line? — Thread-per-request blocking vs event-loop non-blocking; WebFlux wins on massive concurrent slow I/O, MVC on simplicity — and virtual threads narrow the gap.
  • Why did my @Transactional/@Cacheable not fire on an internal call? — Self-invocation bypasses the proxy; only external calls cross the advice.
  • JDK proxy vs CGLIB? — Interface-based vs subclassing; Boot defaults to CGLIB (proxyTargetClass=true); CGLIB can't proxy final classes/methods.
  • @Transactional on a private method? — Silently ignored: the proxy can't intercept it (CGLIB can't override private).
  • REQUIRES_NEW vs NESTED? — New suspended-outer independent transaction vs savepoint within the same transaction (JDBC only).
  • Checked exception thrown — does @Transactional roll back? — No, only unchecked by default; add rollbackFor for checked.
  • What is the persistence context? — The first-level cache / identity map tracking managed entities and flushing dirty changes at commit; one per transaction.
  • LazyInitializationException — why? — Accessing a lazy association after the persistence context closed; fix with fetch joins/EntityGraph/DTOs, not OSIV.
  • N+1 in one line, two fixes? — One query for the list plus one per row for the association; join fetch or @EntityGraph (or batch fetching).
  • Why is open-in-view controversial? — Holds the DB connection through view rendering and hides fetch bugs; disable it and fetch deliberately.
  • Optimistic vs pessimistic locking? — @Version check at commit (retry on conflict) vs SELECT … FOR UPDATE row locks; optimistic for low contention.
  • How does Spring Security process a request? — One FilterChainProxy in the servlet chain runs an ordered SecurityFilterChain (auth filters → exception translation → authorization) around the app.
  • Where does the authenticated user live? — SecurityContextHolder (ThreadLocal), populated per request; async needs context propagation.
  • How is a JWT validated by a resource server? — Signature against the IdP's JWKS keys (fetched via issuer/jwk-set-uri), plus expiry/issuer/audience checks — no session, no IdP call per request.
  • Why is CSRF off for stateless APIs? — CSRF rides ambient cookies; a bearer token isn't sent automatically by browsers, so the attack vector is gone.
  • 401 vs 403? — Unauthenticated (who are you?) vs authenticated but forbidden (you can't do that).
  • @PreAuthorize ignored — first suspect? — Method security not enabled (@EnableMethodSecurity) or self-invocation bypassing the proxy.
  • Kafka ordering guarantee? — Per partition only; same key → same partition → ordered.
  • At-least-once consumer — what must you build? — Idempotent processing (dedupe by key/id in the same transaction), because redelivery after rebalance/retry is guaranteed eventually.
  • What triggers a consumer group rebalance? — Membership change (join/leave/crash/missed poll within max.poll.interval.ms) or topic metadata change; cooperative protocol avoids stop-the-world.
  • Circuit breaker states? — CLOSED → OPEN on failure-rate threshold → HALF_OPEN trial calls → CLOSED on success; OPEN fails fast without calling.
  • Retry + circuit breaker — which wraps which? — Breaker outside, retry inside (Resilience4j default order applies breaker first): retries count against the breaker, and an open circuit isn't hammered by retries.
  • Outbox pattern in one line? — Write the event to a DB table in the same transaction as the state change; a relay publishes it — killing the dual-write problem.
  • What replaced Sleuth/Hystrix/Ribbon/Zuul? — Micrometer Tracing / Resilience4j / Spring Cloud LoadBalancer / Spring Cloud Gateway.
  • traceparent carries what? — traceId + parent spanId + sampling flags (W3C); services continue the trace by extracting it.
  • Liveness vs readiness? — Restart me if broken vs don't send me traffic yet; external deps never belong in liveness.
  • Zero-downtime deploy — three ingredients? — Readiness gating, graceful shutdown, preStop delay (with a grace period exceeding both).
  • @RefreshScope in one line? — The bean is a proxy; refresh evicts the cached target and the next call rebuilds it from new config.
  • Pod OOMKilled but heap fine? — Native memory: thread stacks, Metaspace, direct buffers, code cache — cgroup kills on total RSS.
  • Why database-per-service? — Independent deploys/scaling and enforced ownership; cross-service consistency then needs sagas + outbox, not joins.
  • Boot 2 → 3 in three bullets? — Java 17 baseline, javax → jakarta, observability unified under Micrometer (plus AOT/native support).
